q: A team deploys a payment API as a Swarm service with --replicas 3. During a routine kernel patch, one worker node reboots. When it comes back, the payment API has only 2 running tasks and the missing task was never rescheduled. The service was NOT in global mode. What is the most likely cause?
options: The service was created with a placement constraint the rebooted node no longer satisfies, or the node came back with availability set to drain or pause
Swarm never reschedules tasks after a node reboot; you must run docker service scale manually
The rebooted node lost its Raft log and can no longer accept tasks
The routing mesh removed the node permanently because it missed three consecutive health checks
explain: Swarm's orchestrator DOES reschedule failed tasks automatically — that is its whole job. When a task stays missing, the cause is almost always scheduling: a placement constraint (node.role, node.labels, engine.labels) the node no longer meets, or the node's availability being pause/drain so it accepts no new tasks. A lost Raft log matters for managers, not for running worker tasks, and the routing mesh has nothing to do with scheduling. First checks: docker service ps <svc> (see the task state and error) and docker node ls / docker node inspect <node> (availability and labels).

q: You roll out a new image to a Swarm service with: docker service update --image shop:2.0 --update-parallelism 3 --update-delay 20s --update-failure-action rollback shop. Two tasks fail their health checks under the new image. What happens next?
options: The entire service is removed and must be recreated from the previous spec
All tasks are immediately reverted to shop:1.0 because failure-action is rollback
Swarm keeps retrying the failed tasks indefinitely until they pass
The update pauses after the first failing batch, leaving a mix of old and new tasks, and the service stays in an updating state
explain: With --update-failure-action rollback, a failed update triggers an automatic rollback of the whole service to its previous spec — that is exactly what this flag buys you over the default. The DEFAULT behavior (failure-action pause) is what stops the rollout mid-flight and leaves a mix of old and new tasks. This is one of the most-tested Swarm distinctions: default = pause (manual intervention, service stuck 'updating'), explicit rollback = automatic revert. Know both cold.

q: A three-manager Swarm cluster loses two managers to a datacenter power failure. The remaining manager is healthy, and all application containers on worker nodes are still running and serving traffic. A teammate tries docker service create and it hangs, then fails. Why?
options: The surviving manager automatically demotes itself to worker when it detects the failure
Swarm enters autolock mode after losing managers and requires the unlock key
Raft quorum is lost: with 3 managers, quorum needs 2. One surviving manager cannot elect a leader, so no scheduling or cluster changes are possible — though existing tasks keep running
Worker nodes refuse all traffic when managers are unhealthy, so the whole cluster is down
explain: Raft needs a majority: quorum = (managers / 2) + 1, so 3 managers require 2 healthy ones. Lose quorum and the cluster can't schedule, create, or update anything — the API simply can't commit changes. Crucially, EXISTING tasks keep running on workers; the data plane survives while the control plane is frozen. This is why the exam stresses odd manager counts: 5 managers survive 2 failures, 3 survive 1. Autolock is unrelated (it's an opt-in encryption of the Raft log).

q: Your company runs a metrics collector agent that must run on every single node in a 12-node Swarm — including any nodes added next month. Which service mode, and why?
options: Replicated with a placement constraint of node.role == worker, which covers all nodes
A stack with deploy.replicas: 12, which behaves like global mode
Replicated with --replicas 12, because it guarantees exactly 12 tasks
Global mode (--mode global), because Swarm places exactly one task per node automatically, including future nodes
explain: Global mode is purpose-built for 'one task on every node' — log collectors, monitoring agents, security daemons. It automatically covers nodes added later, which replicated --replicas 12 does NOT (you'd have to rescale). Constraints don't create per-node placement either; they only filter eligible nodes. EXAM TRAP: replicated vs global is the single most-tested service concept — replicated = N tasks spread across nodes (web apps), global = exactly one per node (agents).

q: A developer deploys a stack with docker stack deploy -c app.yml billing. The Compose file includes a deploy: section with replicas: 4 and placement constraints. Then she runs docker compose up -d with the same file on her laptop for testing. Only one copy of each service starts, and the placement constraints are ignored. What happened?
options: The deploy: section is Swarm-only; docker compose up silently ignores it. Replicas and placement only apply under docker stack deploy
The Compose file version is too old — deploy: requires version 2
docker compose up requires a separate --scale flag for every service
Stack deploy and compose up share state, so the laptop deployment conflicted with the swarm one
explain: Fields under deploy: (replicas, update_config, placement, resources) are Swarm/stack-only — plain docker compose up / docker-compose up ignores them silently. That's why her laptop ran single replicas with no constraints. It's the reverse that the exam loves too: docker stack deploy REQUIRES Compose file format version 3+; a v2 file is rejected. Remember the direction: deploy: is stack-only, and stack deploy needs v3+.

q: You need to perform OS patching on worker3 tonight. The node runs 6 service tasks. Which sequence empties the node safely for maintenance and restores it afterward?
options: docker node rm worker3, patch, then docker swarm join to re-add it
docker node update --availability drain worker3, patch and reboot, then docker node update --availability active worker3
docker node demote worker3, patch, then docker node promote worker3
docker service scale to zero for every service, patch, then scale back up
explain: drain is the maintenance answer: existing tasks are shut down and rescheduled onto other nodes, and no new tasks are placed while drained. After patching, set availability back to active. pause would only stop NEW tasks (existing ones keep running — not what you want for a reboot). node rm / demote are destructive and wrong here — demote/promote changes Raft membership on managers and does nothing useful on a worker. Never scale services to zero for node maintenance; drain exists precisely for this.

q: A Swarm service's tasks keep showing as 'Pending' in docker service ps web. The cluster has plenty of CPU and memory free. Which is the most likely cause?
options: The service is in global mode and the cluster has too many nodes
The overlay network ran out of IP addresses
A placement constraint on the service matches no available node (e.g. node.labels.disk == ssd where no node carries that label)
The routing mesh is blocking the tasks from starting
explain: Pending-with-free-resources screams unsatisfiable placement constraints: the service demands node.role == manager, a node label, or a platform (os/arch) that no ready node provides. Swarm will wait forever rather than violate a hard constraint. Debugging order: docker service ps web (look at the task error message — it usually names the constraint problem), then docker node ls and docker node inspect to compare labels/roles. The routing mesh and overlay IPs don't block task startup, and global mode places one task per node — it doesn't cause Pending.

q: Your PostgreSQL primary must always run on a node with fast local SSDs. Two of your six nodes have node.labels.disk=ssd. Which service definition is correct?
options: docker service create --name db --mode global --constraint 'engine.labels.disk == ssd' postgres
docker service create --name db --replicas 1 --constraint 'node.hostname == ssd' postgres
docker service create --name db --replicas 1 --placement-pref 'spread=node.labels.disk' postgres
docker service create --name db --replicas 1 --constraint 'node.labels.disk == ssd' postgres
explain: Constraints are hard rules: --constraint 'node.labels.disk == ssd' pins the task to nodes carrying that label (set with docker node update --label-add disk=ssd). Placement preferences (spread=) are SOFT — they distribute but don't pin, so the DB could land on a spinning-disk node. Custom labels live under node.labels (set by you); engine.labels are Docker Engine labels — different namespace, wrong here. node.hostname matches a specific host name, not a label. And global mode would try to run the DB on EVERY node — the opposite of pinning.

q: A secrets rotation policy requires the database password to change monthly. The Swarm service db uses a secret named db_pass mounted at /run/secrets/db_pass. Which is the correct rotation procedure?
options: Create db_pass_v2 with the new value, run docker service update --secret-rm db_pass --secret-add db_pass_v2 db, then remove the old secret
Delete db_pass and recreate it with the same name; running containers pick up the change automatically
Store the new password in an environment variable and redeploy the service
Edit the secret in place with docker secret update db_pass, then restart the service tasks
explain: Swarm secrets are IMMUTABLE — there is no docker secret update, and recreating under the same name does not propagate into already-running containers (they hold the old secret's mount). The supported rotation: create the new versioned secret, update the service to swap it in (this triggers a rolling task restart with the new secret mounted), then delete the old one. The environment-variable 'shortcut' is exactly what secrets exist to avoid: env values are visible in docker inspect and in the Raft log unencrypted.

q: An MKE (formerly UCP) administrator is planning the control plane. Which statements about MKE architecture are correct? (Choose the best answer.)
options: MKE's web UI listens on port 2377 and the Kubernetes API on port 443
MKE installs its control plane as containers on manager nodes; controllers run MKE/Swarm managers/Kubernetes masters and application workloads should NOT run on controllers in production
MKE requires a separate physical server per role and cannot share nodes with Swarm managers
MKE replaces Swarm entirely; docker swarm commands stop working after MKE install
explain: MKE installs as containers on manager (controller) nodes — you run the mirantis/mke (older: mirantis/ucp) install image with --host-address, admin credentials, and SANs. Controllers host the control plane; workers run workloads — keeping apps off controllers is the production best practice. Port check: web UI is 443, Kubernetes API is 6443, swarm is 2377 — the option swaps them. And MKE sits ON TOP of Swarm/Kubernetes; it doesn't remove them.

q: Your MKE backup script runs: docker container run --rm --name ucp -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock mirantis/ucp:3.3 backup --passphrase 's3cret!' > /backups/mke.tar. A junior admin asks what the passphrase protects and what happens if it's lost. What do you tell them?
options: The passphrase only encrypts the admin password; losing it means resetting the admin user via the web UI
The passphrase is a label for the backup file; any passphrase works at restore time
The passphrase encrypts the backup (Swarm state, configs, access control). Without it the backup cannot be restored — it is effectively useless
Backups are unencrypted; the passphrase is only required to satisfy compliance auditors
explain: The --passphrase encrypts the MKE/UCP backup bundle. Lose it and the backup is cryptographically unrecoverable — no backdoor, no reset. This is the exam's favorite MKE backup fact, and it mirrors the Swarm autolock lesson: encryption keys for control-plane material must be stored somewhere safe and separate (a vault, not the same server). Restore uses the same passphrase on a fresh install.

q: A Swarm cluster spans two datacenters. The team wants VXLAN traffic between nodes encrypted because database replication crosses the WAN link. How is this achieved?
options: Publish the database port with -p so traffic uses TLS automatically
Set "icc": false in daemon.json on every node
Run docker swarm init --autolock on every manager
Create the overlay network with --opt encrypted: docker network create -d overlay --opt encrypted secure-net, and attach the database service to it
explain: --opt encrypted on overlay network creation enables IPsec encryption of the VXLAN traffic between nodes — the exact feature for sensitive east-west traffic crossing untrusted links. Autolock encrypts the Raft LOG (control-plane state), not data-plane traffic. "icc": false restricts container-to-container communication on the default bridge (defense in depth), and publishing a port (-p) does nothing for encryption. Note the performance cost: encrypted overlays add CPU overhead, so use them where the traffic warrants it.

q: A service is published with docker service create --name web -p 8080:80 --replicas 3 nginx on a 5-node swarm. Only two nodes actually run web tasks. A client connects to http://node5:8080 — node5 runs NO web tasks. What happens?
options: The request succeeds: the ingress routing mesh makes every node listen on 8080 and routes to a healthy task
Connection refused — only nodes running tasks listen on published ports
The request succeeds only if node5 is a manager node
The request is forwarded to a random container on node5, which fails
explain: This is the routing mesh (ingress network): publishing a port on a Swarm SERVICE makes EVERY node in the swarm listen on that port, and the mesh routes the request to a node running a healthy task — even nodes with zero tasks. That's the whole point: clients can hit any node IP. Contrast with docker run -p on a single container, where only the host running the container listens. EXAM TRAP: routing mesh applies to services, not to standalone docker run containers.

q: A stateful application behind a Swarm service breaks when connections land on different tasks — it needs each client to reach the SAME task directly. The default service setup load-balances across tasks via a virtual IP. What should you change?
options: Publish the port in host mode with --publish mode=host
Switch the service to --endpoint-mode dnsrr so DNS returns task IPs directly instead of the VIP
Move the application to global mode
Increase --update-parallelism so more tasks serve traffic
explain: The default endpoint mode is VIP: the service name resolves to one virtual IP and the mesh load-balances across tasks. --endpoint-mode dnsrr (DNS round-robin) skips the VIP — DNS queries return the individual task IPs, letting clients connect directly to a specific task. That's what stateful protocols and some databases need. Host-mode publishing is a different tool (bypasses the mesh, binds the host port directly on task nodes). Global mode changes placement, not load balancing.

q: Two managers of a five-manager Swarm are being decommissioned. The correct procedure is:
options: Run docker node rm on both managers; Raft reconfigures automatically
Shut both down simultaneously; the remaining three elect a new leader instantly
Demote them one at a time (docker node demote), verifying quorum after each, then remove them — keeping an odd number of managers throughout
Promote two workers first, then remove the old managers all at once
explain: Raft membership changes must preserve quorum at every step. With 5 managers quorum is 3; removing two at once (even via rm) risks losing quorum mid-operation and freezing the control plane. The safe path: docker node demote one manager (it becomes a worker; Raft membership drops to 4, quorum 3), verify docker node ls is healthy, then demote the second (3 managers, quorum 2). Keep manager counts ODD — 4 managers still only tolerate 1 failure, so an even count buys nothing. Never remove managers abruptly; a lost quorum means no scheduling or changes until managers are recovered.

q: A Compose file for a stack defines a service with deploy.resources.limits: {cpus: '0.50', memory: 512M} and deploy.resources.reservations: {memory: 256M}. What is the difference between limits and reservations in Swarm?
options: Reservations are hard caps; limits are soft suggestions the kernel may ignore
They are synonyms; Swarm accepts either spelling
Limits apply only to CPU and reservations only to memory
Limits are hard caps the task cannot exceed; reservations are the minimum guaranteed resources used by the scheduler to decide placement
explain: limits = the ceiling (the task is throttled/killed if it exceeds them — memory over limit triggers OOM kill of the container); reservations = the floor the scheduler guarantees when placing the task (a node must have the reserved resources free to accept it). The exam loves this pair because the words sound interchangeable. Memory reservations without limits is a common production pattern (guaranteed placement, burst allowed); CPU limits throttle rather than kill.

q: A team runs MKE and needs to give the QA team read-only visibility into the 'production' collection of services, while the release team gets full control over the same collection. In MKE's access model this is expressed as:
options: Two grants: (subject=QA team, role=View Only, resource set=production collection) and (subject=release team, role=Full Control, resource set=production collection)
Two Swarm secrets, one per team, mounted into the services
A single grant with role=Scheduler applied to both teams
Two Linux users on each manager node with different sudo rules
explain: MKE access control is grants = Subject + Role + Resource Set. Nobody has access by default — every permission flows through a grant combining who (user/team, often via LDAP/AD), what they can do (role: Full Control, Restricted Control, Scheduler, View Only...), and where (resource set = a collection of nodes/services/images). Different permissions on the same collection = two grants differing in subject+role. 'Why can't this user deploy?' → check their grants: right subject, right role, right resource set.

q: You create a Swarm service pinned with --constraint 'node.role == manager'. A teammate warns this is risky. Why?
options: The constraint syntax is invalid — node.role only accepts 'worker'

Running application workloads on managers risks starving the Raft/control plane of resources and expanding the blast radius if the app is compromised — managers should be dedicated to cluster management
Constraints on managers are ignored by the scheduler
Manager nodes cannot run service tasks at all; the tasks will stay Pending
explain: The constraint is valid and managers CAN run tasks — the issue is operational: managers run Raft, the API, and scheduling. A hungry or compromised app on a manager can destabilize the control plane (CPU starvation delays Raft heartbeats → leader elections → cluster flapping) and a container escape on a manager is far worse than on a worker. Production rule: keep workloads on workers; reserve managers for the control plane. (MKE formalizes this: controllers vs workers.)

q: A developer asks for the Kubernetes equivalents of Swarm concepts she knows. Which mapping is correct?
options: There are no equivalents — the DCA tests Swarm and Kubernetes as entirely separate topics
Swarm manager → Kubernetes kubelet; Swarm worker → Kubernetes etcd; overlay network → Kubernetes Ingress
Swarm service → Kubernetes Deployment (+ Service); docker stack deploy → kubectl apply -f of manifests; docker service scale → kubectl scale
Swarm service → Kubernetes Pod; docker stack deploy → docker compose up; docker secret → Kubernetes Volume
explain: The analogy the DCA expects: a Swarm service (desired state for N tasks) ≈ a Kubernetes Deployment managing ReplicaSets, plus a Service for the stable VIP/DNS — one Swarm service covers what K8s splits into Deployment+Service. A stack (Compose file deployed as a unit) ≈ a set of manifests applied with kubectl apply -f. Scaling: docker service scale web=5 ≈ kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5. And docker secret ≈ Kubernetes Secret (both mount sensitive data into workloads). The other options scramble the components.

q: During docker swarm init on a multi-homed host (two NICs: 10.0.0.5 on the cluster VLAN, 192.168.1.10 on the office LAN), you forget --advertise-addr. The init succeeds but workers can't join using the printed token. What's wrong?
options: docker swarm init binds to all interfaces by default, so the problem must be a firewall
Workers can only join over the office LAN, so the cluster VLAN must be disabled
The join tokens are interface-specific and must be regenerated with docker swarm join-token --rotate
Swarm requires --advertise-addr on multi-homed hosts so the manager advertises a reachable address; without it, the manager may advertise the wrong interface and join traffic goes nowhere
explain: On multi-homed hosts, --advertise-addr tells the manager which address to advertise to the cluster. Without it, Swarm picks one — possibly the office-LAN interface workers can't route to — and the join address in the token (10.0.0.5:2377 vs 192.168.1.10:2377) points at the wrong place. The exam tests this as a 'workers can't join' scenario: check which address was advertised (docker info / docker node inspect) and re-init with the correct --advertise-addr. Firewalls are a possible cause too, but the advertise-addr omission is the classic trap.

q: A service update is configured with --update-delay 30s --update-parallelism 1. The team complains deployments take forever on a 20-replica service. They ask what each flag does and what to tune. Your answer:
options: parallelism = tasks updated simultaneously (currently 1); delay = wait between batches (currently 30s). For a 20-replica service, raising parallelism to 4-5 with a shorter delay (10s) speeds the rollout while still limiting blast radius
parallelism = total replicas allowed; delay = time before the first task updates. Set parallelism to 20 and delay to 0
delay is the health-check grace period; parallelism is the number of managers. Neither affects rollout speed
These flags only apply to rollbacks; updates always replace all tasks at once
explain: --update-parallelism = how many tasks update at once (default 1 — the safe, slow default); --update-delay = pause between batches. 20 replicas × 30s+ per task ≈ 10+ minutes minimum. Raising parallelism bounds the blast radius while speeding things up — 4-5 at a time with a 10s delay is a sane production compromise. Setting parallelism to 20 = all at once = a failed image takes down the whole service simultaneously. The flags apply to updates (there are separate --rollback-parallelism/--rollback-delay for rollbacks).

q: A monitoring task must run on every node, but the team also wants exactly 3 copies of the web API spread across workers, with the API never landing on managers. Which combination is correct?
options: One stack with deploy.mode: global for both services
Two services: agent with --mode global; web with --replicas 3 --constraint 'node.role == worker'
Two services: agent with --replicas <node-count>; web with --mode global --constraint 'node.role != manager'
One service with --mode global --replicas 3
explain: Two different placement needs = two services. The agent is textbook global mode (one task per node, automatic on new nodes). The web API is replicated (3 tasks) with a hard constraint node.role == worker keeping it off managers. --mode global --replicas 3 is contradictory (global ignores replica counts). Replicas set to today's node count won't cover nodes added tomorrow. Constraints use == / != with node.role, node.hostname, node.labels.*, engine.labels.*, node.platform.os/arch.

q: After a failed update with the default failure action, docker service ps web shows some tasks running the new image and some the old, and the service state is 'updating'. The on-call engineer wants to get back to a known-good state quickly. What should they do?
options: Wait: the default failure action automatically completes the rollout after 5 minutes
Delete the service and recreate it — rollback only works with --update-failure-action rollback
Run docker service rollback web to revert all tasks to the previous spec
Run docker service update --force web to restart the paused update
explain: The default failure action is pause — the rollout halts mid-flight leaving a mixed-version service stuck 'updating'. docker service rollback web reverts every task to the previous service spec; it works regardless of what the failure action was (the flag only controls AUTOMATIC rollback). --force would just restart the same broken update. Don't delete and recreate — rollback preserves the service's networks, ports, and history. Know the pair: pause (default) = manual recovery via rollback; rollback (flag) = automatic.

q: A company is migrating from UCP/DTR-era documentation to current Mirantis products. Which name mappings are correct?
options: UCP and DTR were discontinued with no replacements
UCP → MSR; DTR → MKE
UCP → Docker Desktop; DTR → Docker Hub
UCP → MKE (Mirantis Kubernetes Engine); DTR → MSR (Mirantis Secure Registry)
explain: After Mirantis acquired Docker Enterprise (2019), Universal Control Plane (UCP) became Mirantis Kubernetes Engine (MKE) and Docker Trusted Registry (DTR) became Mirantis Secure Registry (MSR). The DCA still references both names — exam questions may say UCP or MKE interchangeably, so know the mapping cold. MKE = the enterprise control plane (Swarm + Kubernetes management, RBAC grants); MSR = the enterprise registry (image promotion, vulnerability scanning, garbage collection).

q: kubectl get pods shows a pod stuck in Pending. In Swarm terms, and in Kubernetes terms, what does Pending mean and what's the first thing to check?
options: In both: the scheduler couldn't place the workload. Check why: Swarm → docker service ps (constraint/node fit); Kubernetes → kubectl describe pod (events: insufficient CPU/memory, unsatisfiable nodeSelector/affinity, no matching PVC)
Pending means the image is still pulling in both orchestrators; wait and it will resolve
In Swarm Pending means paused; in Kubernetes it means the kubelet is down
Pending is a Swarm-only state; Kubernetes uses 'Waiting' instead
explain: Pending is the universal 'scheduled nowhere yet' state. Causes are the same family in both orchestrators: no node satisfies the requirements (constraints/nodeSelector/affinity), insufficient resources, or a missing dependency (unbound PVC in K8s). The debugging reflex transfers directly: look at the workload's events/status (docker service ps / kubectl describe) for the scheduler's reason, then check node capacity and placement rules. Image-pull problems show as ImagePullBackOff (K8s) or task errors — not Pending.

q:
A Dockerfile ends with:
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
A teammate runs: docker run myimg python worker.py
What executes inside the container?
options: python app.py — CMD cannot be overridden at runtime
python worker.py — CLI arguments replace the CMD instruction
Both: app.py starts first, then worker.py
The container fails because CMD and CLI args conflict
explain: CMD is the DEFAULT command — anything you append to docker run replaces it entirely. So docker run myimg python worker.py runs python worker.py, and app.py never starts. Contrast with ENTRYPOINT: if the Dockerfile had ENTRYPOINT ["python"] + CMD ["app.py"], then docker run myimg worker.py would execute python worker.py (args append to the entrypoint). The exam's #1 Dockerfile trap: CMD = replaced by CLI args; ENTRYPOINT = fixed program that CLI args append to.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q:
A Dockerfile contains:
ENTRYPOINT ["/bin/backup.sh"]
CMD ["--full"]
What runs for each of these invocations?
docker run img  →  ?
docker run img --incremental  →  ?
options: --full is ignored in both; → /bin/backup.sh; → /bin/backup.sh --incremental
→ /bin/backup.sh (no args); → error, CMD and CLI args can't be combined
→ /bin/backup.sh --full; → /bin/backup.sh --incremental
→ /bin/backup.sh --full --incremental in both cases
explain: ENTRYPOINT + CMD is the classic pair: ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable, CMD is the default argument list. With no CLI args, Docker runs ENTRYPOINT + CMD → /bin/backup.sh --full. With CLI args, they REPLACE the CMD (not the entrypoint) → /bin/backup.sh --incremental. This is the pattern for 'a tool with sensible defaults the user can override' — and the single most-tested Dockerfile behavior on the DCA.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q:
Two Dockerfiles:
A: ENTRYPOINT echo hello   (shell form)
B: ENTRYPOINT ["echo", "hello"]   (exec form)
A teammate runs docker stop on containers from each. The container from A takes 10 seconds to stop; B stops instantly. Why?
options: Shell form containers ignore docker stop entirely by design
Exec form is faster because JSON arrays parse quicker
The difference is random; both forms behave identically

Shell form runs the command as a child of /bin/sh, so PID 1 is the shell — SIGTERM goes to sh, which doesn't forward it to echo, and Docker waits out the 10s timeout before SIGKILL. Exec form makes the command PID 1, which receives SIGTERM directly
explain: Shell form wraps your command: /bin/sh -c "echo hello" — PID 1 is sh, not your process. sh doesn't forward SIGTERM to its child, so docker stop's graceful SIGTERM is swallowed and Docker falls back to SIGKILL after the 10-second default timeout. Exec form runs the binary as PID 1 directly, so it receives SIGTERM and can shut down cleanly. Rule: use exec form for ENTRYPOINT/CMD in production images — it also matters for any app needing graceful shutdown (draining connections, flushing buffers).
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile needs a 200MB dataset downloaded from an internal HTTP server and extracted during the build. Which instruction, and why is the alternative wrong here?
options: ADD, because it can fetch remote URLs and auto-extract local tarballs — the two features COPY lacks. COPY cannot fetch URLs at all
RUN curl, because neither COPY nor ADD supports remote files
VOLUME, because datasets should never be baked into images
COPY, because ADD is deprecated and fails on HTTP URLs
explain: ADD's two extras over COPY: fetching remote URLs and auto-extracting local tar archives. Here the URL fetch is needed, so ADD (or RUN curl + tar, which many teams prefer for clarity) is the tool. COPY only copies from the build context — it cannot reach the network. The exam's rule of thumb: prefer COPY everywhere; reach for ADD only when you specifically need URL fetching or tar auto-extraction. (ADD is NOT deprecated — that's a common myth.)
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q:
A team's Node.js Dockerfile:
FROM node:20
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
RUN npm run build
Every code change rebuilds the world: npm ci re-runs even when only app.js changed, and builds take 6 minutes. What's the fix?
options: Switch to ADD instead of COPY for better caching
Reorder: copy dependency manifests first, install, THEN copy source code last — so code changes don't invalidate the cached npm ci layer
Combine the RUN lines into one to reduce layer count
Add more RUN layers so each step caches independently
explain: Layer caching invalidates everything BELOW the first changed layer. COPY . . as the first step means any file change busts the cache for npm ci and the build. The canonical fix — order instructions least-changed → most-changed: COPY package.json package-lock.json . → RUN npm ci → COPY . . → RUN npm run build. Now code edits only invalidate the last two layers; dependency installs reuse cache. This 'dependencies before code' ordering is THE Dockerfile optimization the DCA tests, and .dockerignore (excluding node_modules, .git) keeps the context small too.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Go service's Dockerfile builds to a 1.1GB image (golang:1.22 base + source + toolchain). Production needs only the compiled 25MB binary. Which approach gives the smallest, most secure production image?
options: Run docker image prune after building to shrink the image
Use docker squash to merge the layers into one
Multi-stage build: compile in a golang:1.22 builder stage, then COPY --from=builder only the binary into a minimal runtime stage (alpine or distroless/scratch)
Add a .dockerignore to exclude the Go source from the final image
explain: Multi-stage builds: stage 1 (FROM golang:1.22 AS builder) compiles; stage 2 (FROM alpine or scratch) copies ONLY the binary via COPY --from=builder. Result: ~30MB image with no compiler, no source, no build tools — smaller pulls, faster deploys, and a much smaller CVE surface (no toolchain for an attacker to use). .dockerignore only shrinks the build CONTEXT, not the image. Prune removes unused images, never shrinks one. Squash merges layers but keeps every file — the toolchain is still in there.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile has three CMD instructions (a leftover from merges). The image behaves unexpectedly. What actually happens at container start?
options: All three commands run in sequence
The three CMDs are combined with && automatically
Docker errors out: duplicate CMD is a build failure
Only the LAST CMD takes effect; earlier ones are silently discarded
explain: Only the last CMD (and likewise the last ENTRYPOINT) in a Dockerfile takes effect — earlier ones are silently discarded, no error, no warning. Merged Dockerfiles with duplicate CMDs are a real-world source of 'why is it running the wrong thing?' confusion. docker inspect shows the effective Cmd so you can verify. Same rule applies to ENTRYPOINT.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A deployment manifest pins image: shop/api:latest. Last Tuesday's deploy worked; today's deploy (no manifest change) pulls different code and breaks. The team wants reproducible deploys. What's the root cause and the fix?
options: latest is just the default tag — it's mutable and can be re-pointed at any time. Pin the immutable digest (image@sha256:<digest>) for reproducible deploys
latest is cached aggressively; the fix is docker pull before every deploy
latest always points to the newest build by timestamp, so the CI pipeline is at fault
The registry is corrupted; re-push the image
explain: latest means nothing more than 'the tag applied when you omitted one' — anyone can push a new image under :latest and your next pull silently changes. Tags are mutable; DIGESTS are immutable: image@sha256:abc... always resolves to the exact same bits, forever. Production pinning = digests (or immutable semantic tags like :1.4.2 that your pipeline never re-points). The exam hammers this: 'most reproducible' → digest.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A security review finds a production image built FROM ubuntu:22.04 six months ago. Scanning shows 40+ CVEs, all in system packages the app doesn't use. The app is a static Go binary. What's the best remediation?
options: Run the container with --read-only to neutralize the CVEs
Rebuild on a minimal base: FROM scratch (static binary needs no OS) or distroless — eliminating the unused packages and their CVEs entirely
Switch to ubuntu:24.04, which has no CVEs
Add RUN apt-get upgrade to the Dockerfile and rebuild monthly
explain: The CVEs live in packages the app doesn't need — the fix is to stop shipping them. A static Go binary runs on scratch (empty image) or distroless (minimal runtime, no shell/package manager). No unused packages = no CVEs to patch, tiny image, minimal attack surface. apt-get upgrade is treadmill maintenance on bloat you don't need; no base is CVE-free; --read-only is good hardening but doesn't remove vulnerable code. Minimal bases are the exam's standard 'reduce image CVE surface' answer.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A CI pipeline needs to pull a private base image during docker build, using a registry password. The engineer proposes ARG REGISTRY_PASSWORD in the Dockerfile. Why is this dangerous, and what's the safe alternative?
options: There is no risk; ARG is the documented way to pass secrets
ARG values are printed in build logs; use ENV instead

ARG values persist in the image's history/metadata (docker history shows them) — secrets leak into every layer and anyone with the image can read them. Use BuildKit secret mounts (--mount=type=secret) so the secret never lands in a layer
ARG is only for strings under 10 characters; passwords need ENV
explain: ARG is build-time only (not persisted into running containers) — but it IS baked into the image metadata: docker history and docker inspect reveal ARG values to anyone holding the image. Secrets in ARG/ENV = secrets in the image forever. BuildKit's --mount=type=secret exposes the secret as a file during a single RUN step without creating a layer containing it. Same family of trap: never bake secrets into images, never pass via -e (visible in docker inspect) — use proper secret mechanisms.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A company runs its own registry at registry.internal:5000 over plain HTTP (no TLS yet). Developers' docker push fails with 'http: server gave HTTP response to HTTPS client'. What's the correct client-side fix?
options: Run the push with docker push --insecure registry.internal:5000/img:tag
Registries require TLS; there is no client-side workaround
Log in with docker login --http registry.internal:5000 first
Add "insecure-registries": ["registry.internal:5000"] to /etc/docker/daemon.json on each client and reload the daemon
explain: Docker assumes HTTPS for registries; plain-HTTP or self-signed registries must be allowlisted per-daemon in daemon.json under insecure-registries, followed by systemctl reload docker. There is no --insecure flag on push/pull — that's the trap. (Long-term: terminate TLS properly; insecure-registries is a stopgap.) Also note: this is a DAEMON setting, so it must be configured on every host that pushes/pulls, including Swarm nodes.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An MSR (Mirantis Secure Registry) administrator wants: (1) vulnerable images blocked from reaching production repos, (2) old unreferenced image layers cleaned up automatically. Which MSR features deliver this?
options: Image promotion policies with vulnerability scanning gates, plus garbage collection of unreferenced blobs/manifests
Swarm autolock and Raft log compaction
Content Trust and the routing mesh
Digest pinning and .dockerignore
explain: MSR (formerly DTR) is the enterprise registry: image PROMOTION pipelines move images between repos (dev → staging → prod) with gates — including vulnerability-scan results blocking promotion of CVE-laden images. Garbage collection reclaims storage from unreferenced blobs/manifests (dangling layers from overwritten tags). RBAC on repositories controls who can push/promote. Content Trust is a client-side signing check (related but separate); autolock/Raft are Swarm concerns.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A deploy pipeline sets DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1. A developer tries to pull an image tag that was pushed without signing. What happens, and what does DCT actually guarantee?
options: DCT encrypts the image layers during transfer

The pull is rejected — DCT (via Notary) verifies signatures on push/pull, so unsigned or tampered images are refused. It guarantees provenance/integrity (the image is what the publisher signed), not that the image is vulnerability-free
The pull succeeds with a warning; DCT only logs trust status
DCT scans the image for CVEs before allowing the pull
explain: Docker Content Trust enforces signature verification: with DCT=1, the client refuses to pull (or push) tags that aren't signed via Notary. It answers 'did this image come untampered from the key holder?' — provenance and integrity. It does NOT scan for vulnerabilities (that's MSR scanning / docker scout) and doesn't encrypt anything. Common confusion: signing ≠ scanning. Use both: sign what you ship, scan what you build.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: docker images shows 40 tags of shop/api but disk is nearly full. docker image prune -a is proposed. What does it remove, and what's the risk?
options: It removes stopped containers, not images
It only removes untagged (dangling) images; tagged images are never touched

It removes all images not currently used by a container — including tagged ones. Risk: deleting tagged images you intended to keep (e.g. rollback targets); use filters or prune dangling-only (default) for safety
It compresses image layers in place; nothing is deleted
explain: docker image prune (no -a) removes only DANGLING images (untagged layer leftovers). -a goes further: every image not referenced by a container — including perfectly good tagged ones like last week's rollback target. On a build server that's usually what you want; on a deploy host it can nuke your fallback images. Safer variants: prune without -a, or --filter "until=72h". Know the pair: prune = dangling only; prune -a = all unused.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile sets USER appuser halfway through, then later needs to install a system package. The build fails with 'permission denied' on apt-get. What's the correct fix?
options: Run apt-get with sudo inside the Dockerfile
Add --privileged to docker build
Remove the USER instruction; containers must build as root
Move the apt-get install before the USER instruction (or temporarily switch back with USER root), keeping USER appuser as the final user so the running container stays non-root
explain: USER switches the build user for all SUBSEQUENT instructions — apt-get as appuser fails. Pattern: do privileged work first (as root), then drop privileges with USER appuser as one of the last instructions so the RUNTIME user is non-root. sudo isn't installed in most base images and --privileged is a runtime flag, not a build flag. Defense in depth: non-root runtime user + --read-only filesystem + dropped capabilities.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An image's HEALTHCHECK is defined as: HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --retries=3 CMD curl -f http://localhost/health || exit 1. A container shows 'healthy' then flips to 'unhealthy' during a traffic spike, though the app still serves requests. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The health endpoint is timing out under load (5s timeout, 3 retries) — the probe is too aggressive for spike conditions. Tune interval/timeout/retries or lighten the health endpoint
HEALTHCHECK is broken; unhealthy status always means the app is down
HEALTHCHECK only runs once at container start; the status is stale
Docker kills unhealthy containers automatically, so the app will be restarted
explain: HEALTHCHECK is a probe, not a verdict: 3 consecutive failures (each after a 5s timeout) mark the container unhealthy. Under a traffic spike, a heavy /health endpoint can exceed the 5s timeout even though the app serves real requests fine. Fixes: raise --timeout/--retries, lengthen --interval, or make the endpoint cheap (a static 200, not a full DB check). Note: Docker does NOT restart unhealthy containers by itself — orchestrators (Swarm/K8s) or restart policies act on it. HEALTHCHECK NONE disables a base image's check.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A team tags every CI build as shop/api:ci-<sha> and also moves shop/api:stable to the latest green build. For the production Swarm service, which reference should the service use, and why?
options: shop/api:ci-<sha> — CI tags are the most precise
The immutable digest (shop/api@sha256:...) of the verified build — tags like :stable are mutable and can be re-pointed between scheduling and task startup, causing mixed versions across tasks
shop/api:stable — it's the newest green build by definition
Any tag works identically once the service is created
explain: Mutable tags are a rollout hazard: if :stable is re-pointed mid-rolling-update, some tasks pull the old bits and some the new — a mixed-version service from a single update. The digest is immutable: every task pulls the exact same bits, always. CI sha tags are precise IF your pipeline never re-pushes the same tag (it shouldn't). Production rule: verify a build, record its digest, deploy the digest. This is the same 'tags mutable, digests immutable' principle as Q33, applied to orchestration.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: docker history shop/api:2.0 shows a 900MB layer from a single RUN instruction that downloaded, compiled, and 'cleaned up' temp files. Why is the layer still 900MB, and how should the Dockerfile be fixed?
options: docker history is inaccurate; the layer is actually small
The cleanup command syntax was wrong; rm doesn't work in Dockerfiles

Layers are additive and immutable: files deleted in a LATER layer still occupy space in the earlier layer that created them. Fix: do download → compile → cleanup in a SINGLE RUN (chained with &&) so temp files never become their own layer — or better, use a multi-stage build
Layers can't exceed 500MB; the image is corrupted
explain: Each RUN creates a layer capturing the filesystem diff. Deleting files in a later RUN adds a 'whiteout' marker — the bytes remain in the earlier layer forever. The fix is to never let temp files become a committed layer: chain everything in one RUN (curl && build && rm -rf /tmp/* in the same instruction) or use multi-stage builds so build-time files never reach the final image. docker history is precisely how you spot this: look for giant layers and read which instruction created them.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A developer runs: docker build --build-arg API_KEY=supersecret -t shop/api:2.0 .  with ARG API_KEY in the Dockerfile, used in one RUN to fetch a private dependency. The image is pushed to a shared registry. What's exposed?
options: Only the key's length is exposed, not its value
The key is exposed only if the container is run with --privileged
Nothing — ARG values are never stored anywhere
The API key is visible via docker history / docker inspect to anyone who pulls the image, because ARG values are baked into image metadata
explain: ARG values are embedded in the image config/history — docker history shows the full RUN line including the expanded value, and it's in the image JSON anyone can pull. This is the 'secrets in builds' trap (see also Q35): use BuildKit --mount=type=secret for build-time secrets so they never enter a layer or metadata. Related: ENV secrets are visible in docker inspect of RUNNING containers; image-baked secrets are visible to anyone with the image. Both are wrong — use runtime secret mechanisms.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A registry administrator notices pushes failing for large images with 'blob upload unknown'. Smaller images push fine. The registry sits behind a corporate reverse proxy. What's the most likely cause?
options: The reverse proxy is buffering or timing out the chunked blob-upload PATCH requests — registry blob uploads use PATCH with specific headers that some proxies mishandle; check proxy timeouts/buffering and the registry logs
The developers forgot docker login
Docker Hub rate limits apply to private registries
The images are too large for the registry; registries have a 1GB blob limit
explain: Registry pushes upload blobs via PATCH requests that can be long-lived for large layers. Corporate proxies with small buffers, short timeouts, or request-size limits break exactly these uploads while small images sail through. 'blob upload unknown' means the registry lost track of the upload session — classic proxy interference. Fix at the proxy layer (timeouts, buffering off, max body size) or push directly. Auth failures would say 'unauthorized', not 'blob upload unknown'.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: After adding a developer to the docker group so she can run Docker without sudo, a security engineer flags it as a risk. Why is docker group membership considered root-equivalent?
options: It isn't — the docker group only allows listing containers
Any member can run docker run -v /:/host --privileged ... and read/modify the entire host filesystem as root, so group membership effectively grants host root
Group members can only access their own containers, which is still a risk
The docker group grants sudo access to all commands
explain: The Docker daemon runs as root, and anyone who can talk to it can ask it to mount the host's / into a container (docker run -v /:/host ...) and then read/write /etc/shadow, install keys, etc. — full host root, no exploit needed. That's why 'add user to docker group' is a convenience with root-equivalent consequences: only trusted admins belong there. The exam tests this as a least-privilege question: the convenience is real, the risk is root.

q: A production host's disk filled overnight. Investigation shows /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log at 40GB from one chatty service. The daemon uses default logging settings. What should have been configured, and where?
options: Run docker logs --truncate on a cron schedule
Switch to the none log driver to disable logging
In /etc/docker/daemon.json: set "log-driver": "json-file" with "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"} so logs rotate — the default json-file driver grows WITHOUT bound
Nothing — Docker rotates logs automatically; the disk must be failing
explain: The default json-file log driver NEVER rotates unless you set max-size/max-file — a classic production incident and a favorite exam scenario. The fix is daemon-wide in daemon.json (applies to new containers) or per-container with --log-opt at run time. Also know the flip side: with non-json-file drivers (syslog, journald, gelf...), docker logs often returns NOTHING — that's expected, not a bug, because logs go to the external system. none = no logs kept at all.

q: A team enables "live-restore": true in daemon.json. During the next Docker daemon upgrade, what happens to running containers?
options: They are gracefully stopped before the upgrade and must be restarted manually
They are checkpointed to disk and restored from the checkpoint
live-restore only affects Swarm services, not standalone containers
They keep running across the daemon restart/upgrade — live-restore decouples container lifecycle from the daemon
explain: live-restore keeps containers running while the daemon itself restarts or upgrades — without it, a daemon restart kills every container (and Swarm would reschedule the resulting outage). It's the zero-downtime-daemon-upgrade setting. Note it doesn't cover host reboots (nothing runs without a kernel) and some daemon.json changes still need a full restart rather than a reload — but for daemon upgrades, live-restore is the answer.

q: An engineer changes the storage driver from overlay2 to devicemapper in daemon.json and restarts Docker. All local images and containers are gone. What happened?
options: Each storage driver uses its own separate backing store — switching drivers makes Docker look at a different (empty) store; the old data still exists under the previous driver's directory but is inaccessible until you switch back
The daemon.json change triggered an automatic docker system prune
devicemapper is incompatible with existing images and corrupts them
Docker deleted them as a safety measure when the driver changed
explain: Storage drivers maintain independent backing stores under /var/lib/docker. Changing the driver doesn't migrate or delete anything — it just points the daemon at a different, empty store, so images/containers 'disappear' (switch back and they reappear). Lesson: choose the storage driver ONCE at install time. overlay2 is the default and recommended driver (overlay is legacy; devicemapper loop-lvm was never production-safe). Verify with docker info.

q: A host needs containers to resolve an internal DNS server (10.0.0.53) instead of the host's default resolver. Where is this configured for ALL containers on the host?
options: In each Dockerfile with a DNS instruction
In /etc/docker/daemon.json with "dns": ["10.0.0.53"], then reload the daemon
In /etc/resolv.conf inside each container image
With docker network create --dns on every network
explain: daemon.json's "dns" key sets the default DNS servers for all containers on the host (overridable per-container with docker run --dns). Dockerfiles have no DNS instruction; baking /etc/resolv.conf into images is fragile (Docker manages that file); and --dns is a docker run flag, not a network-create flag. Related daemon.json keys the exam likes: insecure-registries, log-driver/log-opts, live-restore, storage-driver, icc, default-runtime.

q: A Swarm join token was accidentally pasted into a public chat channel. What's the correct response?
options: Run docker swarm leave on all nodes and re-init the swarm
Delete the chat message; tokens are single-use
Rotate it immediately: docker swarm join-token --rotate worker (and manager if exposed). Old tokens stop working at once
Nothing — join tokens expire after 24 hours automatically
explain: Join tokens do NOT expire and are NOT single-use — anyone with a worker token can join your swarm as a worker (a manager token is worse: full Raft membership). docker swarm join-token --rotate invalidates the old token instantly and issues a new one. No need to rebuild the cluster. This is the 'compromised credential' reflex the exam wants: rotate, don't rebuild. Same thinking applies to leaked MKE backup passphrases — except those can't be rotated, which is why they're stored in a vault.

q: An MKE install command includes --san app.mke.corp.example and --san 10.0.0.10. Why are SANs required, and what breaks if a SAN is missing?
options: SANs configure storage area networks for the registry backend
SANs are optional labels for the web UI; nothing breaks
SANs set the admin usernames; missing SANs lock out the admin
SANs (Subject Alternative Names) are embedded in MKE's TLS certificate — any DNS name or IP used to reach MKE must be listed, or clients get certificate errors when connecting via the unlisted name
explain: MKE generates its TLS cert at install time with the provided SANs. Reach MKE via a name/IP not in the SAN list and TLS verification fails (browsers warn, automation breaks, docker logins fail). Include EVERY name and IP clients will use: load balancer VIP, DNS names, direct IPs. This is standard TLS behavior, but the exam tests it in MKE-install context alongside --host-address (which interface MKE binds) and the admin credentials.

q: A firewall engineer asks which ports must be open between Swarm nodes for a new cluster. The correct answer is:
options: 2377 (cluster management), 7946 TCP/UDP (gossip/container network discovery), 4789 UDP (overlay VXLAN data path) — plus 443/6443 if MKE is installed
443 only — Swarm tunnels everything over HTTPS
8080 and 8443 for the Swarm API
No ports — Swarm uses the Docker socket over SSH
explain: The Swarm port trio: 2377/TCP (swarm management/API — the join port), 7946 TCP+UDP (gossip protocol for node discovery and overlay control), 4789/UDP (VXLAN data plane carrying overlay traffic). Block 4789 and overlays silently fail; block 7946 and nodes can't discover each other. MKE adds 443 (web UI) and 6443 (Kubernetes API). This is pure memorization — but it's exactly the kind of 'cluster won't form' troubleshooting fact the DCA tests.

q: docker info on a host shows 'Runtimes: runc io.containerd.runc.v2 nvidia'. A team wants GPU workloads on this host. What does this output tell them, and how do they use a GPU in a container?
options: GPUs work automatically; runtimes are informational only
The nvidia runtime is available; run containers with --runtime nvidia (or --gpus all) so containerd uses the NVIDIA runtime instead of default runc
They must reinstall Docker with GPU support compiled in
Runtimes can't be selected per-container; set "default-runtime": "nvidia" in daemon.json
explain: The stack is Engine → containerd → OCI runtime (runc by default). Additional runtimes (nvidia for GPUs, kata for VM-isolation) appear in docker info and are selected per-container with --runtime <name> (modern Docker also supports --gpus all, which wires the nvidia runtime). You don't reinstall Docker — the runtime just needs installing and registering. The exam only expects the layering (Engine → containerd → runc → your process) and that --runtime selects a non-default one.

q: A container needs to resolve a private registry hostname that isn't in corporate DNS. The engineer adds an entry to the host's /etc/hosts. The container still can't resolve it. What's the proper fix?
options: Restart the container; /etc/hosts changes apply live
Add the entry to the Dockerfile so it's baked into the image
Pass --add-host registry.internal:10.0.0.60 to docker run (or add host entries in the Compose file) — containers get their own network namespace and don't read the host's /etc/hosts
Containers can't use custom host entries; deploy a DNS server
explain: Containers have their own /etc/hosts (managed by Docker) — the host's file is invisible inside the container's network namespace. --add-host injects entries into the container's hosts file (Compose: extra_hosts:). Baking into the Dockerfile is fragile (IPs change; the image becomes environment-specific). This is the same namespace-isolation principle behind --network host (shares the host stack) and why embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) exists on user-defined networks.

q: An admin sets "icc": false in daemon.json. What changes, and what breaks?
options: Nothing changes; icc is a deprecated no-op
All container networking is disabled; only host networking works
It enables encrypted communication between containers

Inter-container communication on the default bridge is disabled — containers can't talk to each other directly (published ports still work). Apps relying on container-to-container traffic on the default bridge break
explain: "icc": false disables inter-container communication (adds iptables DROP rules between containers). It's defense-in-depth: even if two containers share a network, they can't reach each other — external access still works via published ports. What breaks: anything depending on direct container-to-container traffic (common on the default bridge). It's a hardening knob, not an encryption setting, and it requires a daemon restart. The exam pairs it with least-privilege thinking.

q: A team runs Docker Desktop on Macs for development and Linux Engine in production. A developer's bind-mount-heavy Compose app behaves differently on her Mac (slow file sync, permission quirks). What's the underlying reason?
options: Docker Desktop runs the Engine inside a lightweight VM — bind mounts cross the VM boundary (osxfs/gRPC-FUSE), so file performance and permission mapping differ from native Linux mounts
The Compose file version is incompatible with Docker Desktop
Macs can't run Linux containers at all
Docker Desktop doesn't support bind mounts
explain: Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows) runs the daemon in a Linux VM; bind mounts shuttle files between the host OS and the VM through a file-sharing layer — slower and with UID/GID mapping quirks versus native Linux bind mounts. Same CLI, same images, different I/O path. Practical takeaway: keep bind-mounted hot paths small in dev, prefer named volumes for databases even locally, and don't benchmark I/O on Desktop. The exam tests the architectural fact (VM in the middle), not the workarounds.

q: docker version shows the client at 26.1 but the server API at 1.43 with an error contacting the daemon. Actually the output shows 'Cannot connect to the Docker daemon'. What's the systematic check order?
options: Delete /var/lib/docker and restart
1) Is the daemon running? (systemctl status docker) 2) Does the user have permission to reach the socket? (docker group / sudo) 3) Is DOCKER_HOST pointing somewhere unexpected?
The client and server versions must match exactly; downgrade the client
Reinstall Docker immediately
explain: 'Cannot connect to the Docker daemon' is almost always one of three: daemon not running (systemctl start docker / check dockerd logs via journalctl -u docker), socket permissions (user not in docker group and no sudo), or DOCKER_HOST pointing at a dead remote (env | grep DOCKER_HOST — a stale export from a cloud session is a classic). Client/server version skew is tolerated within reason (API negotiation); exact-match is NOT required. Never nuke /var/lib/docker as a first step — that's all your images, volumes, and containers.

q: A company wants containers' stdout to flow into their Splunk infrastructure instead of local JSON files. Which daemon configuration achieves this, and what operational trade-off comes with it?
options: Run a Splunk sidecar container with --volumes-from on every app container
Logging drivers are per-image; rebuild all images with the Splunk driver

Set "log-driver": "splunk" with the Splunk URL/token in "log-opts" in daemon.json. Trade-off: docker logs / docker service logs may return nothing locally (expected — logs go to Splunk), and if Splunk is unreachable, container startup can block depending on driver mode
Mount /var/log/splunk into every container
explain: Logging drivers are a DAEMON-level setting (daemon.json log-driver/log-opts, overridable per-container with --log-driver). splunk/gelf/fluentd/syslog/journald forward to external systems — which is exactly why docker logs goes quiet: there's nothing local to read. That's expected behavior, not a bug (a favorite exam trap). The availability trade-off: if the log endpoint is down, drivers can block container start (unless configured otherwise) — log pipeline outages can halt deploys. none = no logs at all.

q: An MKE upgrade is scheduled. The runbook's first step is a backup with --passphrase. The second step is verifying the backup. Why is backup verification critical for MKE specifically?
options: Verification is only needed for compliance audits
MKE backups are unencrypted and often corrupt
MKE backups can't be verified; the step is ceremonial

An MKE backup contains Swarm state, configs, and access control — and it's encrypted with the passphrase. An untested backup (wrong passphrase recorded, truncated file) is discovered only at restore time, when it's too late. Verify by test-restoring or at minimum validating the archive and passphrase record
explain: The nightmare scenario: upgrade fails, you reach for the backup, and the recorded passphrase is wrong or the file is truncated — the backup is cryptographically useless and there's no recovery. MKE backups bundle the cluster's identity (Swarm Raft state, configs, grants), so their integrity IS your disaster-recovery plan. Best practice: store the passphrase in a vault (separate from the backup), verify archives after creation, and periodically test-restore into a lab. The exam loves the 'lose the passphrase = lose the backup' fact — this is its operational consequence.

q: Two containers on the default bridge network need to talk to each other. The developer tries ping web1 from web2 and gets 'bad address'. Both containers are running. What's wrong, and what's the proper fix?
options: The default bridge has no embedded DNS — containers can't resolve each other by name there (legacy --link aside). Fix: create a user-defined bridge network and attach both; name resolution then works via the embedded DNS server
ICMP is blocked on the default bridge; use TCP instead
Containers on the same host can never communicate
The containers need --privileged to use ping
explain: The default bridge is the odd one out: no automatic DNS resolution between containers (a legacy limitation; --link was the old workaround). User-defined bridge networks get Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11 inside each container), so containers resolve each other by name or network alias. The fix is architectural, not a flag: docker network create appnet + attach both. This default-vs-user-defined bridge distinction is one of the most-tested networking facts on the DCA.

q: A container runs a legacy monitoring agent that must see the host's exact network interfaces and bind to the host's ports directly, with no NAT. Which network mode, and what's the cost?
options: macvlan: gives the container its own MAC on the LAN

--network host: the container shares the host's network stack (no isolation, no port mapping needed). Cost: zero network isolation — port conflicts with host services, and a compromised container sees host network traffic
--network none: maximum performance with no overhead
The default bridge with -p for each port
explain: host mode removes the network namespace boundary: the container uses the host's interfaces and IP directly — localhost in the container IS the host. That's why no -p mapping is needed (and -p is ignored/meaningless with host mode). The cost is total loss of network isolation: port collisions with host daemons, broader blast radius. Use it for network appliances/agents that genuinely need the host stack — never as a lazy substitute for publishing ports.

q: A network team needs containers to appear as physical devices on the corporate LAN — each with its own MAC address and a DHCP-reserved LAN IP — because firewall rules are written per-IP. Which driver fits, and what's the catch?
options: overlay: spans the LAN automatically
bridge: just assign static IPs on the bridge

macvlan: containers get their own MAC + LAN IP and look like physical hosts. Catch: the parent interface must support it (promiscuous mode), the container can't reach the HOST's own IP by default, and MAC limits on switches/VM platforms can bite (ipvlan shares the host MAC where MAC limits apply)
host: containers inherit the host's MAC
explain: macvlan attaches containers directly to the physical network with their own MACs — they look like real devices to switches, DHCP, and firewalls. Requirements: parent interface (-o parent=eth0), subnet/gateway specified, promiscuous mode allowed. Two classic gotchas: (1) the container usually CAN'T talk to the host's own IP (kernel drops it — a known macvlan limitation), and (2) environments limiting MACs per port (some VMs/clouds) break it — that's when ipvlan (shared MAC, separate IPs) is the answer. Bridge IPs are NAT'd privates, not LAN IPs.

q: A developer runs: docker run -d -P nginx (capital P). Then docker port <container> shows 0.0.0.0:32768->80/tcp. What did -P do, and how does it differ from -p 8080:80?
options: -P and -p are identical; the capital letter is cosmetic
-P publishes to all swarm nodes; -p publishes to one
-P only works with the host network driver
-P publishes ALL exposed ports (from EXPOSE in the image) on RANDOM host ports. -p maps specific host:container ports deterministically
explain: -P/--publish-all takes every port the image EXPOSEs and binds each to a random high host port (32768+). -p 8080:80 is explicit: host 8080 → container 80. Use -P for quick throwaway testing; never for anything clients depend on (the ports change every run). And remember the chain: EXPOSE documents, -p/-P actually publishes. Without either, the port is reachable only from within Docker networks.

q: Two app containers share a user-defined network. The developer hardcodes the database container's IP (172.18.0.4) in the app's config. After a routine docker compose down/up, the app can't reach the database. What broke, and what's the durable fix?
options: Container IPs are ephemeral — recreate assigns new ones. Fix: use the container/service NAME (embedded DNS resolves it on user-defined networks); names are stable across recreates
The network subnet changed; pin it with --subnet
Compose randomizes IPs deliberately; use host networking instead
The database lost its data; restore from backup
explain: Container IPs are leased per container lifetime — down/up, rescheduling, or scaling changes them. Names on user-defined networks are the stable handle: embedded DNS always resolves the current IP. This is the same principle behind Swarm service names and Kubernetes Service DNS. Hardcoding IPs is the #1 container networking anti-pattern; the exam tests it as a 'worked yesterday, broken today' scenario. (Data loss would show different symptoms — connection refused vs. wrong-data.)

q: A container must join TWO isolated application networks (frontend and backend) to act as an API gateway. How is this done, and can it be changed at runtime?
options: Run two gateway containers, one per network

docker network connect frontend gateway; docker network connect backend gateway — a container can join multiple networks, and connect/disconnect work LIVE on user-defined networks (no recreate needed)
Connect it at creation to both with --network (only one allowed), so gateways need host networking
Multi-network containers are impossible in Docker
explain: Containers can attach to multiple networks simultaneously (each gets an interface + IP per network) — the standard API-gateway/proxy pattern: frontend net for clients, backend net for services, with the gateway bridging them. On user-defined networks, docker network connect/disconnect are hot operations — no container recreate (unlike the default bridge, which doesn't allow hot attach). The gateway container then resolves names on both networks via embedded DNS.

q: A Swarm service needs to send traffic to external SaaS APIs, but the security team requires all egress to pass through a forward proxy for inspection. The service is on an overlay network. Where should the proxy configuration live?
options: Swarm automatically routes all external traffic through the manager nodes
In the overlay network definition with --opt proxy
In the container/service environment (HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY) — overlay networks don't do egress proxying; the application or its sidecar must be configured to use the proxy
Publish the proxy port with -p and Docker handles it
explain: Docker networks don't implement egress forward proxies — that's application configuration. Set HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY (and NO_PROXY for internal/swarm DNS names — critical: don't proxy the service VIP/DNS or the mesh breaks) in the service env. The exam angle: know what Docker networking does (DNS, VIPs, mesh, overlays) versus what it doesn't (L7 proxying, TLS termination). Sidecar proxy containers are the production pattern when the app can't be configured.

q: docker network inspect ingress shows a 10.255.0.0/16 subnet. A new overlay network fails to create with 'pool overlaps'. What's happening?
options: Ingress networks can't coexist with custom overlays
The daemon's default address pool is exhausted; restart Docker
Overlay networks don't support custom subnets
The ingress network (routing mesh) already occupies 10.255.0.0/16; the new overlay's default subnet collides. Fix: create with an explicit --subnet outside that range
explain: The built-in ingress network (which carries routing-mesh traffic) defaults to 10.255.0.0/16, and Docker's default overlay pool can collide with it. Fix: docker network create -d overlay --subnet 10.200.0.0/16 mynet. Broader lesson: plan subnet allocation for Docker hosts like any network engineering — the default pools (docker0 172.17.0.0/16, user bridges from 172.18+, ingress 10.255.0.0/16) must not overlap corporate ranges, or containers can't reach (or be reached by) those networks.

q: A service is created with --network frontend (an overlay) but tasks can't reach a legacy database on the corporate LAN (192.168.50.20). Other containers on the default bridge CAN reach it. What's the most likely cause?
options: The overlay's subnet or the ingress network overlaps 192.168.50.0/24, so traffic for the database is misrouted into Docker's own networks. Check subnet allocation and re-create the overlay with a non-overlapping --subnet
Overlay networks can't route to external IPs by design
The database firewall blocks overlay traffic specifically
Services can't access the LAN; only docker run containers can
explain: The tell: default-bridge containers (172.17.0.0/16) reach the DB, overlay containers don't — the overlay (or ingress) subnet overlaps the 192.168.50.0/24 LAN, so the container's routing table sends DB-bound packets into Docker's virtual network instead of out the host. Overlays route externally just fine otherwise (NAT via the host). Fix: audit docker network ls subnets vs. corporate ranges and recreate with --subnet outside them. This 'subnet overlap' scenario is a top-tier DCA troubleshooting question.

q: A team wants container-to-container traffic on a custom bridge to be encrypted because it carries PII between app tiers on a shared host. They propose --opt encrypted on the bridge network. Will it work?
options: Encryption is automatic on all user-defined networks
No — --opt encrypted is an OVERLAY driver feature (IPsec for VXLAN between hosts). On a single host, use application-level TLS (or run the tiers on an overlay if you need the feature)
Yes, but only on the default bridge
Yes — encrypted works on any network driver
explain: --opt encrypted applies to overlay networks (encrypts VXLAN traffic between HOSTS). Single-host bridge traffic never leaves the host's memory — there's nothing to intercept on the wire, so the option doesn't exist there. For PII between tiers on one host, the real control is mutual TLS at the application layer (or a service mesh). Know each feature's scope: encrypted = overlay/VXLAN between nodes; icc=false = isolation on bridge; TLS = application.

q: An engineer runs docker run -d --name db --network backend postgres, then docker network connect frontend db. From a container on frontend, ping db resolves. What makes this work?
options: DNS only works on the first network; the ping is using cached IPs
The frontend network automatically routes to all other networks
The db container has two interfaces, each on its network, and Docker's embedded DNS registers the container name on every network it's attached to
postgres enables multi-network mode by default
explain: Each network attachment = a virtual interface + IP in the container. Embedded DNS serves every user-defined network the container joins, so db resolves from both frontend and backend. The networks remain ISOLATED from each other — a frontend-only container still can't reach backend-only containers; only the dual-attached db bridges (at L3, as a participant, not as a router unless IP forwarding is configured in it). This is the controlled way to span network boundaries.

q: A Swarm cluster's overlay-encrypted database traffic shows high CPU on all nodes. The team asks whether encryption is worth it and what the alternative is. Your guidance:
options: Switch to the default bridge to avoid encryption costs
Remove --opt encrypted; overlay traffic is encrypted by default anyway
Encryption overhead is zero; the CPU must be from something else

--opt encrypted adds IPsec overhead per packet — measurable on busy nodes. Keep it only where the underlay is untrusted (multi-DC, cloud). On a trusted single-DC underlay, application TLS on the sensitive flows gives better granularity with less blanket overhead
explain: IPsec on every VXLAN packet costs CPU — real and measurable at high throughput. Security is always a trade-off: encrypt the overlay where the network is untrusted (WAN, shared cloud), skip blanket encryption on a trusted datacenter fabric and use targeted app-level TLS for the sensitive flows. 'Encrypted overlays are free' is the trap — nothing in networking is free. The exam tests this as a design-judgment question, not just a flag-recall one.

q: A developer exposes a container port with -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 instead of -p 8080:80. What's the difference in behavior?
options: -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 binds the host port to LOOPBACK only — reachable from the host itself but NOT from other machines. -p 8080:80 binds all interfaces (0.0.0.0), reachable network-wide
No difference; localhost binding is the default
The 127.0.0.1 form publishes the port inside the container only
Port binding addresses are ignored by Docker
explain: -p [host-ip]:host-port:container-port controls which host interface listens. 127.0.0.1 = localhost-only (safe default for dev tools, admin UIs); bare 8080:80 = 0.0.0.0 = every interface, reachable from the network. This is a least-exposure control: bind admin/debug ports to loopback, and put a real reverse proxy in front for external traffic. The exam tests the syntax and the security implication together.

q: A container on a user-defined bridge can't resolve external domains (google.com fails) but CAN ping 8.8.8.8. Containers on the default bridge resolve fine. What's the likely cause?
options: User-defined bridges don't support external DNS

A firewall/iptables rule is blocking the embedded DNS (127.0.0.11:53) path or outbound DNS from the bridge subnet — user-defined networks use embedded DNS, and corporate firewalls sometimes block DNS except via approved resolvers. Check iptables FORWARD rules and whether the host's firewall allows the bridge subnet's DNS traffic
The user-defined network has no DNS configured
The container needs --dns 8.8.8.8 on user-defined networks
explain: IP works but names don't = DNS problem specifically. User-defined networks use the embedded DNS server (127.0.0.11 inside the container, forwarding to the host's resolvers). When default-bridge containers work but custom-bridge ones don't, the difference is the DNS path: firewall rules (iptables FORWARD, firewalld, ufw) blocking port 53 from the new subnet, or a corporate DNS policy. Debugging: getent hosts google.com inside the container, check /etc/resolv.conf there (should show 127.0.0.11), then inspect host firewall rules for the bridge subnet.

q: A Swarm service with 5 replicas publishes port 443. The team wants clients' source IPs visible to the application for audit logging, but the app sees only internal mesh IPs. What's the explanation and the fix?
options: Enable --opt encrypted to preserve headers
Source IPs are never visible in containers; audit logging is impossible

The routing mesh SNATs client connections — the app sees the ingress network IP, not the client. Fix: publish in host mode (--publish mode=host,target=443) so the task receives the original source IP (at the cost of one task per node per port and no mesh load-balancing on that port)
The app must use the VIP instead of task IPs
explain: The ingress routing mesh performs source NAT: by the time the packet reaches the task, the source is the ingress overlay IP. If the app needs true client IPs (audit, geo, rate-limiting), bypass the mesh with host-mode publishing — the task binds the host's port directly and sees the real source. Trade-offs: only one task per node can use that host port (scheduling constraint), and you lose mesh-level load balancing on it. Design decision, not a bug — the exam wants you to know WHY the IP is masked and the exact fix.
