q: A container runs: docker run -d -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock --name helper ci-helper:latest. A security audit flags this as CRITICAL. Why?
options: The socket mount is read-only and harmless; the audit is wrong
Socket mounts only work on Swarm managers
The risk is log spam, not privilege escalation

The Docker socket is the daemon's API — any process that can write to it has full daemon control: start a --privileged container mounting the host root, and you have host root. A compromised helper container = full host compromise
explain: The daemon runs as root and the socket IS root-equivalent access: docker -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock run --privileged -v /:/host ... = host root in one command. Mounting the socket into a container hands that power to whatever runs inside it. Legitimate uses exist (CI agents, Portainer) but they demand hardened, trusted images, read-only mounts where possible, and network isolation. The exam's favorite 'what's wrong with this setup?' — socket mount + untrusted image = game over.

q: An app needs to bind to port 80 (a privileged port) inside its container but should otherwise run with minimal privileges. Which is the least-privilege approach?
options: docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE app — drop everything, add back only the capability to bind privileged ports
Run as root; capabilities don't apply to port binding
Run the container with --privileged
Use --network host so port binding needs no privileges
explain: Linux capabilities split root's powers: NET_BIND_SERVICE alone allows binding ports <1024. --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE gives the container exactly that and nothing else — least privilege in one line. --privileged grants ALL capabilities and disables seccomp/AppArmor: the nuclear option, almost never correct. Default Docker already drops dangerous caps (SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN); fine-tune from there. The exam pattern: '--privileged' is the distractor; the capability pair is the answer.

q: A Dockerfile for a web app ends with USER www-data, but the container must write upload files to /app/uploads. The directory is root-owned in the image and writes fail. What's the correct fix that keeps the non-root posture?
options: Mount /app/uploads from a privileged volume
In the Dockerfile (as root, before the final USER): create the directory, chown it to www-data, and keep USER www-data as the runtime user — the app writes as non-root to a directory it owns
Run the container with --user root
Switch back to root; uploads require root
explain: Non-root doesn't mean can't-write — it means own-what-you-write. Pattern: RUN mkdir -p /app/uploads && chown www-data:www-data /app/uploads (as root during build), then USER www-data for runtime. The app writes happily as non-root. Reverting to root 'because uploads' surrenders the whole security benefit; --user root at runtime is the same surrender. Pair with --read-only + --tmpfs for scratch space for the full hardening set.

q: A team debates where to put the production database password: (a) baked into the image via ENV, (b) passed with docker run -e, (c) Swarm secret mounted at /run/secrets. Rank them and explain.
options: (b) is best because env vars are ephemeral
(a) is best because the password ships with the image

(c) is correct: secrets are encrypted in the Raft log and mounted read-only only into granted services. (a) bakes the password into every layer forever (visible in docker history to anyone with the image). (b) exposes it in docker inspect and the daemon's process list
All three are equivalent; pick the most convenient
explain: The hierarchy: Swarm/K8s secrets (encrypted at rest, least exposure) > env vars (visible in inspect, process tables, sometimes logs) > baked into the image (immortal — every layer, every registry copy, every docker history reader). The exam tests all three failure modes: 'visible in docker history' → baked in; 'visible in docker inspect' → -e; 'most secure' → secrets at /run/secrets. Bonus: secrets are immutable — rotate by versioning (see Q9).

q: Swarm's mutual TLS is enabled by default. A new worker joins with a token and immediately gets a certificate. An engineer asks: how often do node certificates rotate, and how is rotation tuned?
options: Certificates never expire; rotation requires rejoining every node
Certificates rotate on every docker service update
TLS is only for managers; workers communicate in plaintext
Node certificates auto-rotate with a default 90-day expiry, tunable via docker swarm update --cert-expiry. The swarm CA handles issuance and rotation automatically
explain: Every swarm node gets a mutual-TLS certificate from the swarm CA at join; the CA auto-rotates them (default 90-day validity, --cert-expiry to tune, --external-ca to integrate with an enterprise CA). All control-plane and Raft traffic is mTLS — workers included. This is 'secure by default' done right: the exam contrasts it with the things you MUST configure yourself (join token rotation, autolock, secrets usage). Don't confuse cert expiry (node identity) with token rotation (join credentials).

q: A regulated customer requires that Swarm's Raft logs be encrypted at rest, with a key required whenever a manager restarts. Which feature, and what's the operational risk?
options: Swarm autolock (docker swarm init --autolock / docker swarm update --autolock=true): encrypts Raft logs; managers need docker swarm unlock with the key after each restart. Risk: lose the unlock key and a restarted manager can NEVER rejoin — store it in a vault, not on the manager
MKE backup passphrase; risk is backup size
--opt encrypted on the overlay network; risk is CPU overhead
Docker Content Trust; risk is unsigned images
explain: Autolock encrypts the Raft log (cluster state: services, secrets, configs) at rest; every manager restart requires docker swarm unlock with the key. The operational cliff: no key = that manager is permanently locked out (the data isn't destroyed, but it's unreadable). This is the same key-custody lesson as MKE backup passphrases: encryption keys for control-plane material live in a vault with tested retrieval. --opt encrypted is data-plane (VXLAN between nodes) — different layer, different threat.

q: An MKE user can log in but gets 'access denied' creating a service in the production collection. They ARE in the release-team LDAP group. What's the most likely misconfiguration?
options: They need --privileged on their docker client

The grant chain is incomplete: MKE requires Subject + Role + Resource Set. Being in the LDAP group (subject) isn't enough — there must be a grant binding that subject to a role (e.g. Scheduler/Full Control) on the production resource set. Check grants for the missing link
MKE doesn't support LDAP groups
Their password expired
explain: MKE's model is deny-by-default: no grant = no access, regardless of group membership. The three-legged grant (subject=release-team, role=Scheduler or Full Control, resource set=production collection) must ALL be present. Debugging order: does a grant exist for their subject? Does its role include service creation? Does its resource set cover production? LDAP supplies identity (the subject); grants supply authorization. Conflating authentication (can log in) with authorization (can act) is the trap.

q: A container image from a public registry is compromised at the registry (attacker pushed a malicious :latest). The team's defenses are: digest pinning + Docker Content Trust. Which defense catches this, and how?
options: Digest pinning only works for private registries
Neither helps; registries are trusted implicitly

Digest pinning: the service references the known-good sha256 — the attacker's new bits have a different digest, so pulls still resolve the old, good image. DCT additionally refuses the unsigned/foreign-signed tag
DCT scans the image and detects the malware
explain: Two independent controls: (1) Digest pinning — you deploy sha256:abc (the verified bits); the attacker's push changes :latest's digest, but your reference still resolves the ORIGINAL bits. Immutable reference beats mutable tag. (2) DCT — with DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1, the client verifies the Notary signature; the attacker's tag isn't signed by YOUR publisher key, so it's rejected. DCT proves provenance (who signed), digests prove integrity (exact bits). Neither scans for malware — that's image scanning's job (MSR/docker scout). Layered: pin + sign + scan.

q: A developer runs a container with --read-only and it crashes writing to /tmp. The app can't be modified. What's the correct runtime fix?
options: Run with --privileged so it can remount
Bind-mount the host's /tmp into the container
Remove --read-only; it's incompatible with real apps
Add --tmpfs /tmp (and any other writable scratch paths): keeps the root filesystem immutable while giving the app RAM-backed writable space where it needs it
explain: --read-only + --tmpfs is the standard pairing: immutable image filesystem (an attacker can't modify binaries or plant persistence) with explicit writable scratch areas. --tmpfs /tmp gives a RAM-backed writable /tmp that vanishes with the container — ideal for temp files. Removing --read-only surrenders the hardening; --privileged is wildly disproportionate; bind-mounting host /tmp shares host state (and host /tmp contents) unnecessarily. Also consider: does the app really need /tmp, or is it misconfigured logging?

q: A seccomp profile blocks a containerized backup tool that needs mount(2). The vendor says 'just run --privileged'. What's the least-privilege alternative?
options: --security-opt seccomp=<custom-profile> allowing the mount syscall (or --cap-add SYS_ADMIN if capability-gated), granting only what's needed instead of disabling all isolation
Run the backup on the host instead of in a container
There is none — mount always requires --privileged
Add the tool to the docker group
explain: --privileged disables seccomp, AppArmor, AND grants all capabilities — the vendor's lazy answer nukes every isolation layer for one syscall. The precise fix: a custom seccomp profile permitting mount(2) (via --security-opt seccomp=profile.json), possibly plus the specific capability. Default profiles exist to contain container escapes; you punch minimal, documented holes. The exam's meta-lesson: every '--privileged?' question has a narrower answer (capabilities, seccomp, read-only+tmpfs) — find it.

q: An auditor asks for proof that production images contain no critical CVEs. The pipeline currently builds and pushes with no checks. What's the minimal credible pipeline addition?
options: Scan once a year during the audit

Add image vulnerability scanning (MSR scanning / docker scout / equivalent) as a CI gate BEFORE promotion to production repos, with a policy blocking critical/high CVEs — scanning finds them, promotion gates enforce the policy
Pin all base images to :latest for the newest patches
Sign images with DCT — signing proves no CVEs
explain: Scanning detects, gates enforce: scan every build in CI, and make the promotion pipeline (dev → prod repos in MSR) refuse images violating the CVE policy. Signing (DCT) proves provenance, not cleanliness — a signed image can still be vulnerable. :latest is the opposite of controlled (mutable, unreviewed). Annual scans miss the 364 days of new CVEs between them. The exam wants the full loop: scan in CI + gate promotion + rebuild on patched bases (minimal bases shrink what needs patching).

q: A Swarm manager's disk was stolen from the datacenter. The team used autolock. What does the thief get, and what must the team still do?
options: Nothing is at risk; stolen disks can't be read
The team must rebuild the entire swarm from scratch

The encrypted Raft log is unreadable without the unlock key — cluster state, secrets, and configs stay protected. The team must still rotate join tokens (in daemon config/backups elsewhere), audit what else was on the disk (TLS keys, logs), and verify no other managers are affected
The thief gets everything; autolock only protects running processes
explain: Autolock's whole purpose: Raft data at rest is encrypted, so a stolen disk yields ciphertext without the unlock key. But defense in depth means assuming partial exposure: join tokens might exist in shell history/backups on that disk (rotate them), node TLS keys and logs need review, and the incident gets documented. The remaining managers keep the cluster running (quorum permitting) — no rebuild needed. This is the 'encryption at rest: what does it actually cover' question — Raft log yes, everything-else-on-disk not automatically.

q: A container needs to talk to the host's Docker daemon to spawn sibling containers (a CI runner). The team knows socket-mounting is risky. What's the safer architecture?
options: Use docker-in-docker with --privileged; it's safer than the socket
Give the container --privileged instead of the socket
There is no safer way; mount the socket

Run the CI jobs as Swarm/Kubernetes Jobs via the orchestrator API with scoped credentials (least-privilege service account / client certs) instead of handing the container the root-equivalent daemon socket — or use a dedicated, hardened runner host isolated from production
explain: The socket IS the daemon API with no scoping — whoever holds it is root on that host. Better: go through the ORCHESTRATOR with narrowly-scoped credentials (a CI service account that can only create Jobs in one namespace / collection), so a compromised runner can only do CI things, not host-root things. Alternatives: isolated runner hosts (blast radius containment), or rootless Docker. Docker-in-docker with --privileged is arguably WORSE (full privilege + nested daemon complexity). The principle: replace ambient authority (the socket) with scoped credentials.

q: USER appuser is set in a Dockerfile, but docker exec -it <container> whoami shows root. How is this possible?
options: docker exec always runs as root by default — it doesn't inherit the container's USER. Use docker exec --user appuser to match, and be aware that exec-as-root is an available escalation path for anyone with Docker API access
whoami is broken in containers
The USER instruction was ignored
The image was built with --privileged
explain: docker exec defaults to root regardless of the image's USER — the container's user only governs the ENTRYPOINT/CMD process. Anyone with docker API access (CI systems, teammates, attackers with the socket) can exec as root into your 'non-root' container. Implications: non-root USER hardens the APP's own process (limits what an app-layer exploit gets), but it's not a boundary against Docker-API holders. Use --user to exec as the app user for debugging fidelity, and treat Docker API access as privileged (it is).

q: A company runs untrusted third-party container images (a marketplace of plugins). Which combination MOST reduces the risk of a malicious image?
options: Trust Docker Hub's default scanning and run them normally

Run each with: --read-only, --cap-drop ALL (add back only needed caps), --user non-root, --security-opt no-new-privileges, memory/CPU limits, on isolated networks without the docker socket — layered containment assuming the image is hostile
Scan once and then run with --privileged for compatibility
Only allow images with more than 1M pulls
explain: Assume hostile: --read-only (no persistence/modification), --cap-drop ALL (no privileged syscalls), non-root user + no-new-privileges (blocks setuid escalation), resource limits (fork bombs, miners), isolated network (no lateral movement, no socket). Pull-count is not a security property (popular images get typosquatted). Scanning is necessary but not sufficient (zero-days, obfuscation). This is the exam's 'defense in depth for untrusted code' answer — no single flag saves you; the LAYERING does.

q: A database container is started with docker run -d -v /data/db:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres. The DBA complains this is fragile. What's wrong with this storage choice, and what's the better one?
options: Bind mounts are read-only; databases need write access
Postgres can't run in containers

It's a bind mount: the container depends on a host path that must exist with correct permissions on every host (breaks portability, Swarm scheduling, and SELinux contexts). Better: a named volume (-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data) — Docker-managed, portable, with proper driver support
Nothing — bind mounts are the recommended database storage
explain: Bind mounts tie the container to host paths: the directory must pre-exist with right ownership (a classic 'works on my machine' failure), it breaks when Swarm reschedules to another node, and SELinux/AppArmor need relabeling (:z/:Z). Named volumes are Docker's managed answer: created on demand, live under /var/lib/docker/volumes, work with volume drivers, and are the exam's default 'persistent data' choice. Bind mounts remain right for dev workflows (live code reload) and injecting config files — not for databases.

q: A Swarm service uses a named volume for uploads. After a node failure, the task reschedules to a new node — and the uploads are gone (empty volume). What happened, and what are the two fixes?
options: Swarm deletes volumes on reschedule; use bind mounts instead
The volume driver crashed; restart the daemon
Named volumes don't work in Swarm at all

Volumes are node-local by default: the new node's volume is a fresh, empty one — the data sits on the dead node. Fixes: (1) pin the service to the node with a placement constraint (sacrifices HA), or (2) use a cluster-aware volume driver (REX-Ray, Portworx, cloud drivers) so the volume follows the task
explain: Default (local) volumes are bound to ONE node's disk. Reschedule elsewhere = new empty volume = 'data disappeared' — the single most-tested Swarm storage scenario. Fix 1 (constraint pinning) is simple but the node becomes a single point of failure. Fix 2 (shared/cluster-aware driver) is the production answer: the volume detaches from the dead node and reattaches where the task lands. Design question the exam loves: local volume + rescheduling = data loss by design, not by bug.

q: A container processes credit-card data in temp files that must never touch persistent disk (compliance requirement). Which storage type, and why not the others?
options: tmpfs (--tmpfs /scratch): RAM-only, never written to disk, gone with the container. Volumes persist (wrong), bind mounts live on host disk (wrong)
A named volume with the nocopy option
The container's writable layer — it's deleted with the container
A bind mount to /dev/shm on the host
explain: tmpfs mounts live purely in memory (swap excluded if configured): nothing hits the disk, and the data evaporates when the container stops — exactly the compliance property needed. Volumes persist by design; bind mounts are host disk; the writable layer IS on disk (and worse, it's in the container's filesystem where docker export/commit could capture it). Size caveat: tmpfs consumes RAM — size it (--tmpfs /scratch:rw,size=512m) and monitor.

q: An engineer backs up a database volume with: docker run --rm --volumes-from db -v /backup:/backup ubuntu tar czf /backup/db.tar.gz -C /var/lib/postgresql/data .  Explain why --volumes-from is used and what the -v /backup:/backup does.
options: --volumes-from copies the database into the backup image permanently

--volumes-from mounts the db container's volumes into the throwaway backup container so tar can read the live data; -v /backup:/backup is a bind mount giving the backup container a host path to write the archive to
-v /backup:/backup shares memory between the containers
The command backs up the ubuntu image, not the database
explain: The classic sidecar pattern: --volumes-from db grafts db's volumes onto a disposable container (no need to stop the database; use pg_dump/pg_basebackup for consistency on live DBs), tar reads the files, and the bind mount -v /backup:/backup writes the archive to a host directory. Two mount types cooperating: volumes-from (read the data) + bind mount (land the artifact). Restore reverses it: fresh volume + tar xzf. The exam tests this as THE volume backup procedure.

q: docker volume ls shows dozens of volumes with 64-hex-character names. What are they, and how should the team prevent them?
options: They're Swarm secrets stored as volumes
Hex-named volumes are corrupted and must be deleted immediately

Anonymous volumes — created when a Dockerfile VOLUME instruction has no name at build/run time. They're hard to track and leak on container removal. Prevent: always use NAMED volumes (-v name:/path or --mount type=volume,src=name,...); clean strays with docker volume prune
They're encrypted volumes; nothing to do
explain: VOLUME /data in a Dockerfile with no -v name at runtime = anonymous volume with a hex ID. They accumulate silently (every container recreate mints a new one) and nothing maps them to their purpose. Named volumes are self-documenting and manageable (inspect, backup, remove by name). docker volume prune removes unused ones — but 'unused' is judged at prune time, so don't prune on hosts with stopped-but-precious containers. The exam's hygiene question: named > anonymous, always.

q: Compare -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data and --mount type=volume,src=pgdata,dst=/var/lib/postgresql/data. Why does the DCA call --mount the modern best practice?
options: -v is deprecated and will be removed
They behave identically; the exam doesn't distinguish them
--mount is shorter to type

--mount is explicit and validated: it fails loudly on typos and missing sources instead of silently creating the wrong thing (e.g. -v with a typo'd name creates a NEW empty volume or a bind mount to a wrong path). Verbose syntax documents intent
explain: -v is terse and DWIM (do-what-I-mean): -v pgdata:... with pgdata misspelled silently creates a fresh empty volume — your database 'loses' its data with zero errors. -v /wrong/path:... creates a bind mount to a possibly unintended host path. --mount validates: unknown source type, missing fields, or bad combinations are hard errors at container creation. The exam DOES distinguish them: --mount = explicit/safe/modern; -v = legacy/terse. (Also: --mount is required for some features like tmpfs options.)

q: A Kubernetes pod needs 10Gi of durable storage. The DCA expects you to describe the object chain. Which is correct?
options: Pod → PersistentVolumeClaim (the request: 10Gi, access mode) → binds a matching PersistentVolume → provisioned from a StorageClass (provisioner + parameters). CSI drivers plug third-party storage into this chain
The kubelet provisions storage directly from the container image
Pod → StorageClass → PersistentVolume → PersistentVolumeClaim, in that order
Pods can't use durable storage; use a StatefulSet instead
explain: The K8s storage chain: the pod's volume references a PVC ('I need 10Gi ReadWriteOnce'); the PVC binds to a suitable PV (manually created or dynamically provisioned); dynamic PVs come from a StorageClass (which names the provisioner — e.g. ebs.csi.aws.com — plus parameters like type/iops). CSI is the plugin interface vendors implement. Scope facts the exam likes: PVCs are namespaced (a pod only uses PVCs in its namespace); PVs and StorageClasses are cluster-scoped. StatefulSets add stable identity on top — they still use this same chain.

q: A config file must be injected into a container at /etc/app/config.yaml, read-only, from the host's /srv/app/config.yaml. Which mount, and with what option?
options: tmpfs — config in memory is fastest

A bind mount with :ro — docker run -v /srv/app/config.yaml:/etc/app/config.yaml:ro (or --mount type=bind,src=...,dst=...,readonly). Bind mounts are the right tool for single host files; :ro prevents the container from modifying host config
A named volume — volumes are the only read-only-capable mount
Bake it into the image with COPY
explain: Single host file into a container = bind mount's home turf (dev configs, TLS certs, one-off files). :ro/readonly is the hardening: the container reads but can't alter host config (imagine a compromised app rewriting its own config or escaping via a writable host file). Volumes are for Docker-managed data, not host files; tmpfs is RAM temp space; baking environment-specific config into images kills portability (the image differs per environment — an anti-pattern). Swarm equivalent: configs (docker config create) — but that's Swarm-only.

q: A Dockerfile contains VOLUME /var/lib/mysql. A user runs the image WITHOUT -v, then docker inspect shows a mount to /var/lib/docker/volumes/<hex>/_data. The user is confused — they never created a volume. Explain.
options: The hex directory is the image layer cache, not a volume
It's a bug; VOLUME without -v should use the container's writable layer

Docker auto-creates an anonymous volume for each VOLUME instruction when no explicit mount is given — the data persists in that hex-named volume even though the user didn't ask for one. To control it: run with -v dbdata:/var/lib/mysql
MySQL creates its own volumes at runtime
explain: VOLUME in a Dockerfile declares 'this path holds data' — at container creation, Docker auto-provisions an anonymous volume for it if you don't supply one. Consequences: data DOES persist (survives container removal — a surprise for users expecting ephemerality), and hex-named volumes accumulate (see Q95). Database official images do this deliberately (protecting your data by default). Control it explicitly: named volume at run time, or accept the anonymous one knowingly. The exam tests the mechanism: VOLUME instruction → anonymous volume unless overridden.

q: A team runs Docker on hosts with limited SSD space. They want: (1) container writable layers on the fast SSD, (2) image/blob storage on a larger HDD, (3) no performance surprises. What's the honest guidance?
options: Move /var/lib/docker/volumes to the HDD with a symlink; everything else stays
Storage performance doesn't matter for containers
Docker supports per-path storage splitting natively with two --data-root flags

Docker has a single --data-root (/var/lib/docker): the clean approach is mounting the fast SSD at /var/lib/docker (whole daemon dir on fast disk) or using volume drivers/plugins for tiered data — you can't split writable layers from image storage with stock Docker. For (3): monitor disk with docker system df and prune aggressively
explain: Stock Docker = one data-root; there's no native 'images here, writable layers there' split. Realistic options: whole /var/lib/docker on the fast disk (simplest, best performance), or keep the daemon dir on SSD and put bulk DATA on the HDD via named volumes with explicit bind paths or volume drivers. The symlink trick works but is fragile across upgrades. Operational hygiene the exam touches: docker system df shows reclaimable space; docker system prune is the big hammer (images, containers, networks, build cache — use with care on production hosts).

q: A runbook instructs the on-call engineer to run `docker service scale web=5` during a traffic spike. A teammate objects: 'That's not a real command — the correct way is `docker service update --replicas 5 web`.' Who is right?
options: The teammate — docker service scale only works on Compose stacks, not Swarm services
The runbook — docker service scale is a convenience shorthand that does exactly what docker service update --replicas does, including honoring the service's update_config during the rollout
Both are wrong — replica counts can only be changed in the Compose file followed by a stack redeploy
The runbook command works but bypasses update_config, updating all tasks simultaneously
explain: docker service scale web=5 is literally shorthand for docker service update --replicas 5 web — same API call, same rolling-update behavior, parallelism and delay honored. The teammate is confusing it with docker compose up --scale (the Compose-side equivalent). EXAM TRAP: 'scale bypasses update_config' is invented — scaling IS an update, so all update settings apply.

q: A 6-replica API service runs on a cluster with just enough capacity for 6 tasks. The team needs zero-downtime deploys, but updates keep stalling with tasks stuck Pending. The service uses the default update order. What should change, and what's the trade-off?
options: Set --update-order start-first so the new task starts before the old one stops — zero downtime, but the update temporarily needs capacity for 7 tasks, which this cluster lacks (hence the Pending stall)
Set --update-order stop-first — the default is start-first, which is causing the stall
Increase --update-parallelism to 6 so all tasks update at once
Update order only applies to rollbacks; the stall must be a network issue
explain: Default order is stop-first: old task stops, then the new one starts — brief capacity dip, but safe on tight clusters. start-first reverses it (new before old) for true zero-downtime, at the cost of needing headroom for parallelism+1 tasks. The Pending stall is the scheduler unable to place that 7th task — the diagnostic fingerprint of start-first on a full cluster. EXAM TRAP: parallelism=6 would take all 6 down simultaneously on a bad image.

q: A 50-replica worker service rolls out a new image. Two tasks land on nodes with a corrupted image layer and fail; the whole rollout pauses, leaving 48 tasks on mixed versions. The team expects a couple of bad nodes in a fleet this size. Which flag makes the rollout tolerate a small failure percentage?
options: --update-parallelism 50 to push through failures faster
--update-delay 0 to skip the failure window
--restart-condition none so failed tasks are ignored
--update-max-failure-ratio 0.2 — the update continues unless more than 20% of tasks fail, instead of pausing on the very first failure (the default ratio of 0)
explain: --update-max-failure-ratio sets the tolerated fraction of failed tasks before the rollout pauses (default 0 = any single failure halts it). On large fleets a small ratio absorbs known-bad nodes without human intervention. Parallelism and delay change rollout SPEED, not failure handling; restart-condition governs crashed tasks, not updates. EXAM TRAP: the default 0 is why one bad node freezes a 50-replica rollout.

q: A service update completes 'successfully' in seconds, but the new tasks crash 45 seconds after starting — after Swarm has already moved on to the next batch. The team wants Swarm to watch each updated task longer before declaring that batch a success. Which setting controls this?
options: --update-delay — it already does this
The HEALTHCHECK --timeout value
--update-monitor 60s — how long Swarm watches an updated task for failure before proceeding to the next batch; the default is only 5s, so slow-crashing tasks slip through unnoticed
--restart-delay — it delays the crash
explain: --update-monitor is the observation window per batch (default 5s). A task that starts cleanly then dies at 45s passes a 5s monitor — the rollout 'succeeds' and the failure surfaces later as restarts. Raising the monitor makes the rollout itself catch slow crashes and trigger the failure action. --update-delay is the pause BETWEEN batches, not the watch window; HEALTHCHECK timeout is probe-level. EXAM TRAP: confusing delay (spacing) with monitor (observation).

q: A Compose file includes `build: ./api` for the api service. The developer runs `docker stack deploy -c app.yml prod` and the api tasks fail with 'No such image'. The image builds fine with `docker compose up`. What's wrong?
options: docker stack deploy never builds images — it ignores the build: section entirely. Build and push the image to a registry first (docker build / docker compose build, then docker push), and reference the pushed tag in the file
Stack deploy requires build: to use an absolute path
The build section needs deploy.replicas set to trigger a build
Swarm managers can't reach the build context; copy it to every worker node
explain: docker stack deploy is orchestration-only: it deploys the Compose file's desired state and expects every image to already exist in a registry reachable by all nodes. The build: section is silently ignored (the mirror image of Q5's deploy:-ignored-by-compose-up trap). Building happens client-side with docker build or docker compose build — then push, then deploy. EXAM TRAP: assuming the swarm builds images on nodes.

q: A team stores a TLS certificate (public) and a private key in Swarm. They used a secret for both. A reviewer says the certificate should be a config, not a secret. What's the real difference between Swarm configs and secrets?
options: There is none — configs and secrets are aliases for the same object
Configs are encrypted and secrets are not

Both are immutable and mounted as files into granted services, but secrets are encrypted in the Raft log and mount under /run/secrets/<name> by default, while configs are stored unencrypted and mount under /<config-name> by default — secrets for sensitive material, configs for non-sensitive files
Configs can be updated in place; secrets cannot
explain: The encryption boundary is the whole point: secrets get Raft-log encryption (that's what makes them safe for passwords and keys); configs don't, so they must never hold sensitive data. Both are immutable (no docker config update exists either) and both mount as files — only the default paths and the encryption differ. EXAM TRAP: 'configs are the encrypted ones' inverts the model; 'update in place' is invented for both.

q: A service uses an image from a private registry. The manager pulls it fine (the engineer ran docker login on the manager), but every task scheduled to worker nodes fails with 'No such image' / pull access denied. What's the fix?
options: Run docker login on every worker node manually
Deploy with --with-registry-auth (docker service create --with-registry-auth / docker stack deploy --with-registry-auth) so the manager forwards its registry credentials to the workers for the pull
Make the registry public
Copy the image tarball to each worker with docker save/load
explain: Swarm workers don't share the manager's docker login session — the credential lives in the manager's ~/.docker/config.json only. --with-registry-auth ships the auth token along with the task so workers can pull private images. Manual logins on every node work but rot (tokens expire, nodes get replaced); it's toil, not a solution. EXAM TRAP: 'it pulled on the manager so the cluster can pull' — the manager is not the cluster.

q: A 3-manager swarm loses two managers permanently (hardware destroyed). One manager survives with intact Raft data, but the cluster has no quorum and nothing can be scheduled. What's the recovery path?
options: The cluster is unrecoverable; restore from backup and rebuild
Run docker swarm join on the survivor so it rejoins itself
Wait — Raft will elect the survivor as leader once the others time out
On the surviving manager, run docker swarm init --force-new-cluster --advertise-addr <ip>:2377 to form a single-manager cluster from its surviving Raft data, then join fresh managers and workers
explain: --force-new-cluster is the documented quorum-loss recovery: it bootstraps a new single-manager cluster from one survivor's Raft state — services, networks, secrets and configs come back. Then add managers to restore HA. Without quorum Raft can NEVER elect a leader (waiting changes nothing), and 'rebuild from backup' discards live state you still have. EXAM TRAP: this is disaster recovery, not normal operation — never use it on a healthy cluster.

q: A data-loader task is designed to run once and exit 0 on success. It's defined as a Swarm service, but after each successful run Swarm immediately starts it again, reprocessing the data. Which setting is wrong?
options: The default --restart-condition any restarts the task no matter how it exits — for run-to-completion work use --restart-condition on-failure (or none), so a clean exit 0 is left alone
Services can't run one-shot tasks; you must use docker run instead
Exit code 0 is treated as failure by Swarm
restart-condition only accepts 'always' or 'never'
explain: Restart policies: any (default) restarts regardless of exit code; on-failure restarts only non-zero exits (optionally capped with on-failure:N); none never restarts. A batch job that exits 0 under any gets resurrected forever — the classic 'why does my job run twice' bug. EXAM TRAP: on-failure sounds like 'only when the app fails' — correct — while any means 'even on success'.

q: A monitoring sidecar on the same overlay network needs to scrape metrics from EACH replica of the api service individually — not through the load-balanced VIP. Which DNS name gives it the individual task IPs?
options: api — it always returns every task IP
tasks.api — Docker's embedded DNS resolves tasks.<service> to the individual task IPs (round-robin), while the bare service name resolves to the VIP
vip.api — the special VIP hostname
It can't be done; the VIP is the only endpoint Swarm exposes
explain: tasks.<service> is the documented per-task DNS name on overlay networks — it returns the backing task IPs directly, the DNS-level equivalent of endpoint-mode dnsrr. The bare name resolves to the VIP (default endpoint mode). This is how sidecars, debuggers, and stateful clients address replicas individually without giving up the VIP for normal traffic. EXAM TRAP: assuming the VIP is the only way to reach tasks.

q: A 6-replica service must survive the loss of an entire availability zone. Nodes carry node.labels.az=1a/1b/1c. A hard constraint can't express 'spread across zones'. What can?
options: --constraint 'node.labels.az == 1a' — pin everything to one zone for consistency
Global mode — one task per node automatically guarantees zone spread
--placement-pref 'spread=node.labels.az' — a soft preference that distributes tasks evenly across the AZ label values; combined with enough replicas it yields zone-level HA
Placement preferences are just hard constraints with different syntax
explain: Placement preferences are SOFT distribution hints (spread=), evaluated after hard constraints — they balance tasks across label values but never refuse to schedule. Constraints are hard filters that can leave tasks Pending. Global mode gives one-per-node, which says nothing about zone balance. EXAM TRAP: treating spread= as a guarantee — if two AZs are full, tasks still land in the third; preferences guide, constraints compel.

q: A legacy app refuses to read its mounted secret unless the file is mode 0400 owned by root. The default secret mount doesn't satisfy it. How do you set ownership and permissions on a Swarm secret?
options: chmod the file inside the container at startup — secrets are writable
Secrets always mount 0400 root; the app is misconfigured and must be fixed
Update it in place with docker secret update --mode 0400
At service creation: --secret source=db_pass,target=db.txt,uid=0,gid=0,mode=0400 — target renames the mount point, and uid/gid/mode set ownership and permissions on the mounted file
explain: Secret mount options (source, target, uid, gid, mode) are set when the secret is GRANTED to the service — that's the only place file metadata can be controlled. Secrets mount read-only (chmod at runtime fails), there is no docker secret update (secrets are immutable), and the default is not 0400-root for every app. EXAM TRAP: trying to fix mount metadata after the fact instead of at grant time.

q: A Kubernetes Deployment rolls out a bad image. The Swarm-trained engineer reaches for 'docker service rollback'. What's the Kubernetes equivalent?
options: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> — reverts to the previous revision (ReplicaSet); kubectl rollout status watches progress, mirroring docker service rollback
kubectl delete deployment — then recreate it from scratch
kubectl scale deployment to zero and back up
Kubernetes has no rollback; you must re-apply the old manifest
explain: kubectl rollout undo is the direct analog of docker service rollback — Kubernetes keeps revision history (default 10 ReplicaSets) precisely for this. rollout history shows revisions; rollout status tracks the revert. Delete/recreate loses the Deployment's history and causes an outage; re-applying old manifests works but ignores the built-in revision mechanism the exam expects you to know.

q: A Kubernetes Deployment must never drop below its full replica count during a rollout (a trading API with zero capacity headroom tolerance). Which RollingUpdate strategy settings express this?
options: maxUnavailable: 50% — the default handles it
strategy: Recreate — it replaces everything at once
maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 — no old pod is removed until its replacement is ready and passing; needs headroom for one extra pod, the K8s equivalent of Swarm's start-first update order
RollingUpdate can't guarantee this; use a DaemonSet instead
explain: maxUnavailable: 0 means the available count never dips below desired; maxSurge: 1 permits one extra pod above desired during the swap — the standard zero-downtime pair (the mirror of --update-order start-first). Recreate does the opposite (all old pods die first — maximum downtime). DaemonSet changes placement, not rollout availability. EXAM TRAP: maxSurge alone doesn't protect availability; it's the maxUnavailable: 0 that does.

q: A team keeps a base Compose file plus an environment override: docker stack deploy -c base.yml -c prod.yml shop. The override sets replicas: 6 for web; the base sets replicas: 2. How many web replicas result?
options: 2 — the first file wins
6 — multiple -c files merge with later files overriding earlier ones; base-plus-override is the standard pattern
8 — values are summed across files
The deploy fails — only one -c flag is allowed
explain: Compose files merge in order, later files overriding earlier ones for the same keys — so teams keep a base file and layer environment overrides on top. Multiple -c flags are fully supported (that's what they're for). Values are never summed. EXAM TRAP: 'first file wins' inverts the merge order — it's always last-wins.

q: The engineer who held the Swarm unlock key leaves the company on bad terms. Autolock is enabled on the cluster. What's the correct response?
options: Nothing — the unlock key is tied to the manager's hardware and useless elsewhere
Re-init the swarm; unlock keys can't be changed
Toggle autolock off and on to generate a new key
Rotate it immediately: docker swarm unlock-key --rotate issues a new key and re-encrypts; the old key stops working at once
explain: docker swarm unlock-key --rotate is the documented rotation: new key issued, Raft re-encrypted, old key dead immediately. It's the same reflex as rotating a leaked join token — a departed key holder is a compromised credential. Re-init would destroy the cluster for no reason; toggling autolock doesn't rotate the key material. EXAM TRAP: treating the unlock key as immutable like the backup passphrase — it isn't.

q: A service reads its configuration from an external key-value store at startup. The config was fixed externally, but the running tasks still hold the old values. No service spec change is needed — the tasks just need re-rolling. What's the cleanest command?
options: docker service update --force web — forces a rolling restart honoring the existing update_config, with no spec change required
docker service scale web=0, then scale back up
Delete and recreate the service
docker service update --image with the same image tag
explain: --force triggers a fresh rolling update even when nothing in the spec changed — exactly the 'bounce the tasks' operation. Scaling to zero creates an outage window and loses the rolling discipline; delete/recreate drops networks, ports, and history. Re-pushing the same tag is a hack that may not even register as a change. EXAM TRAP: --force sounds dangerous; here it's the precise, intended tool.

q: With docker compose up, the api container crashes on startup because it tries to connect to postgres before the database finishes initializing. depends_on: [db] is already set. Why doesn't it help, and what's the fix?
options: depends_on is broken; add a sleep to the entrypoint
depends_on waits for the DB to be ready — the crash must be unrelated

depends_on only waits for the dependency container to START, not to be READY. Fix: give db a healthcheck and use the long syntax — depends_on: {db: {condition: service_healthy}} — so api starts only when postgres passes its health check
Compose can't order startup; deploy to Swarm instead
explain: Short-syntax depends_on orders STARTUP only — postgres's container starts in a second, but the database accepts connections much later. The long syntax with condition: service_healthy gates on an actual healthcheck, which is the only reliable 'ready' signal. The sleep hack is timing roulette. (Swarm note: docker stack deploy ignores depends_on entirely — readiness there comes from healthchecks plus update monitoring.) EXAM TRAP: 'started' vs 'ready' — containers are not applications.

q: A Dockerfile ends with USER appuser, but the app can't read its own config files: they were COPY'd as root with mode 600. The build currently runs a separate RUN chown after every COPY. What's the cleaner fix?
options: COPY --chown=appuser:appuser src/ /app/ — set ownership at copy time: no extra layer, no separate chown step, and the non-root posture stays intact
Run the container with --user root to match the file owner
Add chmod 777 in the entrypoint script
COPY can't set ownership; the RUN chown pattern is mandatory
explain: COPY --chown applies ownership during the copy itself, so no additional layer is created just to fix permissions — smaller images, fewer layers, same non-root runtime. --user root surrenders the USER hardening; chmod 777 is a security anti-pattern; and the 'mandatory chown' claim ignores a flag that's existed for years. EXAM TRAP: solving a build-time ownership problem with runtime privilege.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A multi-stage Dockerfile declares ARG VERSION=1.2 BEFORE the first FROM and uses $VERSION in a RUN step of the second stage. The build fails: VERSION is empty in that stage. Why?
options: ARG values can't be used in RUN instructions at all
The syntax requires ${VERSION} with braces
An ARG declared before the first FROM is only in scope for FROM lines. To use it inside a stage, redeclare ARG VERSION (no value needed) after that stage's FROM — it inherits the global default
Multi-stage builds don't support ARG
explain: Pre-FROM ARGs exist so FROM itself can be parameterized (e.g. ARG BASE / FROM $BASE). Inside a stage they're out of scope unless redeclared — the bare redeclaration picks up the outer value. This scoping rule is the #1 multi-stage ARG bug: the build doesn't error at the ARG line, it just expands to empty. EXAM TRAP: assuming 'declared once at top' means 'visible everywhere'.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An engineer builds myimg:2.0 locally and runs docker push myimg:2.0, expecting it to land in the company's registry at registry.internal:5000. Instead it tries Docker Hub and fails on permissions. What's missing?
options: docker login to Docker Hub first
Tag the image with the registry hostname first: docker tag myimg:2.0 registry.internal:5000/team/myimg:2.0, then push that name — the push DESTINATION comes from the image name, not from login state
Push with docker push --registry registry.internal:5000 myimg:2.0
Registries pull images; you can't push to a private registry
explain: Docker derives the registry from the repository name: no hostname = Docker Hub. docker login only supplies credentials; it doesn't choose the destination. The workflow is always tag-then-push with the fully qualified name. EXAM TRAP: the invented --registry flag — there is no such push flag, which is exactly why the tag carries the destination.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A production datacenter has no internet access. The team needs to get a custom image onto those hosts. What's the correct transfer procedure?
options: docker export the running container and import it there
Copy the Dockerfile and rebuild on each host
docker push to Docker Hub and pull from the datacenter
docker save myimg:2.0 -o myimg.tar on a connected host, transfer the tarball (USB, sneakernet), then docker load -i myimg.tar — save/load preserves the image with all layers, tags, and history intact
explain: docker save serializes the IMAGE (layers, tags, metadata); docker load restores it bit-for-bit — the standard air-gap transfer. docker export is the trap: it flattens a CONTAINER's filesystem, discarding layers, history, tags, and image config. Rebuilding per-host is slow and risks divergence; pushing to Hub defeats the air gap. EXAM TRAP: save=images, export=containers — never cross them.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile needs (1) the app version baked in at build time for labeling, and (2) the database hostname the container must read at RUNTIME, which differs per environment. Which instruction for each?
options: ARG for the version (build-time only, not persisted into running containers), ENV for the DB hostname (persisted into the image and visible to the running process) — with the caveat that ENV values are visible in docker inspect, so never use ENV for secrets
ENV for both — ARG is deprecated
ARG for both — ENV values can't be read at runtime
Neither — use EXPOSE for runtime configuration
explain: ARG = build-time inputs (versions, build flags), gone from the running container's environment (though visible in image history — hence never for secrets). ENV = baked into the image config and present at runtime — right for non-sensitive runtime config, wrong for passwords (inspect exposes them). The secrets-in-ARG/ENV failures from Q35/Q44 are the same visibility principle applied to credentials. EXAM TRAP: 'ARG is deprecated' — it's not; it's scoped differently.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A team labels every image with its git commit: LABEL org.opencontainers.image.revision=$SHA. Months later they need to find which local images came from a specific commit. How?
options: docker history shows labels; grep through it
Labels are write-only metadata; they can't be queried
docker images --filter "label=org.opencontainers.image.revision=<sha>" — labels are first-class queryable metadata, and docker image inspect shows them per image
Rebuild every image and compare
explain: Labels (OCI-standard keys like org.opencontainers.image.*) are queryable with --filter label= and visible in docker inspect — that's their purpose: traceability metadata (commit, build date, maintainer) that stays attached to the image. They're not shown in docker history (that's layers/commands). EXAM TRAP: treating labels as decorative comments instead of searchable metadata.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A security scanner flags a container because its image has EXPOSE 6379, claiming 'port 6379 is open'. The container was started with no -p flags on an internal network. Is the port reachable from outside the host?
options: Yes — EXPOSE opens the port on the host automatically
No — EXPOSE is documentation/metadata only. It does not publish anything; the port is reachable only within Docker networks unless explicitly published with -p/-P
Yes, but only on the default bridge network
EXPOSE enables the Swarm routing mesh for that port
explain: EXPOSE declares intent ('this container listens here') for documentation and for -P/--publish-all to consume — it opens nothing. Reachability from outside requires -p/-P (or the routing mesh for services). The scanner is reading metadata, not probing the network. EXAM TRAP: the #1 EXPOSE misconception — confusing declaration with publication.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Java service takes 90 seconds to warm up. Its HEALTHCHECK fails during warmup, so Swarm's rolling update marks each new task unhealthy and rolls back — even though the image is fine. Tuning --interval/--timeout/--retries didn't help. What's the right fix?
options: Remove the HEALTHCHECK entirely
Set --update-failure-action continue to ignore the failures
Increase --retries to 100
Add --start-period=120s to the HEALTHCHECK — a grace period after container start during which health failures don't count toward the unhealthy threshold, designed exactly for slow-starting apps
explain: --start-period says 'don't judge yet': failures during the window don't accumulate toward the retries threshold. Interval/timeout/retries tune the STEADY-STATE probe; none of them grant startup grace. Removing the check or ignoring failures masks real breakage — start-period keeps the protection while accommodating slow starts. EXAM TRAP: reaching for retries when the problem is startup, not flakiness.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: After docker login, ~/.docker/config.json contains an 'auth' field. A developer assumes the password is encrypted. What is it actually, and what's the safer setup?
options: It's base64-encoded, not encrypted — anyone who can read the file recovers the credential trivially. Use a credential helper (credsStore, e.g. desktop keychain/pass/secretservice) so secrets live in the OS keychain instead of the file
It's AES-encrypted with the user's login password
It's a one-time token that expires after an hour
Docker never stores credentials locally
explain: base64 is an encoding, not encryption — the 'auth' blob decodes to username:password in one step. On shared hosts, CI runners, or Swarm managers, that file is a credential treasure chest. Credential helpers move storage into the OS keychain/secret store. Same family as the K8s secret lesson (Q197): encoding is not protection. EXAM TRAP: 'it's in a dotfile so it's safe' — dotfiles are not access control.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A release pipeline pushes shop/api:1.4.2, but a later buggy CI run overwrites the same tag, and production pulls the bad bits. The team wants the registry itself to reject overwrites of release tags. Which MSR feature does this?
options: Image promotion — it signs the tag so overwrites fail
Garbage collection — it removes overwritten tags
Content Trust — it blocks the unsigned push
Immutable tags — an MSR repository setting that rejects any push which would overwrite an existing tag, so release tags can't be re-pointed after publication
explain: Immutable tags enforce tag immutability server-side: once 1.4.2 exists, no push can replace it — the buggy CI run fails loudly instead of silently poisoning production. Content Trust verifies signatures client-side but doesn't stop a signed overwrite; promotion gates movement between repos; GC cleans storage. Layered with digest pinning (Q42), this is the full 'release bits never change' story. EXAM TRAP: confusing signing (who published) with immutability (can't republish).
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: The base image ubuntu:22.04 was rebuilt upstream with a critical OpenSSL fix. The team's docker build still produces images with the vulnerable OpenSSL — the Dockerfile hasn't changed. Why, and what's the fix?
options: The Dockerfile needs a new FROM line pointing at the fixed version
Docker reuses the cached local base image without checking upstream. Build with --pull to always fetch the freshest base image before building
Use --no-cache instead — it also refreshes the base image
Base images update automatically on every build
explain: The FROM layer is cached like any other: if ubuntu:22.04 exists locally, the build reuses it without contacting the registry. --pull forces a fresh base check first. --no-cache is the trap — it ignores the build cache but still starts FROM the local base image. This is why 'rebuild to patch CVEs' silently fails in CI: the pipeline rebuilds on a stale base. EXAM TRAP: no-cache ≠ fresh base.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A CI server's disk is full. docker image prune -a freed almost nothing — most of the space is build cache from hundreds of builds. Which command reclaims it?
options: docker image prune -a — build cache is just unused images
docker container prune — cache is attached to containers
docker builder prune — BuildKit's build cache is accounted separately from images and has its own prune command (with --filter until= for age-based cleanup)
rm -rf /var/lib/docker/buildkit — the only reliable way
explain: Build cache lives outside image accounting — image prune never touches it, which is why the disk stayed full. docker builder prune is the dedicated tool (use --filter until=168h to keep recent cache warm). Never rm -rf daemon internals while the daemon runs — that's how you corrupt the store. EXAM TRAP: assuming 'prune' is one thing; Docker has separate prunes for images, containers, volumes, networks, and builder cache.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile has ADD https://internal.example.com/data.tar.gz /data/. The build succeeds, but /data contains a single file data.tar.gz instead of extracted contents. The engineer expected ADD to auto-extract. What's the rule?
options: ADD never extracts archives
The URL must end with a trailing slash for extraction
Auto-extraction only works with COPY

ADD auto-extracts only LOCAL tar archives — remote URLs are downloaded as-is with no extraction. For a remote tarball, download and extract in a RUN step (curl + tar), or fetch it into the build context first
explain: ADD's two magic behaviors have different scopes: URL fetching works remotely, tar auto-extraction works only for local context files. A remote .tar.gz lands as an opaque file. The explicit RUN curl | tar pattern is also more transparent about what's happening (and keeps the ADD-vs-COPY guidance clean: COPY for files, ADD only when you need its extras). EXAM TRAP: assuming both ADD features apply everywhere.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: docker rmi oldbase:1.0 fails with 'image has dependent child images'. The engineer just wants it gone. What's the safe handling?
options: Remove the dependent child images first (or rebuild them on a new base), then remove the parent — the error protects images built FROM it. docker rmi -f forces removal but leaves children with dangling parent references
The image is corrupted; restart the daemon
Use docker image prune -a instead — it bypasses the check
Child images are deleted automatically after 24 hours
explain: Layers form a parent chain: deleting a base out from under its children orphans them, so the daemon refuses. Work top-down (children first), or retag children onto the replacement base. -f is the footgun — it 'succeeds' and leaves broken references. Prune doesn't bypass parentage checks. EXAM TRAP: -f as a first resort instead of understanding the layer graph.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A team builds on ARM laptops and pushes shop/api:2.0. On x86 production hosts, docker pull fails with 'no matching manifest'. What's happening, and how do official images avoid this?
options: ARM images can never run anywhere else, ever

The pushed image contains only the ARM variant. The tag needs a multi-arch manifest list — one manifest per architecture, built with docker buildx --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 — which is what official images publish, so each host pulls its native variant automatically
x86 hosts need --privileged to pull ARM images
Tags are architecture-specific by design; use a different tag per arch
explain: A plain push uploads a single-arch image; a manifest list wraps per-arch manifests under one tag so the daemon selects its platform. docker buildx --platform builds all variants and assembles the list. The error message is the fingerprint: the tag exists, but has no entry for the pulling host's platform. Per-arch tags (D) work but abandon the seamless UX that manifest lists provide. EXAM TRAP: 'the tag doesn't exist' — it does; it just doesn't speak your architecture.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q:
A Dockerfile has:
WORKDIR /app
WORKDIR src
RUN pwd
What does pwd print, and why does it matter?
options: /src — each WORKDIR resets to the filesystem root
It errors — WORKDIR can only appear once per Dockerfile
/app — the second WORKDIR is ignored
/app/src — relative WORKDIR paths resolve against the previous WORKDIR, and the directory is created if missing; only an absolute path resets to root
explain: WORKDIR behaves like shell cd: relative paths chain, absolute paths reset, and missing directories are created automatically. This is why multi-stage Dockerfiles often do WORKDIR /app then WORKDIR build — each stage sets its own context. Confusing it with a reset-to-root causes files to land in unexpected paths (and COPY destinations to miss). EXAM TRAP: treating the second WORKDIR as absolute.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Every docker build starts with 'Sending build context to Docker daemon' and takes 3 minutes — the context is 4GB including node_modules, .git, and local test data. Builds are slow and the cache keeps busting. What's the fix?
options: Buy a faster disk for the daemon host
Use ADD instead of COPY

Add a .dockerignore excluding node_modules, .git, test data, and other build-irrelevant files — the context is the entire directory shipped to the daemon every build; shrinking it speeds transfers and stops unrelated file changes from busting the COPY layer cache
Build with --no-cache to skip context sending
explain: The build context is tarred and sent to the daemon on EVERY build — 4GB of node_modules rides along even though the Dockerfile never uses it, and any change in it invalidates COPY . . caching. .dockerignore prunes the context at the source. --no-cache doesn't skip context sending (nothing does — the daemon needs the files). EXAM TRAP: optimizing Dockerfile layer order while ignoring the 4GB elephant.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: After editing /etc/docker/daemon.json, the Docker daemon won't start. What's the systematic first check?
options: Reinstall Docker — config edits corrupt the installation

Validate the JSON (a trailing comma or syntax error kills the daemon at startup) and read journalctl -u docker for the parse error — daemon.json must be strictly valid JSON, and the daemon fails fast on invalid config rather than guessing
Delete /var/lib/docker — the data directory conflicts with new config
Reboot the host; daemon.json is only read at boot time
explain: The overwhelmingly common cause is malformed JSON — a trailing comma, a comment, a missing quote. The daemon logs the exact parse failure to the journal, so journalctl -u docker (or dockerd --validate) pinpoints it in seconds. Deleting /var/lib/docker destroys all images/volumes for a config typo — never the first step. EXAM TRAP: treating a config problem as an installation problem.

q: Hosts sit behind a corporate egress proxy. docker pull fails with timeouts, though curl with proxy env vars works fine. The daemon doesn't see the shell's proxy variables. Where do proxy settings for the DOCKER DAEMON live?
options: In daemon.json under a "proxy" key
In each Dockerfile with ENV HTTP_PROXY
In /etc/hosts on the daemon host

In a systemd drop-in (e.g. /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/http-proxy.conf) setting HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY for docker.service, then systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart docker — the daemon is a systemd service and never inherits shell environment
explain: The daemon's environment comes from systemd, not from any shell — proxy vars must be injected via a drop-in Environment= override. (Remember NO_PROXY for internal registries and cluster addresses, or you'll proxy traffic that must stay local.) daemon.json has no proxy key — that's the invented distractor; Dockerfile ENV only affects builds/containers, not the daemon's own pulls. EXAM TRAP: confusing container proxy config (env vars, Q67) with daemon proxy config (systemd).

q: The corporate network uses 172.17.0.0/16. Containers on the default docker0 bridge (172.17.0.0/16) can't reach corporate hosts in that range — return traffic routes into the bridge instead. What's the daemon-side fix?
options: Set "bip": "10.200.0.1/24" in daemon.json to move the docker0 bridge address off the conflicting range, then restart the daemon
Set "icc": false to isolate the bridge
Run every container with --network host
Change the corporate network's addressing
explain: "bip" (bridge IP) re-addresses docker0 itself — the fix when the DEFAULT bridge collides with real infrastructure. This is the daemon-level cousin of the overlay subnet-overlap problems (Q68/Q69): Docker's defaults assume 172.17.0.0/16 is free, and enterprise networks often prove otherwise. icc controls container-to-container traffic, not addressing; host networking 'fixes' it by abandoning isolation. EXAM TRAP: bip only moves docker0 — user-defined networks need default-address-pools (Q139).

q: Same company, but now USER-DEFINED networks keep grabbing 172.18.0.0/16, 172.19.0.0/16... which also collide with corporate ranges. bip is already fixed. What moves the pool Docker carves user-defined networks from?
options: "bip" covers user-defined networks too — just widen it
Nothing — user-defined network subnets are fixed at 172.18.0.0/16+
"default-address-pools": [{"base": "10.50.0.0/16", "size": 24}] in daemon.json — defines the supernets Docker subdivides when creating user-defined networks
Recreate each network manually with --subnet forever
explain: Two different knobs for two different things: bip addresses docker0 (the default bridge); default-address-pools defines the supernets Docker carves up for user-defined bridge networks. Setting pools once in daemon.json fixes every future docker network create. Manual --subnet per network works but doesn't scale and is forgotten under pressure. EXAM TRAP: thinking bip is the universal subnet fix.

q: Containers work fine on the LAN, but traffic to a branch office over a VPN tunnel hangs for large transfers while small requests succeed. What's the likely cause and daemon fix?
options: VXLAN is incompatible with VPNs; stop using overlay networks

MTU black hole: VPN encapsulation overhead means 1500-byte frames get dropped (often silently, when ICMP fragmentation-needed is filtered). Set "mtu": 1400 in daemon.json (or per-network --opt com.docker.network.driver.mtu=1400) so container packets fit inside the tunnel
Increase the MTU to 9000 for jumbo frames
The VPN blocks Docker traffic specifically; allowlist the daemon
explain: The fingerprint — small packets fine, large transfers hang — is classic PMTU failure: encapsulated packets exceed the tunnel MTU and the 'fragmentation needed' ICMP never makes it back. Lowering the container network MTU (1400 is the common safe value) makes packets fit. Raising to 9000 goes the wrong direction. EXAM TRAP: blaming the overlay driver for what is purely a packet-size problem.

q: A security team wants defense in depth: even if a process breaks out of a container, it shouldn't be root on the host. Which daemon setting maps container UIDs to unprivileged host UIDs?
options: "icc": false — it isolates containers from each other
The default (don't run --privileged) is sufficient
A custom seccomp profile
"userns-remap": "default" — enables user-namespace remapping so container root (uid 0) maps to a high, unprivileged host UID; a container escape then yields an unprivileged host user, not root
explain: Userns-remap gives every container its own UID/GID range on the host: root inside the container is an unprivileged subordinate UID outside it — so a breakout lands without host root. Operational caveat: volume file ownership is remapped too, so existing volumes need their ownership migrated. Not running --privileged and seccomp are good layers, but neither changes the UID mapping. EXAM TRAP: thinking non-root USER in the image protects the host — it doesn't change the daemon's root-owned mounts.

q: An engineer manages three Docker hosts (dev, staging, prod) by exporting DOCKER_HOST before each command — and once deployed to prod thinking it was dev. What's the safer workflow?
options: docker context — named endpoints (docker context create prod --docker host=ssh://ops@prod-01), switched with docker context use; the active context is always visible via docker context ls and in the prompt. No more blind environment variables
Run each daemon on a different TCP port
DOCKER_HOST is the only supported method for remote daemons
Copy /var/run/docker.sock between hosts
explain: Contexts make the target explicit, named, and visible — the 'which host am I talking to' question is answered before every command. DOCKER_HOST is invisible ambient state: one stale export in a shell profile and you're operating on the wrong fleet. Contexts also bundle TLS material per endpoint. EXAM TRAP: 'just be careful with env vars' — the incident already proved that doesn't scale.

q: A firewall between datacenters can't open UDP 4789 (VXLAN) for policy reasons, but the security team will allow UDP 5789. How can the Swarm still use overlay networks?
options: Overlays hard-require 4789; fall back to the routing mesh only
Switch every service to the default bridge network
Initialize with docker swarm init --data-path-port 5789 — the VXLAN data-path port is configurable for exactly this situation; every node in the cluster must use the same port
Set "data-path-port" in each container's environment
explain: --data-path-port moves the overlay VXLAN encapsulation off the IANA-assigned 4789 to any allowed UDP port — designed for restrictive firewall policies. The whole cluster must agree on the port (it's set at init). This is separate from --data-path-addr (which NIC, Q151) and --advertise-addr (control plane, Q20). EXAM TRAP: assuming IANA assignments are technically mandatory — they're conventional, and Docker made this one configurable.

q: On an SELinux-enforcing host, a bind-mounted config file gives 'permission denied' inside the container even though host DAC permissions look fine. What's the fix?
options: Disable SELinux on the host

Add :z (shared label — multiple containers may use the mount) or :Z (private label — this container only) to the bind mount — the mount needs SELinux relabeling so the container's MCS context is permitted to access it
Run the container with --privileged
chown the file to root:root
explain: SELinux is mandatory access control on top of DAC: correct Unix permissions mean nothing if the SELinux context denies the container's domain. :z relabels for shared container access, :Z for exclusive access (using :Z on a mount two containers share breaks the second one — a favorite gotcha). Disabling SELinux or --privileged 'fixes' it by demolishing the security layer. EXAM TRAP: debugging this as a Unix permissions problem.

q: docker run mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022 fails on a Linux host with 'image operating system "windows" cannot be used on this platform'. What's the explanation?
options: The image is corrupted; pull it again
Pull with --platform linux to convert it
Enable LCOW on the host to translate the syscalls

Windows containers require a Windows host kernel — containers share the host's kernel, and a Linux kernel cannot execute Windows binaries. Run Windows containers on Windows Server hosts (and Linux containers on Linux)
explain: Containers are not VMs: there is no guest kernel, so the image OS must match the host kernel. --platform can't transmute a Windows image into a Linux one (it selects among variants in a manifest list). LCOW (Linux containers on Windows) goes the other direction and is a separate, limited feature. EXAM TRAP: treating --platform as an OS converter.

q: A team wants Docker volumes backed by their SAN without writing a driver. They found a vendor volume plugin. How is it installed and used?
options: docker plugin install <vendor>/<plugin> (granting the permissions it requests), then docker volume create --driver <plugin> data — plugins extend the daemon itself, and the driver name is then usable anywhere volumes are created
Plugins install through the host package manager only
Copy the plugin binary into every container that needs it
Volume plugins don't exist; every driver must be compiled into the daemon
explain: Plugins are first-class daemon extensions: docker plugin install fetches, installs, and (after you grant its requested privileges) enables the plugin; its driver name then works in volume create, --mount volume-driver, and Compose. That's how REX-Ray, Portworx, and cloud drivers slot in without daemon rebuilds. EXAM TRAP: treating a volume driver as something each container must carry — drivers live in the daemon, not the image.

q: A team needs to manage a remote Docker daemon over TCP. Exposing the API unencrypted is out of the question. What's the correct secure setup?
options: Expose port 2375 and rely on firewall rules alone
Put HTTP basic auth in front of the daemon
Configure the daemon with --tlsverify plus CA/server certificates, and distribute client certificates — mutual TLS authenticates both sides and encrypts all API traffic
The Docker API can't be secured remotely; only use the local socket
explain: --tlsverify enforces mutual TLS: the client verifies the daemon's cert, the daemon verifies the client's — encryption plus two-way authentication in one mechanism. Firewall-only 'security' leaves anyone inside the perimeter with root-equivalent API access; and the daemon has no basic-auth mechanism (that's the invented distractor). For ad-hoc use, DOCKER_HOST=ssh:// over SSH is the simpler secure alternative. EXAM TRAP: confusing network location (firewall) with authentication.

q: An admin changes "log-driver" in daemon.json and reloads the daemon, but existing containers still log via json-file. Is this a bug?
options: Yes — file it upstream

No — most daemon.json settings (log-driver, dns, bip) are captured at container/network CREATION time; existing containers keep the settings they were created with. Recreate containers to pick up the new defaults
The daemon must be rebooted, not reloaded, for any change
log-driver can't be set in daemon.json at all
explain: Daemon defaults are templates for new objects, not retroactive policies: a container created under json-file keeps json-file until it's recreated. Same for dns and bip — creation-time capture. This is why 'I changed the config but nothing happened' is almost always answered with 'recreate the container'. Reload vs restart matters for whether the daemon picks up the file at all; it never rewrites history. EXAM TRAP: expecting config changes to time-travel.

q: A shared build server runs the Docker daemon as root. The security team wants the daemon itself to run without root privileges. What does rootless mode provide, and what's the catch?
options: Nothing — the Docker daemon fundamentally requires root
It removes the daemon entirely; containers run daemonless
It encrypts all container network traffic

Rootless mode runs dockerd and its containers as an unprivileged user, so a daemon compromise doesn't hand over host root. Trade-off: unprivileged operation limits some features (storage drivers, networking modes, and privileged ports behave differently or need extra setup)
explain: Rootless shrinks the blast radius at the top: the daemon — the root-equivalent socket from Q76 — no longer runs as root at all. The cost is real: overlay networking, certain storage drivers, and sub-1024 port binding need workarounds or are restricted, since unprivileged users can't do everything root can. It's a deliberate security/functionality trade, ideal for dev and CI hosts. EXAM TRAP: 'rootless means no isolation trade-offs' — it means different ones.

q: A host installed 'docker.io' from the distro repositories. docker buildx and recent swarm flags are missing, and the version is two years old. What's the guidance?
options: Distro packages track upstream loosely and lag badly — install from Docker's official repositories (download.docker.com) for current Engine releases with all features and security fixes
docker.io is the newest packaging; those features were removed upstream
Compile the Engine from source to unlock them
The missing features require a commercial license
explain: Distribution repositories freeze versions for stability — 'stable' here means 'old', missing features, flags, and CVE fixes the DCA assumes you have. Docker's official apt/yum repos track current releases. When a documented flag 'doesn't exist' on a host, the first check is the Engine version and where it came from — not the documentation. EXAM TRAP: assuming every docker is the same docker.

q: A swarm host has two NICs: eth0 (management) and eth1 (high-throughput storage/VXLAN fabric). The team wants overlay data traffic on eth1 and control traffic on eth0. Which setting separates them?
options: --advertise-addr eth1 — it moves everything to eth1
It's automatic; Docker benchmarks the NICs and picks the faster one
--data-path-addr eth1 at swarm init/join — pins the VXLAN data path to that address while control-plane traffic uses the advertise address
Run two daemons, one per NIC
explain: --data-path-addr splits the data plane from the control plane: Raft/API/gossip use --advertise-addr, VXLAN payload uses --data-path-addr. Multi-homed clusters use this to keep bulky overlay traffic off the management network. --advertise-addr moves control traffic (Q20's topic), not data. EXAM TRAP: assuming one address setting covers both planes.

q: A single-manager swarm needs high availability: the target is 3 managers. Two fresh hosts are ready with Docker installed. What's the correct procedure?
options: Init a new swarm on each host and merge the three swarms
On the existing manager, run docker swarm join-token manager to get the manager join token, then docker swarm join --token <manager-token> <manager-ip>:2377 on each new host
Copy /var/lib/docker/swarm from the manager to the new hosts
Managers can't be added after init; rebuild the swarm with 3 from the start
explain: Manager tokens enroll new hosts directly into the Raft group — quorum grows 1 to 3 with no downtime. (Alternative: join as workers, then docker node promote.) Copying Raft state by hand corrupts the cluster; 'merging swarms' doesn't exist. Do this BEFORE you need it: a single manager is a single point of failure for the control plane. EXAM TRAP: worker vs manager tokens — a worker token can never create a manager.

q: Two containers run postgres primary and replica on the same user-defined network. The app should reach the primary as 'db-primary' without hardcoding the container's actual name. How?
options: Rename the container to db-primary and never rename it again
Use --link db:db-primary
Connect with --network-alias db-primary (Compose: aliases:) — embedded DNS resolves the alias to the container, decoupling the logical service name from the container's identity
Aliases only work on the default bridge network
explain: Network aliases are extra DNS names for a container on a given network — the app targets the stable logical name while the container itself can be replaced, renamed, or rescheduled. --link is the legacy answer (Q154); renaming the container couples identity to addressing.
