EXAM TRAP: aliases are per-network — the same container can present different names on different networks.

q: A 2016 tutorial uses --link db:database for container name resolution. A developer copies it into a new Compose setup. What should they know?
options: --link is legacy and deprecated — it only ever worked on the default bridge and doesn't scale. On user-defined networks, containers resolve each other by name via embedded DNS with no flags at all
--link is still the recommended approach for name resolution
--link now provides encrypted container links
Links are required for DNS on every network type
explain: --link was the pre-DNS workaround for the default bridge's lack of name resolution (Q61). User-defined networks made it obsolete: every container is resolvable by name automatically. It still exists for backward compatibility but is deprecated — new designs should never use it. EXAM TRAP: old tutorials rank high in search results; the exam tests current practice.

q: A backend tier (database, cache) must have NO route to the internet — even if compromised, a container there must not be able to exfiltrate data. Which network option enforces this?
options: --opt encrypted on the network
"icc": false in daemon.json
Simply don't publish any ports
docker network create --internal backend — containers on an internal network get no gateway and no external routing; they can only talk to each other
explain: --internal removes the network's external gateway entirely — no NAT, no egress, enforced at the network layer rather than by policy. Not publishing ports only blocks INBOUND; compromised containers could still phone home. icc=false blocks container-to-container traffic (different threat). EXAM TRAP: 'no published ports = isolated' — egress works fine without published ports.

q: Overlay containers reach the internet via the docker_gwbridge network (default 172.18.0.0/16), which overlaps a corporate range — external access from overlay containers breaks. How is docker_gwbridge's subnet changed?
options: Set "bip" in daemon.json — it controls docker_gwbridge too

docker network rm docker_gwbridge, then recreate it: docker network create --subnet 10.99.0.0/16 --gateway 10.99.0.1 -o com.docker.network.bridge.name=docker_gwbridge docker_gwbridge — it's a regular bridge network Docker recreates on demand
It can't be changed; reinstall Docker with different defaults
Put --internal on every overlay network
explain: docker_gwbridge is just a local bridge network Docker manages — remove and recreate it with a custom subnet and the same bridge name, and overlays use the new one for egress. bip only addresses docker0 (the default bridge), not gwbridge — that's the trap. --internal would kill the egress you're trying to fix. EXAM TRAP: treating Docker's plumbing networks as immutable.

q: A swarm overlay network 'backend' exists. An engineer wants to run a one-off debugging container with docker run and join that same overlay to curl the services directly. docker run --network backend fails. Why, and what's the fix?
options: Swarm overlay networks reject standalone containers unless created with --attachable. Recreate it as docker network create -d overlay --attachable backend — then both Swarm services and docker run containers can attach (reattach services afterward)
Standalone containers can never join Swarm overlay networks
Use --network host for debugging instead
Debugging containers must run on manager nodes
explain: --attachable opens a swarm-scoped overlay to non-service containers — the intended escape hatch for debugging, monitoring sidecars, and one-off tools. Without it, only Swarm tasks may attach, hence the failure. The flag is set at creation, so the network must be recreated (plan the service reattachment). EXAM TRAP: assuming overlays are services-only by nature — they're services-only by DEFAULT.

q: A DNS server container needs UDP port 53 published. The engineer runs -p 53:53 and DNS queries time out, though TCP checks pass. What's wrong?
options: DNS doesn't work inside containers
Port 53 is privileged and can't be published from a container
-p 53:53 publishes TCP only by default — DNS primarily needs UDP: use -p 53:53/udp (and publish both for full DNS). Protocol is part of the port mapping
Publishing never works for UDP; use --network host
explain: Port mappings are protocol-specific and default to TCP — DNS over UDP silently misses a TCP-only mapping (TCP checks passing is the diagnostic tell). The /udp (or /tcp, /sctp) suffix selects the protocol; publish both when the service needs both. EXAM TRAP: '-p 53:53 covers the port' — it covers the TCP port.

q: Containers must sit on VLAN 20 of the corporate network with LAN IPs. The host's eth0 is an 802.1Q trunk port. How is the macvlan network created?
options: macvlan can't do VLANs — use the default bridge
-o parent=eth0 and hope the switch sorts untagged traffic
Use ipvlan instead — macvlan ignores VLAN tags
-o parent=eth0.20 — the sub-interface notation puts the macvlan on the 802.1Q-tagged VLAN 20; specify that VLAN's --subnet and --gateway
explain: The parent sub-interface (eth0.20) is how macvlan attaches to a tagged VLAN on a trunk — the kernel handles the 802.1Q tagging, and containers get IPs from VLAN 20's subnet as if physically plugged into an access port there. Plain eth0 would land containers on the native/untagged VLAN instead. This builds on the macvlan basics (Q63): same driver, trunk-aware parent. EXAM TRAP: 'macvlan = one flat network' — the parent selects the VLAN.

q: A cloud environment forbids promiscuous mode, so macvlan fails. The team tries ipvlan. What's the key difference, and when is L3 mode used?
options: ipvlan is just a slower macvlan with the same requirements

ipvlan shares the host's MAC address (no promiscuous mode needed) while giving containers their own IPs. L2 mode: containers share the host's subnet; L3 mode: containers get a different subnet routed via the host — use L3 when the network team routes a dedicated container subnet to the host
ipvlan requires a DHCP server; macvlan doesn't
L3 mode encrypts the container traffic
explain: ipvlan's trick is one MAC, many IPs — switches with MAC limits or no-promiscuous-mode policies accept it where macvlan is rejected. L2 keeps containers in the host's broadcast domain; L3 gives them their own subnet with the host as router (needs the upstream route). Pick L2 for flat integration, L3 for routed container subnets. EXAM TRAP: 'ipvlan fixes everything macvlan does' — it fixes the MAC problem specifically.

q: A deployment needs containers with IPv6 addresses. The engineer creates a network with --ipv6, but containers get no v6 address. What's missing?
options: The daemon needs "ipv6": true plus a "fixed-cidr-v6" range in daemon.json (and a daemon reload) — IPv6 is opt-in at the daemon level; the network flag alone isn't enough
IPv6 is automatic once the network flag is set
Use --network host for IPv6
Docker doesn't support IPv6 networking
explain: Docker's IPv6 support is daemon-gated: "ipv6": true enables it and "fixed-cidr-v6" (e.g. 2001:db8:1::/64) carves the allocation range; per-network --ipv6 then opts networks in. The network flag without daemon support silently yields v4-only containers. EXAM TRAP: assuming the network flag is the whole configuration.

q: docker network ls shows 40 unused networks left over from months of experiments. What's the safe cleanup?
options: Delete /var/lib/docker/network directly
docker network rm on each one, including ingress and docker_gwbridge
docker system prune without flags doesn't touch networks
docker network prune — removes only unused networks; predefined ones (bridge, host, none) and any network with attached endpoints are left alone
explain: docker network prune targets exactly the clutter: networks with no attached containers. Built-ins and in-use networks are protected, so it's safe to run blind — unlike hand-deleting ingress or docker_gwbridge, which would break the routing mesh and overlay egress until recreated. (docker system prune also prunes networks, but the dedicated command is clearer.) EXAM TRAP: 'prune deletes everything listed' — prune only deletes the UNUSED.

q: Three cache containers on a user-defined network all connect with --network-alias cache. A client resolves 'cache' repeatedly. What does it get?
options: Only the first container's IP, every time
An error — aliases must be unique per network
DNS round-robin across all three container IPs — a shared alias gives client-side load distribution, the same mechanism Swarm uses for service names (minus the VIP)
The network gateway IP
explain: Embedded DNS round-robins all endpoints registered under a name — whether that name is a container name, an alias, or a Swarm service. A shared alias is the lightweight, orchestrator-free way to load-balance across identical containers. Uniqueness is not required; that's the feature. EXAM TRAP: expecting DNS to pick 'the' container — DNS returns the SET.

q: On Docker Desktop, a container reaches the host via host.docker.internal. On Linux Engine, that name doesn't resolve. The container needs to call a mock API running on the Linux host. What's the portable fix?
options: Hardcode the host's public IP in the app config
Start the container with --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway — the special host-gateway value injects the host's gateway IP, bringing the Desktop convention to Linux
host.docker.internal is Desktop-only and can't be replicated on Linux
Use --network host and call localhost
explain: host-gateway is a special --add-host value resolving to the host's gateway address (typically the host itself from the container's view) — it makes host.docker.internal work on Linux Engine exactly as on Desktop. Hardcoding IPs rots; --network host 'works' by deleting isolation. This is the sanctioned bridge between dev (Desktop) and prod (Linux) conventions. EXAM TRAP: 'the name doesn't exist on Linux' — you create it with one flag.

q: Containers on mynet can't reach each other. The network was created weeks ago by someone who's left. What's the first inspection step?
options: docker network inspect mynet — verify the containers are actually attached, check the subnet/gateway for conflicts, and confirm the driver and options are what you expect
Restart the Docker daemon immediately
Recreate all the containers
Check the image registry — it's probably an image problem
explain: Inspect before acting: half of 'can't reach each other' cases are containers attached to DIFFERENT networks, a subnet colliding with the corporate LAN (Q69), or the wrong driver. docker network inspect shows attachments, subnets, and options in one view — the five-second check that prevents an hour of blind restarts. EXAM TRAP: restarting the daemon as a first step — it disrupts everything and rarely fixes addressing.

q: The ingress network's default 10.255.0.0/16 collides with a corporate range, breaking the routing mesh for those destinations. The collision is with ingress itself, not a custom overlay. What's the fix?
options: Renumber the corporate network
docker network rm ingress is impossible — it's protected
Add --opt encrypted to bypass the conflict

Remove and recreate the ingress network with a custom subnet: docker network rm ingress && docker network create --ingress --subnet 10.250.0.0/16 --gateway 10.250.0.1 ingress — do it in a maintenance window, since published service ports ride on ingress
explain: The ingress network is recreatable like any other — the --ingress flag marks the replacement as the routing-mesh network. This is the fix when the overlap from Q68 is with ingress itself rather than a custom overlay. The maintenance-window caveat is real: recreating ingress briefly disrupts published ports. Encryption doesn't change addressing, and nothing about ingress is sacred. EXAM TRAP: 'built-in networks can't be touched'.

q: A batch job crunches files from a mounted volume and needs NO network access at all — the security team wants the kernel to enforce that, not just policy. Which network mode?
options: --network host combined with host firewall rules
--network none — the container gets only a loopback interface; no external network path exists to misconfigure, exploit, or accidentally enable
The default bridge without -p flags
An --internal overlay network
explain: --network none gives the container a network namespace containing only lo — there is no interface to attack or leak through, enforced by the kernel rather than by convention. An unpublished bridge still has full egress; --internal still allows inter-container traffic. For compute-only jobs, none is the strongest and simplest isolation. EXAM TRAP: 'no -p means no network' — egress needs no published ports.

q: Two Swarm services both publish port 8080 in the default ingress mode. The second service create fails with 'port is already allocated'. Why can't both share it?
options: They can — the error must mean something else
Only manager nodes can publish ports

Ingress-mode published ports are cluster-wide singletons: the routing mesh listens on that port on EVERY node, so a second claimant conflicts. Give each service its own published port (or use host-mode publishing / distinct ports)
Swarm allows sharing with --update-parallelism 2
explain: The routing mesh binds the published port on all nodes simultaneously — that's what makes 'any node IP works' (Q13) true, and it's why the port is allocated cluster-wide, not per-node. Two ingress publishers on one port is a genuine conflict, reported at create time. Host-mode publishing binds only on task nodes (different trade-offs, Q75). EXAM TRAP: thinking of published ports as per-container like docker run -p.

q: A platform runs containers with a random UID (OpenShift-style) for security. The vendor image's files are root-owned, and the app running as UID 100071 can't write its data dir. The Dockerfile can't change. What's the runtime approach?
options: Run with --privileged so any UID can write anywhere

Make the data directory group-writable in the image and run with --user 100071 plus --group-add for the file group — arbitrary numeric UIDs work when filesystem permissions allow that UID; images should be built 'UID-agnostic' with no hardcoded user assumptions
Random UIDs are impossible in Docker; the platform must assign fixed ones
chown the files at runtime via docker exec as root
explain: The kernel only sees numbers: any UID works if the permission bits allow it — that's the whole arbitrary-UID model. The pattern is group-writable directories (root group, e.g. :0) plus --group-add, so whatever UID is assigned can write. --privileged 'fixes' it by deleting the security model; exec-chown doesn't survive restarts. This is the runtime counterpart to the build-time USER discipline (Q78). EXAM TRAP: 'the image USER must match the runtime UID' — numeric permission checks don't care about names.

q: A container runs a legacy binary with the setuid bit set. The team worries a vulnerability in it could escalate privileges inside the container. Which flag blocks setuid/setgid privilege gains?
options: --cap-drop ALL — it also disables setuid escalation
--read-only — it prevents privilege changes
--user nobody — setuid binaries can't execute as nobody
--security-opt no-new-privileges — prevents the process and its children from gaining new privileges via setuid/setgid binaries, even if the binary is setuid root
explain: no-new-privileges is the kernel's 'no privilege gains, ever' bit: exec of a setuid-root binary keeps the caller's privileges. --cap-drop ALL is the trap — capabilities and setuid are independent mechanisms; dropping caps doesn't neutralize a setuid binary. --read-only stops filesystem writes, not privilege transitions. Pair it with --user and dropped caps for the full least-privilege set. EXAM TRAP: assuming capability-dropping covers all escalation paths.

q: A containerized app is denied writing to /data/app.db even though Unix permissions allow it; dmesg shows APPARMOR denials. The default docker-default profile is loaded. What's the proper fix?
options: Write a custom AppArmor profile allowing that path and apply it with --security-opt apparmor=<profile> — the denial is mandatory access control, independent of file permissions; never disable AppArmor host-wide to fix one app
chmod 777 the database file
Run the container with --privileged to bypass AppArmor
AppArmor denials are warnings; the writes actually succeeded
explain: AppArmor (like seccomp, Q85) is MAC layered over DAC: the profile decides what the container may do regardless of rwx bits. The fix is a tailored profile granting exactly the needed paths — the same 'punch minimal, documented holes' discipline as custom seccomp profiles. chmod can't override MAC; --privileged demolishes every layer for one denial. EXAM TRAP: debugging a MAC denial as a Unix permissions problem (see also Q144's SELinux cousin).

q: An engineer needs to strace a production process inside a container to diagnose hangs. strace fails with 'Operation not permitted'. The team refuses --privileged. What's the minimal grant?
options: strace fundamentally can't work inside containers
--cap-add SYS_ADMIN — the only capability that enables debugging
--cap-add SYS_PTRACE — the specific capability for process tracing; add it to the debugging session only, keeping everything else dropped
--security-opt seccomp=unconfined
explain: SYS_PTRACE is the surgical grant for ptrace(2)-based tools (strace, gdb): it enables exactly the debugging operation without the 40-capability firehose of --privileged or the syscall free-for-all of seccomp=unconfined. Scope it to the debugging container/session, not the fleet. This is the capabilities model's whole pitch (Q77): replace '--privileged?' with the narrowest yes. EXAM TRAP: SYS_ADMIN as the 'debugging capability' — it's far broader than needed.

q: A buggy worker forks child processes in a loop until the host becomes unresponsive — a fork bomb that sailed past the container's CPU and memory limits. Which setting would have contained it?
options: --memory — it limits process counts too
--pids-limit 256 — caps the number of processes/threads in the container's cgroup; the fork bomb hits the ceiling inside the container instead of exhausting the host's process table
--cpus 1 — fork bombs are CPU-bound so this contains them
A strict restart policy prevents fork bombs
explain: CPU and memory limits don't bound process COUNT — fork bombs consume PIDs and scheduler slots, a different resource. --pids-limit sets the cgroup pids.max ceiling: fork() starts failing inside the container while the host stays healthy. It's the forgotten third resource limit alongside CPU and memory. EXAM TRAP: 'I set memory limits so I'm safe' — each limit guards its own resource only.

q: A container keeps exiting with code 137 during peak load. docker inspect shows "OOMKilled": true. The team set no memory limits. What's happening?
options: Exit 137 means the application crashed on its own
Someone is running docker kill against it
The image layers are corrupted

The kernel OOM killer terminated the container's process (137 = 128 + SIGKILL) — the HOST ran out of memory. Set --memory limits so the container fails predictably at its own ceiling instead of taking the host down, then investigate the leak or size the host properly
explain: 137 is the signature of external SIGKILL, and OOMKilled: true names the killer: the kernel, out of RAM, chose the fattest process. With no --memory limit, the container can grow until the host itself tips over — limits convert a host outage into a contained container restart. Note the direction: limits don't prevent OOMs, they localize them. EXAM TRAP: reading 137 as an application bug — it's the kernel's verdict.

q: Four containers share a host. A batch job starves the latency-sensitive API of CPU. The team wants the API guaranteed responsive while the batch job soaks up spare cycles. Which settings?
options: Give the API --cpus 2 (hard ceiling guaranteeing its share) and leave the batch job unconstrained or with low --cpu-shares — --cpus is an absolute cap, while --cpu-shares is only a relative weight applied when CPUs are contended
Set --cpu-shares 1024 on the API — shares guarantee absolute CPU time
CPU can't be controlled per-container in Docker
Run the batch job with --privileged for efficiency
explain: --cpus is a hard ceiling (2.0 = two full cores max, enforced always); --cpu-shares is a relative weight that only matters under contention (1024 vs 512 = 2:1 split of what's contested, zero guarantee when idle). For latency protection you want the guarantee (--cpus on the API, or shares to deprioritize the batch job) — understand which knob promises what. EXAM TRAP: 'higher shares = reserved CPU' — shares reserve nothing.

q: The private registry uses a corporate CA-signed certificate (not a public CA). docker pull fails with 'x509: certificate signed by unknown authority'. The team considers adding the registry to insecure-registries. What's the proper fix?
options: Use insecure-registries — it's the only option for private CAs
Disable TLS on the registry and use plain HTTP

Install the corporate CA certificate at /etc/docker/certs.d/registry.internal:5000/ca.crt on each Docker host — Docker trusts per-registry CAs from certs.d, keeping full TLS verification intact. insecure-registries would trade away verification for convenience
Log in with docker login --insecure
explain: certs.d is the designed path for private PKI: drop the CA cert in /etc/docker/certs.d/<host>:<port>/ca.crt and the daemon verifies the registry's cert chain normally. insecure-registries is the lazy alternative — it disables the very verification that stops MITM attacks on image pulls. (Same decision as Q36, made correctly this time.) EXAM TRAP: the invented --insecure login flag — there is no such thing.

q: An auditor asks to 'see the secret value' via docker secret inspect db_pass to verify that rotation happened. What will they find?
options: The plaintext value in the Spec field

Only metadata (name, ID, creation time, labels) — secret values are never exposed through the API. Verify rotation via the secret's creation timestamp or versioned name, and confirm running tasks mount the new value at /run/secrets/
The base64-encoded value, which they can decode
Secrets can't be inspected at all — the command errors
explain: Secret values are write-only through the API by design: inspect, service inspect, and the Raft API all omit them — the value only ever appears as a file inside a granted container. Rotation verification therefore uses metadata (timestamps, versioned names like db_pass_v2) plus checking the mounted content from inside a task. Anyone who could read values via the API could bypass the entire secrets model. EXAM TRAP: expecting inspect to be a window into the secret.

q: A container needs access to a USB hardware security module at /dev/hsm0. The vendor docs say to use --privileged. What's the least-privilege alternative?
options: --privileged is required for all hardware access
Bind-mount the entire /dev into the container
--device /dev/hsm0 — exposes just that device node (with optional :rwm permission flags) instead of granting all host devices plus every capability and disabled LSMs
Hardware security modules can't be used from containers
explain: --device grants a single device node with controlled permissions — the HSM and nothing else. --privileged for one USB device hands over all devices, all capabilities, and disables seccomp/AppArmor: the vendor's lazy answer again (Q85's meta-lesson). Bind-mounting all of /dev is barely better. EXAM TRAP: vendor docs that prescribe --privileged as the first resort.

q: A monitoring agent runs with --pid=host so it can see all host processes. The security review flags it. Why?
options: The container joins the host's PID namespace — it can see every host process's metadata and, subject to capabilities, signal them. It breaks process isolation; prefer the Docker API, /proc mounted read-only, or cgroup metrics for observability
--pid=host has no security implications; the flag is cosmetic
It only affects performance, not security
PID namespace sharing is the default for all containers
explain: --pid=host dissolves the PID namespace boundary: ps inside the container lists host processes, and kill can reach them (capability-gated, but the visibility alone leaks architecture). It's occasionally justified for monitoring, but it's namespace-sharing with the host — the same category of risk as --network host and --ipc host. Prefer APIs that expose metrics without sharing the namespace. EXAM TRAP: 'it's read-only visibility' — signaling is not read-only.

q: A compliance program requires Docker hosts to be hardened against a recognized baseline, with evidence. Which is the industry-standard tool for assessing Docker hardening?
options: docker system prune — a clean host is a secure host
The Docker Hub star rating of the images in use

The CIS Docker Benchmark, commonly run via the docker-bench-security script — it checks daemon configuration, file permissions, and container runtime settings against CIS recommendations; findings are then remediated (least privilege, no --privileged, read-only roots, socket protection, and the rest)
Antivirus scans of image tarballs
explain: The CIS Docker Benchmark is the recognized hardening baseline: hundreds of checks across host, daemon, images, and runtime, automated by docker-bench-security. It's an assessment tool — it reports, you remediate — and it directly encodes the exam's greatest hits (no --privileged, dropped capabilities, read-only filesystems, socket mounting, user namespaces). Prune is hygiene, not hardening; Hub stars are popularity, not security. EXAM TRAP: confusing cleanliness with hardening.

q: Inside a container running as root, ip route add fails with 'Operation not permitted'. Why?
options: Containers can't run the iproute2 tools
The NET_ADMIN capability is dropped by default — container root is not full root; network configuration needs NET_ADMIN. Add it explicitly (--cap-add NET_ADMIN) only if genuinely required
The container needs --network host for any ip command
iproute2 always requires --privileged
explain: Docker starts containers with a reduced capability set — NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN, and other dangerous capabilities are dropped by default. Root in the container without NET_ADMIN can't reconfigure networking, mount filesystems, or load modules: that's the point. Grant the single capability when needed (--cap-add NET_ADMIN), not the --privileged bundle. EXAM TRAP: 'root in container = root powers' — capabilities say otherwise.

q: A proxy container drops connections under load with 'too many open files', though the host has file descriptors to spare. What's the container-specific fix?
options: Raise the host's fs.file-max only — containers share it automatically
Restart the container on a schedule to reset the count
Run with --privileged to bypass descriptor limits
Raise the container's descriptor limit: docker run --ulimit nofile=65536:65536 — containers inherit the daemon's default ulimits, which are far below what a connection-heavy proxy needs
explain: Ulimits are per-process and inherited: the container gets the daemon's defaults (often 1024:4096-ish), regardless of host capacity. --ulimit nofile=soft:hard sets the container's ceiling directly. Raising host fs.file-max doesn't propagate into the container's rlimit; restarts just postpone the crash. Connection-heavy workloads (proxies, load balancers) are the classic victims. EXAM TRAP: tuning the host when the limit lives in the container.

q: An app needs --read-only filesystem protection but must persist its SQLite database across restarts. --read-only alone breaks it. What's the correct combination?
options: --read-only plus a named volume mounted at the database path (-v appdata:/data) — the root filesystem stays immutable while the designated data path remains writable and persistent
Drop --read-only; databases fundamentally can't be hardened
--tmpfs for the database path
Bind-mount the host's /var/lib/docker into the container
explain: --read-only is a default-deny on the image filesystem; named volumes (and tmpfs, Q84) are the explicit allowlist. Persistent data goes on a volume — immutable code, mutable designated data, exactly the separation hardening wants. --tmpfs is the trap here: RAM-backed and ephemeral, it would vaporize the database on restart. EXAM TRAP: treating --read-only as all-or-nothing.

q: With DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1, a developer pushes shop/api:2.0 for the first time and is prompted for passphrases. What's happening?
options: The registry enforces two-factor authentication on all pushes
DCT encrypts the image; the passphrase is the decryption key for pullers

The first trusted push initializes the repository's signing keys (root/target keys via Notary) — the passphrases protect the private signing keys. Later pulls with DCT=1 verify the signature, proving the tag was published by the key holder
The passphrases are embedded in the image for verification
explain: Trust bootstrapping: the first DCT push generates the repo's key hierarchy and signs the tag; the passphrases encrypt the private keys at rest. From then on, signature verification (Q38's pull side) can prove provenance. This is why key custody matters: whoever holds the repo keys can publish trusted tags. DCT signs; it never encrypts. EXAM TRAP: 'signing = encrypting' — signatures prove authenticity, not secrecy.

q: A container crashed and won't restart, but a config file inside it needs inspection. The container's filesystem is intact. How do you get the file out?
options: The data is lost — containers are ephemeral by design
docker export the image and grep the tarball
Restart it with --privileged and read the file
docker cp <container>:/etc/app/config.yaml ./config.yaml — copies files between the container's filesystem and the host, and works on stopped containers too
explain: docker cp operates on the container's filesystem directly — running or stopped — no need to revive a crashed container to inspect it. It's the forensics-friendly alternative to restarting something broken just to read a file. Export works but is heavier (whole filesystem tarball); and 'ephemeral' describes the design intent, not a physical law — the data sits there until the container is removed. EXAM TRAP: assuming a stopped container's files are unreachable.

q: A team 'bakes' production images by hand-configuring a container and running docker commit. Builds are unreproducible and nobody can say exactly what's inside. What's the verdict on this workflow?
options: It's the recommended production workflow — faster than Dockerfiles

docker commit is an anti-pattern for production: it creates opaque, unrepeatable images with no audit trail. Use a Dockerfile — version-controlled, reviewable, rebuildable. Reserve commit for emergency forensics, not releases
commit is preferred at scale because it skips the build cache
Dockerfiles can't reproduce manual changes anyway, so commit is equivalent
explain: commit snapshots mutable state into an image nobody can reproduce or review — configuration drift made permanent, and a gift to auditors asking 'what changed?'. Dockerfiles are the source of truth: every step explicit, diffable, and rebuildable from scratch. commit has its niche (capturing a compromised container's state for forensics), but production releases built on it are unmaintainable. EXAM TRAP: 'it works, so it's fine' — reproducibility is the requirement.

q: A write-heavy database runs on the container's writable layer and performs noticeably worse than on bare metal. Why do volumes fix this?
options: The writable layer is a copy-on-write union filesystem — a write to a file that exists in the image first copies the whole file up into the writable layer, adding overhead to every write. Volumes bypass the union filesystem and write directly to the host filesystem
Volumes compress data on write
The writable layer is network-attached storage
There is no difference; the slowdown is mismeasured
explain: Copy-up is the hidden tax: first write to any image-origin file copies it into the top layer before the write proceeds — fine for config tweaks, punishing for database I/O patterns. Volumes sidestep the union mount entirely with direct host-filesystem I/O. This is the performance half of the 'databases belong on volumes' rule (Q91 covered portability). EXAM TRAP: blaming the database engine for storage-layer overhead.

q: An image ships 500MB of seed data at /app/seed. The team mounts a named volume there but wants the volume to START EMPTY (they'll load their own dataset). By default the new volume gets populated from the image. How do they prevent that?
options: They can't — volumes always inherit image content
Delete the seeded data after the first start

Mount with the nocopy option (-v seedvol:/app/seed:nocopy, or --mount type=volume,src=seedvol,dst=/app/seed,volume-nocopy=true) — disables the initial population of the volume from the image's directory
Use a bind mount to an empty host directory instead
explain: Volume initialization (Q189) copies image content into fresh volumes — usually helpful, wrong here. nocopy opts out: the volume starts empty and the image's seed data stays unreachable under the mount. The bind-mount 'fix' changes the storage model entirely (host-path coupling) to dodge a one-flag behavior. EXAM TRAP: not knowing the population happens at all, then wondering where 500MB went.

q: A fresh named volume mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data already contains database files on first run — the team never put them there. Where did they come from?
options: Postgres downloads seed files on first start
A previous container leaked them into the volume
The volume driver synthesizes default content

On first use, Docker populates a new named volume with the image's existing content at that path (copy-up initialization). That's why official database images 'just work' with empty named volumes — and why the nocopy option exists to disable it
explain: Named-volume initialization is a deliberate convenience: the volume starts as a copy of what the image had there, so data-container paths work out of the box. It only happens on FIRST use of an empty volume — existing data is never overwritten. Understanding this explains both the 'magic files' surprise and the nocopy escape hatch (Q188). EXAM TRAP: assuming volumes always start empty.

q: Three containers need read access to the same 20GB dataset (ML models). The team wants one copy on disk, and no container should be able to modify it. What's the setup?
options: COPY the dataset into each image
One named volume mounted into all three containers with :ro — a single copy on disk, read-only in each container, so a compromised container can't poison the models for the others
Three separate named volumes with rsync between them
A bind mount with chmod 777 so everyone can read
explain: A shared read-only volume is the efficient pattern: one copy, N consumers, and the :ro mount option enforces integrity per-container — even a fully compromised container can't alter the shared data. Baking 20GB into images triples storage and slows every pull; separate volumes triple storage and drift. chmod 777 'for reading' grants writing too. EXAM TRAP: solving a sharing problem with duplication.

q: Two hosts need shared read-write access to the same files, but there's no cluster-aware volume plugin available. The company has an NFS server. How can Docker consume it as a volume?
options: docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=10.0.0.5,rw --opt device=:/exports/share sharevol — the local driver can mount NFS directly via driver options; then use -v sharevol:/data as usual
NFS can't be consumed by Docker volumes
Mount NFS on the host and run containers with --privileged
Only Swarm cluster drivers support NFS
explain: The local volume driver's --opt type=nfs turns Docker into an NFS client: the daemon performs the mount with the given options, and containers just see a normal volume. No plugin, no host-level fstab coupling per container. The NFS server remains the single point of truth (and failure) — this is shared storage, not replicated storage. EXAM TRAP: assuming 'local driver' means 'local disk only' — it's the driver name, not a limitation.

q: An engineer removed the old database container (docker rm db) intending to recreate it against the same named volume later — then ran docker system prune -a --volumes to 'clean up'. The volume and all its data are gone. What happened?
options: Prune never touches named volumes; the data loss is unrelated
The database deleted its own data on container removal

Once no container references a volume, prune considers it fair game — --volumes extends the cleanup to ALL unreferenced volumes, named or not. The moment the container was removed, the volume became 'unused'. Never run --volumes where unreferenced volumes hold precious data; back up first
Only anonymous volumes are ever pruned
explain: docker system prune --volumes is the nuclear option: it deletes every volume no existing container references — named volumes included. Removing the container first is what doomed the data; the volume was perfectly safe while referenced. The safe sequence is back up (Q94's --volumes-from pattern), then prune, then recreate. EXAM TRAP: 'named volumes are protected' — nothing is protected from an explicit --volumes prune.

q: A Swarm service needs its named volume provisioned by the REX-Ray driver instead of the default local driver. What's the service-level syntax?
options: -v rexray-vol:/data — the driver is auto-detected from the volume name
Volume drivers can't be selected per service
Install the driver on manager nodes only
--mount type=volume,src=sharedata,dst=/data,volume-driver=rexray — the long syntax carries the driver selection; the plugin must be installed and enabled on every node where tasks may land
explain: volume-driver= in the --mount long syntax is how services request non-default drivers — the short -v form can't express it. And the plugin must exist cluster-wide: a task landing on a node without the driver fails to mount. This is the mechanism behind the shared-storage fix from Q92 — the driver is what makes the volume follow the task. EXAM TRAP: installing the plugin once on a manager and expecting workers to use it.

q: Two containers in one Kubernetes pod need a shared scratch space for intermediate files that must vanish when the pod dies. Which volume type?
options: A PersistentVolumeClaim — it's the only way to share storage
emptyDir — ephemeral storage with the pod's lifetime, shared between the pod's containers, deleted when the pod is deleted. Ideal for scratch/cache; wrong for anything durable
hostPath — it's temporary by nature
configMap — it provides writable scratch space
explain: emptyDir is 'pod-local temp': created when the pod is scheduled, shared by its containers, destroyed with the pod — the K8s answer to tmpfs-with-sharing. A PVC would persist (wrong lifecycle and heavier); hostPath ties to the node (Q195); configMaps are read-only. Match the storage lifetime to the data lifetime — that's the whole decision. EXAM TRAP: reaching for durable storage for ephemeral data.

q: A pod uses hostPath: /data on its node for 'persistence'. After a node failure, the replacement pod scheduled to another node starts with empty data. What's the lesson?
options: hostPath ties the pod to one node's disk — rescheduling elsewhere loses the data, and it exposes host filesystem paths to the pod (security risk). It's for single-node/system use (e.g. /var/log); durable multi-node data needs PVCs backed by networked storage
hostPath replicates data across nodes automatically
Kubernetes syncs hostPath directories between nodes
The data is still there; the kubelet just hides it from new pods
explain: hostPath is node-local by definition — the scheduler treats the pod as portable but the data isn't, so 'persistence' silently becomes 'ephemeral on node failure'. It also punches a hole into the host filesystem (a privileged hostPath is a breakout aid). Legitimate uses are narrow: node-level logs, device files, single-node system daemons. Everything else goes through the PVC → PV → StorageClass chain (Q97). EXAM TRAP: 'it's a volume, so it's persistent' — persistence has a scope.

q: A Kubernetes app needs its configuration as a FILE at /etc/app/config.yaml, and the config differs per environment. What's the idiomatic approach?
options: Bake each environment's config into a separate image
Use a Secret — configs and Secrets are interchangeable

A ConfigMap mounted as a volume — decouples config from the image; the pod spec maps ConfigMap keys to files, and updating the ConfigMap (followed by a pod restart) changes the file without rebuilding anything
hostPath to a config file placed on every node
explain: ConfigMaps are K8s's non-sensitive config objects (the analog of Swarm configs, Q106): mounting one as a volume projects keys as files, keeping environment specifics out of the image. Per-environment images multiply build/test burden; hostPath reintroduces node coupling; Secrets are for sensitive data (and are base64 'protected', Q197). Note the restart caveat: mounted ConfigMaps update on a delay, and many apps only read config at startup — hence the pod restart. EXAM TRAP: env vars for file-shaped config — volumes are the file-shaped answer.

q: A developer base64-encodes a password into a Kubernetes Secret and considers it 'encrypted'. The cluster has NOT enabled encryption at rest. What's the reality?
options: base64 is a form of encryption — the password is safe

base64 is encoding, not encryption — anyone with API or etcd read access decodes it trivially. Real protection needs etcd encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration, ideally with a KMS provider) plus RBAC limiting who can read Secrets
Kubernetes encrypts all Secrets in etcd by default
Kubernetes Secrets can't hold passwords — use ConfigMaps
explain: base64 is a transport encoding from the JSON API era, not a security boundary — decoding it is one command. Without etcd encryption at rest, Secrets sit as near-plaintext in etcd backups and on disk. Defense is layered: encryption at rest (so stolen etcd data is useless) plus RBAC (so few can read them via the API). Same lesson as Docker's registry credentials (Q127): encoding is not protection. EXAM TRAP: 'it's in a Secret object, so it's secret' — the object name is not a guarantee.

q: How does docker export differ from docker save, and when would you use it?
options: They're identical — two names for one command
export is for images; save is for containers
export uploads directly to a registry

docker export flattens a CONTAINER's filesystem into a tarball — losing layers, history, and image metadata — while docker save preserves an IMAGE with all of that. Use export to capture a container's filesystem contents (e.g. forensics on a compromised container); use save to move images between hosts
explain: export = container filesystem, flattened, no history; save = image, complete with layers and tags (Q122). The forensics use case is export's real home: snapshot what an attacker changed without needing the image. For every image-distribution need, save is the answer — export can't recreate an image's layer structure. EXAM TRAP: the eternal save/export swap — containers vs images, always.

q: A container behaves differently from its image, and the team suspects files were modified inside it at runtime. How do you list exactly what changed?
options: docker diff <container> — lists filesystem changes against the image as A (added), C (changed), D (deleted)
docker history — it shows container runtime changes
docker inspect — it diffs the filesystem automatically
You can't — the writable layer is opaque to inspection
explain: docker diff compares the container's writable layer against its image and reports every added/changed/deleted file — the quickest way to answer 'what did it touch?' for debugging and forensics (pairs with docker cp, Q185, to extract the evidence). docker history shows IMAGE build layers, not runtime changes; inspect shows configuration, not file diffs. EXAM TRAP: history-vs-diff confusion — history is build-time, diff is run-time.

q: Two database containers are pointed at the SAME named volume for 'high availability'. Within hours the data is corrupted. What went wrong?
options: Named volumes can't be shared between containers at all
The volume driver has a bug

Most filesystems — and database engines — assume a single writer. Two DB engines writing the same data files concurrently corrupt them. A shared volume is not HA: use real replication (primary/replica) or a cluster-aware filesystem/driver designed for multi-writer access
Volumes are read-only by default, causing the corruption
explain: Sharing block-level storage between writers that don't coordinate is corruption by design — databases guard their files with the assumption of exclusive access. Real HA is replication at the application layer (primary/replica, consensus), with storage shared only through cluster-aware systems built for it. The volume did exactly what it was told; the architecture was wrong. EXAM TRAP: 'shared disk = shared-nothing HA' — shared disk is the opposite of shared-nothing.

q: An engineer SSHes into a Swarm WORKER node and runs `docker service logs web -f` to tail a service's logs. The command fails outright. Nothing is wrong with the service itself. What's the problem?
options: Service-level commands run against the Raft-backed control plane, so `docker service logs` (like create, update, rm, ps) is manager-only — run it from a manager node or point DOCKER_HOST at one
The `-f` flag isn't supported by `docker service logs`; rerun without it
Service logs are only available if the service was created with `--log-driver json-file`
Logs can only be read on the node where each task runs, so the command must be repeated on every node
explain: Swarm orchestration commands are served by managers — workers only run tasks, so `docker service logs` from a worker fails with a 'not a swarm manager' style error. `-f` IS supported, and the log driver doesn't gate the command itself. EXAM TRAP: 'run it where the task runs' confuses `docker service logs` (aggregated, manager-side) with `docker logs` (per-container, node-local).

q: The team re-pushes `app:latest` with a hotfix, then runs `docker service update --image app:latest web`. The tasks restart — but they are still running the OLD code. What happened, and what's the fix?
options: Swarm caches images forever; the only fix is `docker system prune` on every node before updating

The update reused the tag's previously resolved digest — Swarm pins tag-to-digest at creation/update time, and re-resolving the SAME tag requires `--force`: `docker service update --force --image app:latest web`
The `--image` flag is ignored during updates; you must remove and recreate the service
Each node needs a manual `docker pull app:latest` before the update runs
explain: A service spec stores the resolved digest, not the floating tag — updating with the same tag is a no-op for the image unless `--force` forces re-resolution and a fresh pull. Manual pulls don't help because the spec still pins the old digest. EXAM TRAP: 'just pull on the nodes' ignores that the pinned digest in the service spec is what tasks actually run.

q: You must reboot worker3 for kernel patching and want its 6 tasks rescheduled elsewhere BEFORE the reboot. Separately, on worker4 you want to stop NEW tasks from landing while keeping its current tasks running during an investigation. Which pair of commands?
options: `docker node update --availability pause worker3` and `--availability drain worker4`
`docker node update --availability drain worker3` and `--availability active worker4`
`docker node update --availability drain worker3` (existing tasks are shut down and rescheduled elsewhere) and `--availability pause worker4` (no new tasks scheduled, existing tasks keep running)
`docker swarm leave` on both nodes, then rejoin them afterward
explain: `drain` evicts and reschedules — the pre-reboot move; `pause` freezes scheduling while leaving running tasks untouched — the investigation hold; `active` is the default normal state. EXAM TRAP: swapping drain and pause — draining worker4 would kill the very tasks under investigation.

q: After `docker stack rm billing`, the team redeploys and finds yesterday's upload data still present. They expected a completely clean slate. Why?
options: `docker stack rm` only stops tasks; images and configs stay cached on the nodes
The redeploy reused the same overlay network, which caches volume data
Named volumes are node-local, so the data followed the rescheduled task

The engineer is wrong about what `stack rm` removes — it deletes services, networks, secrets, and configs, but NOT named volumes; volumes persist until `docker volume rm`, so remove them explicitly for a clean slate
explain: Volumes are the deliberate data-protection boundary: `stack rm` tears down the compute and network plumbing but never touches named volumes, so redeploys reattach the old data. EXAM TRAP: assuming `rm` means total teardown — data survives by design, which is also why `stack rm` is safe to run against production.

q: Security rotates the database password monthly. The engineer creates the new secret (`docker secret create db_pass_v2 -`), then hunts for a `docker secret update` command to swap it into the running service. It doesn't exist. What's the correct rotation sequence?
options: Create the new secret, then `docker service update --secret-rm db_pass --secret-add db_pass_v2 web` — secrets are immutable, so rotation is a service update that rolls tasks onto the new secret with zero downtime
Pipe the new value through `docker secret inspect` to edit it in place
Delete the old secret first, then recreate the new one under the SAME name — running tasks pick it up automatically
Restart the Docker daemon on each manager to reload secret values
explain: Secrets can't be edited in place — rotation means minting a versioned replacement and rolling the service onto it via `--secret-rm/--secret-add`. Deleting the in-use secret first would break running tasks (they mount by secret ID, not name). EXAM TRAP: the same-name recreate — tasks reference the old secret's ID, so they'd keep the stale value.

q: A service should PREFER spreading tasks across racks (nodes carry label `rack`), but must still schedule even where the label is missing. The engineer used `--constraint 'node.labels.rack==a1'` and tasks went Pending on unlabeled nodes. What's the right primitive?
options: Constraints are the only placement control — label every node and keep the constraint

`--placement-pref 'spread=node.labels.rack'` — preferences are soft, best-effort hints (spread here if you can), while constraints are hard requirements that block scheduling when unmatched, which is exactly the Pending cause
Use `--constraint 'node.labels.rack!=a1'` to invert the match
Placement preferences only work with `--mode global` services
explain: Constraints filter (hard: no match, no task); placement preferences rank (soft: spread where possible, schedule anyway). The Pending tasks were the constraint doing its job. EXAM TRAP: treating a preference as a guarantee — prefs never block scheduling, so they can't strand tasks.

q: A team runs 2 managers 'for HA' and loses one to a hardware failure. They expect the survivor to keep managing the cluster. What actually happens?
options: The survivor keeps working — 1 of 2 is still a majority
The cluster promotes worker nodes as temporary managers

Quorum needs a majority: for 2 managers that's 2 of 2. With one lost, the survivor can't reach quorum — no scheduling, no updates, no joins; already-running tasks keep running but the control plane is frozen. Two managers tolerate ZERO failures, which is why odd counts (3, 5) are recommended
Swarm automatically promotes a worker to restore the pair
explain: Raft quorum is (n/2)+1 — for n=2 that's 2, so a single failure kills writability; nothing auto-promotes to fix it. EXAM TRAP: '2 is better than 1' — for Raft consensus it genuinely isn't; an even count adds failure modes without adding tolerance.

q: A bad image reached production via `docker service update`. The team wants the previous spec back immediately without reconstructing all the original flags. What's the command, and what governs the rollout back?
options: `docker service rollback web` — it reverts instantly with no rollout
Redeploy the old Compose file with `docker stack deploy`; rollbacks aren't a Swarm concept
The only safe path is deleting and recreating the service from scratch

`docker service update --rollback web` reverts to the previous service spec, and the rollout follows the ROLLBACK settings (`--rollback-parallelism`, `--rollback-delay`, `--rollback-failure-action`) — a separate config from the update settings, not governed by them
explain: `--rollback` restores the prior spec in one command, rolling out under the rollback config (defaults: one at a time, no delay) rather than `update_config`. EXAM TRAP: the invented `docker service rollback` command, and assuming update parallelism/delay apply to rollbacks — they're independent knobs.

q: Each replica of a logging-agent service must report a unique hostname containing its slot number. The engineer hardcoded `--hostname agent` and every replica reports 'agent', breaking per-replica log attribution. What's the fix?
options: `--hostname 'agent-{{.Task.Slot}}'` — Swarm expands Go templates in `--hostname` (and `--env`) per task, with values like `.Task.Slot`, `.Task.ID`, and `.Node.Hostname`
Hostnames can't differ between replicas of a single service — run one service per replica
Switch to `--mode global` so each task lands on a differently-named node
Bake unique hostnames into the image's /etc/hostname at build time
explain: Template expansion gives each task its own identity (slot, ID, node) while the service definition stays identical — the Swarm way to do per-task uniqueness. EXAM TRAP: baking identity into the image, which destroys the 'every task runs the same spec' model and breaks scaling.

q: A Compose file sets `restart: always` on every service. Deployed with `docker stack deploy`, containers that exit stay down. Deployed with `docker compose up` on a dev box, they restart fine. Why the difference?
options: Swarm forcibly overrides all restart policies to 'no' for security

`restart: always` is a `docker compose` (non-Swarm) directive — `docker stack deploy` ignores it entirely. Service restart behavior comes from `deploy.restart_policy` (condition any/on-failure/none, plus delay and max attempts); the default condition is `any`
The stack needs `--restart-condition any` passed to `stack deploy`
Restart policies only apply to `--mode global` services
explain: Top-level `restart:` belongs to the Compose (single-host) world; Swarm stacks read `deploy.restart_policy` instead — same file, different orchestrator, different keys. This is the same class of trap as `build:` being ignored by stacks. EXAM TRAP: assuming every Compose key works under Swarm.

q: A Kubernetes-trained engineer needs the Swarm equivalents before node maintenance: K8s `kubectl drain` evicts pods AND blocks new scheduling, while `kubectl cordon` only blocks new scheduling. What are the Swarm mappings?
options: `docker node rm` equals drain; Swarm has no cordon equivalent
There are no equivalents — remove the node and rejoin it after maintenance

`docker node update --availability drain <node>` evicts tasks and reschedules them elsewhere (like `drain`); `--availability pause` blocks new scheduling while keeping existing tasks running (like `cordon`)
`docker swarm leave` on the node equals `drain`
explain: drain ≈ drain (evict + reschedule + block), pause ≈ cordon (block only, running workloads untouched). EXAM TRAP: `node rm` / `swarm leave` — those destroy cluster membership instead of gracefully shifting workloads.

q: A team stores a non-sensitive Nginx config as a Swarm config and the database password as a Swarm secret. An auditor asks which of the two is encrypted at rest in the Raft log. What's the correct answer?
options: Both — everything persisted in Raft is encrypted
The config — configs are mounted read-only, which implies encryption
Neither — Swarm only encrypts the join tokens
Only the secret — secrets are encrypted at rest (and in transit to workers); configs are stored UNENCRYPTED in Raft, which is exactly why credentials must never go in configs
explain: Encryption at rest is a secrets-only property; configs trade that away for convenience with non-sensitive data. Read-only mounting is about writability, not confidentiality. EXAM TRAP: 'read-only = encrypted' — unrelated axes.

q: An engineer runs `docker service create --mode global --replicas 3 monitoring-agent` and it errors out. What's wrong?
options: `--replicas` is only valid for replicated services — `--mode global` means one task per matching node BY DEFINITION, so a replica count is meaningless; drop the flag
Global mode multiplies: it would create 3 tasks per node, which the scheduler rejects as ambiguous
Global mode silently converts to replicated mode with 3 replicas
The flags are fine together; the error must be the image name
explain: Global services schedule exactly one task per node matching the constraints — there is no count to set. `--replicas` belongs to `--mode replicated` (the default). EXAM TRAP: '3 per node' — no such multiplication exists.

q: The team deletes the `worker` service from `app.yml` and re-runs `docker stack deploy -c app.yml billing`. The worker service keeps running. Why, and what's the fix?
options: Stack deploy can only add services; removed ones must always be deleted by hand with `docker service rm` — there is no automatic cleanup
A plain redeploy leaves services that vanished from the file alone; add `--prune` — `docker stack deploy --prune -c app.yml billing` removes services (and networks) no longer defined in the file
Rename the stack to force a clean redeploy
Prune was removed from `stack deploy`; `docker stack rm` followed by a fresh deploy is the only way
explain: Without `--prune`, redeploy is additive — file-removed services are orphaned, not deleted. `--prune` reconciles the stack to the file. EXAM TRAP: assuming redeploy equals full reconciliation (compare `docker compose up --remove-orphans` in the Compose world).

q: The deploy pipeline wants a bad rollout to REVERT ITSELF automatically instead of pausing halfway with a mix of old and new tasks awaiting a human. Which update settings deliver that?
options: `--update-failure-action continue` — it pushes through the bad image until the rollout completes
The failure action is fixed at cluster creation and can't be changed per service
`--update-failure-action rollback` — when failures exceed `--update-max-failure-ratio`, Swarm automatically rolls back to the previous spec instead of pausing (the default action is `pause`)
`--update-parallelism 0` disables failure detection so nothing pauses
explain: Failure actions are `pause` (default: stop and wait for a human), `continue` (plow through failures — the opposite of safety), or `rollback` (auto-revert to the last good spec). EXAM TRAP: `continue` sounding like recovery — it means keep rolling out the broken image.

q: A 5-manager cluster must decommission one manager — and it's the current LEADER. The runbook says `docker node demote` then `docker swarm leave`. A teammate fears demoting the leader will break the cluster. What actually happens?
options: The leader can't be demoted; you must wait for leadership to move on its own
Demoting the leader permanently destroys quorum
Skip demote and run `docker swarm leave --force` directly on the leader — demote is only for followers

Demoting the leader is safe — the remaining managers immediately hold a Raft election and pick a new leader; then the demoted node leaves cleanly as a worker. Never `leave --force` a manager without demoting first
explain: Leadership is not sticky — Raft re-elects automatically the moment the leader steps down, so demote-then-leave works on any manager including the leader. EXAM TRAP: treating the leader as special; the dangerous move is actually `leave --force` on a manager, which can strand quorum.

q: Map the concepts for a K8s-trained hire: a Swarm service with a published port uses the routing mesh (every node listens; traffic routes to healthy tasks). What's the closest Kubernetes equivalent, and what maps to Swarm's internal VIP?
options: NodePort ≈ published port / routing mesh (a port opened on every node, routed to the service's pods); ClusterIP ≈ the Swarm VIP (cluster-internal virtual IP used for service discovery)
LoadBalancer ≈ the VIP; ClusterIP ≈ the published port
Ingress ≈ the routing mesh; NodePort ≈ the VIP
There are no equivalents — Kubernetes networking shares nothing with Swarm's model
explain: NodePort opens the same port on every node and routes into the service (mesh-like); ClusterIP is the stable internal virtual IP clients dial (VIP-like). LoadBalancer is a cloud-provisioned external LB — a different thing. EXAM TRAP: LoadBalancer-sounds-like-mesh; it isn't.

q: During code review, a Dockerfile shows `COPY config/ /app/config/` followed later by `USER appuser` — and then a separate `RUN chown -R appuser /app/config` layer just to fix ownership, because the app couldn't read its own root-owned 600-mode configs. The reviewer wants that extra layer gone. What's the idiomatic fix?
options: Run the container as root instead and drop the USER instruction
`COPY --chown=appuser:appuser config/ /app/config/` — ownership is set AT COPY TIME with no extra layer; alternatively keep root ownership and widen to 644 if the threat model allows
Add `USER root` after the COPY so the app runs privileged
Ownership can only be fixed with a separate RUN layer — there is no copy-time option
explain: `COPY --chown` (and `--chmod`) bake ownership into the same layer as the copy — no extra layer, no root runtime needed. `USER` only sets the runtime user; it never retroactively fixes file ownership. EXAM TRAP: 'USER fixes permissions' — it doesn't; the files stay root-owned and unreadable.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A multi-stage Dockerfile has stages named `deps`, `build`, and `runtime`. CI needs an image containing ONLY the `build` stage output (compiled artifacts plus toolchain) for debugging — without editing the Dockerfile. How?
options: Impossible without editing the Dockerfile to reorder stages
`docker build --from build .` selects the stage to tag
`docker build --target build -t app:debug .` — builds through the named stage and tags THAT intermediate result instead of the final stage
`docker build --stage build .` stops at the named stage
explain: `--target` names the last stage to build, letting you capture intermediate stages (debug images, test runners, artifact extractors) from one Dockerfile. `--from`/`--stage` aren't build flags. EXAM TRAP: inventing `--stage` — the real flag is `--target`.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI must produce ONE tag, `shop/api:2.0`, that works on both amd64 servers and arm64 edge nodes. Today the pipeline builds on amd64 only, and arm64 pulls fail with 'exec format error'. What's the fix?
options: Push two tags (`shop/api:2.0-amd64`, `shop/api:2.0-arm64`) and document which node type uses which
arm64 can't run the same image definition; maintain a separate Dockerfile per architecture
Have the edge nodes pull with `--platform linux/arm64` to convert the image on the fly

`docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t shop/api:2.0 --push .` — BuildKit builds both architectures and pushes a manifest list, so the single tag resolves to the correct image per node's architecture
explain: A manifest list (fat manifest) lets one tag serve many architectures; `--platform` at pull time can't conjure an arm64 image out of an amd64-only tag. EXAM TRAP: pull-time `--platform` as a converter — it only SELECTS among architectures the manifest already contains.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: After getting burned by the `latest` tag moving under them (n=33), the team wants deploys that can NEVER silently change, even if someone re-pushes the tag. What's the strongest pinning available?
options: Reference the image by digest — `shop/api@sha256:9f3a...` — digests are content-addressed and immutable; a tag can be re-pointed, a digest cannot
Use a longer, more specific tag like `shop/api:2.0.1-final-v2`
Pin the tag inside the Dockerfile's FROM line
Digests change on every pull, so digest pinning is unstable — stick with tags
explain: A digest names exact content — it cannot drift, be overwritten, or be 'latest' by accident. Any tag, however specific-looking, remains mutable. EXAM TRAP: 'digests change on pull' — no; the digest IS the content's identity, which is why `docker images --digests` exists.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Upstream rebuilt `ubuntu:22.04` with a security fix. The team runs `docker build --no-cache .` expecting the fix, but the resulting image still contains the OLD base. Why?
options: `--no-cache` is broken in recent Docker versions; file a bug

`--no-cache` rebuilds every Dockerfile layer but still starts FROM the locally cached base image — it never contacts the registry. `--pull` forces the daemon to check for a newer base first; combine them (`--pull --no-cache`) for a fully fresh build
The Dockerfile's FROM line must be deleted to refresh the base
Base images are immutable once pulled; rebuild FROM scratch instead
explain: `--no-cache` = rebuild my layers; `--pull` = refresh the base image. They're independent axes, and the classic mistake is expecting one flag to do both jobs. EXAM TRAP: conflating the two — a `--no-cache` build on a stale base bakes the stale base into a 'fresh' image.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: The team's .dockerignore excludes `*.log`, but `audit.log` MUST be included in the build context — a compliance check baked into the image reads it. How do you carve out the exception?
options: Remove `*.log` from .dockerignore — exceptions aren't supported, so list files individually
Enumerate every other log file explicitly instead of using the wildcard
Add `!audit.log` AFTER the `*.log` line — later negation patterns re-include previously excluded paths; order matters, last match wins
Prefix it with double negation: `!!audit.log`
explain: `.dockerignore` supports `!` exceptions evaluated in order — the last matching pattern decides. So the exception must come after the broad exclusion. EXAM TRAP: `!!` (not a thing) and assuming order doesn't matter.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A team publishes a base image `corp/python-base` that should AUTOMATICALLY copy in `requirements.txt` and pip-install it whenever anyone builds FROM it. Which instruction implements this, and when does it execute?
options: A plain `RUN pip install` in the base image — it re-runs for every child automatically
There is no such instruction; ship a shell script instead
`CMD pip install` — it runs at every child container's startup

`ONBUILD COPY requirements.txt /app/` plus `ONBUILD RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt` in the base image — ONBUILD triggers are stored in the image metadata and execute during the NEXT build that uses this image as its base
explain: ONBUILD defers instructions to the downstream build — the base image records them, and they fire when a child Dockerfile's FROM references it. They run at child BUILD time, not at base build time or container runtime. EXAM TRAP: thinking ONBUILD runs when the base is built.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An app handles SIGQUIT for graceful shutdown but ignores SIGTERM. `docker stop` waits the full 10-second timeout, then SIGKILLs — causing unclean shutdowns. The app code can't change. What's the Dockerfile-level fix?
options: `STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT` — overrides which signal `docker stop` sends instead of the default SIGTERM
STOPSIGNAL only takes effect combined with `--init`
Add `STOPTIMEOUT 60` to extend the graceful window
The stop signal can't be changed; the app must be rewritten
explain: `STOPSIGNAL` sets the signal the daemon sends on stop (default SIGTERM); the timeout is a separate knob (`--time` on `docker stop`, `--stop-timeout` at create). EXAM TRAP: the invented `STOPTIMEOUT` instruction — and blaming the timeout when the wrong signal is the real problem.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A build needs a private PyPI token to install dependencies. `ARG` leaks it into image history; COPYing it in and `rm`-ing later still leaves it in an earlier layer. What's the BuildKit-native pattern that leaves NO trace?
options: Pass it as an ENV — environment variables don't appear in history

`RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pypi pip install ...` with `docker build --secret id=pypi,src=token.txt .` — the secret is mounted only for that single RUN step and is never persisted in any layer or in history
COPY the token in, use it, and `RUN rm` it in the very next layer
Build-time secrets are impossible; only runtime secrets exist
explain: Secret mounts exist only for the duration of one RUN — nothing is written to a layer, so there's nothing to leak via history or layer export. ARG values ARE baked into history; a later `rm` can't erase an earlier layer. EXAM TRAP: 'rm removes it' — layers are immutable, so the secret stays recoverable.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: `docker images` shows several `<none>:<none>` entries left over from rebuilds. Someone suggests `docker image prune`, but the team fears losing tagged release images. What does a PLAIN `docker image prune` actually remove?
options: Everything unused, including tagged releases — back them up first
Nothing at all — prune requires `-a` to do anything
Only DANGLING images (untagged `<none>:<none>` layers with no children) — tagged images are untouched; `-a` is the dangerous variant that removes all unused images, tagged or not
Only the build cache, never images
explain: Default prune is conservative: dangling (untagged, childless) images only. `-a` escalates to every image not referenced by a container. EXAM TRAP: assuming prune defaults to the `-a` behavior — that's how release images get deleted on a Friday.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile needs a local `assets.tar.gz` extracted into the image. Compare `COPY assets.tar.gz /static/` vs `ADD assets.tar.gz /static/`. What's the actual difference?
options: Nothing — they're identical for local files
COPY extracts archives; ADD copies verbatim
Neither extracts; you must add a `RUN tar` step
`ADD` auto-extracts LOCAL tar archives into the destination; `COPY` places the file as-is. (Separately: ADD never extracts REMOTE downloads — a common second mix-up)
explain: Archive auto-extraction is ADD-only and local-only: remote URLs are downloaded verbatim, never extracted. Prefer COPY unless you specifically want one of ADD's two magic behaviors. EXAM TRAP: the reversed 'COPY extracts' claim, and expecting URL downloads to unpack.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A CI host is under disk pressure and the suspects are images, build cache, and volumes. What's the fastest native way to see which category is eating space — and how much of it is reclaimable?
options: `docker system df` — breaks down Images, Containers, Local Volumes, and Build Cache with SIZE and RECLAIMABLE columns; `-v` adds per-object detail
`docker images` — it includes volume and cache usage
`du -sh /var/lib/docker` is the only reliable measurement
`docker system prune` prints a usage report before deleting
explain: `docker system df` is the built-in space audit across all four object types, showing what's reclaimable before you delete anything. EXAM TRAP: `du` on /var/lib/docker — overlayfs double-counts shared layers, wildly overstating usage.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An engineer runs `docker tag shop/api:2.0 shop/api:stable` and pushes both tags. A teammate worries this DOUBLES registry storage. Is that right?
options: Yes — each tag is a full independent copy in the registry
No — a tag is just a named pointer to the same image ID, and layers are content-addressed blobs: pushing the second tag uploads each blob once (the second push is nearly instant)
Yes, unless `docker tag --shared` is used
Tags share layers only within the same repository name
explain: Tags are pointers; blobs are deduplicated by digest across the whole registry. Retagging costs metadata, not storage. EXAM TRAP: the tag-as-copy mental model — the same fallacy behind 'don't retag, it wastes space'.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A containerized DNS server listens on TCP AND UDP port 53. The Dockerfile declares `EXPOSE 53`. A scanner flags UDP 53 as unexposed. What's missing?
options: Nothing — a bare EXPOSE covers all protocols
`EXPOSE 53/tcp 53/udp` on one line is invalid syntax
A bare `EXPOSE 53` means TCP ONLY — declare the protocol explicitly: `EXPOSE 53/udp` (alongside `EXPOSE 53/tcp` if both are needed)
EXPOSE can't declare UDP at all; protocol must be set with `--publish` at runtime
explain: EXPOSE defaults to TCP; `/udp` (or `/sctp`) must be stated per port. This is documentation-only metadata, but scanners and tooling read it literally. EXAM TRAP: 'bare port covers both' — it doesn't.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI needs to build an image straight from a GitHub repo WITHOUT a separate clone step in the pipeline script. Is that possible with plain `docker build`?
options: No — `docker build` requires a local directory as context
Only with a separately installed BuildKit git driver
A clone step is mandatory; restructure around multi-stage builds instead
Yes — `docker build https://github.com/org/repo.git#branch:subdir .` treats the remote repo as the build context (with optional `#branch` and `:subdir` selectors); the daemon fetches it directly
explain: Remote git contexts are native: the daemon clones the repo (optionally a branch/subdirectory) and uses it as the context — no local clone needed. EXAM TRAP: 'local context only' — the context can be a tarball stream, stdin, or a git URL.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A child image (`FROM corp/base`) inherits a HEALTHCHECK that curls a port the child doesn't serve, so orchestrators mark the child unhealthy. How does the child Dockerfile disable the inherited check?
options: `HEALTHCHECK NONE` — explicitly disables any inherited healthcheck (a new HEALTHCHECK instruction would override it instead)
Inherited healthchecks are permanent and can't be removed
Set `HEALTHCHECK --interval=0s` to disable it
Override it with an empty `CMD []`
explain: `HEALTHCHECK NONE` is the documented off-switch for inherited checks; otherwise the last HEALTHCHECK instruction wins. `--interval=0s` is invalid, and CMD is unrelated to healthchecks. EXAM TRAP: reaching for interval tricks instead of the explicit NONE.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A build must `git clone` a PRIVATE repo during `docker build`. The SSH key must never land in any layer, and `--mount=type=secret` doesn't fit the SSH-agent protocol git needs. What's the BuildKit answer?
options: COPY the private key in, clone, then delete it in a later layer
`docker build --ssh default .` with `RUN --mount=type=ssh git clone ...` — forwards the host's SSH agent socket into that single RUN step; the key material never enters a layer
Embed a deploy token in the git URL — URLs aren't stored in layers
Private clones are impossible during builds; vendor the code into the context first
explain: SSH mounts forward the agent (not the key) for exactly one RUN — git authenticates, nothing persists. A token-in-URL WOULD be baked into the layer history. EXAM TRAP: 'delete it later' — the key remains recoverable from the earlier layer forever.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An engineer manages dev, staging, and prod daemons by exporting DOCKER_HOST before every command — and once deployed staging's stack to prod after forgetting to switch. What's the safer NATIVE mechanism for juggling multiple daemons?
options: `docker context create` one context per environment, then `docker context use prod` — contexts store endpoints (and TLS material) by name, the active one is always visible in `docker context ls`, and switching is a single deliberate command instead of an invisible, forgettable env var
DOCKER_HOST is the only supported mechanism; the fix is discipline
Keep one terminal window open per environment
Contexts only work with Swarm clusters, not standalone daemons
explain: Contexts make the target explicit, named, and listable — DOCKER_HOST is ambient state that's easy to get wrong (as the staging-to-prod incident proves). Contexts work with any daemon endpoint, including SSH ones. EXAM TRAP: 'env vars are the only way' — contexts replaced that pattern years ago.

q: An admin sets log-level to debug in daemon.json AND starts dockerd with `--log-level info` for a one-off test. The daemon refuses to start at all. Why?
options: debug isn't a valid log level for the daemon

The daemon fatally errors when the SAME option is set in BOTH daemon.json and CLI flags ('unable to configure the Docker daemon with both options') — pick one source; flags for experiments, daemon.json for persistence
daemon.json is only read on SIGHUP, never at startup
Two log levels require comma syntax: `--log-level debug,info`
explain: Duplicate configuration across the two sources is a hard startup error, not a precedence decision — Docker refuses to guess which you meant. Remove one of them. EXAM TRAP: 'flags override the file' — that's true for many tools, but dockerd treats the conflict as fatal.

q: A host's security team sets iptables management to false in daemon.json so they can own the firewall rules by hand. After the daemon restarts, containers lose internet access and published ports stop working. What's the relationship?
options: The setting only affects Swarm overlay networks, so something else broke
The setting is deprecated and silently ignored

With daemon iptables management disabled, Docker stops programming the NAT/MASQUERADE and port-forwarding (DNAT) rules — outbound container traffic and `-p` publishing depend on those rules, so the team must now maintain them manually (or re-enable daemon management)
Containers need `--privileged` when the daemon doesn't manage iptables
explain: The daemon's iptables rules ARE container connectivity: MASQUERADE for egress, DNAT for published ports. Disabling management means you own every rule. EXAM TRAP: blaming the application or reaching for `--privileged` — the packets are fine, the NAT is just gone.

q: The corporate LAN uses 172.17.0.0/16 — colliding with Docker's default docker0 bridge subnet — so containers can't reach corporate hosts. What's the daemon-level fix?
options: Re-address the corporate LAN
Run everything with `--network host`
Delete docker0; the daemon works fine without a bridge
