Set 'bip' to '10.200.0.1/24' in daemon.json (the bridge IP for docker0) and restart the daemon — new containers get addresses from the new range; existing containers and networks must be recreated to pick it up
explain: `bip` (bridge IP) re-addresses docker0 away from the collision. It's a daemon-startup setting, so already-created containers keep their old addresses until recreated. EXAM TRAP: expecting live containers to migrate subnets — they won't.

q: Containers on an overlay network hang on LARGE transfers over a VPN path with reduced MTU, while small requests work fine. The daemon `--mtu` was already lowered, but overlay traffic still fragments. Why didn't that fix it?
options: Daemon `--mtu` only sets docker0's MTU — each overlay network takes its MTU from its OWN option: `docker network create -d overlay --opt com.docker.network.driver.mtu=1450 ...`. VXLAN encapsulation adds roughly 50 bytes of overhead, so overlays need their own (lower) MTU
MTU can't be set on overlay networks at all
Lower the physical host interface MTU instead
This is a VXLAN bug; restart the daemon
explain: The daemon MTU governs the default bridge; overlay networks are separate interfaces with their own MTU option — and VXLAN headers eat into the payload budget, so the overlay MTU must sit below the path MTU. EXAM TRAP: 'one MTU knob covers everything' — it's per-network.

q: Every container on a host needs a default nofile limit of 65536 instead of the low default — WITHOUT adding `--ulimit` to every `docker run` invocation. Where does this belong?
options: It can't be defaulted; wrap `docker run` in a helper script
In daemon.json as `default-ulimits` (e.g. nofile with Hard/Soft 65536) — it applies to all newly created containers, and a per-container `--ulimit` still overrides it
In /etc/security/limits.conf on the host
Ulimits are per-image and must be baked into the Dockerfile
explain: `default-ulimits` in daemon.json sets the baseline for every container the daemon creates. Host limits.conf doesn't propagate into containers, and Dockerfiles can't set ulimits. EXAM TRAP: limits.conf — it governs host login sessions, not container processes.

q: `docker info` shows `Runtimes: runc io.containerd.runc.v2 nvidia`. The team runs GPU jobs with `--runtime nvidia`. A teammate says there's a simpler modern flag. What is it — and does it remove the need for the NVIDIA runtime installation?
options: `--gpu all` — and it works with zero NVIDIA setup
There is no alternative; `--runtime` is mandatory

`--gpus all` (or `--gpus 2`) — the device-request API. NO, it doesn't remove the need: the NVIDIA container toolkit/runtime must still be installed; the flag just selects GPUs declaratively instead of swapping the entire runtime
`--privileged` exposes GPUs automatically
explain: `--gpus` is the modern interface over the same NVIDIA stack — it doesn't replace the toolkit, it just consumes it more cleanly (count, device IDs, capabilities). EXAM TRAP: 'the flag replaces the driver install' — the runtime must still be present and registered.

q: The daemon won't start with overlay2 on a host whose /var/lib/docker sits on XFS. If it could start, `docker info` would report `Supports d_type: false`. What's the underlying requirement?
options: overlay2 requires ext4; XFS is unsupported as a backing filesystem
The kernel is too old for any storage driver
Bypass the check with a storage-opt override

overlay2 REQUIRES d_type support from the backing filesystem — XFS must be formatted with ftype=1 (check with `xfs_info`). Without d_type the daemon can't use overlay2; the fix is a d_type-capable filesystem (reformat XFS with ftype=1, or use ext4)
explain: Overlayfs needs directory entry type info (d_type) from the lower filesystem; XFS only provides it when formatted with ftype=1 — a mkfs-time decision that can't be changed later. EXAM TRAP: kernel-override storage opts — those bypass version checks, not filesystem capability checks.

q: An admin secures the remote daemon API with `--tlsverify` plus `--tlscacert`, `--tlscert`, and `--tlskey` against TCP port 2376. A colleague tries `--tlsverify` ALONE 'to keep it simple'. What happens?
options: The daemon fails to start — `--tlsverify` REQUIRES the CA, server cert, and key flags; verify-mode with nothing to verify against is a contradiction, and Docker refuses the configuration
It works, generating self-signed certs on the fly
It silently falls back to unencrypted TCP
Clients can then connect without presenting certs
explain: `--tlsverify` means 'require and verify client certs against my CA' — without the CA/cert/key material that's incoherent, so the daemon won't start. TLS without verify (`--tls` alone) encrypts without client auth, which is a different (weaker) mode. EXAM TRAP: verify-without-certificates as a valid minimal setup.

q: A host's disk filled with container logs under /var/lib/docker/containers/. The team assumed Docker rotates logs by default. What's the actual default behavior, and the fix?
options: Docker rotates at 100MB by default; the disk problem must be elsewhere

The default json-file driver keeps ALL logs with NO rotation — set `log-opts` (`max-size: 10m`, `max-file: 3`) in daemon.json to bound them; it applies to newly created containers, so existing ones must be recreated
Log size can't be limited; logs must be shipped off-host instead
Schedule `docker logs --clear` nightly via cron
explain: json-file's default is unbounded growth — rotation is opt-in via max-size/max-file, and like most daemon.json changes it only affects containers created after the change. EXAM TRAP: the invented `docker logs --clear` — and assuming defaults protect you.

q: A new worker fails to join the swarm: `x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid`. The CA is healthy and the join token is fresh — but the node's system clock shows last year. What's the mechanism?
options: Join tokens expire after 24 hours; generate a new one
The manager's clock is authoritative, so set the manager's clock back to match
Swarm node certificates are time-bound — mutual-TLS enrollment validates not-before/not-after against the node's LOCAL clock. Fix time sync (NTP/chrony) so the clock is correct, then rejoin
Certificates are only validated on managers, so the worker should skip validation
explain: x509 validity is checked against local time — a skewed clock makes a perfectly good certificate look expired (or not-yet-valid). The fix is time sync, not new tokens or certs. EXAM TRAP: blaming the token or CA when the error names the certificate's validity window.

q: An engineer creates a user-defined network with `--ipv6` and assigns IPv6 addresses, but containers get no IPv6 connectivity at all. What daemon-level prerequisite was missed?
options: Nothing — IPv6 works automatically once the network flag is set
Containers need `--privileged` for IPv6 packet flow
IPv6 networking requires Swarm mode

The daemon itself must enable IPv6: `ipv6: true` plus `fixed-cidr-v6` (a routed /64 to allocate from) in daemon.json, then restart — the network flag only marks the network; the daemon needs the address pool to hand out
explain: Docker's IPv6 is opt-in at the daemon level: without `ipv6` + `fixed-cidr-v6`, the `--ipv6` network flag is decoration. The /64 must actually be routed to the host. EXAM TRAP: 'the network flag is sufficient' — it's necessary but not sufficient.

q: The platform team wants DAEMON-level metrics (engine operations, queue depths) in Prometheus. `docker stats` only shows per-container CPU/memory. What's the native option?
options: Set `metrics-addr` (e.g. `0.0.0.0:9323`, experimental) in daemon.json — the daemon exposes Prometheus-format metrics on that address for scraping
Prometheus can't consume Docker metrics; poll the API and convert manually
Pipe `docker events` into Prometheus
Daemon metrics require a commercial Docker edition
explain: The experimental `metrics-addr` exposes engine internals in Prometheus format — a different telemetry layer from container stats. EXAM TRAP: confusing container stats with daemon metrics; `docker stats` will never show engine internals.

q: Compliance demands a TECHNICAL guarantee (not a policy doc) that developers can start/stop containers but can NEVER create `--privileged` ones. Which daemon mechanism enforces this?
options: Remove the `--privileged` flag from the Docker CLI binary on dev machines
`--authorization-plugin` (e.g. an OPA-based plugin) — EVERY API request is passed to the plugin, which allows or denies based on request content (like Privileged=true); denials come back as 403s
Set `privileged: false` in daemon.json
Authorization plugins only gate image pulls, not container creation
explain: Authz plugins intercept all API calls and can deny on payload inspection — the only native way to forbid a specific create-time flag cluster-wide. No daemon.json toggle for this exists. EXAM TRAP: CLI-side 'removal' — anyone with API access bypasses the CLI entirely.

q: Before a risky Swarm change, the team wants a backup of the CLUSTER STATE (services, networks, secrets definitions) — not the MKE wrapper around it. What's the actual procedure?
options: Run `docker swarm backup` to produce a tarball
Back up /etc/docker — cluster state lives there

Quiesce writes, then back up `/var/lib/docker/swarm` on a manager — that directory IS the Raft store holding all cluster state; restore means placing it on a fresh manager before the daemon starts. (There is no `docker swarm backup` subcommand — that's the trap)
Snapshot etcd — Swarm stores state there
explain: Swarm's state is the Raft log under /var/lib/docker/swarm — a filesystem-level backup of a manager is the documented safety net. Swarm doesn't use etcd and ships no backup subcommand. EXAM TRAP: the invented `docker swarm backup` and the etcd confusion (that's Kubernetes).

q: On Docker Desktop for Mac, bind-mounting `~/projects/app` works, but mounting `/opt/legacy/data` shows an EMPTY directory in the container — though the path exists on the Mac. What's going on?
options: Bind mounts are unsupported on Docker Desktop
The container needs `--privileged` to see host paths
macOS permissions block Docker from reading /opt entirely

Docker Desktop runs the daemon inside a Linux VM — only host paths shared INTO the VM (Settings → Resources → File Sharing, e.g. /Users by default) are visible; add `/opt/legacy/data` to file sharing or move the data under an already-shared path
explain: Desktop's VM boundary means the daemon only sees the allowlisted shared paths — unshared host paths mount as empty dirs, not errors. EXAM TRAP: treating Desktop like native Linux; the file-sharing allowlist is the whole story.

q: A team on Docker 24+ hears the containerd image store improves performance and unlocks newer features, but their daemon still uses the classic image store. How do they opt in?
options: Set `containerd-snapshotter: true` in daemon.json and restart — the daemon then uses containerd for image pull/store; existing images must be re-pulled under the new store (it's effectively a one-way migration per data-root)
It's automatic on Docker 24 and later
Install containerd separately and point DOCKER_HOST at it
The snapshotter only affects Swarm scheduling, not images
explain: The containerd image store is opt-in via daemon.json — not default, not automatic — and the two stores don't share images, so plan a re-pull. EXAM TRAP: 'automatic on 24+' — the feature shipped as opt-in precisely because migration has sharp edges.

q: Containers on a macvlan network reach every LAN host EXCEPT the Docker host's own IP. The team suspects a host firewall rule. What's the actual cause?
options: By design, macvlan child interfaces cannot talk to the parent host's IP — the kernel filters that traffic. Workarounds: create a second macvlan interface ON the host for host↔container traffic, or route through another LAN host
The host firewall blocks macvlan traffic by default; open the container ports
macvlan needs `--internal` for the host to be reachable
The containers need the host's MAC passed via `--mac-address`
explain: This is kernel macvlan behavior, not a firewall: the parent interface never receives packets from its own macvlan children. The standard fix is a macvlan sub-interface on the host itself. EXAM TRAP: firewall blame — no rule change will ever fix a kernel-level filter.

q: An engineer runs `docker run -d --network host -p 8080:80 nginx`, then is confused: `docker port` shows nothing and the app answers on port 80, not 8080. Explain.
options: Port publishing is broken in host mode; switch to bridge networking
In host network mode the container shares the host's network stack directly — there is no NAT, so `-p/--publish` is meaningless and silently ignored; the app's own port (80) is what the host sees
Host mode requires `--publish mode=host` syntax instead
Host mode remaps published ports randomly
explain: Host mode = no network namespace, no NAT, no port mapping layer — publish flags have nothing to act on. If you need remapping, you need a namespaced driver (bridge/macvlan). EXAM TRAP: expecting NAT semantics where no NAT exists.

q: A metrics sidecar must scrape `localhost:9100` on an app container — but the app only listens on loopback and can't be reconfigured. How can two containers share ONE network stack?
options: Put both on the same user-defined network and dial the app by container name
Link them with the legacy `--link` flag
`docker run --network container:app metrics-sidecar` — the sidecar joins the app container's network namespace: same interfaces, same localhost, same port space (so port conflicts are possible)
Share the stack with `--volumes-from`
explain: `--network container:<name>` shares the entire netns including lo — the ONLY way for two containers to share localhost. Same-network name resolution doesn't merge loopbacks. EXAM TRAP: assuming a shared user-defined network shares localhost — it doesn't.

q: The security team asks how often the IPsec keys for `--opt encrypted` overlay networks are rotated — and who performs the rotation. What's the answer?
options: Never — the admin rotates them manually with `docker network update`
On every service update touching that network
The admin must run `docker swarm ca --rotate` on a schedule
Automatically by the Swarm managers on a schedule — no manual rotation step exists or is needed (`docker network` has no key-rotation command at all)
explain: Data-path keys rotate automatically under manager control; there's simply no manual command for it. `swarm ca --rotate` rotates the CLUSTER CA (control-plane identity), not the overlay data-path keys. EXAM TRAP: ca --rotate — right command family, wrong keys.

q: Firewall rules reference the bridge interface by name, but Docker names it `br-a3f9c2...` unpredictably per network. How do you pin a deterministic host-side interface name for a user-defined bridge?
options: `docker network create -d bridge --opt com.docker.network.bridge.name=br-billing mynet` — the driver option sets the host-side interface name explicitly
Interface names are always random; firewall by subnet instead
Rename it afterward with `ip link set`
Pass `--hostname` to set the interface name
explain: `com.docker.network.bridge.name` pins the veth-bridge interface name at creation. Renaming afterward fights the daemon (it manages that interface). EXAM TRAP: `ip link set` — the daemon recreates/overwrites its interfaces, so manual renames don't stick.

q: A standalone debug container must join the existing Swarm overlay `backend`, but `docker run --network backend` fails: the network 'is not attachable'. The engineer looks for a flag to flip on the existing network. What actually works?
options: `docker network update --attachable backend`

Nothing can change the existing network — attachable is a CREATE-TIME property, and `docker network` has no update subcommand. Recreate it (`docker network create -d overlay --attachable backend2`) and reattach the services
Restart the daemon with an `--attachable` default
Use `--network container:` to bypass the check
explain: There is no `docker network update` — network options are immutable after creation, so the only path is recreate-with-attachable. (Stack-created networks hit this constantly since stacks never set attachable.) EXAM TRAP: the invented update subcommand.

q: A container is attached to `frontend` with `--network-alias api`, and is ALSO connected to `backend` via `docker network connect`. From a container on `backend` only, the name `api` does NOT resolve. Why?
options: Network aliases are broken on multi-network containers
The flag should be `--alias`, not `--network-alias`
Aliases are registered PER NETWORK — the alias landed on `frontend`, so it only resolves there. Register it on the second network too: `docker network connect --alias api backend <container>`
Embedded DNS doesn't work across overlay networks at all
explain: A network alias is scoped to the attachment that registered it; each additional network needs its own `--alias` registration. Cross-overlay DNS works fine — the name was simply never registered on `backend`. EXAM TRAP: 'alias = global name' — it's per-network by design.

q: The ingress network's default 10.255.0.0/16 overlaps the corporate WAN, breaking the routing mesh. How do you change the ingress network's subnet?
options: Edit it in place with `docker network update`
Set the new subnet in daemon.json and SIGHUP the daemon
Reinstall Docker with a different built-in default

Remove and recreate it: `docker network rm ingress` (no published-port services may exist at that moment), then `docker network create --driver overlay --ingress --subnet=10.10.0.0/16 --gateway=10.10.0.2 ingress` — ingress is just an overlay network carrying the ingress flag, recreated like any other
explain: The documented procedure is rm + recreate with `--ingress` and your chosen subnet/gateway — ingress has no special immutability. daemon.json's address pools govern FUTURE user networks, not ingress. EXAM TRAP: reaching for daemon.json for a network that already exists.

q: A service publishes port 8080 with `--publish mode=host` instead of the default ingress mode. The external load balancer health-checks EVERY node on 8080, but nodes running no task report connection refused. Why?
options: With `mode=host`, the port binds ONLY on nodes actually running a task — there is no routing mesh to forward from task-less nodes. Aim the LB at task nodes only (or use ingress mode if every-node listening is the goal)
`mode=host` is invalid for Swarm services
The tasks must have crashed on those nodes
Host-mode publishing requires `--endpoint-mode dnsrr`
explain: `mode=host` bypasses the mesh: the port exists exactly where tasks run and nowhere else — which also preserves client source IPs, the usual reason for choosing it. EXAM TRAP: expecting mesh behavior (every node answers) from the mode that explicitly opts out of it.

q: `docker exec web1 ip addr` on an overlay-connected container shows an interface on the overlay subnet (10.0.x.x) AND another on 172.18.x.x. Is the second interface a misconfiguration?
options: Yes — containers should have exactly one interface; remove the extra network

No — this is normal: one interface is the OVERLAY (container-to-container and service traffic); the other attaches to `docker_gwbridge`, which provides the default route for EXTERNAL traffic (SNATed out). Overlay networks don't route to the outside world by themselves
It's a leftover interface from a previous network attachment
One is the IPv4 stack and the other is IPv6
explain: Every overlay-attached container gets dual attachment: overlay for east-west, docker_gwbridge for north-south egress. Deleting docker_gwbridge 'to clean up' kills external access. EXAM TRAP: 'extra interface = misconfiguration' — it's the egress path.

q: A Compose file uses `expose: - '5432'` for postgres, but the developer can't reach the database from her laptop. She insists `expose` should publish the port. What's the real distinction?
options: `expose` is deprecated and does nothing at all
`expose` publishes to the host on a random high port
`expose:` only documents/opens the port for container-to-container traffic on shared networks — it NEVER publishes to the host. `ports:` (the `-p` equivalent) is what binds host ports
`expose` only works in Swarm stacks, not `docker compose`
explain: `expose` is inter-container metadata (like Dockerfile EXPOSE); `ports` creates the host binding. Reaching it from a laptop needs `ports:`. EXAM TRAP: carrying the Dockerfile-EXPOSE confusion ('EXPOSE publishes') into Compose — neither publishes.

q: A RUNNING Swarm service must join a second overlay network — with no downtime and without recreating the service. Is that possible?
options: No — a service's networks are fixed at creation time
Only by editing the Compose file and redeploying the whole stack
`docker network connect` works directly on service tasks
Yes — `docker service update --network-add backend web` attaches the new network (rolling the tasks through it); `--network-rm` detaches. It's an update operation, not a recreate
explain: `--network-add/--network-rm` are first-class service update operations — the service rolls onto the new network like any other update. `docker network connect` targets standalone containers, not service tasks. EXAM TRAP: 'networks are immutable on services' — they're updatable.

q: A firewall allowlist needs the logging container at a predictable 10.5.0.50. The engineer runs `docker run --network mynet --ip 10.5.0.50`, but it errors — `mynet` is 10.5.1.0/24. What's wrong?
options: The requested static IP must fall INSIDE the network's subnet — 10.5.0.50 isn't in 10.5.1.0/24. Pick an address inside 10.5.1.0/24, or recreate the network with a covering subnet
Static IPs aren't supported on user-defined networks
Use `--ip-range` on the container instead of `--ip`
The address must be the network's gateway address
explain: `--ip` is an assignment from the network's IPAM pool, not an arbitrary claim — outside the subnet it can't be routed or allocated. EXAM TRAP: 'any IP goes' — IPAM still owns the address space.

q: A SaaS vendor allowlists client IPs. Containers on a Swarm overlay call the SaaS API, but the vendor sees ever-CHANGING source IPs as tasks reschedule across nodes. Which IPs must actually be allowlisted?
options: The container IPs — they're stable per task slot
The Swarm NODES' egress IPs — overlay traffic to the outside leaves via docker_gwbridge and is SNATed to the node's own IP, so the vendor sees node IPs, never container IPs
The service VIP address
The ingress network's addresses
explain: Egress from overlays SNATs at the gwbridge to the node's IP — container/overlay addresses never leave the cluster. Allowlist the nodes' outbound IPs (or front the traffic with a fixed-egress proxy). EXAM TRAP: allowlisting overlay/container IPs, which are invisible past the cluster edge.

q: An engineer runs `docker run --network billing_backend debug-tools` to troubleshoot a stack's network and gets 'network is not attachable'. The name is right — so why the refusal?
options: Stacks don't create real Docker networks
The network doesn't exist under that name

Networks created by `docker stack deploy` are NOT attachable by default — only Swarm services may use them, so standalone containers are rejected. Debug via a one-off SERVICE on that network, or manage the network outside the stack with `--attachable`
Debug containers must use `--network host` instead
explain: Stack networks are service-only unless created attachable — a standalone `docker run` is refused by design. The idiomatic debug move is a temporary `docker service create --network billing_backend` one-shot. EXAM TRAP: assuming the name is wrong — `billing_backend` (stack_network) naming is correct.

q: The team puts containers on macvlan expecting the corporate DHCP server to assign their LAN IPs automatically. Instead, containers get IPs that Docker picks. Why no DHCP?
options: The Docker host firewall blocks DHCP requests
macvlan can't provide LAN IPs at all
Containers need a `--dhcp` flag to request leases
Docker's built-in IPAM allocates from the `--subnet` YOU declare at network creation — there is no built-in DHCP client for containers; getting real DHCP leases needs a third-party IPAM plugin
explain: Built-in IPAM is static allocation from your declared subnet — 'on the LAN' doesn't mean 'uses LAN DHCP'. Coordinate your `--subnet`/`--ip-range` with the network team to avoid collisions. EXAM TRAP: physical-network intuition ('it's on the LAN, so DHCP') applied to Docker's IPAM.

q: A hardening guide says to run containers with `--cap-drop ALL` plus only the capabilities actually needed. A developer objects: 'Dropping ALL capabilities will break everything — containers need their default capability set to function.' Who's right?
options: The guide — capabilities are granular privileges, and dropping ALL then adding back the minimum is textbook least privilege; most apps run fine on a tiny set (many need none of the defaults they never exercise). Test, then add back only what's proven necessary
The developer — the default capability set is mandatory for any container to run
`--cap-drop` only works combined with `--privileged`
Capabilities are a VM concept; they don't apply to containers
explain: The default capability set is broad for compatibility, not necessity — least privilege means starting from zero and justifying each add. EXAM TRAP: 'defaults = requirements' — defaults are a convenience superset, and every unneeded capability is unneeded attack surface.

q: A backup container needs to perform mounts inside the container (the mount(2) syscall), currently blocked by the default seccomp/capability set. The vendor says 'just use --privileged'. What's the precise, less-dangerous alternative — and what does `--privileged` actually do?
options: `--privileged` is the only way to allow mounts in containers

`--cap-add SYS_ADMIN` grants the mount privilege specifically — while `--privileged` disables nearly ALL isolation at once (all capabilities, seccomp filtering, AppArmor confinement, full host /dev access). The vendor's shortcut trades one blocked syscall for removing every guardrail
Mounts are impossible inside containers by design
Use `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` — equivalent capability, but safer than privileged
explain: Mounting needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN — grant exactly that. `--privileged` is the nuclear option: it doesn't just add one capability, it removes the entire containment model. EXAM TRAP: seccomp=unconfined as 'safer' — it removes syscall filtering while adding nothing back.

q: A container's app spawns worker subprocesses. Over days, `ps` inside shows dozens of `<defunct>` zombie processes, and `docker stop` hangs until the kill timeout. The image runs the app directly as PID 1. What's the standard fix?
options: Zombies are harmless kernel bookkeeping; ignore them
Give the container more memory so children exit cleanly

Add `--init` (tini) — PID 1 in a container inherits orphaned children and MUST reap them, plus forward signals; most apps aren't written as init systems. tini reaps zombies and forwards SIGTERM so `docker stop` completes promptly
The image is corrupted; rebuild it from scratch
explain: PID 1 has init duties (reaping, signal forwarding) that normal apps don't implement — `--init` inserts a minimal init (tini) as PID 1 to do them. EXAM TRAP: resource blame — zombies are a reaping failure, not a memory failure.

q: An engineer runs `docker run --secret db_pass ...` on a standalone host and gets an 'unknown flag' error — yet she uses secrets successfully in Swarm services. What's the boundary?
options: The standalone flag is `--secrets` (plural)
Standalone hosts need the secret created with a `--driver local` option first
`docker run` supports secrets only alongside `--privileged`

Swarm secrets are a Swarm-orchestrator feature — they're only mountable into Swarm SERVICE tasks. Standalone `docker run` containers cannot consume them; use env files, bind-mounted files, or an external secrets manager instead
explain: Secrets live in the Swarm Raft store and are delivered by the orchestrator to service tasks — there's no secrets machinery for standalone containers. EXAM TRAP: the plural-flag invention; the real answer is architectural, not syntactic.

q: Where does a Swarm service task's secret actually live at RUNTIME — and why does that matter for forensics?
options: In a tmpfs (in-memory) mount at `/run/secrets/<name>` — never written to disk, never baked into image layers, and hidden from `docker inspect`. A disk image of the node won't contain the secret values (memory forensics aside)
In the container's writable layer under /etc/secrets — `docker export` captures them
In an environment variable the orchestrator injects at startup
In the image layer belonging to the service's image
explain: Secrets are delivered to tmpfs — RAM-only, mode 0444 by default, invisible to inspect and to disk forensics. That's the whole point of secrets-vs-env-vars. EXAM TRAP: the env-var mental model — secrets are files, deliberately NOT environment.

q: The Swarm CA key is suspected compromised. Rotating the join tokens isn't enough — every node certificate chains to that CA. What's the recovery procedure?
options: Nothing can be done — CA keys can't be rotated; rebuild the cluster from scratch
`docker swarm ca --rotate` — generates a new CA and the managers automatically re-issue node certificates; follow up by rotating the join tokens too
`docker swarm leave --force` on every node, then re-init the swarm
Rotate the autolock key — that re-keys the CA as a side effect
explain: `swarm ca --rotate` re-keys the root of trust and re-issues the whole node certificate chain automatically. Token rotation alone leaves the compromised CA signing new certs. EXAM TRAP: the autolock key — that encrypts Raft logs at rest, a completely different key.

q: Swarm node certificates expire after 90 days by default (`--cert-expiry`). A team fears a quarterly outage cliff where nodes suddenly drop. What actually happens at expiry?
options: Nodes drop out of the cluster until an admin manually renews each certificate
The cluster must be re-initialized every 90 days

Nothing breaks — managers automatically renew node certificates BEFORE expiry (the 90-day default is tunable via `--cert-expiry`). Expiry only bites if the managers are down or unreachable at renewal time
Certificates are valid forever; the 90-day figure applies to join tokens
explain: Certificate lifecycle is manager-automated — renewal happens well before expiry with no operator action. The cliff only exists if the control plane itself is unhealthy. EXAM TRAP: the manual-renewal cliff — Swarm handles this like any managed PKI.

q: A service runs with `--read-only` for hardening, but the app legitimately needs scratch space in /tmp and /run. Removing `--read-only` entirely defeats the purpose. What's the established pattern?
options: Drop `--read-only` — it's fundamentally incompatible with real applications
Bind-mount the host's /tmp into the container
Give the container a named volume mounted at /tmp
Keep `--read-only` and add `--tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run` — tmpfs mounts are writable RAM disks that don't weaken the read-only root; the data is ephemeral, which is exactly right for scratch space
explain: tmpfs carve-outs give you writable scratch while the image filesystem stays immutable — the standard read-only-container pattern. A host /tmp bind would punch a hole in the isolation you're buying. EXAM TRAP: 'read-only means nothing writable anywhere' — tmpfs is the designed exception.

q: In MKE, the QA lead needs read-only access to the `production` collection. The admin creates a grant to do it. What three things does every MKE grant bind together?
options: Subject (user/team) + Role (the permission set, e.g. View Only) + Collection (the resource scope) — the grant is the binding of WHO, WHAT they can do, and WHERE
Username + password + collection
Role + node + network
Team + join token + secret
explain: MKE's RBAC triple is subject–role–collection: identity, permission set, and scope. Everything else (LDAP users, teams) feeds into the subject side. EXAM TRAP: credential-flavored distractors — grants are authorization bindings, not authentication material.

q: A hardened RHEL host runs containers with SELinux in enforcing mode. Two requirements: a config directory that must be readable by MULTIPLE containers, and a data directory that must be exclusive to ONE container. Which mount suffixes satisfy both, and what's the hazard?
options: `:z` on both — SELinux makes no shared/private distinction

`:z` (shared — relabels the content for shared container access) on the config dir, `:Z` (private — relabels it exclusively for that one container) on the data dir. Hazard: relabeling host system directories can lock out the host itself or other containers — never `:Z` a dir others need
`:Z` for shared, `:z` for private — capital means shared
SELinux suffixes are deprecated; use `--privileged` instead
explain: Lowercase `:z` = shared label, uppercase `:Z` = private label — and relabeling is a host-visible mutation, so `:Z`-ing a shared system path is a classic self-inflicted outage. EXAM TRAP: the swapped letters, and reaching for `--privileged` to dodge MAC entirely.

q: Four containers share a host. The team sets `--cpu-shares 1024` on the latency-sensitive API 'to guarantee it a full CPU'. During the batch job's spike, the API still starves. Why didn't the setting guarantee anything?
options: cpu-shares are ignored outside Swarm
The value must be expressed as a percentage: `--cpu-shares 100%`

`--cpu-shares` is a RELATIVE weight, not a reservation — 1024 against the default 1024 means equal weight, so it guarantees nothing. For hard guarantees use `--cpus` / CFS quota-period (absolute bandwidth caps), which actually bound and reserve CPU
Shares only take effect combined with `--cpuset-cpus`
explain: Shares divide the pie proportionally during contention; they never reserve a slice. `--cpus 2` is the absolute mechanism. EXAM TRAP: shares-as-guarantee — the single most common CPU-limit misconception on the exam.

q: A scanner reports 200 CVEs in the team's Ubuntu-based image — but the app is a STATIC Go binary needing no shell, package manager, or OS utilities. What's the structural fix?
options: Stay on Ubuntu and patch faster
CVEs in unused packages are false positives; document and ignore them
Switch to a larger base with more debugging tools

Rebuild FROM `scratch` or a distroless/minimal base — unused OS packages are still attack surface AND scanner noise; a static binary needs no distribution at all, which eliminates whole CVE classes by construction
explain: You can't exploit (or be scanned for) what isn't in the image — minimal bases shrink both the attack surface and the CVE backlog structurally, not by patching faster. EXAM TRAP: 'unused = harmless' — unused setuid binaries and libraries are still reachable in many exploit chains.

q: With Docker Content Trust, the team wants developers able to sign `testing` images, but ONLY release managers able to sign `production` tags. Which DCT/Notary concept implements per-tag signing rights?
options: Delegations — Notary delegation roles (e.g. targets/releases-style) grant signing rights scoped to specific tag paths, so devs can hold `targets/testing` while release managers hold `targets/production`; `docker trust inspect` shows who signed what
Run a separate registry per environment
DCT can't distinguish between signers
Use a different Docker Hub account per team
explain: Delegations split the targets role per repository path — cryptographic enforcement of 'who may sign what', verified at pull time. Separate registries/accounts are organizational workarounds, not signing policy. EXAM TRAP: account-per-env as the mechanism — it doesn't scope signing rights.

q: A CI agent container needs the host's Docker socket to build images, but running the agent as ROOT with the socket mounted was flagged in review. What's the least-privilege improvement?
options: There is none — socket access equals host root anyway, so running as root changes nothing

Run the agent as non-root with `--group-add <docker-group-gid>` so its user can read/write the socket via GROUP permission — the socket stays root-owned and the container process isn't root. (Honest caveat: socket access is still ~host-root; this removes the container-root vector, not the socket's inherent power)
`chmod 777` the socket on the host so any user can use it
Use `--privileged` instead of mounting the socket
explain: Group membership grants socket access without container root — strictly better than root+socket, while staying honest that the socket itself remains highly privileged. 777 would let EVERY host user drive the daemon. EXAM TRAP: 'socket = root so why bother' — defense in depth still counts; remove each privilege you can.

q: MKE currently uses built-in users. The company wants single sign-on via corporate Active Directory so that deprovisioning happens in exactly one place. What's supported?
options: MKE supports built-in users only
Sync /etc/passwd from the AD domain controllers
MKE supports external authentication backends — LDAP/AD and SAML/OAuth providers — so users authenticate against the corporate directory while MKE maps them to teams, roles, and collections
AD integration requires reinstalling MKE from scratch
explain: MKE delegates authentication to LDAP/AD or SAML and keeps authorization (teams/roles/collections) internal — joiners/leavers are handled in the directory. EXAM TRAP: the reinstall myth — it's a configuration change, not a rebuild.

q: A team sets DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 on their BUILD server and assumes deployments are now protected against unsigned images. But the deploy agent pulls with DCT unset. What's the gap in their thinking?
options: No gap — signing at build time protects every downstream pull automatically
DCT only works against Docker Hub
Unsigned images can't be pushed once DCT is enabled anywhere

Trust is ENFORCED AT PULL TIME, where the signature is actually verified — so DCT must be enabled on EVERY client that pulls, especially deploy agents. Build-side signing without pull-side verification leaves the deploy path trusting whatever the tag resolves to
explain: Signing and verifying are two halves: the build signs, the puller verifies — and verification only happens where DCT=1 is set at pull time. An unverifying deploy agent will happily run a tampered tag. EXAM TRAP: 'build-side DCT is enough' — the signature is worthless if nobody checks it.

q: A Swarm service runs 3 database replicas, each needing its OWN persistent volume (shared-nothing — one shared volume corrupts, per n=200). How do you get one dedicated named volume per task from a single service definition?
options: `--mount type=volume,source=pgdata-{{.Task.Slot}},target=/var/lib/postgresql/data` — the `{{.Task.Slot}}` template expands per task, so each replica gets its own named volume (pgdata-1, pgdata-2, pgdata-3)
Swarm can't do per-task volumes; run three separate services
Use one volume with a 'shared' driver option
Go templates only work in `--hostname`, not in mounts
explain: Mount sources support the same Go templating as hostnames — `.Task.Slot` (and `.Task.ID`, `.Node.Hostname`) expand per task, giving shared-nothing persistence from one service spec. EXAM TRAP: the single shared volume — the exact corruption scenario from n=200.

q: `docker volume ls` shows dozens of 64-hex-character anonymous volumes from months of `docker run` without `-v`. Plain `docker rm` didn't remove them. How do you remove a container AND its anonymous volumes — and why do NAMED volumes survive the same command?
options: Anonymous volumes are permanent once created

`docker rm -v <container>` removes the container plus its anonymous volumes; NAMED volumes are deliberately preserved (they're the durable-data contract) — `docker volume prune` reclaims unused ones, but it never touches volumes attached to any container
`docker volume rm` deletes volumes even while containers use them
Restart the daemon to garbage-collect orphaned volumes
explain: The `-v` on rm is the anonymous-volume cleanup; named volumes survive because they're presumed to hold data worth keeping. Prune only targets truly unused volumes. EXAM TRAP: expecting prune to nuke everything — in-use volumes are always protected.

q: An engineer hand-configures a container (installs tools, loads 2GB of data into a VOLUME-mounted path), then `docker commit`s it as the new golden image. New containers from that image start EMPTY at that path. Why?
options: `docker commit` is broken for data over 1GB
The data needs `--change` flags to be captured by the commit

`docker commit` captures ONLY the container's writable layer — VOLUME contents are explicitly EXCLUDED (volumes live outside the layered filesystem). The 2GB never entered the image; bake data with COPY in a Dockerfile instead
Commit only works on stopped containers
explain: Volumes are mounts, not layers — commit serializes layers only, so volume data is silently dropped. This is one more reason golden images come from Dockerfiles, not commits. EXAM TRAP: 'commit = snapshot of everything' — volumes are the exception by design.

q: A container bind-mounts `/mnt/backups`. Later, the HOST mounts a new NFS share at `/mnt/backups/nightly` — but the container can't see it. What mount concept controls this, and what's the fix?
options: Bind mounts are point-in-time snapshots; recreate the container after every host mount
Mount the NFS share from inside the container instead
Replace the bind with a named volume

Mount PROPAGATION — the bind defaults to `private`, so new sub-mounts under the source don't propagate in. Use `--mount type=bind,source=/mnt/backups,target=/mnt/backups,bind-propagation=rshared` (and the host mount itself must be shared) so sub-mounts appear in the container
explain: Propagation mode decides whether mount/unmount events cross the bind boundary; `private` (default) isolates them, `rshared` lets sub-mounts flow both ways recursively. EXAM TRAP: recreating the container — the bind itself is fine; it's the propagation that's private.

q: A stack's Compose file needs a host path mounted, but the team wants it declared as a NAMED volume (uniform volume semantics, driver options) rather than a bare bind mount. What's the trick?
options: Create it through the local driver with bind options: `docker volume create --driver local --opt type=none --opt device=/srv/data --opt o=bind srvdata` — the 'volume' IS a bind mount under the hood, usable as a named volume everywhere including stacks
Stacks forbid host paths entirely; it's impossible
Named volumes can never reference host paths
Declare it with `external: true` and a filesystem path
explain: The local driver's `type=none, o=bind, device=<path>` options turn any host path into a first-class named volume — the standard way to get bind behavior with volume ergonomics in Swarm stacks. EXAM TRAP: 'forbidden' — it's fully supported, just spelled through driver opts.

q: A Kubernetes team is tired of admins pre-creating a PersistentVolume for every single claim. They want PVCs to trigger AUTOMATIC volume creation from their cloud block storage. Which object enables that?
options: A larger etcd cluster for faster binding
A StorageClass (with a provisioner) — PVCs referencing it trigger DYNAMIC provisioning: the provisioner creates the PV automatically. Without one, binding needs a pre-created static PV
A hostPath volume with auto-create enabled
An emptyDir with `persistent: true`
explain: StorageClass + provisioner = dynamic provisioning; no StorageClass = static PVs an admin must create. This is the K8s answer to 'who creates the disk'. EXAM TRAP: the invented `persistent: true` emptyDir flag — emptyDir is never persistent.

q: A PVC is deleted during a namespace teardown — and the team discovers the backing cloud disk was deleted WITH it. The data is gone; they wanted the disk preserved for forensics. What controls this, and what's the safer setting?
options: Nothing controls it; cloud disks always delete with their PVC
The StorageClass name determines deletion

`persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy` — `Delete` (common default with dynamic provisioning) removes the backing storage along with the PV; `Retain` keeps the disk so it can be manually reclaimed. For precious data use Retain — though Retain is NOT a backup strategy
Mark the PV read-only to prevent deletion
explain: Reclaim policy is the data-lifecycle knob: Delete = disk goes with the claim, Retain = disk survives for manual recovery. Dynamic provisioning often defaults to Delete, which is the surprise here. EXAM TRAP: 'Retain = backup' — it preserves the disk, not a restorable backup.

q: An image ships seed data at `/app/seed`. The FIRST deploy populates the named volume correctly — but a v2 image with UPDATED seed data deploys and the volume still holds v1 data. Why, and what's the robust pattern?
options: Named volumes re-sync from the image on every container start; this is a daemon bug
Clear the image layer cache on the nodes
Volumes fundamentally can't hold seed data

Docker copies image content into a named volume ONLY when the volume is brand-new and empty — afterward the volume always wins. For re-seeding on every deploy, use an entrypoint/init script that syncs or version-checks the seed data at container start
explain: First-use population is a one-time bootstrap, not a sync mechanism — the volume is authoritative after that. Versioned entrypoint seeding is the standard pattern for evolving seed data. EXAM TRAP: expecting continuous image→volume sync; it happens exactly once.

q: A `docker run` includes `-v cfg:/etc/app -v ./local.cfg:/etc/app/config.yaml`. The app sees NEITHER the volume's files NOR the bind file reliably. What's the mount-order rule being violated?
options: Last mount wins on the same target — the second `-v` SHADOWS (hides) the first at overlapping paths. Mounts never merge; restructure so targets don't overlap (e.g. mount the volume at /etc/app and the file beside it)
Docker merges both mounts into a union view
The first mount always wins over later ones
Bind mounts are silently ignored whenever a named volume is present
explain: Mounts stack by hiding, not merging — the later mount obscures whatever was at that path, including an earlier volume's content. Overlapping targets are the bug. EXAM TRAP: the union/merge mental model — that's overlayfs layers, not mounts.

q: A container uses `--tmpfs /scratch` for temp files, but a runaway job filled host RAM and tripped the OOM killer. How do you put a hard bound on a tmpfs mount?
options: tmpfs mounts can't be bounded; switch to a named volume

`--mount type=tmpfs,target=/scratch,tmpfs-size=512m` — caps that mount's RAM usage (writes past it fail with 'no space left'). The `--tmpfs` shorthand takes no options, which is exactly why the long syntax exists
Append `size=512m` to the `--tmpfs` shorthand flag
tmpfs is exempt from all limits by kernel design
explain: `tmpfs-size` bounds the mount independently of the container's memory limit — but only via the long `--mount` syntax, since the shorthand accepts no options. EXAM TRAP: inventing shorthand options; the shorthand is deliberately minimal.

q: A Swarm config holding the app's feature flags must change weekly. The engineer edits the local file and re-runs `docker config create app_cfg` — 'already exists'. What's the correct rotation procedure?
options: Run `docker config update app_cfg` with the new file
Configs are immutable and can never change — rebuild the cluster

Create `app_cfg_v2`, then `docker service update --config-rm app_cfg --config-add source=app_cfg_v2,target=/etc/app/flags.yaml web` — like secrets, configs are immutable; rotation is version-plus-service-update (rolling, no downtime)
Edit the config file directly on each manager's filesystem
explain: Configs are immutable objects — same rotation dance as secrets: mint a versioned replacement, roll the service onto it. There is no update-in-place. EXAM TRAP: the invented `docker config update`; and editing manager filesystems, which changes nothing in Raft.

q: A stack's database needs its named volume provisioned by a SHARED-storage driver (not local) — and in prod the volume is pre-created by the storage team. How is this declared in the Compose file?
options: Stacks can't use non-local volume drivers
The driver is auto-detected at deploy time
Put the driver choice under the service's `deploy:` key

In the top-level `volumes:` block — `dbdata:` with `driver:` (plus `driver_opts:`) to select provisioning, or `external: true` (optionally with `name:`) to consume the pre-created volume instead of creating one
explain: Volume driver selection lives in the top-level `volumes:` declaration (`driver`/`driver_opts`); `external: true` says 'don't create it, it already exists'. Driver choice is a volume property, not a deploy property. EXAM TRAP: stuffing it under `deploy:` — that's for placement/resources, not storage.

q: A Kubernetes pod needs ~2GB of RAM-disk scratch space shared between its two containers — blazing fast, and guaranteed GONE when the pod dies. Which volume fits?
options: `emptyDir` with `medium: Memory` (and a `sizeLimit`) — a tmpfs-backed emptyDir shared by all containers in the pod, wiped with the pod. (Without `medium: Memory`, emptyDir is node DISK, not RAM)
A hostPath mount of the node's /dev/shm
A 2Gi PersistentVolumeClaim
A configMap with binaryData
explain: `medium: Memory` turns emptyDir into a pod-scoped RAM disk — shared, ephemeral, fast. hostPath ties you to a specific node; a PVC is persistent overkill. EXAM TRAP: plain emptyDir — that's disk-backed unless you ask for Memory.

q: On Docker Desktop for Mac, a bind-mounted PHP app takes ~8 seconds per page load; on native Linux it's instant. Same code, same container. What's the known Desktop-specific tuning?
options: Buy a faster Mac — it's a hardware problem

Set a mount consistency flag, e.g. `-v ~/app:/app:delegated` (or `cached`) — it relaxes host↔VM file-sync consistency for speed where the container's view may lag slightly; the default `consistent` (perfect sync) is brutally slow through the macOS VM boundary
Run the container with `--privileged` for faster I/O
Bind mounts are unusable on Desktop; switch everything to COPY
explain: Desktop's Linux VM syncs every filesystem event across the macOS boundary under `consistent` — `cached`/`delegated` trade a little staleness for an order-of-magnitude speedup on file-heavy workloads. EXAM TRAP: hardware blame for what's really a sync-consistency tax.

q: A container writes to a bind-mounted NFS share as root, but the files land owned by `nobody:nogroup` and the app can't read them back. The identical container on local disk works fine. What's happening?
options: Docker automatically remaps root on NFS mounts
The NFS export must be read-only

NFS `root_squash` (the default on most servers) maps client-side root to `nobody` — the container's root is NOT the server's root. Fix server-side (`no_root_squash` for trusted hosts, or align anonuid/anongid) or run the writer as a non-root UID the server recognizes
Bind mounts don't function over NFS
explain: root_squash is a server-side NFS protection: remote root gets squashed to nobody. It's the NFS server doing this, not Docker — local disk works because there's no squash in play. EXAM TRAP: blaming Docker for the server's access policy.

q: A host is out of disk and a named volume is the prime suspect — but `docker system df` only shows aggregate volume usage. How do you find exactly where that volume's data lives on the host?
options: Volume data lives inside the daemon's memory, not on disk
`docker volume ls` prints the host path
Guess under /var/lib/docker/volumes by hashing the name
`docker volume inspect <name>` → the `Mountpoint` field (e.g. /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data) — that's the host path; `du -sh` it directly for the real size
explain: `volume inspect` exposes the Mountpoint — the host-side directory backing the volume — so you can measure and examine it directly. `volume ls` shows names and drivers only. EXAM TRAP: assuming ls-level commands reveal paths; inspect is the introspection tool.

q: An engineer copies a data directory OUT of a container: `docker cp web:/app/data ./data`. The files land owned by root with mangled permissions, breaking the restore. What preserves ownership and modes?
options: `docker cp -a web:/app/data ./data` — archive mode preserves UIDs, GIDs, and permission bits; without `-a`, ownership and modes are not faithfully preserved, and root-owned copies are the classic surprise
`docker cp` always preserves permissions; the problem must be the destination filesystem
Use `docker export` instead of `docker cp`
chown the files inside the container before copying
explain: Archive mode (`-a`) is what makes `docker cp` permission-faithful — default copies don't carry ownership/modes reliably, especially across the root-owned daemon boundary. EXAM TRAP: 'cp preserves everything' — only with `-a`.

q: A service pulls its image from AWS ECR, created with `--with-registry-auth` after `docker login`. It works fine for 12 hours — then newly rescheduled tasks start failing with pull access denied, while already-running tasks are unaffected. Repeating the login and redeploy fixes it for another 12 hours. What is happening?
options: ECR deletes images 12 hours after push — the images must be re-pushed on a schedule

ECR registry tokens expire (12 hours); the credential stored in the swarm's Raft state goes stale, so newly scheduled tasks can't authenticate. Fix: re-login and run `docker service update <svc> --with-registry-auth` on a schedule to refresh the stored credential
The `--with-registry-auth` flag itself expires — it must be combined with `--detach=false` to persist
Workers cache the registry token for 12 hours — restart the worker daemons to clear the cache
explain: With expiring registries (ECR, ACR), the auth captured in Raft at create/update time goes stale — running tasks are fine (they already pulled), but NEW tasks fail to authenticate. The documented practice: a periodic `docker login` plus `docker service update <svc> --with-registry-auth`, which refreshes the stored credential without otherwise changing the service. 'Re-push images' and 'restart workers' misdiagnose a credential-expiry problem as an image or node problem — the error is auth, and it's time-bound.

q: A stateful queue worker needs up to 60 seconds to drain in-flight jobs on SIGTERM before exiting. During `docker service update`, tasks are SIGKILLed 10 seconds after SIGTERM and jobs are lost mid-flight. Which service setting fixes this, and what is the default it overrides?
options: `--update-delay 90s` — it pauses 90 seconds between task updates so jobs finish
`--restart-delay 90s` — it delays the restart, giving jobs time to drain
`--health-interval 90s` — it slows health checks so the task isn't marked unhealthy during drain
`--stop-grace-period 90s` on the service — it extends the wait between SIGTERM and SIGKILL, whose default is 10s
explain: `--stop-grace-period` controls how long the daemon waits after SIGTERM before sending SIGKILL (default 10s) — the exact knob for graceful drain. `--update-delay` only spaces out batches of the rolling update, `--restart-delay` spaces restart attempts after failure, and health check timing doesn't change how a task is stopped. Set the grace period longer than the worst-case drain, and make sure the app actually handles SIGTERM.

q: A nightly reconciliation task must run exactly 3 parallel workers, each processing a shard, and STOP when all three finish — never restart, never linger. Defined as a normal replicated service with `--restart-condition none`, the tasks finish but the service keeps its 'desired state' semantics, and updates/VIPs make no sense for it. Which service mode is designed for run-to-completion work?
options: `--mode global` — it runs the task on every node exactly once, which equals 3 workers
Keep the replicated service — jobs are just services with `--restart-condition none`; no separate mode exists
`--mode replicated-job` — Swarm runs the tasks to completion (3 in parallel here) and stops; finished jobs aren't resurrected the way long-running services are
`--mode global-job` — it runs exactly 3 jobs total, spread across the swarm
explain: Swarm's job modes (`replicated-job`, `global-job`) change the orchestrator's goal from 'keep N running forever' to 'run to completion': replicated-job runs N tasks until they finish; global-job runs one per node until done. A replicated service with `restart-condition none` approximates it but keeps service semantics (rolling updates, VIPs, endless desired-state) that jobs don't need. The trap is 'jobs are just services' — the mode genuinely changes reconciliation behavior.

q: The daemon default log driver is `json-file`, but the `payments` service must ship its logs to the corporate syslog server — without changing the daemon default for every other service. Can one service use a different log driver?
options: No — the log driver is daemon-wide; every service uses the default, no exceptions
Yes — set it in the Dockerfile with a `LOGDRIVER=syslog` instruction
Yes — run `dockerd --log-driver syslog` on whichever nodes run the payments tasks

Yes — `docker service create --log-driver syslog --log-opt syslog-address=tcp://logs.corp:514 payments` — services accept their own `--log-driver`/`--log-opt`, overriding the daemon default per service
explain: `--log-driver` and `--log-opt` on `docker service create` (or the `logging:` section in Compose) override the daemon default for that service's tasks only — the standard way to route one service to syslog/splunk/awslogs while everything else stays json-file. 'Daemon-wide only' is the trap; there is no LOGDRIVER Dockerfile instruction, and changing the daemon flag affects the whole host. Remember the consequence: with a remote driver, `docker logs` on the node stops working for those tasks.

q: A 3-manager Swarm lost two managers permanently — disks destroyed, no backups of those nodes. The surviving manager holds an intact Raft log but has no quorum, so the cluster is frozen. What is the documented recovery procedure?
options: On the survivor, run `docker swarm init --force-new-cluster --advertise-addr <its-ip>` to start a new single-manager Swarm from its Raft state, then join fresh managers and workers
Run `docker swarm join-token --rotate` on the survivor; the new tokens restore quorum automatically
Delete `/var/lib/docker/swarm` on the survivor and re-init — the workers will repopulate the state
Wait 72 hours; Raft automatically elects the survivor as leader once the others' leases expire
explain: `--force-new-cluster` is the disaster-recovery escape hatch: it converts the surviving manager's Raft data into a fresh single-manager cluster, discarding the dead managers' membership. Afterwards you join new managers (to rebuild an odd-numbered control plane) and rejoin workers. Rotating tokens changes credentials, not Raft membership; deleting the swarm directory destroys the very state you're trying to save; and Raft never self-heals a lost quorum — a majority is a majority.

q: `docker node ls` shows worker4 with `Status: Down` and `Availability: Active`. A teammate says 'it's drained, that's why tasks left it.' Another says 'the node is unreachable.' Who is right, and where is the distinction recorded?
options: The first teammate — Down and Drained mean the same thing in the node listing

The second — `Status` (Ready/Down/Disconnected) is the node's health as seen by the manager via heartbeats; `Availability` (Active/Pause/Drain) is the admin-set scheduling intent. Down + Active means the node stopped heartbeating unexpectedly, not that it was drained
Neither — a node can't be Down and Active at the same time; the listing is corrupted
The first — Availability Active is just the default label and carries no meaning
explain: Status and Availability are independent columns: Status reflects liveness (the manager hasn't heard heartbeats → Down), Availability reflects intent (you set Drain for maintenance). Down + Active = the node died or lost network without warning — tasks get rescheduled, and you investigate the host. Down + Drain = you drained it deliberately and it went offline. `docker node inspect` shows both fields; confusing them leads to 'maintaining' a node that's actually crashed.

q: A stack is deployed with `docker stack deploy --resolve-image never -c app.yml shop`. A teammate worries this is dangerous. What does the flag do, and when is `never` actually the right choice?
options: It skips pulling entirely — tasks reuse whatever image is cached on each node; correct only for fully air-gapped hosts where images are pre-loaded

It tells Swarm not to contact the registry to resolve the tag to a digest at deploy time — every task pulls whatever the tag currently points to. `never` fits air-gapped or digest-pinned workflows where you don't want deploy-time resolution
It disables image resolution for the lifetime of the stack — tasks can never pull new images again
It forces Swarm to resolve the digest once and pin it forever, which is the safest option
explain: By default (`always`/`changed`) Swarm resolves each tag to a digest at deploy time so all tasks run identical bits. `--resolve-image never` skips that registry lookup — useful when the registry is unreachable (air-gapped) or when you've already pinned digests and want zero deploy-time registry dependence. The trade-off is exactly what the teammate fears: with a mutable tag, different nodes can pull different bits. It's not 'skip pulling' — nodes still pull; they just don't pre-resolve.

q: A 6-replica cache service must spread across 6 nodes — never two replicas on the same node — for blast-radius isolation. Placement preferences (`spread=node.id`) are only soft hints. Which hard mechanism enforces 'at most one replica per node'?
options: Switch the service to `--mode global`, which places exactly one task per node
`--replicas-max-per-node 1`, which caps how many tasks of the service can land on any single node
Add a constraint `node.hostname != node.hostname`, which forces unique hosts
Set `--update-parallelism 1` so tasks start one at a time on different nodes
explain: `--replicas-max-per-node 1` is the hard cap: the scheduler will never place two tasks of this service on one node. Global mode also yields one-per-node but runs on EVERY node (including future ones) — wrong when you want exactly 6 replicas. Spread preferences are soft hints the scheduler may violate under pressure, and update-parallelism only paces rollouts. Note the exam wording: 'max replicas per node' = `--replicas-max-per-node`, not a placement preference.

q: A Swarm cluster has GPU-equipped nodes for an inference service. Each task needs exactly 2 GPUs, and tasks must never land on non-GPU nodes. The nodes expose GPUs through the Docker Engine's generic resources. Which service definition is correct?
options: `docker service create --name infer --replicas 4 --generic-resource "NVIDIA-GPU=2" infer:2.0` — the scheduler only places tasks on nodes advertising that generic resource, 2 GPUs per task
`docker service create --name infer --gpus 2 infer:2.0` — Swarm schedules GPUs with the same flag as `docker run`
`docker service create --name infer --constraint node.labels.gpu==true --env NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2 infer:2.0`
GPUs can't be scheduled by Swarm; the inference service must run as standalone `docker run --gpus` containers
explain: `--generic-resource "NVIDIA-GPU=2"` is Swarm's GPU scheduling: nodes advertise discrete resources (configured on the daemon), and the scheduler matches tasks to nodes that have them — no manual node labels needed. `--gpus` is a `docker run`-only flag; Swarm doesn't accept it. The label+env hack schedules correctly only if you maintain the labels by hand and doesn't reserve the GPUs. Swarm has scheduled generic resources since Engine 19.03.

q: A team configures automatic rollback on update failure (`--update-failure-action rollback`), but the rollback itself slams all 30 tasks at once and overloads the database on restart. Which flags pace the ROLLBACK independently of the update?
options: There are none — a rollback always mirrors the update's parallelism and delay settings

`--rollback-parallelism`, `--rollback-delay` (and `--rollback-monitor`, `--rollback-order`, `--rollback-max-failure-ratio`) — rollbacks have their own full set of tuning flags, separate from the `--update-*` family
`--update-parallelism` and `--update-delay` — rollbacks reuse whatever the update used, so lower those
Rollbacks can't be paced; the only fix is `--update-failure-action pause` and a manual rollback
explain: Every `--update-*` flag has a `--rollback-*` twin: `--rollback-parallelism`, `--rollback-delay`, `--rollback-monitor`, `--rollback-order`, `--rollback-max-failure-ratio`, `--rollback-failure-action`. The rollback is its own rolling operation with its own pacing — a thundering-herd rollback is fixed with rollback flags, not by slowing normal updates. 'Rollback mirrors the update' is the trap; the two configurations are fully independent.

q: An MKE control plane is destroyed by a datacenter fire, but the encrypted backup (`mke-backup.tar`, passphrase stored in the vault) survived. The team has fresh hosts. What is the correct restore sequence?
options: Untar the backup on one host and copy the files into `/var/lib/docker` — the daemon picks up the state
Run `docker swarm init` on the fresh hosts, then `docker config create` for each entry found by inspecting the tar

Install a fresh single-node MKE, then run the `mirantis/ucp restore` container with the same `--passphrase`, feeding it the backup tar — it rebuilds Swarm state, configs, and access control from the backup
Restore is impossible — MKE backups only work on the original hosts
explain: MKE restore = fresh install first (so there's a working Engine and swarm), then `mirantis/ucp restore --passphrase <same> < backup.tar` replays the backed-up Swarm state, configs, secrets and grants. Manually untarring into `/var/lib/docker` corrupts Raft state, and rebuilding by hand from tar inspection is error-prone fiction. The passphrase point from the backup question returns here: wrong or lost passphrase = unusable backup, on any hosts.

q: A company runs MKE with 3 controller (manager) nodes and 10 workers. After joining a 4th manager to the Swarm for extra Raft resilience, the engineer is surprised that MKE's control-plane components are already running on it — no separate MKE install step was needed. Why?
options: MKE components are deployed as global Swarm services, so any node joining as a manager automatically gets the controller workloads scheduled onto it
The new manager inherited the components through the Raft log replication
MKE only runs on the first manager; what the engineer sees are stale `docker ps` entries
Joining with the manager token automatically re-runs the MKE installer
explain: MKE installs its control plane (ucp-agent, ucp-auth, Kubernetes components) as Swarm services — many in global mode constrained to managers. Joining a new manager extends the Swarm, and the orchestrator schedules the controller workloads onto it with no extra install step. The Raft log carries cluster state, not container images; nothing 're-runs the installer.' This is also why keeping user workloads off managers matters: controllers share those nodes with the control plane.

q: A CI pipeline runs `docker service update --image shop/api:2.1 web` and immediately reports success — but the pipeline needs to block until every task is actually running the new image before running smoke tests. As written, the command returns as soon as the update STARTS. Which flag makes it wait for convergence?
options: Append `--detach=false` — the CLI blocks until the update converges (or fails) instead of returning after dispatch
Append `--quiet` — it suppresses output until the update finishes
Use `docker service update --wait web` — the dedicated wait flag
Nothing can do this; the pipeline must poll `docker service ps` in a loop
explain: `docker service update` defaults to `--detach=true` (fire and forget — the opposite of `docker service create`, which defaults to detach=false). `--detach=false` makes the CLI follow the rollout to convergence or failure, which is what a pipeline gate needs. `--quiet` only trims output, `--wait` isn't a real flag here, and hand-rolled polling duplicates what `--detach=false` already does — including surfacing the failure exit code.

q: A Compose file sets `depends_on: [db]` for the api service so the database starts first. Deployed with `docker stack deploy`, the api tasks still start before db is ready and crash-loop until db accepts connections. The developer insists `depends_on` is broken. What is actually happening?
options: `depends_on` is broken in Compose file version 3 — downgrading to version 2 fixes stack deploys
Stack deploy requires `depends_on` under the `deploy:` section; at the service top level it's ignored

`depends_on` only controls startup ORDER, never readiness — and `docker stack deploy` ignores it entirely. Swarm has no startup ordering; services must retry connections (or use healthcheck-gated logic) until dependencies are ready
The db service needs `restart: always` for `depends_on` to take effect
explain: Two truths: `depends_on` never waited for readiness even under `docker compose up` (it only orders container START), and `docker stack deploy` ignores `depends_on` completely — Swarm schedules all services' tasks concurrently with no ordering guarantees. The robust pattern is retry-with-backoff in the app (or an entrypoint wait-for-it script), not orchestration ordering. Moving it under `deploy:` is invented syntax, and version 2 vs 3 doesn't change stack behavior.

q: A Kubernetes Deployment was updated 4 times today; the latest rollout is bad. The engineer knows `kubectl rollout undo` reverts to the previous revision, but she wants to see WHAT changed in each revision first, and possibly jump back TWO revisions. Which commands?
options: `kubectl rollout history deployment/api` lists revisions with their change causes; `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api --to-revision=2` jumps to a specific one
`kubectl get revisions deployment/api` and `kubectl rollback deployment/api --revision=2`
Kubernetes only keeps the current and previous ReplicaSet — older revisions are unrecoverable
Revisions aren't tracked; she must re-apply the old manifest from git
explain: Deployments keep a revision history (old ReplicaSets, capped by `revisionHistoryLimit`, default 10): `kubectl rollout history` shows each revision and its change-cause annotation, and `rollout undo --to-revision=N` targets any retained revision — not just the previous one. The wrong options invent commands (`get revisions`, bare `kubectl rollback`) or claim only one revision is kept. Swarm analogy: this is the K8s equivalent of `docker service rollback`, with finer revision control.

q: In MKE, the release team needs to deploy and update services in the `production` collection but must NOT be able to exec into running containers or change cluster-wide settings. The QA team needs read-only visibility. Which role assignments express this?
options: Both teams get Full Control on the collection — MKE can't split deploy from exec permissions
QA gets View Only; release gets Full Control, since deploy rights always include exec
Both teams get the Restricted Control role, which is read-only plus deploy
QA team → View Only grant; release team → Scheduler grant (can create/update services and schedule workloads, but not exec into containers or manage the cluster)
explain: MKE's role ladder is None → View Only → Scheduler → Operator/Full Control. Scheduler is precisely 'deploy and manage workloads without host-level access': it can create/update services but can't `docker exec` into containers or touch cluster settings. View Only is read-only dashboards and logs. The trap answers either claim the split is impossible or invent semantics for Restricted Control — the Scheduler/View Only pairing is the textbook least-privilege answer.

q: `docker service ps web` shows dozens of `Shutdown`-state tasks from weeks of updates, burying the two `Running` tasks the engineer is debugging. She wants old task history trimmed automatically going forward. Which setting controls this?
options: `docker service update --prune-history web` — removes shutdown tasks for that service
The task history limit, set cluster-wide with `docker swarm update --task-history-limit 5` (default 5) — only that many non-running tasks per service are retained
Task history can't be trimmed; `docker service ps` always shows every task ever created
`docker system prune` — it also cleans shutdown service tasks
explain: Swarm retains a bounded history of shut-down tasks per service (default 5), controlled cluster-wide by `docker swarm update --task-history-limit N`. Dozens of Shutdown entries means someone raised it (or the default display is just noisy — the running tasks sort to the top with `--filter desired-state=running`). `--prune-history` isn't a real flag, `system prune` doesn't touch Swarm task history, and history is never infinite.

q: A Dockerfile runs `pip install` of 2GB of dependencies on every build because each build starts from an empty package cache, adding 8 minutes. The cache must NOT end up in the final image layers. Which BuildKit feature solves this?
options: Add the package cache directory to `.dockerignore` so it's excluded from the image
`RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt` — a BuildKit cache mount persists the package cache across builds without creating a layer containing it
Copy the cache into the image with `COPY --from=cache` and delete it in a later `RUN`
Set `ENV PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=off` — the cache then lives in a layer Docker reuses automatically
explain: `--mount=type=cache` gives a RUN step a persistent cache directory that survives across builds but is never committed to any layer — the package downloads happen once, subsequent builds reuse them, and the image stays lean. `.dockerignore` only affects the build context, COPY-then-delete still bloats the earlier layer (layers are additive), and `PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=off` inside a layer just bakes megabytes of cache into the image. Cache mounts are the BuildKit answer to 'fast rebuilds, small images.'
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: During `docker build`, a `RUN` step must reach an internal artifact server at `artifacts.corp` that only resolves via the host's `/etc/hosts` — and another step needs the host's network stack directly. Which build flags provide these?
options: `--add-host=artifacts.corp:10.0.0.50` adds the hosts entry for build steps; `--network=host` gives the build access to the host's network stack
`--dns=10.0.0.50` for the hosts entry and `--network=bridge` for host networking
Neither is possible — builds always run on an isolated network with no host access
Set both in the Dockerfile with `HOSTS` and `NETWORK` instructions
explain: `docker build` accepts `--add-host` (extra `/etc/hosts` entries during the build) and `--network` (which network build containers use, including `host`). There are no `HOSTS`/`NETWORK` Dockerfile instructions, `--dns` sets resolvers not static entries, and builds are not forced onto isolation — the flags exist precisely for artifact servers, internal proxies, and license servers reachable only from the host network.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A company proxies all external traffic. Every `docker pull` of Docker Hub images should be served from the internal pull-through cache at `mirror.corp:5000` to save bandwidth and survive Hub rate limits — without developers changing their image references. How is this configured?
options: Run every pull as `docker pull mirror.corp:5000/library/nginx` — there is no transparent way
Set `"registry-mirrors": ["https://mirror.corp:5000"]` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` on each host and reload the daemon — pulls for Hub images transparently try the mirror first
Add the mirror to `insecure-registries` — that also enables mirror mode
Configure the mirror in each developer's `~/.docker/config.json` under `mirrors`
explain: `registry-mirrors` in daemon.json is the transparent pull-through cache: the daemon tries the mirror first for Hub images and falls back to Hub on miss — no image reference changes needed anywhere. `insecure-registries` only allowlists plain-HTTP registries (unrelated to mirroring), there is no `mirrors` key in the client config.json, and rewriting every reference defeats the purpose. This is a daemon-level setting, so it must be rolled out to every host (or baked into the provisioning).
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: After the `latest`-tag incident, a team pins their base image too: `FROM ubuntu:22.04` silently changed underneath them when upstream rebuilt the tag. They want the base image pinned to exact bits, not a mutable tag. What is the correct Dockerfile syntax?
options: `FROM ubuntu:22.04 --immutable` — the flag freezes the tag at first build
`FROM ubuntu:22.04` plus `docker build --no-cache` — the fresh pull guarantees the newest bits, which is the same thing
Base images can't be pinned; only final deployment images support digests
`FROM ubuntu@sha256:9c8c7...` — referencing the base by digest pins the exact content; tags can move but digests are immutable
explain: Digests work in FROM exactly as in deployment specs: `FROM repo@sha256:<digest>` locks the base to immutable bits, so upstream tag rebuilds can't silently change your build. `--immutable` isn't a real FROM flag, `--no-cache` does the opposite (it guarantees you get the MOVED tag), and digest pinning applies to any image reference including bases. Record the digest when you vet a base, and bump it deliberately like any dependency.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An image uses a custom entrypoint script that does setup work, then starts the app. After adopting it, `docker stop` takes the full 10 seconds and config reloads via SIGHUP never reach the app. The script ends with `$@` instead of `exec "$@"`. Why does that one word matter?
options: `exec` is only a performance optimization; the signal problem must come from the app ignoring signals
The script needs `#!/bin/bash -e` instead; `exec` is unrelated to signals
Docker can't send signals to entrypoint scripts at all — only to the CMD process
Without `exec`, the app runs as a child of the shell script, which stays PID 1 — signals from `docker stop` go to the shell (which doesn't forward them), and the app never receives SIGTERM or SIGHUP
explain: `exec "$@"` REPLACES the shell process with the app, making the app PID 1 so it receives SIGTERM/SIGHUP directly. Without it, the shell remains PID 1 and the app is its child — the shell doesn't forward signals, so `docker stop`'s SIGTERM is swallowed and Docker waits out the 10s timeout before SIGKILL. This is the same PID-1 lesson as shell-form vs exec-form ENTRYPOINT, applied to wrapper scripts: end every entrypoint script with `exec "$@"`.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
