q: An image sets `ENTRYPOINT ["/app/server"]` and `CMD ["--prod"]`. For a one-off debug session, the engineer needs a shell instead of the server — without rebuilding the image. Which command does it?
options: `docker run img --entrypoint /bin/sh` — the flag goes after the image name like CMD overrides
`docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh img` — `--entrypoint` overrides the image's ENTRYPOINT, and any trailing args become the shell's arguments
It's impossible — ENTRYPOINT is baked in; only CMD can be overridden at runtime
`docker run -e ENTRYPOINT=/bin/sh img` — entrypoint is controlled by an environment variable
explain: `--entrypoint` (before the image name) replaces the image's ENTRYPOINT for that run; trailing CLI args then feed the NEW entrypoint. So `docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh img -c "..."` gives a debug shell. The flag must precede the image name (everything after is the command), ENTRYPOINT is absolutely overridable at runtime, and no env var controls it. Contrast with Q26: bare args after the image replace CMD only — `--entrypoint` replaces the executable itself.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A monorepo keeps Dockerfiles at `docker/Dockerfile.api`, `docker/Dockerfile.worker`, etc. — there is no `Dockerfile` at the context root. The pipeline runs `docker build -t api .` and fails with `Dockerfile: no such file`. What's the fix, and what does the context remain?
options: Move the Dockerfiles to the root — Docker only ever reads `./Dockerfile`
`docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.api -t api .` — `-f` points at the Dockerfile while the context stays `.` (the repo root), so `COPY` paths are still relative to the root
`docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.api docker/` — both the file and context move into `docker/`
Rename one to `Dockerfile` per build — `-f` doesn't exist for `docker build`
explain: `-f` decouples the Dockerfile location from the context: `-f docker/Dockerfile.api` with context `.` keeps all `COPY`/`ADD` paths relative to the repo root — exactly what a monorepo wants. Pointing the context at `docker/` instead would break every `COPY src/...` in the file. Moving files per build is toil, and `-f` very much exists. Remember the pairing: `-f` = which recipe, final arg = which context.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A pipeline builds an image with `cat Dockerfile | docker build -t quickfix -`. The build fails at `COPY app/ /app/` with `COPY failed: no such file`. The Dockerfile is valid and `docker build .` works locally. What is different about the stdin build?
options: Stdin builds are deprecated and silently ignore all COPY instructions
The pipe corrupted the Dockerfile — stdin builds require `--no-cache`
A build from stdin has NO build context, so `COPY`/`ADD` have nothing to copy from; only instructions that don't reference the context (RUN, ENV, etc.) work
The `-t` flag is incompatible with stdin builds; the tag must be applied with `docker tag` afterwards
explain: `docker build -` reads the Dockerfile from stdin, but there is no context tarball — the daemon receives only the recipe, no files. Any `COPY`/`ADD` referencing context paths fails, while `RUN curl ...` style builds work fine. `-t` works normally with stdin builds. If you need both stdin convenience and files, use `docker build -f- . < Dockerfile` (Dockerfile from stdin, context from `.`) or BuildKit's named contexts.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A developer wants to check a freshly built image for known CVEs on her laptop — BEFORE pushing it to the registry where MSR scanning would catch it. No registry-side scan has run yet. Which command gives her a local vulnerability report?
options: `docker scout cves shop/api:2.0` — Docker Scout analyzes the local image against vulnerability databases and reports CVEs by package, no push required
`docker scan` is the only local option, and it requires pushing first
`docker images --vulnerabilities shop/api:2.0` — the flag lists CVEs from the local image store
Local scanning is impossible; she must push and wait for the registry scan
explain: Docker Scout (`docker scout cves`, `docker scout quickview`) scans local images against its vulnerability database without any push — shift-left scanning for the laptop. The wrong options invent flags (`--vulnerabilities`) or claim locality is impossible. Complement, don't confuse: Scout is the client-side scanner, MSR/DTR scanning is the registry-side gate that can block promotion — the exam pairs them as defense in depth, and neither replaces signing (DCT).
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: On a shared CI runner, `~/.docker/config.json` holds registry credentials as base64 `auth` blobs — anyone with read access to the home directory can decode them. The team wants credentials kept in the OS keychain instead of the JSON file. Which client configuration does this?
options: Set `"insecure-registries"` — it moves credentials out of config.json automatically
Set `"credsStore": "secretservice"` (Linux) or `"credsStore": "desktop"` (Docker Desktop) — Docker stores credentials in the OS-native credential helper instead of base64 in config.json
Run `docker login --encrypt` — it encrypts the auth blob in place
Credentials can't leave config.json; the fix is `chmod 600` and nothing more
explain: `credsStore` delegates credential storage to an external helper (OS keychain, `pass`, cloud KMS helpers) — config.json then holds only a marker, not the secret. This is the documented answer to the base64-is-not-encryption problem from Q128. `insecure-registries` is about TLS, `--encrypt` isn't a login flag, and while `chmod 600` is good hygiene, it doesn't change the storage mechanism on a shared runner where the job user itself can read the file.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A BuildKit build fails deep inside a multi-stage Dockerfile, and the default condensed progress output hides the actual error — the engineer only sees a summary line. She needs the full, untruncated build log to find which RUN step failed and why. Which flag gives it?
options: `--verbose` — Docker's build flag for full logs
`--debug` — it re-runs the build step by step interactively
`--progress=plain` — BuildKit emits the complete plain-text log with every command's full stdout/stderr instead of the interactive condensed view
`--no-cache` — the error only appears on uncached rebuilds
explain: BuildKit's default `auto`/`tty` progress condenses output and can swallow the failing command's context; `--progress=plain` streams everything — each step's full output, in order — which is what you paste into a bug report or CI log. `--verbose` isn't a build flag, `--debug` isn't an interactive build debugger, and `--no-cache` just slows the rebuild without changing log verbosity. First debugging move on any opaque BuildKit failure: re-run with `--progress=plain`.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI builds a multi-arch image with `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64`. The engineer tries `--load` to test the image locally, and the build errors out. She switches to `--push` and it works. What is the rule she's hit?
options: `--load` only works for single-platform builds — the local image store can't hold a multi-arch manifest, so multi-platform results must go to a registry with `--push` (or `--output`)
`--push` is deprecated; she should use `--load --multi-arch` instead
Buildx can't build multi-arch at all without a remote builder; the `--push` success was a fluke
`--load` requires `--provenance=false`; the error was about attestations, not platforms
explain: The classic docker image store holds one image per tag — a multi-arch manifest list can't be `--load`ed into it, so buildx refuses. `--push` sends the manifest list (plus per-arch images) to a registry, which is the whole point of multi-arch delivery. Workarounds: build one platform with `--load` for local testing, or push to a local registry and pull. `--load --multi-arch` isn't a flag, buildx builds multi-arch fine with the default docker-container driver, and provenance settings are unrelated to this error.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile needs files from a sibling directory `../shared-protos` that lives OUTSIDE the build context — and `COPY ../shared-protos` is rejected because context paths can't escape the root. The team doesn't want to restructure the repo. How can BuildKit make the sibling directory available?
options: `COPY --from=../shared-protos ./protos/` — `--from` accepts relative host paths directly
Symlink `../shared-protos` into the context — Docker follows symlinks that point outside
`ADD` with an absolute host path — ADD isn't bound by the context root

`docker buildx build --build-context protos=../shared-protos .` then `COPY --from=protos ./ ./protos/` — named build contexts expose extra local directories (or images, or URLs) as additional `--from` sources
explain: Named build contexts (`--build-context name=path|image|url`) add extra sources a Dockerfile can reference via `COPY --from=name` — the clean answer to 'I need files from outside the context.' Relative `..` paths are rejected, symlinks escaping the context are blocked, and ADD obeys the same context boundary as COPY. This is also how you inject a config repo or a prebuilt artifact without restructuring.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A multi-stage Dockerfile needs the stock `nginx.conf` from the official nginx image as a starting point — but the build defines no nginx stage, and adding a throwaway stage was rejected as clutter. Can a single COPY pull a file out of an image that isn't a build stage?
options: No — `COPY --from` only references stage names defined earlier in the same Dockerfile
Only with `ADD` — COPY can't reference external images, ADD can
Yes — `COPY --from=nginx:alpine /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /tmp/nginx.conf.default` works: `--from` accepts any image reference, and BuildKit pulls it as an additional build source
Yes, but only if the image is already in the local daemon cache — remote references are rejected
explain: `COPY --from=` takes a stage name OR any image reference — BuildKit resolves `nginx:alpine` like a base image and copies out of it, no dedicated stage required. The 'stages only' belief is the trap; the remote-reference restriction is invented. This is handy for lifting default configs, CA bundles, or tools out of upstream images without bloating your stage graph.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A legacy Dockerfile starts with `MAINTAINER ops@example.com`. The build prints a deprecation warning. What is the current, supported replacement?
options: `AUTHOR ops@example.com` — the renamed instruction
Nothing — maintainer metadata was removed from the image spec entirely, so delete the line
`LABEL maintainer="ops@example.com"` (or the `org.opencontainers.image.*` label set) — MAINTAINER is deprecated in favor of LABEL
`ENV MAINTAINER=ops@example.com` — environment variables replaced it
explain: MAINTAINER was deprecated in favor of the generic `LABEL` mechanism — `LABEL maintainer="..."` or the OCI-standard `org.opencontainers.image.authors`/`title`/`revision` labels. There is no AUTHOR instruction, the metadata wasn't removed (it moved), and ENV would leak the value into every running container's environment — exactly the wrong place for documentation metadata.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An audit suspects an AWS key was baked into `shop/api:2.0` via `ARG` months ago. The current Dockerfile no longer contains it, and the image was rebuilt since — but the old tag still exists in the registry. How can the auditor confirm whether the key is recoverable from that image?
options: `docker inspect` on the current image — if the Dockerfile no longer has it, the key is gone
It's impossible — rebuilt images contain no trace of old build arguments
`docker history --no-trunc shop/api:2.0` on the suspect tag — build arguments are recorded in layer history metadata, so the key persists in the image even though the Dockerfile changed
Only the CI build logs can show it — the image itself never records ARG values
explain: `docker history` shows the full build command per layer, and ARG values are baked into that metadata — anyone who can pull the old tag can read the key. Rebuilding without the ARG doesn't clean the registry's old tag, and `docker inspect` alone won't show it (history is the forensic view). This is the same lesson as Q35/Q44: secrets must never travel via ARG/ENV — use BuildKit secret mounts so they never enter a layer or its metadata.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI builds on ephemeral runners — every build starts with an empty layer cache, so `npm ci` re-runs from scratch each time. The team pushes images to their registry and wants each build to reuse the previous build's layers as cache. Which build setting enables registry-based layer caching?
options: Pass `--cache-from=shop/api:latest` — it automatically pulls and reuses the registry image as cache
Build with `--export-cache` — the flag embeds cache metadata into the pushed image
Build with `--build-arg BUILDKIT_INLINE_CACHE=1` — it embeds cache metadata into the pushed image, so a later `--cache-from` build can reuse its layers
Registry-based caching is impossible — build cache only lives on the builder's local disk
explain: A pushed image carries layer blobs but NOT build-cache metadata by default, so `--cache-from` alone finds nothing reusable. `BUILDKIT_INLINE_CACHE=1` embeds the metadata into the image config at push time, turning every pushed image into a cache source — pair it with `--cache-from` on subsequent builds. (Buildx also offers `--cache-to type=registry` for dedicated cache manifests — same idea, separate artifact.) The 'disk-only cache' claim is outdated; the trap is assuming `--cache-from` works without the metadata.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: The security team mandates monthly daemon upgrades. Each `systemctl restart docker` kills every running container, causing brief outages. Which daemon setting lets containers keep running straight through a daemon restart or upgrade?
options: `"live-restore": true` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` — the daemon hands container supervision to containerd, so containers survive daemon restarts and upgrades without interruption
`--restart=always` on every container — the daemon restarts them fast enough that nobody notices
`docker update --live <container>` — marks individual containers as restart-proof
Nothing — a daemon restart always stops all containers by design
explain: live-restore keeps containers running while the daemon itself restarts — the use case is exactly daemon upgrades without workload disruption. `--restart=always` does restart containers AFTER the daemon returns, but there's still a kill-and-restart outage window (and it doesn't help if the daemon fails to come back). `--live` isn't a real update flag, and 'always kills' ignores a feature that's existed since Engine 1.12. Note: live-restore doesn't cover host reboots — only daemon restarts.

q: An admin sets `"iptables": false` in `daemon.json`, and a colleague ALSO adds `--iptables=false` to the systemd drop-in for the docker service. The daemon now fails to start, logging that the option is set in both the config file and flags. What is the rule?
options: The systemd flag wins and daemon.json is ignored — remove the file entry to silence the error
The same option must not be set in both `daemon.json` and daemon flags — the daemon treats it as a conflict and refuses to start. Keep each option in exactly one place
daemon.json always overrides flags — the error is a bug, upgrade Docker
Restart the daemon twice — the conflict resolves once the flag file is re-read
explain: Docker explicitly forbids configuring the same option via both daemon.json and command-line flags — startup fails rather than guessing precedence. This bites during migrations (flags → daemon.json) when both linger. Pick one source of truth per option (daemon.json is the modern default) and remove the other. The 'flag wins' and 'json wins' answers invent a precedence that doesn't exist.

q: Before restarting the production daemon with a hand-edited `daemon.json`, the admin wants to catch JSON syntax errors WITHOUT touching the running daemon. Which command validates the configuration file?
options: `docker config validate` — it checks daemon configuration files
`systemctl dry-run docker` — systemd previews the daemon start
`dockerd --validate` — it parses and validates `daemon.json`, then exits without starting the daemon
`docker info --validate` — the client checks the daemon config remotely
explain: `dockerd --validate` is the pre-flight check: it loads daemon.json and reports syntax/semantic errors without disturbing the running daemon. `docker config validate` doesn't exist (configs are Swarm objects), systemd has no dry-run for this, and `docker info` talks to the live daemon rather than checking a file. Cheap insurance before every daemon.json change — a typo otherwise takes down the daemon on restart.

q: On the default bridge network, any container can open connections to any other container's ports. The security team wants containers isolated from each other by default on this host, while keeping normal outbound internet access. Which daemon setting does this?
options: `--iptables=false` — it stops Docker from linking containers together
Start every container with `--network none` — no network means no container-to-container traffic
Set `"icc": true` — it enables inter-container communication lockdown
`"icc": false` in `daemon.json` — it disables inter-container communication on the default bridge; containers keep external egress and published ports still work
explain: `icc: false` is the default-bridge isolation knob: containers can't reach each other directly, but outbound traffic and published ports are unaffected (defense in depth for multi-tenant hosts). `--iptables=false` disables ALL of Docker's firewall management — far broader and usually wrong. `--network none` removes networking entirely, and `icc: true` is the permissive default, the opposite of what's asked. Note: `icc` only governs the default bridge; user-defined networks manage their own isolation.

q: A new worker must join the swarm but stay out of scheduling until it's hardened — the admin doesn't want any task landing on it during the join window. How can the node join already drained?
options: `docker swarm join --availability drain --token <worker-token> <manager>:2377` — the node joins with availability=drain and accepts no tasks until an admin sets it active
Join normally, then immediately run `docker node update --availability drain` — there's no race because the manager waits for new nodes
`--availability` isn't a valid join flag — drain can only be set after joining
Block the VXLAN port until hardening is done — the node joins but can't receive tasks
explain: `docker swarm join` accepts `--availability` (active/pause/drain), so a node can enter the cluster already drained — no window where the scheduler might place tasks on an unhardened host. The 'join then drain' sequence has a real race: the orchestrator can schedule tasks in between. Blocking ports breaks cluster communication rather than scheduling intent, and the flag very much exists.

q: The team wants to schedule GPU workloads with `--constraint 'engine.labels.gpu == true'`, but no engine labels exist yet. A teammate runs `docker node update --label-add gpu=true worker1` and the constraint still matches nothing. What went wrong?
options: Constraints can't reference labels at all — only `node.role` and `node.hostname` are valid

`docker node update --label-add` sets `node.labels.*` (the node's own labels); `engine.labels.*` come from the daemon's `labels` array in `daemon.json` (e.g. `"labels": ["gpu=true"]`) — different namespaces
Engine labels are set with `--engine-label` on `docker swarm join`
Docker auto-detects GPUs and sets `engine.labels.gpu` itself — the manual label conflicts with it
explain: Two label namespaces: `node.labels.*` (set via `docker node update --label-add`, describe the Swarm node object) and `engine.labels.*` (set in the daemon's `labels` array in daemon.json, describe the Engine). A constraint on `engine.labels.gpu` never matches `node.labels.gpu`. Pick one namespace and be consistent — this node-vs-engine mixup is a classic 'constraint matches nothing, tasks Pending forever' root cause.

q: A Kubernetes distribution runs its kubelet with the systemd cgroup driver, but Docker defaults to cgroupfs. The mismatch causes unstable CPU/memory accounting and kubelet warnings. How should the Docker daemon be configured?
options: Nothing — Docker auto-detects the kubelet's cgroup driver at startup
Change the kubelet to cgroupfs — Docker's cgroup driver is compiled in and can't be changed
Set `"exec-opts": ["native.cgroupdriver=systemd"]` in `daemon.json` so Docker and the kubelet share a single cgroup manager
Run the daemon with `--cgroup-parent=kubelet` — it inherits the kubelet's driver
explain: Docker and the kubelet must use the same cgroup driver, and systemd is the recommended one on systemd-based hosts. `native.cgroupdriver=systemd` in daemon.json's exec-opts switches Docker over. Docker does not auto-detect, the driver is very much configurable, and `--cgroup-parent` only nests containers under a cgroup path — it doesn't change the driver. The cgroupfs/systemd mismatch is a classic source of flapping resource stats.

q: Swarm nodes on a high-latency WAN link keep flapping between Ready and Down, causing spurious task rescheduling. Node heartbeats every 5 seconds sometimes arrive late. Which tuning addresses the flapping?
options: Increase `--update-delay` — it spaces out the rescheduling
Raise the Raft election timeout with `--election-tick` on `swarm init`
Set `--heartbeat-period` on each worker node

`docker swarm init --dispatcher-heartbeat 20s` (or `docker swarm update --dispatcher-heartbeat 20s`) — lengthening the dispatcher heartbeat period tolerates transient latency without marking nodes Down
explain: `--dispatcher-heartbeat` controls how often nodes check in; on laggy links the default 5s period produces false Down events and churn. Raising it trades slower genuine-failure detection for stability — the right call on a WAN. `--update-delay` paces rollouts (unrelated), and `--election-tick` / `--heartbeat-period` aren't swarm flags at all — invented distractors. Tune heartbeats for the network you have, not the datacenter you wish you had.

q: During fleet-wide deploys, 50 nodes pulling a 3GB image saturate the registry link — each daemon opens many parallel layer downloads. Which daemon setting caps per-daemon download parallelism?
options: `"max-concurrent-downloads": 3` in `daemon.json` — it limits how many layers a single daemon pulls simultaneously (`max-concurrent-uploads` is the push-side twin)
`--update-parallelism 3` on the service — it throttles pulls across the fleet
`"max-download-bandwidth": "100mbit"` — it rate-limits each daemon's pulls
Nothing — pull parallelism is hardcoded in the Engine
explain: `max-concurrent-downloads` (default 3) is the per-daemon throttle for parallel layer fetches — lowering it smooths registry load during fleet rollouts; `max-concurrent-uploads` does the same for pushes. `--update-parallelism` paces task replacement, not network fetches. There is no `max-download-bandwidth` daemon setting — the invented option sounds plausible, which is exactly why it's the trap.

q: A four-node swarm was initialized with `--advertise-addr` on each host's management interface (10.0.0.0/24). The site also has a dedicated high-throughput storage fabric (192.168.100.0/24), and all VXLAN overlay data traffic must ride the fabric instead of the management network. Which setting pins the data path to the fabric?
options: `--listen-addr 192.168.100.5` — it moves both control and data traffic onto the fabric
`--data-path-addr 192.168.100.5` at `swarm init`/`join` — it selects the interface for VXLAN data-plane traffic, independent of `--advertise-addr`
`--data-path-port 7789` — changing the data-path port also selects the interface
Nothing — VXLAN always follows the advertise address, so the fabric can't be used
explain: Swarm separates the planes: `--advertise-addr` is the address the node tells others to reach it for Raft/API traffic; `--data-path-addr` is the interface VXLAN data traffic uses. On multi-homed hosts with a dedicated fabric, set both. `--listen-addr` only binds the local control socket, and `--data-path-port` remaps the UDP port (the fix when 4789 is blocked) — neither chooses the interface. Don't conflate the three flags.

q: An engineer runs `docker swarm leave --force` on the SOLE manager of a single-node swarm, expecting the worker nodes to keep running their tasks in standalone mode. What actually happens?
options: The manager steps down and the oldest worker is auto-promoted to keep the swarm alive
Nothing — the last manager is protected and cannot leave a swarm
The swarm is dissolved on that node — it leaves swarm mode entirely, and its services, overlay networks, secrets and configs are removed with it
The node converts to a worker and its tasks keep running under the remaining managers
explain: The last manager leaving destroys the swarm from that node's perspective: swarm-mode state (services, networks, secrets, configs) is torn down and the node returns to standalone Engine. There is no auto-promotion, no 'protected last manager,' and no graceful conversion — `--force` is required precisely because the consequences are total. Workers that lose all managers keep RUNNING their existing tasks (data plane survives) but can't be managed until rejoined to a healthy swarm.

q: worker9 died permanently — a hardware failure, the host will never return. It shows `Down` in `docker node ls`, and its tasks already rescheduled elsewhere. What is the proper cleanup of the dead node object?
options: Run `docker swarm leave` on worker9 — the standard way to remove any node
Nothing — Down nodes are garbage-collected automatically after 24 hours
Run `docker node demote worker9` first, then wait for it to disappear
Run `docker node rm worker9` from a manager — it removes the unreachable node from the cluster definition
explain: `docker node rm` is the cleanup for dead nodes — it works on Down/unreachable nodes from any manager. `swarm leave` must run ON the node itself (impossible — it's dead), nothing auto-prunes node objects, and demote only applies to managers' Raft roles. Leaving the corpse in `docker node ls` isn't just untidy: stale Down nodes confuse capacity math and future constraint planning.

q: A developer on Docker Desktop for Windows needs to run a Linux image for one project and a Windows Server Core image for another. How does Desktop handle the two container modes?
options: Right-click the Docker tray icon and choose 'Switch to Windows containers' / 'Switch to Linux containers' — Desktop toggles the daemon between Linux and Windows container modes, one at a time
Both modes run simultaneously — Desktop runs Linux and Windows containers side by side by default
Windows images run under Linux mode through automatic emulation
Install a second copy of Docker Desktop — one per container mode
explain: Docker Desktop runs ONE daemon mode at a time — the tray-icon switch flips between Linux containers (via the Linux VM) and Windows containers (native). There's no side-by-side mode and no emulation of Windows images on Linux (the reverse of the classic 'Windows image on Linux host' failure from Q145). Plan accordingly: switching modes restarts the daemon, so don't flip it mid-workflow.

q: After switching the daemon's default log driver to `splunk`, `docker logs web` fails with `configured logging driver does not support reading`. The events ARE arriving in Splunk. What is going on?
options: The splunk driver is broken — switch back to `json-file` to restore logging
Only local log drivers (`json-file`, `local`, `journald`) support `docker logs` — remote drivers stream to the external system and keep no locally readable logs, so you read them in Splunk
`docker logs` requires `--follow` when the driver is remote
The container must be recreated with `--log-opt read=true`
explain: `docker logs` reads from the daemon's local log store, which only local drivers maintain. Remote drivers (splunk, awslogs, syslog, gelf...) ship entries off-host and support no local read — the error message is telling you exactly that. This is the operational trade-off of centralized logging: you gain aggregation and lose `docker logs`. (Dual logging/cache options exist for bridging, but the default remote-driver behavior is ship-only.)

q: A fleet must stay on Docker Engine 26.1.x — an unattended `apt upgrade` once jumped a host to 27.x and broke a storage plugin. How can the team install and hold a specific Engine version with apt?
options: Apt always installs the latest — version pinning isn't possible; use the convenience install script instead
`apt-mark hold docker-ce` with no version — it freezes whatever happens to be installed
`apt-get install docker-ce=5:26.1.4-1~ubuntu.22.04~jammy docker-ce-cli=...` (then `apt-mark hold`) — apt supports exact-version installs, and holding blocks surprise upgrades
Set `"engine-version": "26.1"` in `daemon.json` — the daemon refuses newer binaries
explain: Apt version pinning (`package=version`, with Docker's epoch prefix like `5:`) installs the exact build, and `apt-mark hold` prevents upgrades from moving it — the standard fleet discipline for version-sensitive plugins. 'Apt can't pin' is false, hold-without-version is fragile (it freezes accidents too), and no daemon.json key controls the binary version. Pair this with staged rollouts: pin in testing first, promote the known-good version fleet-wide.

q: A running production container was started with `--restart no`, and the team now wants `unless-stopped` — without recreating it, because it holds local state they'd rather not migrate. Is the restart policy changeable on a live container?
options: No — restart policy is fixed at creation; the container must be recreated
Only by committing the container to an image and re-running it
Only by hand-editing `/var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/hostconfig.json` while the daemon is stopped
Yes — `docker update --restart unless-stopped <container>` changes the restart policy of a running (or stopped) container in place
explain: `docker update` mutates several container settings live, and `--restart` is one of them — no recreate, no state migration, no daemon downtime. The 'immutable' belief confuses `docker update`'s limits (it can't change images, ports, or mounts) with a blanket ban. Hand-editing hostconfig.json is the dangerous folk alternative — it corrupts state if the daemon is running. Note the Swarm parallel: services use `--restart-condition`, updated via `docker service update`.

q: A bank's policy requires all cluster certificates to be issued by its corporate CA rather than Docker's built-in swarm CA. Can Swarm honor this, and how?
options: No — Swarm always uses its own internal CA; external CAs are unsupported
Yes — set `"ca-cert"` in `daemon.json` to point at the corporate CA
Yes — pass the corporate CA certificate with `docker swarm join --ca-cert`
Yes — `docker swarm init --external-ca` (or `docker swarm ca --external-ca`) delegates node certificate signing to an external CA such as Cloudflare's cfssl
explain: Swarm supports an external CA for node certificates via `--external-ca` (protocol cfssl, with the CA's URL and options) — the swarm CA then acts as an intermediary to the corporate PKI instead of being its own root. daemon.json has no `ca-cert` key for this, join has no `--ca-cert` flag, and 'unsupported' ignores a documented enterprise feature. This is separate from the TLS certificates on the remote daemon API — it's about the mutual-TLS identity of swarm nodes themselves.

q: `cat /etc/resolv.conf` inside an app container on a user-defined network shows `nameserver 127.0.0.11`. The engineer worries DNS is broken because nothing appears to listen on localhost:53. What is 127.0.0.11?
options: Docker's embedded DNS server — every container on a user-defined network gets it; it resolves container and service names and forwards external queries to the host's upstream resolvers
A stale entry baked into the image — it should be replaced with the host's real resolver
The Docker daemon's own IP — containers query the daemon process directly for DNS
A randomly chosen link-local address — its value differs per container and carries no meaning
explain: 127.0.0.11 is the embedded DNS resolver present in every container network namespace on user-defined networks (bridge and overlay) — it's how `ping db` resolves without any manual DNS setup. It's not in the image (Docker injects resolv.conf at runtime), not the daemon, and not random — it's the well-known address of the per-container resolver. If external names fail but container names work, the problem is upstream forwarding (check the daemon's `--dns` / host resolvers), not 127.0.0.11 itself.

q: Containers must resolve `db.corp.internal` through the corporate resolver at 10.0.0.53, and short names like `db` should expand via the `corp.internal` search domain. The host's own resolver configuration can't be changed. Which `docker run` flags configure this per container?
options: `-e DNS=10.0.0.53 -e DNS_SEARCH=corp.internal` — environment variables configure the resolver
`--dns 10.0.0.53 --dns-search corp.internal` — they set the container's nameserver and search domain in its resolv.conf, independent of the host
`--add-host db:10.0.0.53` — it installs both the resolver and the search domain
Exec into the container and edit `/etc/resolv.conf` by hand after starting it
explain: `--dns` and `--dns-search` (plus `--dns-opt`) are the per-container resolver knobs — Docker writes them into the container's resolv.conf without touching the host. No ENV var controls DNS, `--add-host` only adds static entries (useful, but not a resolver or search domain), and hand-editing resolv.conf is ephemeral toil that vanishes on recreate. For fleet-wide defaults, the same keys exist in daemon.json.

q: The corporate network owns 10.0.0.0/8. New overlay networks misbehave because Docker's default address pool hands out subnets inside that range. The team can't renumber the corporation. How should they create overlays that stay clear?
options: Overlays always take 10.0.0.0/24 — the only fix is carving an exception in the corporate range
Create every overlay with `--internal` — internal networks auto-select non-conflicting subnets
`docker network create -d overlay --subnet 192.168.200.0/24 app-net` — explicit subnets per network (or `--default-addr-pool` at `swarm init` for the fleet default) keep Docker off corporate space
Set the subnet inside each service's `deploy:` section — networks inherit it
explain: Overlay subnets are yours to choose: `--subnet` on `docker network create` (or `--default-addr-pool 192.168.0.0/16 --default-addr-pool-mask-length 24` at swarm init for the fleet-wide default) keeps Docker's allocations out of corporate ranges. `--internal` only blocks egress — it doesn't pick subnets — and services have no subnet setting. This is the same class of problem as the docker0/docker_gwbridge collisions, solved one layer up.

q: Windows containers need real LAN IPs from the corporate network — the Windows equivalent of what macvlan gives Linux containers. The default Windows `nat` network only provides internal IPs. Which Windows network driver attaches containers directly to the physical LAN?
options: `--driver macvlan` — it works identically on Windows and Linux
Windows containers can't receive LAN IPs — `nat` is the only option
`overlay` — it transparently bridges containers onto the LAN
`transparent` — the Windows driver that puts containers directly on the physical network with their own LAN IPs, the counterpart to Linux macvlan
explain: Windows' `transparent` driver is the macvlan analog: containers get LAN-routable IPs on the physical network. macvlan is Linux-only, `nat` (the Windows default) hides containers behind the host like a home router, and overlay is for multi-host container networks — not LAN attachment. The exam tests driver parity across OSes: know which driver gives LAN IPs on each platform (`macvlan`/`ipvlan` on Linux, `transparent` on Windows).

q: A developer sets `--hostname web1` expecting other containers to reach it at `web1`, but name resolution fails — while `--network-alias web1` works. What is the distinction between the two?
options: `--hostname` sets the container's own UTS hostname (what it calls itself, seen in its shell prompt); `--network-alias` registers an additional DNS name for the container on that network, which is what other containers resolve
They're synonyms — the resolution failure must be a typo in the alias
`--hostname` only takes effect on the default bridge network
Aliases require the deprecated `--link` flag; `--hostname` works everywhere
explain: Hostname is identity (UTS namespace — `hostname` inside the container); alias is addressability (a DNS entry in the network's embedded DNS). Other containers never resolve your `--hostname` — they resolve network aliases and container names. The common confusion comes from `docker run --name`, which does double duty as both hostname default AND dns name on user-defined networks. If others must reach it, give it an alias (or a `--name`).

q: A service publishes with `--publish mode=host,target=80,published=8080` and 3 replicas. Two tasks land on the same node and one fails with a port allocation error. Why does this happen in host mode but not in ingress mode?
options: Host-mode publishing is broken with more than one replica — ingress mode is the only supported option

In host mode the port binds directly on each task's host network stack, so two tasks on one node collide on 8080. Ingress mode shares one mesh-wide listener per node, so replicas never collide. Fix with `--replicas-max-per-node 1` or a spread placement
Each replica needs a distinct published port — Swarm assigns them automatically in ingress mode only
Port 8080 is in the privileged range — host mode requires ports above 32000
explain: Host mode bypasses the routing mesh: the container port binds straight onto the host's interface, so co-located tasks fight over the same host port. Ingress mode's mesh owns the port once per node and load-balances to tasks — no collision possible. The standard fixes are `--replicas-max-per-node 1` (at most one task per node) or placement that spreads tasks. 8080 isn't privileged (that's <1024), and ingress isn't 'the only supported option' — host mode is legitimate when you need source IPs or direct binding.

q: While testing port mappings, an engineer types `docker run -d -p 8080:80 -p 8081:80 nginx`, half-expecting Docker to complain — instead, the site answers on BOTH host ports. Is this valid?
options: No — the second `-p` silently replaced the first; only 8081 actually works
No — Docker merged them into the range 8080-8081, which behaves differently
Yes — one container port can be published on multiple host ports at once; each `-p` mapping is independent
Yes, but only with `--network host` — bridge networks allow a single mapping per container port
explain: Port mappings are independent: `-p 8080:80 -p 8081:80` creates two host listeners forwarding to the same container port — no conflict, no merging, no replacement. This is genuinely useful (e.g. internal and external listeners on different host ports). The 'one mapping per port' belief is the trap; Docker only complains when two mappings claim the SAME host port.

q: `docker network rm mynet` fails with `has active endpoints`, even though the network looks unused. What must happen before the removal succeeds?
options: `docker network rm -f mynet` — force detaches the endpoints and removes the network
Restart the Docker daemon — stale endpoints clear on restart
Delete every container on the host — networks can't be emptied any other way
Disconnect each attached container with `docker network disconnect mynet <container>` — a network can't be removed while endpoints are attached to it
explain: Networks are reference-counted by their endpoints: `docker network rm` refuses while any container (running or stopped) is still attached. Disconnect each one first, then remove. There is no `-f` for network rm, daemon restarts don't clear attachments, and deleting containers is overkill when a disconnect suffices. (`docker network prune` hits the same rule — it only removes networks with zero endpoints.)

q: A backend network is created with `--internal`, and the developer assumes container name resolution will break too — so she hardcodes IP addresses. Is she right?
options: No — `--internal` only blocks external egress; Docker's embedded DNS still resolves container and service names on the network, so hardcoding IPs is unnecessary
Yes — internal networks ship without DNS; hardcoded IPs are required
Yes, unless `--dns` is also passed to `docker network create`
Internal networks disable the network stack entirely — containers can't even ping each other
explain: `--internal` is an egress firewall, not a DNS switch: name resolution on the network works exactly as before, only traffic to the outside world is dropped. Hardcoding IPs reintroduces the fragility Docker networking exists to remove (IPs change on recreate). The exam's pairing: `--internal` = no internet, full service discovery; `--network none` = no network at all.

q: Intending 'host port 8080 → container port 80' (the app listens on 80), a developer types `docker run -d -p 80:8080 webapp`. The app answers on host port 80 instead, and nothing is on 8080. What happened?
options: The container remapped its own listening port — the app now serves on 8080 internally
The syntax is `hostPort:containerPort` — she published container port 8080 (where nothing listens) on host port 80. The fix is `-p 8080:80`
Host ports below 1024 require `--privileged` — without it Docker silently swaps the order
Port order is negotiated at runtime — retry until the mapping lands correctly
explain: `-p` reads left-to-right as host:container — `80:8080` exposes the container's (empty) 8080 on the host's 80. The mnemonic: the container port is the one the app actually listens on, and it goes LAST. The privileged-port theory is wrong (binding low host ports needs host privilege, but Docker had it and mapped exactly what was asked), and there is no negotiation — the mapping is literal.

q: A host has 10.0.0.5 (public) and 192.168.1.10 (management). The admin wants a container's port 80 reachable ONLY via the management address — `-p 8080:80` binds it on both interfaces. Which publish form restricts it to one interface?
options: `-p 8080:80 --bind management` — the flag selects the interface by name
It's impossible — published ports always bind every host interface
`-p 192.168.1.10:8080:80` — the `hostIP:hostPort:containerPort` form binds the published port to a single host interface
Switch to `--network host` and add a host firewall rule — publishing can't select interfaces
explain: The three-part `-p` form pins the listener to one IP: `192.168.1.10:8080:80` never opens on 10.0.0.5. This is the standard way to keep admin/debug ports off public interfaces (compare Q73's `127.0.0.1` loopback binding — same mechanism). There's no `--bind` flag, 'always all interfaces' ignores the documented form, and host networking plus firewall rules is a heavier solution to a solved problem.

q: A batch container must start with NO network access, perform local setup, and only then join `backend` to fetch its workload. Can network attachment be staged like this?
options: No — a container's networks are fixed at `docker run` time and can't change
Yes — start with `--network backend` and block traffic with an internal firewall until setup finishes
Yes — run with `--network none`, then `docker start` the container a second time naming the network
Yes — `docker run --network none job ...`, then `docker network connect backend <container>` when ready; networks can be attached to (and detached from) running containers
explain: `docker network connect/disconnect` work on running containers — attachment is dynamic, not a creation-time property. `--network none` gives the clean 'no network' starting state (stronger than firewall games), and connect adds `backend` exactly when the job is ready. The 'fixed at run' belief is the trap; only the container's FIRST network has any special status, and even that can be disconnected later.

q: Two stacks, `billing` and `shop`, share an overlay network. From a `shop` container, `ping db` fails — but `ping billing_db` succeeds. Why does the short name fail?
options: Stack deploy prefixes service names with the stack name — the DNS name is `billing_db` (stack_service); the bare `db` only resolves inside its own stack's scope
Cross-stack DNS is blocked by design — stacks are isolated even on shared networks
The overlay needs `--attachable` before cross-stack names resolve
Service names are global — `db` should resolve; this indicates a DNS outage
explain: `docker stack deploy` names every service `<stack>_<service>`, and that's the DNS name on shared networks — `billing_db`, not `db`. Within one stack's own network the short name works via the stack's naming, but across stacks you must use the prefixed name. There's no cross-stack DNS block (shared networks are meant for exactly this), `--attachable` is for standalone containers, and nothing is broken — the name was just wrong.

q: A legacy license server binds licenses to MAC addresses. A container needs the fixed MAC `02:42:ac:11:00:02` on a user-defined bridge network. Which flag assigns it?
options: `--mac 02:42:ac:11:00:02` — the short flag for MAC assignment
`--mac-address 02:42:ac:11:00:02` — it sets the container's MAC address on user-defined networks
MAC addresses can't be assigned — they're always generated from the container ID
`--hostname 02:42:ac:11:00:02` — Docker derives the MAC from the hostname
explain: `--mac-address` pins the container's MAC on user-defined networks (bridge, overlay) — the escape hatch for MAC-licensed software and deterministic DHCP. There is no `--mac` shorthand, generated MACs are only the default, and hostname has no bearing on the MAC. Caveat: duplicate MACs on one L2 segment cause chaos, so keep them unique — this flag is a scalpel, not a default.

q: The team runs ufw with a default-deny policy, yet a container's published port 8080 is reachable from the internet — and ufw shows no allow rule for it. How is the traffic getting through, and where should the block go?
options: Docker is illegally bypassing the firewall — the only fix is disabling Docker's iptables management
Ufw is misconfigured — published ports always respect ufw rules
Docker inserts its NAT/forward rules ahead of ufw's chains, so published ports bypass ufw. Put custom drop rules in the `DOCKER-USER` chain, which Docker preserves and evaluates before its own rules
Published ports can't be firewalled at all — the port must be unpublished
explain: Docker manages iptables directly and jumps ahead of ufw — that's why 'deny everything' in ufw still leaves published ports open. `DOCKER-USER` is the supported hook: Docker creates the chain, never flushes your rules in it, and evaluates it before its own. 'Disable Docker's iptables' breaks publishing and networking outright; 'respect ufw' misdescribes the packet path. If you firewall a Docker host, DOCKER-USER is where your rules live.

q: After a network change, containers on `app-net` reach each other but nothing external — even the package proxy that worked yesterday. `docker network inspect app-net` shows `"Internal": true`, which nobody remembers setting. What does it mean?
options: The network is corrupted — delete it and recreate it identically
`Internal` is just a descriptive label — it doesn't affect traffic
The network's gateway container crashed — restart it to restore egress
The network was created with `--internal`, which drops all external egress. Recreate it without the flag (or attach a second, external network) to restore outside access
explain: `"Internal": true` means the network was built with `--internal`: inter-container traffic and DNS work, but anything leaving the host is dropped — which matches the symptoms exactly (peers reachable, proxy dead). It's not corruption and not a label; someone (or some script) passed the flag at creation. Fix: recreate without `--internal`, or keep the isolated network and attach containers to a second external network for the proxy.

q: A Kubernetes hardening baseline requires every pod to run under the container runtime's default seccomp profile — blocking dangerous syscalls without maintaining a custom profile per application. Which pod security setting applies it?
options: `securityContext.seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }` — the kubelet applies the runtime's default seccomp filter to the pod's containers
`--security-opt seccomp=default` in the pod spec — the Docker-style flag works in Kubernetes manifests
`privileged: false` — it automatically enables the default seccomp profile
Seccomp can't be set per pod — it's a node-wide daemon setting only
explain: Kubernetes exposes seccomp per pod/container via `securityContext.seccompProfile`: `RuntimeDefault` (the runtime's curated filter), `Localhost` (a custom profile placed on the node), or `Unconfined`. It's the K8s counterpart to Docker's `--security-opt seccomp=` — the exam's cross-platform pairing. `privileged: false` governs capabilities/devices, not syscall filtering, and Docker CLI flags don't exist in pod specs. Baseline policy: RuntimeDefault everywhere, Localhost only where an app proves it needs more.

q: A deploy script runs `docker secret create` on a WORKER node and fails with `this node is not a swarm manager`. The secret was already created earlier on a manager. Does every node need its own copy created locally?
options: Yes — secrets are node-local objects; each node that runs the service needs `docker secret create` run on it
No — secret management is manager-only by design, and that's sufficient: the swarm distributes the secret (encrypted) to exactly the workers running services granted that secret
Yes — promote the worker to manager, create the secret, then demote it back
Workers can create secrets if you pass `--force` to override the manager check
explain: Secrets live in the Raft store, which only managers write to — workers never create them, and never need to. Distribution is automatic and least-privilege: encrypted in transit, delivered only to nodes running tasks of services granted the secret. The 'node-local copy' mental model is wrong for Swarm (that's the pre-orchestration world of copying env files around), promotion-churn is unnecessary, and no `--force` override exists.

q: A hardened-image policy bans setuid binaries entirely — the runtime `no-new-privileges` flag is good defense, but the team wants the bits GONE from the image so there's nothing to exploit even if the flag is forgotten at deploy time. How should the Dockerfile enforce this?
options: Set `USER nobody` — non-root users can't execute setuid binaries, so the bits are harmless
Add `--cap-drop ALL` to the Dockerfile — it clears setuid bits at build time
`RUN find / -xdev -perm -4000 -exec chmod u-s {} +` (plus `-2000`/`g-s` for setgid) near the end of the build — it strips every setuid/setgid bit from the image
Setuid bits can't be removed from base-image files — only from files you COPY in yourself
explain: Defense in depth across the lifecycle: strip the bits at BUILD time (`find` + `chmod u-s`/`g-s`) so the image ships with no setuid binaries at all, AND keep `no-new-privileges` at RUNTIME for anything that slips through. `--cap-drop` is a runtime-only flag with no Dockerfile equivalent; USER doesn't remove bits; and base-image files are fully mutable during your build. Verify with a post-build scan: `docker run --rm img find / -xdev \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \)` should return nothing.

q: A container runs as non-root user `app`, but it needs read access to a host device node owned by group `dialout`. Changing the device's host ownership is forbidden by policy. How can the container's user gain the group's permission without running as root?
options: `--privileged` — the only way to reach host devices is full privilege
Run the container as root instead — group membership doesn't cross the container boundary
`--cap-add DAC_OVERRIDE` — it grants the equivalent of the device's group access
`--group-add dialout` — it adds the container's user to supplementary groups, conferring the device's group permissions without uid 0
explain: `--group-add` appends supplementary GIDs to the container's user — the kernel's normal group-permission check then passes for the device node. It's the least-privilege answer: no root, no broad capabilities. `--privileged` and `DAC_OVERRIDE` are sledgehammers for a group-membership problem, and group membership absolutely crosses the boundary — the container user is just a UID/GID as far as the kernel is concerned.

q: `docker secret create big-bundle bundle.tar.gz` fails — the bundle is 4MB. The team assumed secrets could hold arbitrarily large blobs. What is the documented limit, and what's the right approach for a 4MB archive?
options: Secrets and configs are capped at 500KB — they're for credentials, keys, and small files, not archives. Extract just the needed cert/key into the secret, or distribute the archive another way (image layer, volume)
There is no size limit — the failure must be a disk-space problem on the manager
The limit is 1GB, so 4MB should work — retry with `--force`
Split the bundle into eight 500KB secrets and reassemble them at container startup
explain: The Raft store isn't a file server: secrets and configs are limited to 500KB each, sized for passwords, keys, and config files. A 4MB bundle doesn't belong there — put the archive in the image (if static) or on a volume, and keep only the actual secret material in the secret. The split-and-reassemble hack technically fits the limit but multiplies rotation pain and misses the point: the limit is a design signal about what secrets are for.

q: A Kubernetes cluster policy forbids root containers entirely — a pod whose image tries to run as UID 0 must be rejected before it starts. Which pod spec field enforces this at admission?
options: `privileged: false` — it blocks containers from running as root
`securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` — the kubelet refuses to start any container whose effective UID is 0
`runAsUser: 0` — it forces the container into non-root mode
Kubernetes can't enforce this — it has to be done with image scanning in CI
explain: `runAsNonRoot: true` is the admission-time UID gate: if the image's user resolves to 0 (and no explicit non-zero runAsUser overrides it), the container never starts. `privileged: false` governs extended privileges (devices, capabilities), not the UID; `runAsUser: 0` explicitly SETS root — the backwards trap; and while CI scanning helps, the kubelet enforces this natively. Pair with `runAsUser: 1000` (or similar) to be explicit rather than relying on the image's USER.

q: In a Kubernetes namespace, the `payments` pods must accept traffic ONLY from the `api` pods — nothing else in the cluster. Pods currently reach each other freely. Which resource implements this microsegmentation?
options: A host firewall rule on each node — Kubernetes has no native network isolation
An RBAC Role — it controls which pods may send traffic to which
A NetworkPolicy selecting the `payments` pods, with an ingress rule whose `from` matches only the `api` pods' labels — the CNI plugin enforces the allowlist
A ClusterIP Service — it isolates backend pods automatically
explain: NetworkPolicy is Kubernetes' data-plane firewall: podSelectors choose the protected pods, ingress/egress rules with `from`/`to` podSelectors define the allowlist, and a CNI that supports policy enforces it. RBAC governs API access (who can `kubectl`), not pod-to-pod packets; host firewalls don't understand pod identity; Services provide stable endpoints, not isolation. Default-deny plus explicit allows is the production pattern — and note the policy only works if the CNI implements it.

q: The company runs its own Notary server for Docker Content Trust instead of Docker Hub's. Developers export `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1`, but signing still contacts the public Notary. Which setting points DCT at the internal server?
options: `DOCKER_NOTARY_URL=https://notary.corp:4443` — DCT reads the server address from this variable
`NOTARY_SERVER=https://notary.corp:4443` — the shorter variable both the CLI and Notary recognize
Add `"trust-server": "https://notary.corp:4443"` to `daemon.json`
`DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST_SERVER=https://notary.corp:4443` — DCT uses this Notary server for signing, verification, and delegation operations
explain: `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST_SERVER` is the documented variable redirecting all DCT/Notary traffic to a private server — essential for air-gapped or regulated environments. The shorter invented names (`DOCKER_NOTARY_URL`, `NOTARY_SERVER`) are plausible traps, and daemon.json has no `trust-server` key — DCT is a client-side concern, not a daemon one. Remember the pair: `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` turns enforcement on, `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST_SERVER` says where trust lives.

q: After a suspicious container ran overnight, the team wants a timeline: when it was created, started, and from which image. The container is gone — `docker ps -a` shows nothing. Where can they still reconstruct this audit trail?
options: `docker events --since <time>` — the daemon's event stream records the container lifecycle (create, start, die, destroy) with image, name, and timestamps; filterable by time, type, and container
`docker logs` — container logs persist after the container is removed
`/var/log/docker.log` — the daemon writes a structured audit record of every container action there
It's unrecoverable — a removed container leaves no trace anywhere
explain: `docker events` is the daemon's audit log: every create/start/stop/die/destroy with actor attributes (image, name, labels). `--since`/`--until` bound the window, `--filter` narrows by event or container. `docker logs` dies with the container (unless a remote driver shipped them), the daemon log is unstructured operational noise, and 'no trace' ignores the event stream entirely. For serious forensics, ship events to your SIEM — the local buffer is finite.

q: In MSR, the `payments` repository must be pushable only by the payments team, while `base-images` is pullable by everyone but pushable only by the platform team. Where is this access control enforced?
options: In the Dockerfiles' `LABEL` instructions — labels carry the repository permissions
MSR's team-based repository permissions — create teams, grant each team per-repository pull, push, or admin access; the registry enforces it at push/pull time
In MKE grants — MKE's Subject/Role/Resource-Set model covers registry repositories too
In Docker Hub organizations — MSR inherits its permissions from Hub
explain: MSR (formerly DTR) has its own RBAC: organizations contain teams, and each repository grants teams pull-only, push/pull, or admin. The registry enforces it on every push and pull — least privilege for image supply chains. MKE grants govern MKE resources (nodes, services), not MSR repos; Dockerfile LABELs are metadata, not policy; and MSR is self-hosted — Hub permissions are irrelevant. The exam loves the MKE-grants vs MSR-teams boundary.

q: An engineer accidentally joins a new host with the WORKER token, then promotes it with `docker node promote` — it becomes a manager fine. Later, another host joins with the same worker token, and the team expects it to become a manager too. What happens?
options: It becomes a manager — the first promotion 'upgraded' the worker token cluster-wide
The join fails — promoting a worker-token node invalidates that token

It joins as a worker — join tokens are role-specific and immutable; `docker swarm join-token manager` and `docker swarm join-token worker` issue different tokens, and promotion is a separate per-node action
Tokens are identical — the node's role is chosen by a flag at join time
explain: Swarm issues two distinct tokens, one per role — the token IS the role at join time. Promoting a node changes that node's role, not the token's meaning; every future join with the worker token yields a worker. There's no role flag on `docker swarm join`, tokens aren't invalidated by promotions, and 'upgraded token' confuses a per-node action with a cluster credential. Guard the manager token accordingly — anyone holding it can join managers.

q: A monitoring container is configured with `-v /:/host` so it can 'see everything on the host'. The security review flags this as critical. Why?
options: It's merely untidy — as long as the container runs non-root, there's no real risk
Docker blocks mounting `/` — the container won't even start
It only risks disk space from runaway writes, not a security boundary
It exposes the entire host filesystem inside the container — a container-root compromise (or a careless recursive delete) becomes a host compromise. Monitor through narrower mounts instead
explain: Mounting host `/` dissolves the container/host boundary: with the host's binaries, configs, and keys visible (and writable), privilege escalation is trivial and accidents are catastrophic. 'Non-root is safe' ignores how easily container root is obtained; Docker absolutely allows the mount. The right pattern is minimal, read-only, purpose-scoped mounts (`/proc`, `/sys`, specific config paths) — or a proper agent. This is the same lesson as the docker.sock question: the mount defines the blast radius.

q: What is the Kubernetes analog of Docker's `--security-opt=no-new-privileges` — preventing a container's processes from gaining privileges through setuid binaries?
options: `securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` — the kernel blocks privilege escalation via setuid/setgid execution for the pod's containers
`securityContext.privileged: false` — it disables setuid behavior
`securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` — it also suppresses setuid escalation
Kubernetes has no equivalent — only PodSecurityPolicies (now removed) could do this
explain: `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` maps directly to Docker's no-new-privileges (both set the kernel's no_new_privs flag). `privileged: false` merely declines the all-capabilities super-mode — a non-privileged root container can still exploit setuid; `runAsNonRoot` gates UID 0, not setuid mechanics. The Docker/Kubernetes security-setting mapping (no-new-privileges ↔ allowPrivilegeEscalation, capabilities ↔ capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem ↔ readOnlyRootFilesystem) is exactly the kind of cross-platform pair the DCA probes.

q: A team allowlists a plain-HTTP internal registry via `insecure-registries` and runs `docker login` against it. What is the security consequence specific to the login itself?
options: None — the daemon encrypts credentials before transmission, even over HTTP
The login is refused — Docker requires TLS before it will send any authentication
The base64-encoded `auth` credentials travel in cleartext HTTP — anyone on the network path can sniff the registry password. Insecure registries are a temporary stopgap, never the plan
The credentials are broadcast to every swarm node — that's the real exposure
explain: Base64 is encoding, not encryption — over plain HTTP the registry password is readable to any network observer, and it then sits in config.json too. `docker login` happily works over HTTP once the registry is allowlisted; there's no TLS requirement and no broadcast to swarm nodes (that's what `--with-registry-auth` is for, and it's equally sniffable over HTTP). The exam's pairing: `insecure-registries` solves the connectivity error and creates a credential-exposure problem — terminate TLS properly.

q: Two services share a swarm: `api` is granted the `db_pass` secret, `worker` is not. A `worker` task gets compromised. Can the attacker recover `db_pass` from the worker task?
options: Yes — any task on a node can read the `/run/secrets` of co-located tasks
Yes — secrets are swarm-global; granting only controls which services mount them conveniently
No — a secret is delivered only to tasks of services explicitly granted it. The worker task never receives the secret, so there is nothing on its filesystem to steal
No, because the secret is encrypted with a key unique to the `api` service
explain: Swarm secrets are least-privilege by construction: encrypted in transit, mounted (via tmpfs) only into tasks of granted services. An ungranted task has no copy, no mount, nothing to exfiltrate — the Raft-encrypted original never leaves manager storage except to authorized workers. The 'node-local readable' theory misunderstands tmpfs mounts (per-container namespaces), and there's no per-service encryption key — the protection is distribution control, not per-service crypto.

q: A Kubernetes pod runs a third-party image that never needs the API server, yet every pod gets a service-account token auto-mounted. The team wants to remove that credential from this pod's attack surface. Which setting does it?
options: Delete the `default` service account from the namespace — pods then mount no token
`runAsNonRoot: true` — it suppresses token auto-mounting as a side effect
Tokens are mandatory — every pod must carry one, no exceptions
`automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the pod spec (or on the service account) — the token volume is not mounted into the pod
explain: `automountServiceAccountToken: false` opts the pod out of the default token mount — no credential, nothing to steal if the image is compromised. Deleting the `default` service account is cluster vandalism affecting everything; `runAsNonRoot` is about UIDs, not tokens; and tokens are default-on, not mandatory. Set it on the ServiceAccount to cover all its pods at once — defense in depth for workloads that never call the API.

q: A high-performance database pod needs RAW block device access — no filesystem layer — for its data volume, and the storage class provisions block devices. How does the pod claim the volume as a raw device instead of a formatted filesystem?
options: Set `volumeMode: Block` on the PersistentVolume/PVC — Kubernetes exposes the device (e.g. `/dev/xvda`) to the pod without formatting or mounting a filesystem, referenced via `volumeDevices`
Use `hostPath` with the device path — it's the only way to get raw block access
Block mode isn't supported — Kubernetes always formats volumes before attaching
Set `volumeMode: Filesystem` and skip the mount — the raw device then appears automatically
explain: `volumeMode: Block` (paired with `volumeDevices` in the pod spec instead of `volumeMounts`) hands the pod a raw block device — for databases and storage systems that manage their own on-disk layout. `Filesystem` (the default) formats and mounts. hostPath can expose a device node but abandons dynamic provisioning, scheduling, and portability. The exam's pairing: Block goes with volumeDevices, Filesystem goes with volumeMounts — and the storage class must actually support block.

q: An engineer runs `docker volume prune` to clean up the 64-hex anonymous volumes, assuming her NAMED volumes are safe because they're 'in use by the project'. What does the command actually remove?
options: Only anonymous volumes — named volumes are never pruned
ALL unused local volumes — including NAMED ones not currently attached to any container. Referenced or not, if no container uses it, it's deleted
Only volumes older than 24 hours — recent ones are kept regardless
Nothing without `-f` — prune only lists candidates unless forced
explain: `docker volume prune` deletes every local volume with no container referencing it — anonymous AND named. 'Named means safe' is the dangerous assumption: a database volume survives only while a container (even stopped) references it; remove that container and the next prune takes the data. Without `-f` it prompts for confirmation, but the selection is the same. Guardrails: keep a container referencing precious volumes, label them, or back them up — prune doesn't ask what the data was worth.

q: A developer switches the storage driver to `vfs` because 'it's the simplest one'. Builds become extremely slow and disk usage explodes. Why is `vfs` unsuitable for production?
options: vfs is deprecated and refuses to start on modern kernels
vfs doesn't implement layers — every image is flattened into one
vfs has no copy-on-write — each layer is a full directory copy, so builds and pulls duplicate every file and devour disk and time. It's a debugging fallback, not a production driver
vfs only works when paired with the `local` volume driver
explain: vfs is the naive driver: no CoW, no diffs — layer N+1 is a complete copy of layer N plus changes. A 10-layer image stores ~10 copies of the base files. It exists for correctness testing and kernels without overlayfs support, never for production. overlay2 is the default for a reason: shared, CoW, fast. The 'deprecated/won't start' and 'no layers' options invent limitations; the real one is architectural.

q: A Kubernetes PVC requests `accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]`, but two pods on DIFFERENT nodes must share the volume read-write. The second pod stays Pending with an attach error. Which access mode fits, and what constrains it?
options: ReadWriteOnce already allows multi-node sharing — the Pending status is a scheduler bug
Switch to `ReadOnlyMany` — it permits multi-node read-write sharing
Access modes are advisory labels — only the storage class determines sharing
`ReadWriteMany` — shareable read-write across nodes, but the underlying storage must actually support it (NFS/file shares yes, plain block devices no)
explain: ReadWriteOnce = one node at a time (multiple pods on THAT node are fine); the second pod's node can't attach an already-attached block volume. ReadWriteMany is the multi-node mode — but it's a contract the storage must honor: NFS, CephFS, and file shares qualify; EBS-style block doesn't. ReadOnlyMany is read-only by definition, modes are enforced (not advisory), and no scheduler bug is involved — the topology constraint is working as designed.

q: A namespace teardown deletes a PVC whose StorageClass sets `reclaimPolicy: Retain`. The team expects the cloud disk to be deleted, as usual. What actually happens to the disk and its data?
options: The PV is released but NOT deleted — the disk and its data survive; an admin must manually reclaim or delete it. `Retain` is the data-safe policy
The disk is deleted — `Retain` only delays deletion by 24 hours
The PVC becomes undeletable — the teardown hangs on the `Retain` policy
`Retain` encrypts the disk in place instead of deleting it
explain: `Retain` means the PV (and its backing disk) outlives the claim: the PV goes to `Released`, the data sits intact, and a human decides — manually reclaim, delete, or reuse. It's the policy for data you can't afford to lose to an accidental namespace deletion. `Delete` (the common default) is the one that destroys the disk with the PVC. The exam's contrast: Delete = disk dies with the claim; Retain = disk survives and waits for an admin.

q: A pod mounts a ConfigMap volume at `/etc/app/`, but the app ALSO keeps its own writable files in `/etc/app/` — mounting the ConfigMap obscures the whole directory. How can the pod mount just ONE key as `/etc/app/config.yaml` without hiding the rest?
options: Mount the ConfigMap twice at the same path — Kubernetes merges the two mounts
`volumeMounts: [{ mountPath: /etc/app/config.yaml, subPath: config.yaml }]` — `subPath` mounts a single file or directory from the volume, leaving the rest of the mount point intact
Switch to `hostPath` — it merges with existing directory contents automatically
ConfigMaps can only be mounted as whole directories — restructure the app instead
explain: `subPath` carves one entry out of a volume and mounts it at the given path — the classic fix for 'I need one config file inside a directory the app also writes to.' Double-mounting doesn't merge (the second obscures the first), hostPath has the same obscuring behavior, and single-file mounting is fully supported. Note the trade-off the exam likes: subPath mounts don't receive ConfigMap updates — whole-directory mounts do.

q: A container needs the host's `/srv/certs` CA bundle, but it must NEVER modify it — a bug once truncated the host's bundle through the mount. Which mount option enforces read-only access?
options: `-v /srv/certs:/certs:rw` — the default mode is already safe against writes
Bind mounts are always read-only from inside the container
`-v /srv/certs:/certs:ro` (or `--mount type=bind,src=/srv/certs,dst=/certs,readonly`) — the kernel enforces read-only; write attempts fail inside the container
Copy the files into the image at build time — mounts can't be made read-only
explain: `:ro` / `readonly` is the kernel-enforced guard: the mount is read-only inside the container's namespace, so even a root process in the container gets EROFS on write — the host's bundle is safe. The default is `rw` (that's how the truncation happened), bind mounts are not read-only by nature, and while baking certs into the image works for static bundles, it doesn't help when the host rotates them. Read-only mounts are cheap defense in depth — use them for every mount the container doesn't need to write.

q: `docker ps -s` shows a container as `1.2kB (virtual 150MB)`. The engineer concludes the container is consuming 150MB of disk. What do the two numbers actually mean?
options: 1.2kB is the image size; 150MB is the container's memory usage
The container really uses 150MB — virtual size is the true disk figure
Both numbers measure RAM — the container is about to be OOM-killed
`1.2kB` (size) is data written to the container's writable layer; `150MB` (virtual) is that plus the shared read-only image. Image bytes are shared, not duplicated per container
explain: `-s` shows two figures: size = the container's own writable-layer writes (here, almost nothing), virtual = size + the image it runs on. Ten containers from one 150MB image don't use 1.5GB — they share the read-only layers and each add only their own writes. This is the payoff of the layered filesystem (and why Q187's database-on-writable-layer warning matters): measure the first number when hunting container disk bloat, not the second.

q: A container bind-mounts the single host file `/srv/app/config.yaml`. The engineer edits it on the host with vim and saves — but the container still sees the OLD content. Restarting the container picks up the new file. What happened?
options: Bind mounts cache file contents — only a daemon restart refreshes them
Single-file mounts require `--mount` instead of `-v` to stay live
Single-file bind mounts are read-only snapshots by design
vim saves by writing a new file and renaming it over the old — the container's bind holds the ORIGINAL inode, so it keeps seeing the stale file. Edit in place instead, or restart the container
explain: A bind mount pins an inode, not a pathname. Editors like vim replace the file (new inode, rename over), so the container keeps reading the orphaned original — the classic 'config change didn't take' mystery. In-place edits (redirection, `sed -i` without backup... careful: GNU sed -i also renames by default) or a container restart fix it. This inode-vs-path distinction is also why mounting a file that gets log-rotated behaves the same way.

q: Two Kubernetes pods mount the SAME PVC (ReadWriteOnce) for 'high availability'. The second pod never starts — it waits on a multi-attach error while the team blames the scheduler. What is the real problem?
options: The scheduler is broken — RWO volumes support multi-attach across nodes

ReadWriteOnce means one node at a time — the volume is already attached to the first pod's node, so the second pod can't attach it. RWO is not shared storage; use ReadWriteMany or a replicated database for HA
A PVC can never be mounted by two pods — each pod needs its own claim
The pods should use `hostPath` instead — it supports multi-node sharing
explain: RWO is a single-node attachment contract — the second pod's node physically cannot attach the volume while node one holds it, hence Pending (not a scheduler bug; the scheduler is correctly refusing the impossible). 'HA via one shared disk' is the architectural error: real database HA is replication (or a RWX-capable store), not two writers on one block device — which would corrupt data anyway (the Docker-side twin of this lesson is Q200's two-containers-one-volume corruption).

q: On a rootless Docker host, the admin checks `/var/lib/docker` for disk usage — it's nearly empty. Yet `docker system df` reports 40GB used. Where does rootless Docker actually store its data?
options: In memory — rootless Docker keeps all state ephemeral by design
In `/var/lib/docker` anyway — the 40GB figure must be a reporting bug
`~/.local/share/docker` under the invoking user's home — the unprivileged daemon keeps its data root where it has write access
In `/tmp/docker-<uid>` — it's wiped on every reboot
explain: Rootless daemons can't write to `/var/lib/docker`, so the data root moves into the user's home (`~/.local/share/docker` by default). The admin looked in the wrong place — `docker system df` and `docker info` (Docker Root Dir) report against the real one. Operational consequence: home-directory quotas and backups now cover Docker's storage, and `du` on `/var/lib/docker` tells you nothing on a rootless host.

q: A pod uses `emptyDir: { sizeLimit: 2Gi }` for scratch space. A runaway job writes 5GB into it. What does Kubernetes do?
options: Nothing — `sizeLimit` is advisory and never enforced
Writes fail with 'no space left' at exactly 2Gi, but the pod keeps running normally
Kubernetes transparently expands the emptyDir — `sizeLimit` only guides scheduling
The kubelet evicts the pod for exceeding its emptyDir `sizeLimit` — the limit is an eviction threshold, not a writable quota
explain: `sizeLimit` doesn't cap writes like a quota — it arms an eviction tripwire: once the kubelet measures usage past the limit, the pod is evicted (with disk-pressure-style handling). The runaway job doesn't get a graceful ENOSPC at 2Gi; the whole pod gets killed. Lesson: sizeLimit protects the NODE from scratch-space abuse, not the pod from its own bugs — fix the runaway writer, and size scratch honestly.

q: An image ships its application at `/app`. The engineer runs `-v /srv/empty:/app` (an empty host directory) and the container crashes — `/app` is empty inside. Last week a NAMED volume at `/app` worked fine. What is the difference?
options: A new named volume is initialized with the image's content at that path on first use; a bind mount is NOT — the empty host directory simply obscures `/app`
Bind mounts are broken for non-empty image directories — only named volumes work there
The host directory needs the `:z` flag before Docker copies the image content into it
