Named volumes also start empty — last week's success must have been a cached layer
explain: Docker populates a fresh named volume with the image's directory content the first time it's mounted — a convenience that exists ONLY for named volumes. Bind mounts do no such thing: the host path wins verbatim, empty or not, hiding whatever the image shipped. `:z` is SELinux relabeling (unrelated), and 'bind mounts are broken' misdiagnoses documented behavior. If the host dir must start populated, copy the content in yourself — or use the named volume.

q: `docker run -v /data/newdir:/data ...` works even though `/data/newdir` doesn't exist on the host — Docker created it. But `docker run --mount type=bind,src=/data/newdir,dst=/data ...` fails outright. Why the difference?
options: `--mount` is deprecated — `-v` is the only supported syntax now
`-v` auto-creates a missing host path as a root-owned directory (a classic footgun); `--mount` is explicit and errors if the source doesn't exist
`--mount` requires `src=` to be a volume name — host paths aren't allowed
Bind sources only need to exist on SELinux-enforcing hosts
explain: The old `-v` syntax silently mkdirs missing host paths — as root, which then causes the permission-denied surprises of Q119's family. `--mount` refuses to guess: the source must exist. This is one of the concrete reasons the long syntax is recommended — explicitness over magic. The exam's takeaway: prefer `--mount`, and when `-v` auto-creates a directory, expect root ownership fallout.

q: A pod mounts a ConfigMap holding a TLS private key, and the files appear as `0644` (world-readable) inside the container. The team wants `0400`. How is the file mode controlled on a ConfigMap volume?
options: `chmod` in an init container — ConfigMap mount modes are fixed at 0644 and can't be set natively
They can't be changed — private keys must use Secret volumes instead
`defaultMode: 0400` on the volume (or per-item `mode:`) — ConfigMap and Secret volumes both support setting the file mode directly
Set `fsGroup` — it forces the mode to 0400
explain: `defaultMode` (and per-item `mode`) sets the permission bits on files projected from ConfigMaps and Secrets — `0400` for keys is the textbook use. Init-container chmod works but fights the kubelet's periodic remounts; Secret volumes share the same defaultMode mechanism (they're not a mode workaround); and `fsGroup` changes group OWNERSHIP, not the mode bits. Default 0644 on a private key is a finding in any audit — set the mode where the volume is defined.

q: A nightly cron runs a backup container sharing the Postgres container's volumes and tars the live data directory: `docker run --rm --volumes-from pg -v /mnt/backups:/backups busybox tar cf /backups/pg.tar /var/lib/postgresql/data` — while Postgres is RUNNING. Restores intermittently yield a corrupt database. What is wrong with this backup?
options: `--volumes-from` doesn't work against running containers — the tarball is empty
tar can't read volume data — `docker cp` must be used instead
The backup container needs `--privileged` to read the files consistently

Copying live database files at the filesystem level races with writes — the tar captures a torn, inconsistent state. Quiesce the database (or use `pg_dump` / storage snapshots) for a consistent backup
explain: Filesystem copies of a running database are crash-consistent at best: tar happily archives pages mid-write, producing a backup that sometimes restores and sometimes doesn't — the worst kind of failure. The `--volumes-from` technique itself is sound (it's the documented volume-backup pattern); the error is doing it HOT without quiescing. Proper options: `pg_dump` to a file, stop the DB briefly, or snapshot the storage underneath. A backup you've never test-restored is a rumor.

q: A StatefulSet's pods land in different availability zones, but their volumes were provisioned in a single zone first — so pods stay Pending, unable to reach their storage. Which StorageClass setting delays provisioning until the pod's zone is known?
options: `volumeBindingMode: Immediate` — it predicts the pod's zone from the StatefulSet
Add a `nodeSelector` to the StorageClass — it pins provisioning to the right zone
Use `hostPath` volumes — they always match the pod's zone
`volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` — binding and provisioning wait for a pod to be scheduled, so the volume is created in the pod's actual topology
explain: `WaitForFirstConsumer` defers volume binding (and dynamic provisioning) until a pod using the PVC is scheduled — the provisioner then sees the pod's node/zone and creates storage there. `Immediate` (the default) provisions first and hopes the pod lands nearby — the exact failure in the question. StorageClasses take no nodeSelector, and hostPath is node-local ephemera, not zoned durable storage. For any multi-zone cluster, WaitForFirstConsumer is the correct default.

q: A service runs v1. An engineer updates it to v2 (a bad image), then immediately runs `docker service update --rollback web` and confirms v1 is back. Panicking during the incident review, she runs `docker service update --rollback web` a second time 'to be extra sure we're on the safe version.' What does the second rollback do?
options: It re-deploys the BAD v2 image — Swarm keeps only the current Spec and one PreviousSpec, so the first rollback already made v2 the 'previous' spec
Nothing — rollback is idempotent and the second invocation is a no-op once the service is stable
It rolls back to the version before v1, since Swarm keeps a full history of service specs
It fails with an error because a service can only be rolled back once per update
explain: Swarm retains exactly two specs: Spec (current) and PreviousSpec. The first rollback swapped them — v1 became current, v2 became previous. A second rollback swaps them again, re-deploying the bad v2. There is no deeper history to fall back to; `docker service inspect` shows both specs explicitly. The 'extra sure' instinct is the trap: rollback is a toggle, not a ratchet. To get back to v1 after the double rollback, you'd update --image to v1 explicitly.

q: A database migration runs as a Swarm service. It succeeds on the first attempt 90% of the time, but a flaky network dependency makes it fail spuriously on some runs. With the default restart policy it loops forever on genuine failures; with `--restart-condition none` a spurious failure kills the whole migration with no retry. Which restart configuration retries transient failures but eventually gives up?
options: `--restart-condition any` with `--restart-delay 0s` — it retries instantly and forever until success

`--restart-condition on-failure --restart-max-attempts 5 --restart-delay 10s` — only failed tasks restart, backing off 10s between tries, and Swarm stops after 5 failed attempts instead of looping forever
`--restart-condition none` — failed tasks must never be retried, so the operator reruns the migration by hand each time
`--restart-condition on-failure` alone — the max-attempts and delay flags don't exist for Swarm services
explain: `on-failure` restarts only tasks that exit non-zero (a clean exit 0 stays finished), `--restart-max-attempts 5` caps the retry loop so a genuinely broken migration stops instead of churning forever, and `--restart-delay` spaces attempts so a flapping dependency can recover. `any` would also restart successful completions — wrong for run-to-completion work — and `none` gives up on the first spurious failure. All three flags are real service-create options; the exam loves combining them into one scenario.

q: Four GPU nodes in the Swarm carry `node.labels.gpu=true`. A new web frontend must run on every node EXCEPT the GPU nodes, which are reserved for inference workloads. Which placement constraint expresses 'everywhere but the GPU nodes'?
options: `--constraint 'node.labels.gpu == false'` — nodes without the label evaluate the comparison as false
Placement constraints can't express negation; you must label all 40 non-GPU nodes instead
`--placement-pref 'spread=node.labels.gpu'` — preferences are the only way to avoid labeled nodes
`--constraint 'node.labels.gpu != true'` — the != operator matches nodes where the label is absent or has any other value
explain: Constraints support both `==` and `!=`. With `!=`, a node that lacks the label entirely still satisfies the constraint (absent != true), so the frontend lands everywhere except the four GPU nodes — no need to label the other 40. `== false` would only match nodes explicitly labeled `gpu=false`, leaving unlabeled nodes unschedulable. Preferences are soft hints, not exclusion rules, and can't guarantee the reservation.

q: A Swarm service mounts a config as `/etc/app/config.yaml` via `--config source=app_cfg,target=/etc/app/config.yaml`. The config must change weekly, but the app hardcodes that exact path. The engineer looks for a `docker config update` subcommand and finds there isn't one. How is the value rotated while keeping the same in-container path?
options: Edit the config object in place with `docker config edit app_cfg` — configs are mutable, only secrets are immutable
Delete the config and recreate it with the same name; running tasks pick up the new content automatically on next read
Configs can't be rotated without recreating the service from scratch

`docker config create app_cfg_v2 newfile.yaml`, then `docker service update --config-rm app_cfg --config-add source=app_cfg_v2,target=/etc/app/config.yaml web` — configs are immutable, so rotation means a new object plus a service update that swaps it at the same target path
explain: Swarm configs (like secrets) are immutable: there is no update command. Rotation is always create-new-object plus `service update` to detach the old and attach the new. The `--config-add source=...,target=...` form keeps the in-container path stable so the app never knows the object name changed. Editing in place is impossible (no such commands), and running tasks never re-read a swapped object — the update is what recreates tasks with the new mount.

q: The security team pre-creates the production database password with `docker secret create db_prod < /vault/dbpass` and tells the app team to consume it in their stack file — but NOT to manage its lifecycle. The app team's first deploy attempt fails with an 'already exists' error on the secret. What's wrong with their Compose file, and what's the fix?
options: Declare it as `secrets: { db_prod: { external: true } }` — without `external: true`, `docker stack deploy` tries to CREATE the secret and collides with the pre-created one
Secrets can't be shared between teams; each stack must create its own copy
The security team must grant the app team's stack access with `docker secret grant` — there is no such grant command for secrets
Rename the secret in the file; Swarm forbids two stacks referencing the same secret name
explain: `external: true` tells stack deploy the object already exists and must be looked up, not created — the standard pattern when another team (or Terraform, or a prior deploy) owns the lifecycle. Without it, deploy attempts creation and fails on the name collision. Secrets are cluster-global objects any granted service can reference regardless of which stack created them; there is no per-stack secret namespace and no grant command involved.

q: A packet-capture sidecar needs raw socket access, so the engineer adds `privileged: true` to its service in the Compose file and runs `docker stack deploy`. The deploy prints `Ignoring unsupported options: privileged`, and the sidecar's captures fail. What's the reality, and what's the workable alternative?
options: The warning is cosmetic — Swarm applies privileged anyway after a short delay, so the captures will start working
The option belongs under `deploy:` as `deploy.privileged: true`; at the service level it's ignored

Swarm never supported privileged services — the option is silently dropped by design, because a manager scheduling privileged containers onto workers would hand out host root remotely. Run that component as a standalone `docker run --privileged` container (or a global-mode equivalent outside Swarm scheduling) instead
Add `cap_add: [ALL]` to the Compose file, which stack deploy honors as a privileged equivalent
explain: Privileged containers were deliberately never supported in Swarm mode: letting any manager schedule `--privileged` tasks would let a compromised manager (or anyone with service-create rights) get host root on every worker. The deploy warning is real — the option is dropped, not deferred, and there is no `deploy.privileged` spelling. The supported workaround is running that one component outside Swarm scheduling (standalone container, or host-level agent) while the rest of the app stays orchestrated. `cap_add: [ALL]` is not equivalent and the v3 Compose reference historically marked capability options as ignored for stacks.

q: A Swarm service bind-mounts a 200GB ML model directory: `--mount type=bind,src=/data/models,dst=/models,readonly`. It works perfectly when the engineer tests it on a manager, but tasks placed on workers fail with a mount error. The path exists on the manager. What's the most likely cause?
options: Bind mounts are forbidden in Swarm services; only named volumes are allowed
The manager has the directory but the workers don't — a bind mount references a host-local path, so EVERY node that runs the task must have /data/models present with the same content
Swarm encrypts bind mounts and the workers lack the decryption key
The readonly flag is incompatible with bind mounts in Swarm mode
explain: A bind mount is just a host path — Swarm doesn't distribute the data. Testing on the manager masked the problem because that one host happened to have the directory. Every worker needs /data/models populated (via config management, a shared filesystem, or better: a named volume with a shared-storage driver). Bind mounts are legal in services but they're a scheduling landmine for exactly this reason; the exam positions named volumes as the portable answer and bind mounts as the 'works on my node' trap.

q: A Swarm cluster mixes Linux and Windows workers. A Linux-only API service keeps getting tasks scheduled onto Windows nodes, where they fail instantly with platform errors. The service must never land on a Windows node. Which constraint fixes this?
options: `--constraint 'node.role == worker'` — workers are Linux by convention
`--constraint 'engine.labels.os == linux'` — engine labels carry the OS
`--constraint 'node.platform.os == linux'` — the platform constraint matches the node's OS directly
No constraint can do this; Linux and Windows services must run in separate swarms
explain: `node.platform.os` (and `node.platform.arch`) are built-in node attributes describing the actual platform — the precise tool for mixed-OS clusters. `node.role` says nothing about OS (Windows nodes can be workers), and `engine.labels` are custom daemon labels that don't exist unless someone sets them. Mixed-OS swarms are fully supported; the scheduler just needs the platform constraint to keep Linux images off Windows nodes and vice versa.

q: A service was created passing `--with-registry-auth` for a private registry and runs fine. Weeks later the engineer runs `docker service update --image registry.corp/web:2.1 web` WITHOUT the flag. New tasks fail with `no basic auth credentials` while old tasks keep running. `docker login` is still valid on the manager. What happened?
options: The registry revoked the service's credentials because the image tag changed
`docker login` on the manager expired; the engineer must log in again before any update

`--with-registry-auth` only attaches the credentials to that single create/update request — it is not stored in the service spec. Every update that pulls a private image must pass the flag again, or workers pull anonymously and fail
Swarm caches registry credentials per image tag; new tags always require `docker logout` first
explain: The flag's effect is per-request: the CLI forwards your local registry auth with that one create/update call so workers can pull. Nothing about the credentials is persisted into the service definition, so a later update without the flag pulls anonymously and gets `no basic auth credentials`. The manager's own login is irrelevant — workers do the pulling. The operational rule is simple: any `service update` (or `stack deploy`) touching a private image repeats `--with-registry-auth`.

q: A vendor image ships a HEALTHCHECK that curls port 8080, but the app in this deployment listens on 9090 — so every task is marked unhealthy and Swarm keeps rescheduling it. The image can't be rebuilt (signed vendor image). How do you neutralize the bad healthcheck at deploy time?
options: Set `--update-monitor 0s` so Swarm stops watching health during updates
Pass `--no-healthcheck` (or a corrected `--health-cmd`) on `docker service create` — service-level flags override/disable the image's HEALTHCHECK without touching the image
Add `HEALTHCHECK NONE` to a wrapper Dockerfile — the only way to override an image healthcheck is at build time
Healthchecks are advisory in Swarm; the rescheduling must be caused by something else
explain: `--no-healthcheck` disables the image-baked HEALTHCHECK for the service's tasks, and `--health-cmd` (with `--health-interval/timeout/retries/start-period`) replaces it with a correct one — all without rebuilding the signed image. Service-level health settings take precedence over the Dockerfile's. `HEALTHCHECK NONE` is the Dockerfile-side equivalent but requires a rebuild, which the scenario forbids. `--update-monitor` only tunes rollout observation, not the health verdict itself.

q: A third-party image defaults to running as root. The security policy says this service must run as UID 9999, but the team can't modify the vendor's Dockerfile. Which `docker service create` flag enforces the runtime user, and what does it override?
options: `--user 9999` — it overrides the image's USER (or the default root) for every task's main process
`--privileged-user 9999` — the dedicated flag for dropping privileges on Swarm services
There is no such flag; the USER can only be set in the Dockerfile at build time
`--env USER=9999` — the container runtime reads the USER variable to switch identities
explain: `--user` (aka `-u`) sets the UID/GID for the task's processes, overriding whatever the image declares — including an explicit `USER root` or the default. It's the runtime escape hatch when the image can't be rebuilt. There is no `--privileged-user` flag (invented), and the `USER` environment variable is just a string to the process — the runtime never interprets it. Note `docker exec -u` only affects that one exec session, not the service.

q: An engineer sees a misbehaving task `web.3.abc123` in `docker service ps web` and runs `docker exec -it web.3.abc123 sh` from the manager. It fails: `no such container`. The task is Running. Why did exec fail, and what's the correct procedure?
options: `docker exec` only works on managers for global services; replicated tasks can't be exec'd at all

Task names aren't containers — `docker exec` targets a container ID/name on the Docker host actually running it. Find the task's node via `docker service ps`, SSH to that node, then `docker exec` the container there (or use the container ID shown in the task details)
The task ID must be prefixed with the service name twice: `web.web.3.abc123`
Exec is blocked by Swarm's mutual TLS; you must `docker node promote` yourself first
explain: `docker exec` is a single-host operation against a container, not a Swarm-aware one — `web.3.abc123` is a task slot identifier, not a container name the local daemon knows (especially from a manager that doesn't run the task). The workflow is: `docker service ps web` shows the NODE column, then on that node `docker ps` reveals the actual container (named `<stack>_<service>.<slot>.<taskid>`), which is what exec accepts. Mutual TLS and promotion are irrelevant; this is purely about which daemon owns the container.

q: A Prometheus setup must scrape a node-exporter on EVERY Swarm node at a fixed per-node address, e.g. `http://node7:9100/metrics`. The exporter runs as a global service. With the default ingress publish mode, scrapes hit random nodes' exporters instead of the intended one. Which publish configuration gives each node its own directly-addressable exporter port?
options: `--publish mode=host,target=9100,published=9100` — host mode binds the task's port directly on its own node, bypassing the routing mesh, so node7:9100 always reaches node7's exporter
`--publish mode=ingress,target=9100,published=9100` — ingress mode already pins each task to its own node
Add `--endpoint-mode dnsrr` — DNS round-robin makes each scrape land on a different node deterministically
Publish mode can't fix this; run the exporter as a replicated service with one replica per node instead
explain: Ingress mode publishes through the routing mesh: every node listens on 9100 but mesh routing load-balances to a random task, so per-node scraping breaks. `mode=host` skips the mesh — the port binds only where the task actually runs, and with a global service that's exactly one exporter per node at a predictable address. DNSRR changes name resolution, not port routing, and replicated-with-N-replicas can't guarantee one-per-node the way global mode does.

q: A worker service is created with `--limit-memory 256M`. After deploy, its tasks repeatedly show `OOMKilled` in `docker service ps` and Swarm keeps restarting them — a hot restart loop burning CPU. The tasks ran fine in staging without the limit. What's the correct diagnosis and fix?
options: The limit is too low for the workload's real footprint — raise `--limit-memory` to match measured usage (or fix the leak); the OOM killer is doing its job and Swarm's restart policy is dutifully resurrecting the tasks
Add more replicas — the OOM kills mean the service is under-provisioned
Set `--restart-condition none` so Swarm stops resurrecting killed tasks
Memory limits don't apply to Swarm services; the OOMKilled status must come from the host kernel randomly killing processes
explain: `--limit-memory` sets the cgroup cap; exceeding it gets the task OOM-killed, and the restart policy (default `any`) immediately starts a replacement that gets killed again — the classic limit-too-low loop. The fix is sizing the limit to reality (measure with `docker stats` under load) or fixing the memory leak, not adding replicas (each new task hits the same cap) or disabling restarts (which just converts the loop into a dead service). Limits absolutely apply to Swarm tasks — that's their purpose.

q: Two nodes get new SSDs. The engineer labels them via `docker node update --label-add disk=ssd node3 node4`, expecting the Postgres service (constrained with `node.labels.disk == ssd`) to migrate onto them. Nothing moves — Postgres stays on its old nodes. The labels are confirmed present. Why didn't the service reschedule, and what triggers it?
options: Node labels only take effect after `docker swarm leave` and rejoin; the engineer must cycle both nodes

Placement constraints are evaluated only when a task is (re)scheduled — existing tasks don't migrate on label changes. Run `docker service update --force postgres` to roll the tasks so the scheduler re-evaluates against the new labels
The label syntax is wrong — it must be `--label-add node.labels.disk=ssd`
Constraints can't reference labels added after service creation; the service must be removed and recreated
explain: The scheduler evaluates constraints at task creation time; mutating a node's labels doesn't evict or migrate already-running tasks. `--force` triggers a rolling update with no spec change, forcing every task to be rescheduled — now against the current labels. The label syntax used is correct, no rejoin is needed, and constraints absolutely can reference later-added labels; they just only apply to new scheduling decisions.

q: Nodes carry two labels: `az` (1a/1b/1c) and `rack` (r1-r6). The team wants tasks spread across availability zones FIRST, then across racks within each zone. They pass two spread preferences: first `node.labels.az`, then `node.labels.rack`. How does Swarm interpret multiple placement preferences?
options: Only the last preference is used; earlier ones are overwritten
Preferences are evaluated in order — spread across AZs first, then use the rack preference to break ties within each AZ
Multiple preferences are OR'd: a task satisfies the placement if it matches ANY of them
Placement preferences can't be combined; the service create is rejected
explain: Placement preferences form an ordered list — i.e. `--placement-pref 'spread=node.labels.az'` followed by `--placement-pref 'spread=node.labels.rack'`: the scheduler applies them sequentially, using each subsequent preference to spread within the groups formed by the previous one. So AZ spread happens first, then rack spread refines placement inside each AZ. They don't overwrite each other and they aren't alternatives — and they're still soft preferences, not hard constraints, so a task will still schedule (unspread) rather than stay pending if perfect spreading is impossible.

q: A nightly reconciliation job runs as `--mode replicated-job` with 3 tasks, each handling one shard. Every worker needs to know its shard index (0, 1, 2) at startup. The engineer doesn't want three separate services. How can each task learn its own shard number?
options: It can't — Swarm tasks are identical, so sharded workers require one service per shard

Use `--env SHARD={{.Task.Slot}}` — Swarm templates `{{.Task.Slot}}` into the env value per task, so each worker gets its own slot number (note: slots start at 1, so the app should map slot→shard or subtract one)
Set `--hostname shard-worker` and parse the trailing digit from the hostname
Read the slot from `/run/secrets/slot` — Swarm writes each task's slot into a secret automatically
explain: `--env` (like `--hostname` and `--mount`) supports Go templating with placeholders including `.Task.Slot`, `.Service.Name`, and `.Node.Hostname` — each task renders its own value. That's the built-in way to differentiate otherwise-identical tasks. Hardcoding one hostname gives all three tasks the same name, no slot secret exists, and one-service-per-shard defeats the purpose of the replicated-job mode. The slot-numbering caveat (1-based) is the detail that bites: shard math must account for it.

q: A Dockerfile for Windows Server Core needs `RUN` steps using PowerShell cmdlets (`Get-ChildItem`, `Expand-Archive`). The steps fail because the default shell is `cmd.exe`, which doesn't understand them. Which instruction switches the shell used for subsequent `RUN` instructions, and what's its correct form?
options: `CMD ["powershell", "-Command"]` — it changes the shell for all following RUN steps
`SHELL ["powershell", "-Command"]` — it sets the default shell for RUN (and shell-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT); on Windows the default is cmd, so PowerShell syntax needs this override
`RUN powershell -Command "..."` prefixed on every line — SHELL doesn't exist on Windows builds
`ENV SHELL=powershell` — the SHELL environment variable controls the build shell
explain: SHELL exists precisely for this: it sets the default shell used to execute shell-form RUN instructions (JSON exec-form RUN is unaffected). On Windows the default is `cmd`, so PowerShell syntax requires `SHELL ["powershell", "-Command"]` before those RUN steps. CMD only sets the container's default command (nothing to do with build shells), and while prefixing every RUN with `powershell -Command` works, it's the verbose workaround SHELL was invented to replace. The ENV variable named SHELL is just a string — the builder ignores it.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI exports `CI_COMMIT_SHA` in the pipeline environment. The Dockerfile declares `ARG CI_COMMIT_SHA`. The pipeline runs `docker build --build-arg CI_COMMIT_SHA -t shop/api:2.0 .` — note: no `=value` after the flag. What value does the build receive?
options: The value of the `CI_COMMIT_SHA` environment variable from the build environment — a bare `--build-arg NAME` inherits the local env value
An empty string — without `=value` the arg is always empty
The build fails: `--build-arg` requires an explicit value
The value from the Dockerfile's `ARG CI_COMMIT_SHA=<default>` line, ignoring the environment
explain: A valueless `--build-arg NAME` pulls NAME from the environment where the CLI runs — the documented way to pass values without writing them into scripts or Dockerfiles. If the env var is unset AND the Dockerfile declares no default, the arg is empty (with a warning), not an error. The Dockerfile default only applies when neither `=value` nor an environment value is provided.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile starts with `ARG APP_VERSION=1.0`, then `RUN npm ci` (8 minutes), then `COPY . .`, then `RUN npm run build`. Every release bumps `--build-arg APP_VERSION=1.1`, and every bump re-runs the 8-minute `npm ci` even though dependencies didn't change. Why does the cache break, and what's the fix?
options: Build args are never cached; every `--build-arg` forces a full `--no-cache` build — move the version into a LABEL instead

Changing an ARG's value invalidates the cache for that layer AND every layer after it. Move `ARG APP_VERSION` below the expensive `RUN npm ci` (or after the dependency steps) so version bumps only invalidate the cheap tail of the build
The cache breaks because `COPY . .` comes after the ARG; reordering COPY before ARG fixes it
`npm ci` is inherently uncacheable across builds regardless of ARG placement
explain: An ARG instruction is a cacheable layer whose cache key includes its value — change the value and that layer plus everything downstream is rebuilt. Placing volatile ARGs (versions, build dates, SHAs) as late as possible, after expensive stable steps like dependency installation, confines the invalidation to the cheap tail. `COPY . .` placement matters for source-change invalidation, but here the ARG is the cache-buster. `npm ci` caches fine when its inputs (package.json/lockfile layer) are unchanged.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: The team deletes hundreds of old tags from their self-hosted registry via the API, but disk usage doesn't drop at all. `docker system prune` on the registry host changes nothing. What's actually holding the disk space, and how is it reclaimed?
options: The registry caches tag metadata in memory; restart the registry container to free the disk
Tag deletion is asynchronous; the disk frees itself after 24 hours with no action needed
`docker system prune` must be run INSIDE the registry container, not on the host

Deleting a tag only removes the manifest reference — the underlying blobs stay until `registry garbage-collect /etc/docker/registry/config.yml` runs (with the registry stopped or in read-only mode), which deletes blobs no manifest references anymore
explain: Registry storage is content-addressed: tags are pointers to manifests, manifests point to blobs. Deleting tags removes pointers but orphans nothing until garbage collection walks the manifests and deletes unreferenced blobs. `docker system prune` only cleans the local Docker engine's images/containers — it knows nothing about the registry's blob store. GC must run against a quiesced registry (stopped or read-only) so it doesn't delete blobs being pushed.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Before rolling `shop/api:2.0` to ARM edge nodes, the release engineer wants to confirm the tag actually contains BOTH amd64 and arm64 images — not just the amd64 build someone pushed last time. Which command inspects the registry's manifest list without pulling anything?
options: `docker buildx imagetools inspect shop/api:2.0` — it shows the manifest list including each platform's digest
`docker images shop/api:2.0` — the PLATFORM column lists all architectures in the tag
`docker manifest inspect shop/api:2.0` — the standard GA command for this on any modern CLI
`docker pull --platform linux/arm64 shop/api:2.0 --dry-run` — dry-run lists the platforms
explain: `buildx imagetools inspect` queries the registry and prints the manifest list with per-platform digests — the reliable pre-deploy check. `docker images` only shows what's in the LOCAL store (one platform after a pull). `docker manifest inspect` exists but still requires experimental CLI features enabled, so it's not the dependable answer. There is no `--dry-run` flag for pull (invented) — pull always pulls.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A team shrinks a Go service with a multi-stage build ending in `FROM scratch` plus `COPY --from=build /app/server /server`. The container fails instantly: `exec /server: no such file or directory` — but the file is definitely in the image. What's happening, and what's the fix?
options: The binary isn't executable — add `RUN chmod +x /server` after the COPY

`scratch` has no dynamic linker — a dynamically-linked binary can't start because its loader (e.g. /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2) doesn't exist. Build a static binary (`CGO_ENABLED=0`) or copy the needed libraries in
`COPY --from=build` can't target `/` in a scratch image; copy to `/app/` instead
scratch images require an ENTRYPOINT; CMD alone can't launch the binary
explain: The classic misleading error: the kernel reports the missing *interpreter*, not the binary, as 'no such file or directory'. A `scratch` image contains literally nothing — no libc, no loader — so any dynamically-linked binary fails at exec time. The fix is a fully static binary (CGO_ENABLED=0 for Go, or `-static`), or a minimal base (distroless/static) instead of bare scratch. chmod and ENTRYPOINT/CMD form are red herrings; the file is present and executable, its loader is what's missing.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A developer runs `docker build -t MyApp:2.0 .` and gets `invalid reference format`. The Dockerfile is fine. What's wrong?
options: Tags can't contain dots — use `MyApp:2-0` instead
Repository names must be lowercase — `MyApp` is invalid; use `myapp:2.0`
The `-t` flag requires a registry hostname; bare names are rejected
Build tags can't start with an uppercase letter but can contain them elsewhere
explain: Docker reference rules: the repository name component must be lowercase (regex enforced by the daemon). `MyApp:2.0` fails parsing entirely — it's not a warning. Tags themselves MAY contain uppercase, dots, and underscores; it's the name that's restricted. And bare names without a registry hostname are perfectly fine (they default to Docker Hub).
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI must stamp every image with its git SHA for traceability, but the team doesn't want developers editing the Dockerfile for it (merge conflicts on every commit). How can the pipeline add the label at build time?
options: It can't — LABELs can only come from Dockerfile instructions
`docker build --label org.opencontainers.image.revision=$SHA -t img .` — build-time labels are added to the image config and override any LABEL of the same key in the Dockerfile
`docker tag --label` after the build — tags carry labels
Set `ENV org.opencontainers.image.revision=$SHA` in the CI environment; the builder picks it up automatically
explain: `docker build --label` injects labels into the resulting image's config without touching the Dockerfile, and a build-time label wins over a Dockerfile LABEL with the same key. `docker tag` only creates a name alias — it carries no metadata. Environment variables on the CI host are invisible to the build unless passed via `--build-arg`, and even then they'd need an ARG/LABEL instruction to land in the image config.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A multi-stage Dockerfile has `FROM registry-a.corp/base:1.0 AS build` and `FROM registry-b.corp/runtime:2.0` as the final stage. The engineer ran `docker login registry-a.corp` only. The build fails pulling the final stage. Why, and what's required?
options: Only the FINAL stage's registry needs authentication — but the login must use `--registry-b` flag syntax
Multi-stage builds can't span registries; all stages must come from one registry
Every `FROM` that references a private registry needs its own `docker login` — the build must authenticate to BOTH registry-a.corp and registry-b.corp
BuildKit forwards the first login to all registries automatically; the failure must be a network issue
explain: Each FROM is an independent pull against its own registry with its own auth — credentials are per-registry-host in the Docker config, never shared across hosts. Logging into registry-a does nothing for registry-b. There's no `--registry-b` login flag (invented), multi-registry builds are fully supported, and BuildKit forwards nothing across registry boundaries. The fix is simply `docker login` to each private host before building.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: On an ARM64 laptop, an engineer needs to test the amd64-only image `vendor/tool:3.1` (no arm64 variant exists). `docker pull vendor/tool:3.1` fails with `no matching manifest for linux/arm64`. What's the correct pull?
options: `docker pull --platform linux/amd64 vendor/tool:3.1` — it requests the amd64 manifest from the manifest list explicitly
`docker pull --arch amd64 vendor/tool:3.1` — the --arch flag overrides platform detection
It can't be done — Docker refuses images whose architecture doesn't match the host
`docker pull vendor/tool:3.1@amd64` — the architecture goes after the @ digest separator
explain: `--platform linux/amd64` tells the daemon which manifest to select from the image's manifest list instead of defaulting to the host's platform. There is no `--pull --arch` flag (invented), and `@` takes a digest, not an architecture name. (Whether it *runs* then depends on emulation like Rosetta/QEMU — but the pull itself is the question's ask, and cross-arch pulls are routine in multi-arch pipelines.)
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A multi-stage Dockerfile has three UNNAMED stages (no `AS` names). The final stage needs a binary from the FIRST stage. Which `COPY --from` reference works?
options: `COPY --from=0` — stages are indexed from 0 in build order when they have no names
`COPY --from=1` — stage numbering starts at 1
Unnamed stages can't be referenced; you must add `AS` names to every stage
`COPY --from=first` — Docker assigns positional keywords automatically
explain: Build stages are zero-indexed: `--from=0` is the first FROM, `--from=1` the second, and so on. Named stages (`AS builder`) can be referenced by name OR still by index. You never need names just to copy between stages — the index always works. `first` is not a keyword (invented), and 1-based indexing would silently grab the wrong stage.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A team adopts a third-party image with no documentation. Before running it, they want to know: what it executes by default, what env vars it sets, and which ports it declares. Which inspection answers all three WITHOUT running a container?
options: `docker history img` — it shows the effective entrypoint, env, and ports
`docker inspect --format='{{.Config.Entrypoint}} {{.Config.Cmd}} {{.Config.Env}} {{.Config.ExposedPorts}}' img` — the image config records exactly the effective defaults
You must `docker run` it first — image metadata isn't queryable until a container exists
`docker image ls --verbose img` — the verbose listing includes config details
explain: Everything asked lives in the image's config JSON, readable via `docker inspect` with a Go template — no container needed. `docker history` shows layer *creation commands* (truncated, build-time), not the merged effective config. There is no `--verbose` for image ls (invented), and running an unknown image just to read its metadata is both unnecessary and a security anti-pattern.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A multi-stage Dockerfile sets `ENV NODE_ENV=production` in the `build` stage, then the `runtime` stage (`FROM node:20-slim`) runs the app — which behaves as if NODE_ENV were unset. Why?
options: ENV is scoped to the stage that declares it — each FROM starts a fresh stage and nothing (ENV, ARG defaults, shell state) carries over unless redeclared
The ENV was overridden by the base image's own ENV; base images always win
ENV only applies to RUN instructions, not to the final container's runtime
Multi-stage builds strip all ENV for security; use --build-arg instead
explain: Each stage is an independent build rooted at its FROM: ENV, ARG values, WORKDIR, and USER all reset. The runtime stage never saw the declaration. The fix is redeclaring `ENV NODE_ENV=production` (or an ARG+ENV pair) in the runtime stage. Base images don't 'win' over later instructions, ENV absolutely reaches runtime containers, and multi-stage strips nothing — scoping is the whole story.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q:
A `.dockerignore` contains:
```
tests/
!tests/fixtures/seed.csv
```
The build still can't see `tests/fixtures/seed.csv`. The file exists on the host. Why doesn't the exception work?
options: The `!` exception syntax only works for file extensions, not paths

You cannot re-include a file if any PARENT directory is excluded — excluding `tests/` blocks everything beneath it, and the `!` exception for a child path is silently ignored. Exclude selectively (e.g. `tests/*` with exceptions) instead
Exceptions must come BEFORE the exclusion they override
`.dockerignore` doesn't support exceptions at all; the build context always includes everything not excluded
explain: This is the documented .dockerignore gotcha: once a parent directory is excluded, no `!` rule can resurrect anything inside it — the matcher never descends into excluded directories. Order doesn't matter here (later rules do normally override earlier ones), and `!` exceptions absolutely exist for paths. The fix is excluding the directory's *contents* (`tests/*`) rather than the directory itself, so the exception for the one needed file can match.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A build's integration-test step needs a mock API that only listens on the build host's loopback interface (`127.0.0.1:8081`) — it's firewalled from the LAN. From the default build network, `127.0.0.1` is the build container itself, so the connection fails. How can the build reach the host's loopback service?
options: `docker build --network=host .` — the build containers share the host's network namespace, so 127.0.0.1 is the host's loopback
`docker build --add-host=mockapi:127.0.0.1 .` — it maps the hostname to the host's loopback
Publish the port with `docker build -p 8081:8081` — builds accept port publishing like run does
Bind mounts can expose the socket; network settings can't change this
explain: `--network=host` puts build-time RUN containers in the host's network namespace, making host loopback reachable (at the cost of build isolation — use only for trusted Dockerfiles). `--add-host` with 127.0.0.1 just points the name at the *build container's own* loopback — the same failure with extra steps. `docker build` has no `-p` flag (invented), and bind mounts move files, not network reachability.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q:
A Dockerfile has:
```
RUN cd /app
RUN ./migrate.sh
```
The second RUN fails: `./migrate.sh: not found` — even though the first RUN succeeded and the script is in /app. What went wrong?
options: Each RUN executes in a fresh shell starting from the image's WORKDIR (here `/`) — `cd` never persists between RUN instructions because each is its own layer. Chain with `&&` or set `WORKDIR /app`
The `cd` needs to be `WORKDIR` — but only the LAST instruction's directory matters, so this should have worked
RUN instructions share a shell within a build stage, but `cd` requires the `-w` flag to persist
The script lost its execute bit between layers; chmod is required after every cd
explain: Every RUN starts a new container from the previous layer's filesystem state — only filesystem changes persist, never shell state (cwd, env vars, aliases). So the second RUN starts back at `/` (no WORKDIR was set) and `./migrate.sh` resolves wrong. The idiomatic fixes are `WORKDIR /app` once, or `RUN cd /app && ./migrate.sh`. There is no persistent-shell mode and no `-w` flag for cd (invented); execute bits survive layers fine.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A build must download `https://artifacts.corp/build/data.tar.gz` with `ADD`, but the server requires an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header and returns 401 without it. The engineer tries `ADD --header "Authorization: Bearer ..." https://... /data/`. What happens, and what's the correct approach?
options: It works — ADD supports `--header` for authenticated downloads

ADD sends no custom headers and has no `--header` flag (invented) — the 401 persists. Use `RUN curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -o /data/data.tar.gz https://...` (with the token via a BuildKit secret mount, never a baked-in ARG)
Set `ENV AUTHORIZATION="Bearer ..."` — ADD reads credentials from the environment automatically
ADD can only download from registries, not arbitrary HTTPS servers
explain: ADD's remote download is a plain unauthenticated GET — no header flags exist, and environment variables are never sent as headers. The correct tool is RUN with curl/wget carrying the header, with the token injected via `--mount=type=secret` so it never lands in a layer (an ARG would be visible in `docker history`). ADD absolutely downloads from arbitrary HTTPS URLs — authentication is simply outside its feature set.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A team pushes a Windows Server Core-based image to their internal registry, but `docker push` fails on the base layers with foreign-layer errors (`blob upload unknown`). Linux images push to the same registry fine. What's the daemon-side fix?
options: Windows images can't be pushed to a registry running on Linux; the registry must be hosted on Windows Server
Rebuild the image FROM scratch — foreign layers are a Dockerfile problem, not a daemon one
Add the registry to `insecure-registries` — nondistributable layers require plain HTTP

Set `"allow-nondistributable-artifacts": ["registry.corp:5000"]` in daemon.json (and restart) — Windows base layers are 'foreign' nondistributable blobs that registries may refuse; by default the daemon won't push them, and this key allowlists the registries they'll go to
explain: Windows base layers are marked nondistributable (foreign): the daemon refuses to push them unless the target registry is allowlisted via `allow-nondistributable-artifacts`. The registry OS is irrelevant (it's just a blob store), the Dockerfile is fine, and insecure-registries governs TLS — not layer eligibility. Without the allowlist, only the team's own layers push and the base layers fail.

q: The platform team wants `docker run --gpus all` to work on every GPU host WITHOUT developers passing `--runtime nvidia` on each command. `docker info` already lists `nvidia` under Runtimes. Which daemon.json setting makes the NVIDIA runtime the default?
options: There is none — `--runtime nvidia` is the only supported way to request GPUs
Set `"default-runtime": "nvidia"` in daemon.json — then plain `docker run --gpus all` (or bare `docker run`) uses the NVIDIA runtime without repeating `--runtime` on every invocation
Add `"gpus": "all"` to daemon.json — it attaches GPUs to every container automatically
GPU access requires `--privileged`; the runtime setting is irrelevant
explain: `default-runtime` changes which OCI runtime the daemon uses when none is specified, so the NVIDIA runtime (with its GPU device injection) becomes the default path for `--gpus` requests. There is no `"gpus": "all"` daemon key (invented) — GPUs are still requested per-container, just without the legacy `--runtime` flag. `--privileged` is neither required nor advisable for GPU access.

q: A team allowlists their plain-HTTP registry in daemon.json as `"insecure-registries": ["registry.corp"]`. Pushes to `registry.corp:5000` STILL fail with an HTTP/HTTPS protocol mismatch error. The daemon was restarted. What's wrong?
options: The entry must include the port — `"registry.corp:5000"`. A bare hostname doesn't match `host:port`, so the daemon still tries HTTPS
insecure-registries only accepts CIDR ranges, not hostnames
The registry must also be added to `registry-mirrors` for pushes to work
HTTP registries are no longer supported at all; TLS is mandatory
explain: insecure-registries entries match against `host:port` (or CIDR). `registry.corp` without a port doesn't match `registry.corp:5000`, so the daemon defaults to HTTPS and gets a plaintext HTTP response. Hostnames are fine (no CIDR required), `registry-mirrors` is for pull-through caching (not pushes), and HTTP registries remain supported via this exact allowlist — the longer-term fix is still adding TLS.

q: The default bridge hands containers addresses from a /16, but the network team will only route a /28 for container traffic from this host. `bip` sets the bridge's own address. Which daemon.json key restricts the *container* address range on the default bridge?
options: `"fixed-cidr": "10.20.0.0/28"` — it carves the container IP allocation range out of the bridge subnet, independent of the bridge's own address set by `bip`
`"bip": "10.20.0.0/28"` — bip controls both the bridge IP and the container range
`"default-address-pool"` — it restricts the default bridge's container range
Container ranges can't be restricted on the default bridge; only user-defined networks support `--subnet`
explain: `bip` sets the bridge interface's address; `fixed-cidr` (v4) restricts which subset the daemon allocates to containers. They're complementary, not interchangeable. `default-address-pool` governs *user-defined* network subnet allocation, not the default bridge. And the default bridge absolutely supports a restricted range — that's what fixed-cidr is for.

q: A host enables user namespace remapping (`"userns-remap": "default"`). Afterwards, a Postgres container can't read its pre-existing data volume: files that were `root:root` now appear owned by `nobody:nogroup` (uid 65534), and Postgres refuses to start. What happened?
options: The remap only affects new containers; the volume is corrupt and must be restored from backup

Userns-remap shifts the UID/GID mapping for the daemon's storage — files written BEFORE the remap keep their host UIDs, which now fall outside the mapped range and show as nobody. The data must be chown'd into the new mapped range (or migrated) after enabling remapping
Postgres is incompatible with user namespaces; disable userns-remap on database hosts
The volume needs `docker volume update --userns` to adopt the new mapping
explain: With userns-remap, container UID 0 maps to a high host UID (e.g. 100000). Files created before the remap are owned by real host UIDs like 0 — outside the subordinate range — so inside the remapped view they belong to nobody. The fix is `chown`ing the data into the mapped range (or restoring into a fresh volume). The volume isn't corrupt, Postgres works fine under userns, and there is no `--userns` volume flag (invented).

q: On a rootless Docker host, `docker run -p 80:80 nginx` fails with a permission error, while `-p 8080:80` works fine. The engineer suggests `--privileged` to fix it. What's the real explanation and the correct response?
options: Rootless daemons can't bind privileged ports (<1024) — the daemon runs unprivileged, so binding low ports is denied by the kernel. Serve on 8080+ (or put a reverse proxy on 80); `--privileged` doesn't grant host root in rootless mode
`--privileged` restores full root, so it's the correct fix for port 80
Rootless mode blocks ALL port publishing; use host networking instead
The port is in use by the system daemon; pick any other low port
explain: Binding ports below 1024 requires CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE in the *host* user namespace — which a rootless daemon doesn't have, by design. `--privileged` inside rootless still runs within the user namespace, so it can't conjure host-level capabilities either. The supported answers are high ports, a host-level reverse proxy, or `setcap` on a rootful setup — not privilege flags. Rootless publishes high ports normally; only the privileged range is restricted.

q: On Docker Desktop, a Linux container gets OOM-killed at ~2GB even though the Mac has 32GB RAM and the container was started with `--memory 8g`. `docker stats` shows the 8g limit, but the kernel kills the container far below it. What's going on?
options: The `--memory` flag is ignored on Docker Desktop; container limits can't be raised there

Containers run inside the Desktop Linux VM, whose total memory defaults to a small allocation (2 GB on a fresh install) — the VM cap, not the container limit, is the ceiling. Raise it in Settings → Resources → Memory
The Mac's memory pressure is killing the VM; close applications on the Mac
OOM kills on Desktop are a known bug with no workaround; use a Linux host
explain: Docker Desktop runs the engine inside a Linux VM: `--memory 8g` caps the container, but the VM itself only has its allocated RAM (default 2 GB) — the container can never exceed the VM. The fix is the Resources slider in Desktop settings, then the VM restarts with more memory. The flag isn't ignored (stats proves it's applied), Mac-side app memory is unrelated to the VM's fixed allocation, and this is configured behavior, not a bug.

q: A runaway container once filled the host disk through its writable layer. The team wants a daemon-wide cap so no single container's writable layer can exceed 20GB. Which daemon.json setting does this for the overlay2 driver?
options: `"storage-opts": ["overlay2.size=20G"]` — it sets the default base size of each container's writable layer (overridable per-container with `--storage-opt size=`)
`"dm.basesize": "20G"` — the universal writable-layer cap for all storage drivers
`"max-container-disk": "20G"` — the daemon.json key for per-container disk quotas
Writable-layer size can't be capped; only `--memory` constrains containers
explain: `overlay2.size` in `storage-opts` sets the default quota for the per-container writable layer (xfs project quotas underneath). `dm.basesize` is devicemapper-only — wrong driver, silently inapplicable. There is no `max-container-disk` key (invented). And disk usage is independent of memory limits — `--memory` constrains RAM, not the filesystem.

q: The daemon default is json-file logging with `max-size=100m`. One extremely chatty service needs tighter rotation (`max-size=10m`, `max-file=2`) while leaving the daemon default untouched for everything else. How?
options: It can't be done — log options are daemon-wide; the service needs its own daemon
`docker run --log-driver json-file --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=2 ...` (or the Compose `logging.options` equivalent) — per-container log options override the daemon defaults
Set the options in the image's LABELs — the daemon reads logging config from image metadata
Per-container options exist but only for the syslog driver, not json-file
explain: Log driver *selection* and *options* are both overridable per container: `--log-opt` on `docker run` (or `logging:` in Compose) beats daemon.json for that container. Daemon defaults remain for everything else. Image LABELs carry no logging configuration (invented), and json-file fully supports max-size/max-file — that's the canonical rotation pair, not a syslog exclusive.

q: The root filesystem is nearly full, but a large secondary disk is mounted at `/mnt/docker`. The team wants ALL Docker storage (images, containers, volumes) moved there. What's the supported daemon-level move?
options: Symlink `/var/lib/docker` to `/mnt/docker` — the only supported method
Set `"data-root": "/mnt/docker"` in daemon.json, stop the daemon, rsync `/var/lib/docker/` to the new path, and restart — the daemon then uses the new root for everything
Set `"storage-path": "/mnt/docker"` in daemon.json and restart; the daemon migrates data automatically
Reinstall Docker with a custom `--datadir` configure flag
explain: `data-root` is the supported knob for relocating the daemon's entire storage directory. The procedure is stop → copy (preserving permissions/ownership) → point → start; skipping the copy orphans all images and containers. Symlinks technically work but are fragile and unsupported; there is no `storage-path` key and no automatic migration (invented), and Docker ships as packages, not source builds with configure flags.

q: An engineer tries `docker checkpoint create web cp1` to snapshot a running container for fast restore experiments. The CLI errors that the daemon doesn't support it. What's required?
options: Checkpoint/restore (CRIU) is an experimental daemon feature — enable `"experimental": true` in daemon.json (or `--experimental`) and restart the daemon
Checkpoints require Swarm mode; `docker swarm init` first
The container must be started with `--checkpointable`; existing containers can't be checkpointed
CRIU checkpoints were removed from Docker; use `docker commit` instead
explain: Container checkpoint/restore via CRIU lives behind the experimental flag — the daemon must be started experimental for the API endpoints to exist. It's a single-host engine feature, unrelated to Swarm. There is no `--checkpointable` create flag (invented), and `docker commit` snapshots the filesystem only — it can't capture running process state the way CRIU does.

q: A Swarm manager sits behind NAT: its LAN address is 10.0.0.5, but other nodes must reach it at public 203.0.113.10. Which `docker swarm init` address flags separate 'what I bind locally' from 'what others dial'?
options: `--advertise-addr 203.0.113.10 --listen-addr 10.0.0.5` — advertise-addr is the address other nodes dial; listen-addr is the local interface/port the manager binds
`--advertise-addr 10.0.0.5 --listen-addr 203.0.113.10` — advertise is always the local address
Only `--advertise-addr` exists; the manager always binds the advertised address
NAT traversal isn't supported; managers need public interfaces directly
explain: `--listen-addr` controls the local socket bind (interface:port the daemon listens on); `--advertise-addr` is the address published to the cluster for other nodes to connect to. Behind NAT they legitimately differ: listen on the LAN interface, advertise the public IP. Reversing them binds a non-local address (fails) and advertises an unreachable one. Swarm-behind-NAT is supported — this flag pair is exactly the mechanism.

q: A host runs 300 containers. The daemon starts logging `too many open files` and new containers fail to start, though each container is far below its `--ulimit nofile`. Raising the per-container ulimit changes nothing. Where's the actual ceiling?
options: The daemon inherits its file-descriptor limit from systemd (`LimitNOFILE`), not from any container setting — add a drop-in (`/etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/limits.conf` with `LimitNOFILE=1048576`), daemon-reload, and restart the daemon
The kernel's `fs.file-max` is per-container; raise it inside each container
Container ulimits stack: 300 containers × nofile exceeds the daemon's `--default-ulimit`, which caps the SUM
Reboot the host; descriptor leaks can't be fixed at runtime
explain: Two different limits are in play: `--ulimit`/`default-ulimits` constrain processes *inside* containers, while the *daemon process itself* holds sockets and files for every container it manages — its ceiling comes from the systemd unit (`DefaultLimitNOFILE`/`LimitNOFILE`), unaffected by container flags. `fs.file-max` is system-wide, not per-container; ulimits don't sum into a daemon cap (invented); and a restart with the raised service limit fixes it — no reboot needed.

q: During daemon upgrades, a database container needs 60 seconds to flush and shut down cleanly, but the daemon's restart SIGKILLs it after 15 seconds, risking corruption. `--stop-timeout` was already raised on the container with no effect on daemon shutdown. Which daemon.json key controls how long the DAEMON waits for containers during its own shutdown?
options: `"shutdown-timeout": 60` — the daemon-wide grace period for container shutdown (default 15s); `--stop-timeout` governs `docker stop`, not daemon shutdown
`"stop-timeout": 60` in daemon.json — the daemon reads the same key as the container flag
`"live-restore": true` — it makes the daemon skip stopping containers entirely
The daemon always waits indefinitely; the 15s kill must come from systemd's TimeoutStopSec
explain: `shutdown-timeout` is the daemon's own shutdown grace period (15s default) — distinct from per-container `--stop-timeout`, which only applies to explicit `docker stop`. Raising the container flag can't help when the *daemon* is the one initiating shutdown. `live-restore` keeps containers running across daemon restarts (a different strategy with its own trade-offs), and while systemd's TimeoutStopSec also exists, the 15s observed here is the daemon's documented default.

q: After a hardening script runs, containers can talk to each other but nothing outside the host — even `ping 8.8.8.8` fails, while the host itself reaches the internet fine. `iptables` rules look Docker-normal. Which kernel setting did the script most likely disable?
options: `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` — the host must forward (route) container traffic; with forwarding off, packets from container subnets are never routed outward
`net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_all` — it blocks ping specifically, which explains everything
`fs.file-max` — descriptor exhaustion breaks new connections
`net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables` — without it, container traffic bypasses Docker's rules entirely
explain: Docker relies on the host acting as a router for container subnets (NAT via MASQUERADE). With `ip_forward=0`, the kernel won't forward packets between interfaces at all — containers are stranded on their bridges while the host's own traffic (locally generated, not forwarded) works fine. The icmp sysctl would only affect ping, not all traffic; file-max would break the host too; bridge-nf-call-iptables affects *filtering*, not basic forwarding.

q: On Windows, an engineer needs the Docker CLI to talk to the local Docker Desktop daemon. `DOCKER_HOST=tcp://localhost:2375` connects but is unencrypted and isn't the default. What's the native local endpoint?
options: `npipe:////./pipe/docker_engine` — the Windows named pipe Docker Desktop listens on by default
`tcp://localhost:2376` — the default TLS endpoint on Windows
`unix:///var/run/docker.sock` — the socket path works on Windows too
Windows requires SSH (`ssh://`) to reach the daemon; direct pipes aren't supported
explain: Docker Desktop on Windows exposes the engine over the `docker_engine` named pipe — the default the CLI uses with no DOCKER_HOST set. Port 2375 is the legacy *unencrypted* TCP opt-in (never the default; enabling it without TLS is the security anti-pattern). Unix sockets don't exist on Windows, and SSH is for *remote* daemons, not the local Desktop engine.

q: The security team must add custom firewall rules on Docker hosts (e.g. rate-limiting SSH attempts). Rules added to the INPUT chain are silently bypassed for container-published ports, and Docker rewrites its own chains on restart. Where should custom rules go so they're honored and survive daemon restarts?
options: The INPUT chain — Docker only manages the FORWARD chain, so INPUT rules always apply
The `DOCKER-USER` chain — Docker guarantees this chain is evaluated before its own rules and never flushes it, making it the documented home for administrator firewall customizations
The `DOCKER` chain — it's Docker's primary chain and the natural place for custom rules
Custom firewall rules are incompatible with Docker; use a separate firewall appliance
explain: Docker inserts its DNAT/forwarding rules ahead of plain INPUT/FORWARD filtering (that's why ufw 'allow' rules get bypassed for published ports), and it recreates the DOCKER chain on startup — custom rules there get wiped. `DOCKER-USER` is the documented exception: evaluated before Docker's own rules and left alone across restarts. INPUT-chain rules still apply to *host* traffic but never see the container DNAT path; and host firewalls coexist with Docker fine once rules live in the right chain.

q: A platform creates dozens of overlay networks per day. One morning, new overlays fail with `could not find an available subnet` — Docker's default address pool is exhausted. The team can't change the daemon's `default-address-pool` (change-control freeze). How can the next network still be created?
options: Delete the ingress network to free its /16 back into the pool
Pass an explicit subnet: `docker network create -d overlay --subnet 10.60.0.0/24 app-net-41` — a user-specified subnet bypasses pool allocation entirely
Overlays always consume pool space; wait for the freeze to lift — there is no per-network workaround
Reuse an existing network's name; Docker recycles its subnet automatically
explain: Pool exhaustion only blocks *automatic* allocation — `--subnet` (with `--gateway`/`--ip-range` as needed) assigns the range explicitly, sidestepping the pool. Deleting ingress would break the routing mesh and wouldn't return space to the pool anyway. Name reuse doesn't recycle subnets, and waiting is unnecessary: explicit subnets are the designed escape hatch (just ensure they don't collide with corporate ranges).

q: The `docker_gwbridge` network's default 172.18/16 overlaps a new corporate range, breaking overlay containers' external access. The team learns the fix is recreating docker_gwbridge with a custom subnet. What's the correct procedure?
options: Set `"gwbridge-subnet"` in daemon.json and restart the daemon

Disconnect all containers from it, `docker network rm docker_gwbridge`, then `docker network create --subnet 10.99.0.0/24 --gateway 10.99.0.1 -o com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false -o com.docker.network.bridge.name=docker_gwbridge docker_gwbridge` — Docker recreates it on demand, but only honors the custom config if the name and bridge options match
Edit `/var/lib/docker/network/files/local-kv.db` to change the subnet in place
docker_gwbridge is immutable; the corporate range must be renumbered instead
explain: There is no daemon.json key for the gwbridge subnet (invented) — the documented procedure is delete-and-recreate with the exact name `docker_gwbridge` plus the standard bridge options; the daemon then adopts it instead of creating a default one. Hand-editing the local-kv.db corrupts network state. The bridge isn't immutable, and renumbering the corporate network for Docker's default is backwards.

q: A legacy FTP server in passive mode needs host ports 8000–8010 mapped to the container's port range. The engineer runs `docker run -d -p 8000-8010:8000-8010 ftp-server`. What does Docker do?
options: Publishes the whole range — `-p` accepts `hostStart-hostEnd:containerStart-containerEnd` and maps each port 1:1
Fails: `-p` only accepts single ports; ranges require one `-p` flag per port
Maps only port 8000 and silently ignores the rest of the range
Publishes the range but assigns RANDOM host ports regardless of the 8000-8010 request
explain: Port ranges are first-class in `-p`: `8000-8010:8000-8010` maps each host port to its matching container port. A single `-p` per port also works but is verbose for eleven ports. Docker never silently drops ports from a range, and it honors the requested host ports (a conflict errors out rather than randomizing).

q: Containers need LAN IPs on corporate VLANs 10 and 20. The host's eth0 is a trunk carrying both VLANs. The engineer creates one macvlan network with `-o parent=eth0`. Containers get IPs, but they can't reach VLAN 20 resources and the network team sees untagged traffic. What's missing?
options: One macvlan network can't span VLANs — create a separate macvlan network per VLAN with sub-interface parents: `-o parent=eth0.10` and `-o parent=eth0.20`
Add `--vlan 20` to the network create — macvlan takes a native vlan flag
Set `-o macvlan_mode=bridge` — bridge mode tags VLANs automatically
Macvlan can't do 802.1Q at all; use ipvlan L3 mode instead
explain: A macvlan parent of plain `eth0` sends untagged traffic — VLAN membership comes from using the 802.1Q sub-interface (`eth0.10`, `eth0.20`) as the parent, one network per VLAN. There is no `--vlan` network flag (invented); `macvlan_mode=bridge` controls inter-container hairpin behavior, not tagging; and macvlan handles 802.1Q fine via sub-interfaces (ipvlan L3 is a different answer for routed, not switched, VLAN access).

q: Two services sit behind one Swarm VIP: `/api` must route to the api service and `/web` to the web service, by URL path. The engineer publishes both on port 80 and expects the mesh to split traffic by path. What happens?
options: It works — the routing mesh inspects HTTP paths and routes to the matching service's VIP

The mesh load-balances at L4 (IPVS, TCP/UDP) with no HTTP awareness — both services can't share port 80 on ingress, and path-based routing needs a Layer-7 reverse proxy (Traefik/Nginx/HAProxy) in front
DNSRR mode enables path-based routing; switch both services to `--endpoint-mode dnsrr`
Publish one on 80 and one on 8080; clients must use different ports because VIPs are per-port
explain: The Swarm VIP is implemented with IPVS: it balances TCP/UDP connections to task IPs and never parses HTTP. Path/host routing is Layer 7 — the standard pattern is one ingress point (a reverse proxy service) doing L7 routing to the backend services' VIPs or DNSRR names. DNSRR only changes name resolution (all task IPs returned), not request routing. Different ports 'works' but dodges the requirement; the proxy is the real answer.

q: Containers on most overlays are fine, but one overlay crossing a VPN path with 1400-byte MTU sees large transfers hang while small requests succeed. The daemon-wide `--mtu` was already lowered once for another path and the team doesn't want to touch it again. How do you set MTU for just this overlay?
options: `docker network create -d overlay -o com.docker.network.driver.mtu=1400 vpn-net` — the MTU is a per-network driver option
`docker run --mtu 1400` on each container — MTU is a per-container run flag
MTU can only be set daemon-wide; per-network MTU doesn't exist
Set the MTU inside the containers with `ip link set mtu` at startup
explain: The MTU driver option (`com.docker.network.driver.mtu`) applies per network at creation — exactly the tool for one low-MTU path without disturbing every other network. There is no `--mtu` run flag (invented), and while `ip link set` inside the container technically works, it's manual per-container toil that vanishes on reschedule. Daemon-wide `--mtu` is the blunt instrument; the driver option is the scalpel.

q: A firewall runbook references Docker's three default subnets, but the engineer keeps mixing them up: the default bridge, `docker_gwbridge`, and the Swarm ingress network. Which mapping is correct?
options: Default bridge 172.17.0.0/16, docker_gwbridge 172.18.0.0/16, ingress 10.255.0.0/16
Default bridge 10.255.0.0/16, docker_gwbridge 172.17.0.0/16, ingress 172.18.0.0/16
All three default to 172.17.0.0/16; Docker distinguishes them by interface name only
Default bridge 172.18.0.0/16, docker_gwbridge 10.255.0.0/16, ingress 172.17.0.0/16
explain: The defaults are: `docker0` bridge 172.17.0.0/16, `docker_gwbridge` (overlay containers' external egress) 172.18.0.0/16, and Swarm `ingress` 10.255.0.0/16. Knowing which is which matters because they collide with different corporate ranges (the classic bip / gwbridge / ingress overlap tickets) and each has its own remediation. They are three distinct /16s by design, not one shared range.

q: A legacy billing app is hardcoded to reach its database at the hostname `ledger`. The database runs as a Swarm service named `ledger_db`. From the app's containers, `ping ledger` fails but `ping ledger_db` works. The app can't be reconfigured. How do you make `ledger` resolve to the database service?
options: Add `--hostname ledger` to the database service — hostname registers in Swarm DNS
Recreate the service named `ledger` — Swarm DNS only resolves exact service names
Give the service a network alias: `docker service create --network-alias ledger --name ledger_db ...` — aliases register alongside the service name in the embedded DNS
Add an entry to each node's /etc/hosts — Swarm DNS can't be extended
explain: `--network-alias` adds extra DNS names for the service on its networks — `ledger` then resolves to the VIP (or task IPs with DNSRR) just like the real service name. `--hostname` sets the *container's own* hostname and doesn't publish it swarm-wide the way aliases do. Renaming the service works but churns every other consumer of `ledger_db`; /etc/hosts edits don't propagate into Swarm's embedded DNS at all.

q: After the `web` service was created, the app gained a metrics endpoint on port 9090. The team needs that port published on the live service — no teardown, no recreate. Is it possible, and how?
options: No — published ports are immutable after creation; remove and recreate the service
`docker service update --publish-add published=9090,target=9090 web` — publish-add attaches the new port mapping to the running service via a rolling update
`docker network connect --publish 9090` — networks accept port mappings at connect time
Edit the port in `docker service inspect` output and the mesh picks it up
explain: `--publish-add` (and `--publish-rm`) mutate a live service's port mappings through the normal rolling-update machinery — no recreate needed. Published ports aren't immutable; they're part of the service spec like everything else. `docker network connect` manages network *attachments*, not port publishing, and inspect output is read-only state, not a config editor.

q: The daemon's default DNS (inherited from the host) can't resolve internal `corp` names. ALL containers need the corporate resolver — except one legacy container that must use 8.8.8.8 because the corp DNS blocks its telemetry domain. How do you give that one container a different resolver?
options: It's impossible — DNS is daemon-wide; the legacy container needs its own Docker host
`docker run --dns 8.8.8.8 legacy-app` — the per-container `--dns` flag overrides the daemon/host default for that container
Edit `/etc/resolv.conf` inside the running container — changes persist across restarts
Set `--dns-search` — search domains override the nameserver
explain: `--dns` (plus `--dns-opt`/`--dns-search`) is evaluated per container and wins over the daemon default — the standard escape hatch for the one container with different resolution needs. Hand-editing resolv.conf inside the container is lost on every recreate (it's regenerated from daemon config at container start). Search domains only suffix short names; they never change *which server* is queried.

q: `docker network rm stale-net` fails with `has active endpoints`, yet no container exists — `docker network inspect` still lists an endpoint for a long-gone container ID (the host crashed mid-removal). What clears this?
options: `docker network disconnect -f stale-net <endpoint-id>` — force-disconnect removes the stale endpoint record so the network can be deleted
Restart the daemon — stale endpoints are only cleared on restart
Delete `/var/lib/docker/network/files/local-kv.db` to wipe all network state
Networks with any history can't be removed; rename it and leave it
explain: A stale endpoint (container removed without clean disconnect, e.g. after a crash) blocks removal; `docker network disconnect -f` forcibly detaches it by container/endpoint ID, after which `network rm` succeeds. No daemon restart is needed, hand-deleting the boltdb corrupts network state for *all* networks, and 'abandoned but undeletable' is never the intended end state.

q: On a macvlan network created with `--subnet 192.168.20.0/24 --gateway 192.168.20.1 --ip-range 192.168.20.0/24`, a container is sometimes assigned 192.168.20.1 — the LAN gateway — causing an IP conflict that breaks external access. How do you exclude specific addresses from Docker's allocation without shrinking the usable range?
options: Remove `--gateway` — the gateway option is what causes the conflict
Containers can't be kept off specific IPs; assign every container a static `--ip` instead
Add `--aux-address "gw=192.168.20.1"` (repeatable per address) — aux addresses are excluded from IPAM allocation, reserving them while the rest of the range stays usable
Set `--ip-range` to a /25 — shrinking the range is the only supported exclusion method
explain: `--aux-address` reserves addresses out of IPAM's allocation pool — the designed mechanism for gateways, load-balancer VIPs, or any infrastructure IP inside the subnet. Removing `--gateway` doesn't stop allocation of .1 (it only drops the containers' default route hint). Static `--ip` on everything is toil that breaks the moment someone forgets, and shrinking ip-range wastes addresses to solve a reservation problem.

q: The daemon-wide `"icc": false` would isolate EVERY bridge, but other networks on this host rely on inter-container traffic. For just the new `app-net` bridge, the team wants containers unable to reach each other directly, while preserving their normal outbound internet access. How do you scope the isolation to one network?
options: `docker network create --opt com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false app-net` — inter-container communication can be disabled per bridge network
It can't be scoped — `icc` is daemon-wide or nothing
Add `--internal` to the network — it also disables container-to-container traffic
`icc` can't be changed after the daemon starts; rebuild the host
explain: `com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false` is the per-network version of the daemon's `icc` setting — containers on `app-net` can't reach each other directly (they can still reach the outside world). `--internal` is the bigger hammer: it kills *external* egress too, which isn't asked for. And the daemon-wide `icc: false` would indeed affect every bridge — the driver option is precisely how you scope it to one network.

q: The corporate resolver IP changes. The admin updates the host's `/etc/resolv.conf`, and NEW containers resolve correctly — but containers started yesterday still use the OLD resolver. Is this a bug, and how do you fix the old containers?
options: Yes, it's a bug — file a report; resolv.conf should hot-reload everywhere
Not a bug: each container gets a COPY of the host's resolv.conf at creation time. Running containers keep their copy — recreate them to pick up the new resolver
The daemon caches DNS forever; restart the daemon to flush it for running containers
Send `SIGHUP` to the containers — they re-read resolv.conf on hangup like most daemons
explain: Docker populates each container's resolv.conf once, at creation, from the host's file (or daemon `--dns` flags) — it's a bind-mounted copy, not a live symlink. Updating the host file only affects containers created afterwards; existing ones must be recreated.
