Running dockerd bare as a user fails without the mappings, it does not run containerized, and the `docker` group grants root-equivalent daemon access — the opposite of rootless.

q: `docker swarm init --advertise-addr 10.0.0.5 --listen-addr 0.0.0.0:2377` — what does each flag control?
options: They are synonyms — the last flag on the command line wins

`--advertise-addr` is the address other nodes dial to reach this manager; `--listen-addr` is the local socket the manager binds — they answer different questions (how peers reach me vs what I bind locally)
`--listen-addr` sets the VXLAN data-plane port
`--advertise-addr` only accepts interface names, never IP addresses
explain: Advertise is gossiped to the cluster as this node's reachable address; listen is the local bind (address and port). They are independent settings. The VXLAN port is `--data-path-port`, and `--advertise-addr` accepts IPs, DNS names, or interface names such as eth0.

q: CI installs a volume plugin non-interactively: `docker plugin install vendor/plugin` hangs waiting for a privilege-grant prompt. Which flag avoids the prompt, and what is the security note?
options: `--yes` — the standard non-interactive confirmation flag
Plugins cannot be installed non-interactively by design
`--grant-all-permissions` — accepts the plugin's requested privileges without prompting; use it only for trusted plugins, since plugins run with deep host access
`--privileged` — grants the plugin its privileges at install time
explain: `--grant-all-permissions` is the documented non-interactive install flag for plugins. There is no `--yes` on plugin install (invented), non-interactive install is fully supported, and `--privileged` is a container flag — not a plugin install flag.

q: A firewall between datacenters blocks UDP 4789 (VXLAN) with no exception possible, but UDP 5789 is open. How can the Swarm data plane still function?
options: Initialize/join with `--data-path-port 5789` — it moves VXLAN data-plane traffic to a custom UDP port (every node must use the same value)
Add `--opt encrypted` to the overlay — encryption automatically picks an open port
VXLAN is hardcoded to 4789; there is no workaround
Set `--advertise-addr` with a port suffix — that changes the VXLAN port
explain: `--data-path-port` exists exactly for firewalls that cannot open 4789 — all members must agree on the port. Encryption does not change the port (it still rides 4789 by default), the port is not hardcoded, and `--advertise-addr` controls manager reachability, not the data plane.

q: A manager's IP changes after a DHCP reassignment. `docker node ls` shows it unreachable at the old address, and restarting the daemon does not fix it. What is the recovery?
options: Hand-edit `/var/lib/docker/swarm` state files to the new IP
`docker node update --advertise-addr <new-ip>` — updates it in place
On the node: `docker swarm leave`, then rejoin with a fresh `docker swarm join-token manager` token — a node's advertised address is fixed at join time and cannot be edited in place
Restarting the daemon re-advertises the new address automatically
explain: The advertise address is baked into the node's cluster identity at join; there is no in-place update, so leave-and-rejoin is the supported path. Hand-editing Raft state risks corruption, no such `node update` flag exists (invented), and a restart re-uses the stored address.

q: The team wants `docker logs` to keep working AND log rotation without hand-tuning `max-size`/`max-file`. Which log driver fits?
options: `local` — binary format with built-in rotation, and `docker logs` works normally (unlike syslog/splunk/gelf drivers, which break `docker logs`)
`json-file` — it rotates logs by default with no configuration
`syslog` — it supports `docker logs` and rotates
`none` — it discards logs, which trivially 'rotates' them
explain: The `local` driver was built for this: efficient binary storage, rotation out of the box, and full `docker logs` support. `json-file` only rotates when you configure max-size/max-file. Third-party drivers like syslog/splunk forward logs away and break `docker logs`, and `none` keeps nothing at all.

q: During `docker build`, `RUN apt-get update` times out — the site needs an egress proxy. The DAEMON's proxy is already configured via systemd and pulls work. Why does the build still fail, and what is the fix?
options: The daemon proxy only covers pulls; builds additionally need `--network host`
`apt-get` cannot use HTTP proxies
Build containers do not inherit the daemon's proxy environment — pass `--build-arg http_proxy=... --build-arg https_proxy=...` (plus `no_proxy`) so the RUN steps proxy their own traffic
The only fix is baking `ENV http_proxy=...` into the Dockerfile
explain: Daemon-level proxy settings affect the daemon's own traffic (pulls/pushes), not the environment inside build containers — each RUN step needs the variables itself, and build-args are the clean injection point. `--network host` changes build networking, not proxying; apt handles proxies fine; and baking proxy ENV into the image leaks site-specific config into every deployment.

q: A firewall will sit between all future Swarm nodes (managers and workers). Which ports and protocols must be open between them?
options: TCP 2377 (cluster management), TCP and UDP 7946 (control-plane gossip), UDP 4789 (VXLAN data plane)
TCP 80 and 443 only
TCP 2377 only — the remaining ports are negotiated dynamically
UDP 4789 only — management rides the data plane
explain: These are the three documented port groups: 2377/tcp for swarm management API, 7946/tcp+udp for Raft/gossip control traffic, and 4789/udp for overlay VXLAN. HTTP ports are irrelevant to clustering, nothing is dynamically negotiated, and management does not ride the VXLAN port.

q: An admin renames a Swarm worker with `hostnamectl` and reboots. Afterwards `docker node ls` still shows the OLD hostname. Why, and does it matter?
options: The node is now fenced as a suspected imposter and will not receive tasks
`docker node update --hostname <new>` corrects it in place
The node registered under its old hostname at join time and Swarm never re-reads it — it is cosmetic, scheduling works fine; to rename, have the node leave and rejoin
Swarm requires the hostname to equal the node ID, so the rename broke the node
explain: The Swarm node name is captured from the hostname at `docker swarm join` and stored in Raft; later hostname changes are not picked up. It is purely a display label — task scheduling uses the node ID. There is no fencing on rename, no `--hostname` flag on `node update` (invented), and the hostname never had to equal the node ID.

q: Two containers run on the DEFAULT bridge network. `db` was started with `--network-alias database`, but from `app`, `getent hosts database` fails while pinging the container IP works. Why?
options: The default bridge has no embedded DNS — network aliases and automatic name resolution only exist on user-defined networks; create one and attach both containers
`--network-alias` was removed in recent Docker versions
Aliases on the default bridge require the legacy `--link` flag as well
The alias must be qualified with the network name, e.g. `bridge.database`
explain: Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) is only injected into containers on user-defined networks; the default bridge inherits the host's resolv.conf, so no Docker names resolve there. `--network-alias` is current (not removed), `--link` is the deprecated legacy mechanism, and aliases are never prefixed with the network name.

q: From a shell on a Swarm worker node, `docker network create -d overlay app-net` returns an error, while the identical command succeeds on a manager. Why?
options: Worker nodes cannot use overlay networks at all
The worker is not joined to the swarm
Swarm-scoped overlay networks can only be created on manager nodes — the network is then instantiated automatically on workers when tasks needing it are scheduled there
Overlay creation from a worker requires `--attachable`
explain: Network lifecycle is a control-plane operation: managers own it, and workers receive the network on demand as tasks land. Workers absolutely use overlays (their tasks' data plane), a joined worker in Active state is the normal case here, and `--attachable` governs standalone-container attachment — not where the network may be created.

q: The team wants a second ingress network for the routing mesh on a different subnet. What happens when they try to create it?
options: Only one ingress network can exist at a time — to customize it, remove the default `ingress` network (only possible when no service publishes ports) and create the replacement with `--ingress`
Multiple ingress networks coexist fine; the mesh load-balances across them
Use `--ingress-private` for the second one
Ingress networks cannot use custom subnets
explain: The daemon enforces a single ingress network — the routing mesh's entry point. Customizing means replacing the default via `docker network create --ingress` with your subnet/options, and the default can only be removed once nothing depends on it. There is no `--ingress-private` flag (invented), and custom subnets are fully supported on the replacement.

q: An engineer claims 'Swarm services cannot use `--network host`.' Is that true?
options: Yes — the daemon rejects host networking for services
It works and additionally enables the routing mesh over host ports

No — `docker service create --network host` works: task data traffic uses the host's network stack while control traffic still rides the overlay; limits are that only one task per node can bind a given port, and there is no VIP or embedded-DNS discovery for the data path
It works, but only combined with `--mode global`
explain: Host networking is supported for Swarm services with documented semantics: control plane stays on the overlay, data plane goes native. The classic exam traps still apply: port mappings are discarded with host mode, one binder per port per node, and no VIP/service discovery without an overlay attachment. The daemon does not reject it, the routing mesh does not extend to host ports, and replicated mode works — global is merely the common pairing.

q: A stateful TCP service breaks behind the Swarm VIP: the application pins each client session to whichever replica answered first, but the VIP sprays later packets across replicas and sessions collapse. Which endpoint mode resolves it, and what capability do you give up?
options: `--endpoint-mode dnsrr` — no VIP is created; DNS returns every task IP, each client picks one replica and sticks to it, at the cost of losing the built-in L4 load balancing
`--endpoint-mode vip-sticky` — enables session affinity on the VIP
`--publish mode=host` — host-mode publishing adds stickiness
Raising `--update-delay` — slower rollouts preserve sessions
explain: DNSRR removes the virtual IP: with no load balancer in the path, the client's own choice provides natural stickiness. There is no `vip-sticky` mode (invented), host-mode publishing changes routing rather than affinity, and update pacing is unrelated to per-packet forwarding.

q: Containers behind the corporate firewall must present their REAL container IPs to an upstream IDS — the default NAT masquerading hides them. Which bridge-network option disables the masquerade?
options: `--internal` — internal networks skip NAT
Publish a port for each container — published ports preserve the real source IP upstream

`-o com.docker.network.bridge.enable_ip_masquerade=false` at network create — disables the SNAT masquerade so external hosts see container IPs (the upstream network must route the container subnet back)
Bridge networks always masquerade — use macvlan instead
explain: `enable_ip_masquerade=false` is the documented opt-out of bridge SNAT — the trade-off is that the outside world needs a route back to the container subnet. `--internal` removes external connectivity entirely rather than de-NATing it, port publishing does not change source-IP masquerading, and masquerading is optional, not mandatory.

q: The network team forbids broadcast and multicast from container hosts, which rules out macvlan. Which ipvlan mode fits, and why?
options: `ipvlan_mode=l3` — containers are routed at Layer 3 across subnets with no broadcast domain at all
`ipvlan_mode=l2` — it behaves identically to macvlan without the broadcasts
`macvlan_mode=passthrough` — the passthrough mode suppresses broadcasts
Host networking — it never uses broadcast
explain: ipvlan L3 mode routes container traffic between subnets at L3, so no L2 broadcast/multicast domain is needed on the parent interface. L2 mode still needs the broadcast domain (that is the point of the restriction), passthrough is a macvlan mode not an ipvlan one, and host networking is a different axis entirely.

q: The `backend` overlay was created with `--internal`, so its containers have no external route — yet the app must reach exactly one external SaaS API. Which design preserves the isolation?
options: `--internal` is only advisory; add a static route for the SaaS IP
Publish the SaaS port into the network with `-p`
Remove `--internal` — per-destination isolation is a myth
Run a forward proxy (e.g. Squid) attached to both the internal network and an external network, and point the app at the proxy — containers stay internet-less except through the controlled egress
explain: The dual-homed proxy is the standard pattern: the internal network keeps no external route, and all egress funnels through one inspectable choke point. `--internal` is enforced, not advisory; `-p` publishes container ports inbound rather than granting outbound access; and dropping `--internal` destroys the isolation instead of scoping it.

q: The command `docker network create -d overlay --ingress --attachable my-ingress` is rejected. Why?
options: It succeeds — attachable ingress is the recommended pattern for debugging
`--attachable` is the default for ingress networks, so the flag is redundant
It creates two networks: one ingress, one attachable
It fails — the ingress network cannot be attachable; `--attachable` is for standalone containers on regular overlays, while ingress exists solely for the routing mesh
explain: The documented ingress options are 'any overlay option besides --attachable' — the two concepts are mutually exclusive by design. Attachable overlays serve standalone `docker run` containers; ingress serves Swarm published ports. There is no silent defaulting and no splitting into two networks.

q: A DNS service must run as a Swarm service on UDP port 53, reachable from outside the cluster. Which publish configuration works?
options: Swarm cannot publish UDP — use `--network host` instead
`-p 53:53` only covers TCP; UDP publishing requires host networking
Authoritative DNS cannot run as a Swarm service
`--publish published=53,target=53,protocol=udp` — the routing mesh and VIP handle UDP as well as TCP
explain: Swarm port publishing supports `protocol=udp` (and sctp), and the mesh routes UDP through the VIP like TCP. The 'UDP needs host networking' claim is false, `-p`/`--publish` accept an explicit protocol, and DNS runs fine as a replicated service.

q: On a macvlan network, containers must NOT communicate with each other directly — all inter-container traffic must hairpin through the external firewall. Which mode enforces this?
options: `-o macvlan_mode=bridge` — the default already isolates containers from each other
Switch to `ipvlan` L2 mode — it isolates by default
Add `--internal` to the macvlan network
`-o macvlan_mode=private` (or `vepa`) — the parent interface drops direct container-to-container frames, forcing traffic up through the upstream switch/firewall
explain: Private/VEPA mode is the isolation switch for macvlan: frames between macvlan interfaces are not delivered locally, so the external switch (and its firewall policy) sees everything. Bridge mode — the default — deliberately allows direct container-to-container traffic. ipvlan L2 does not add this isolation, and `--internal` blocks external routing rather than inter-container traffic.

q: Every task of the `api` Swarm service must use the corporate resolver at `10.2.0.53` rather than the daemon default. Which service flag does this?
options: Only the daemon-wide `dns` setting in `daemon.json` can change resolver config for services
`--env DNS_SERVER=10.2.0.53` — the resolver reads the environment
Bake the nameserver into the image's `/etc/resolv.conf`
`--dns 10.2.0.53` — `docker service create` supports per-service `--dns`, `--dns-search`, and `--dns-option`, mirroring `docker run`
explain: Service create/update accept the same DNS flags as docker run, applied per task. Daemon-wide DNS is the default, not the only option. The resolver does not read environment variables, and Docker manages each container's resolv.conf — hand-baked files get overwritten.

q: An engineer expects the Swarm VIP to pin each client to one replica (sticky sessions) for a shopping-cart app. Load testing shows requests bouncing between replicas and carts breaking. What is the reality?
options: Add `--update-delay` — slower rollouts enable stickiness
The VIP is sticky by source IP by default; the test must be flawed
Use `--endpoint-mode vip-persistent` for affinity

The VIP is stateless IPVS load balancing with no session affinity — implement stickiness in the app or edge LB (cookies), or switch to `--endpoint-mode dnsrr` so each client resolves to and sticks with one replica
explain: The Swarm VIP does round-robin L4 forwarding with no notion of sessions — stickiness was never a feature. Update pacing is unrelated, source-IP affinity does not exist on the VIP, and `vip-persistent` is invented. The fixes are application-level affinity or removing the VIP via dnsrr.

q: A host has public `203.0.113.5` and management `10.0.0.5`. The team wants every published port on a given bridge network to bind the management IP by default, without adding the IP to each `-p` flag. Which network option does this?
options: `"ip": "10.0.0.5"` in `daemon.json` — but that is daemon-wide, not per-network
Impossible — the bind IP must be specified on every `-p`
`--gateway 10.0.0.5` — the gateway doubles as the bind address
`-o com.docker.network.bridge.host_binding_ipv4=10.0.0.5` at `docker network create` — sets the default host IP for published ports on that network
explain: `host_binding_ipv4` is the per-network default bind for published ports. The daemon.json `ip` key exists but applies daemon-wide rather than per network (which is why it is the wrong answer to this per-network ask). Per-invocation `-p IP:...` remains available as an override, and `--gateway` sets the subnet gateway — unrelated to port binding.

q: On a Windows Docker host, `docker network ls` shows a network named `nat`. A Linux-trained engineer asks what it corresponds to. What do you tell him?
options: It is the Swarm ingress network, renamed on Windows
Windows containers have no default network — `nat` is a leftover
`nat` is Windows' name for host networking
It is the default Windows container network — the counterpart of Linux's bridge (NAT'd container segment); Windows also offers `transparent` (like macvlan) and `overlay` drivers
explain: `nat` is Windows' default container network, giving containers NAT'd access like the Linux bridge does. `transparent` puts containers directly on the LAN (the macvlan analog), and `overlay` serves Swarm. It is not the ingress network, not a leftover, and not host networking.

q: To get encrypted container traffic, an operator creates a bridge network with the overlay encryption option: `docker network create -d bridge --opt encrypted backend`. What is the result?
options: Bridge traffic is now encrypted with IPsec
It enables TLS on the containers' published ports
It encrypts the `docker0` bridge for every container on the host
The option has no effect on a bridge network — `--opt encrypted` is an overlay-driver feature that enables IPsec for Swarm VXLAN traffic only
explain: Encryption is implemented in the overlay driver for the Swarm data plane; the bridge driver has no such feature and ignores (or rejects) the option. It does not add TLS anywhere and does not touch docker0. For encrypted multi-host traffic, the answer is an overlay network with `--opt encrypted`.

q: Two Windows containers on one host must be isolated at the kernel level — a kernel exploit in one must not affect the other. Which isolation mode, and what does it cost?
options: `--isolation=process` — process isolation gives each container its own kernel
Windows containers always share the host kernel; kernel isolation is impossible
`--privileged` — it enables Hyper-V isolation

`--isolation=hyperv` — each container runs in its own lightweight VM with its own kernel; stronger isolation than the default `process` mode (which shares the host kernel) at the cost of more overhead
explain: Hyper-V isolation puts a VM boundary (and separate kernel) around each container; process isolation — the default — shares the host kernel like Linux containers do. The trade-off is density and startup cost. The claim that process mode isolates the kernel is backwards, kernel isolation is very much available, and `--privileged` is a Linux flag unrelated to Windows isolation.

q: A Swarm manager created with `--autolock` reboots for patching. On boot, the manager shows as locked and cannot rejoin Raft. What must happen before it resumes?
options: Wait — locked managers auto-unlock once the daemon restarts
Re-run `docker swarm init` to re-create the cluster state
Restore the manager from the encrypted backup
Run `docker swarm unlock` and supply the unlock key — autolock encrypts the manager's Raft keys at rest, and a reboot requires the key to decrypt them
explain: Autolock's entire purpose is encrypting Raft logs and TLS keys at rest; after any manager restart the operator must present the unlock key via `docker swarm unlock`. There is no auto-unlock (that would defeat the feature), re-init would destroy the cluster, and backups are for disaster recovery — not for a routine reboot.

q: The private Notary signing key for `shop/api` Docker Content Trust signatures is suspected compromised, and a new key has been generated. What completes the rotation for already-pushed tags?
options: Nothing further — publishing signatures with the new key automatically invalidates the old ones
Delete and re-push the tags — tag deletion purges the trust data
`docker trust sign --revoke shop/api:2.0` — revocation is a flag on `sign`
`docker trust revoke shop/api:2.0` for each affected tag — it removes the old signatures so DCT-enforcing clients stop trusting them; then sign fresh with the new key
explain: Trust metadata lives in Notary independently of the image: key rotation alone leaves the old signatures valid, so `docker trust revoke` must explicitly remove them before re-signing. New signatures do not cancel old ones, tag deletion does not reliably purge trust data, and revocation is its own command — `--revoke` is not a `sign` flag.

q: A container must create and use serial devices as they are hot-plugged (`/dev/ttyUSB*` appearing at runtime), without `--privileged` and without knowing device names in advance. What is the least-privilege approach?
options: `--privileged` — dynamic devices are impossible without it
`--device=/dev/ttyUSB0` — it covers devices plugged in later
`-v /dev:/dev` — bind-mounting /dev is sufficient on its own
`--device-cgroup-rule='c 188:* rwm'` — permits the container's cgroup to create/read/write character devices with major 188 (USB serial), so the app can `mknod` nodes as devices appear
explain: `--device-cgroup-rule` whitelists device classes by type/major/minor pattern — the least-privilege answer for hot-plug devices, since the cgroup (not a static node) grants the permission. `--privileged` is the sledgehammer this avoids, a static `--device` only covers the one node present at start, and a /dev bind-mount gives visibility without the cgroup permission to actually use the devices.

q: A performance-debug container requires a syscall denied by the daemon's default seccomp filter. The team rejects `--privileged`. Which option lifts the restriction, and what is the downside?
options: `--cap-add SYS_ADMIN` — capabilities override seccomp blocks, so this unblocks the syscall
`--security-opt apparmor=unconfined` — that disables the seccomp filter
Seccomp cannot be disabled per container
`--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` — disables the seccomp filter for that container; it is the weakest option, and a custom profile allowing just the needed syscalls is preferable
explain: `seccomp=unconfined` removes the syscall filter for the container — effective but maximally permissive, hence the custom-profile recommendation. Capabilities do NOT override seccomp (the filter applies regardless of caps), AppArmor and seccomp are independent mechanisms, and per-container seccomp control is fully supported.

q: A chargeback system bills CPU by cgroup hierarchy. The team wants all CI build containers placed under `/ci.slice` instead of Docker's default hierarchy. Which flag does this?
options: `--cpuset-cpus` — that controls cgroup placement
Container cgroup paths are fixed and cannot be changed
`--parent-cgroup` — that is the flag's name
`docker run --cgroup-parent /ci.slice` (or the daemon's `cgroup-parent` setting) — nests the container's cgroup under the given parent
explain: `--cgroup-parent` sets the parent cgroup for the container's resource controllers — the supported hierarchy knob, also available daemon-wide. `--cpuset-cpus` pins CPUs (a different concern), cgroup placement is configurable, and the flag is `--cgroup-parent`, not `--parent-cgroup` (invented).

q: A multi-tenant cluster keeps hitting noisy-neighbor problems: `LimitRange` caps each pod's size, but tenants simply run MORE pods and exhaust the namespace. Which object caps the namespace's aggregate usage?
options: A second `LimitRange` with smaller per-pod caps
A `PodDisruptionBudget` — it limits total disruption, which caps usage
`ResourceQuota` only governs storage, not CPU or memory
`ResourceQuota` — sets namespace-wide aggregates for CPU, memory, and object counts; pods that would exceed it are rejected at admission
explain: ResourceQuota is the namespace-aggregate mechanism: total CPU/memory requests/limits and counts across all pods, enforced at admission time. LimitRange is per-pod (the tenant just scales out around it), PodDisruptionBudgets govern voluntary evictions — not resource totals — and quotas cover compute as well as storage.

q: Before deploying `shop/api:2.0`, an auditor wants proof of WHO signed it — which keys/roles vouched for the image — not just that a signature exists. Which command provides this?
options: `docker images --digests` — it lists the signing identities
`docker trust view shop/api:2.0` — the signer-listing command
Signer identity is not recorded — signatures only prove 'signed by someone'
`docker trust inspect --pretty shop/api:2.0` — shows signers, roles, and the signed digests
explain: `docker trust inspect` dumps the Notary trust metadata: signers, delegation roles, and digests — the audit trail. `docker images --digests` shows content digests only, `docker trust view` does not exist (invented), and signer identity is precisely what the delegation/role model records.

q: A legacy application uses System V shared memory heavily, and an engineer proposes `--ipc=host` for performance. What is the security implication?
options: It is the default IPC mode, so there is no change
It only affects the container's network stack
Shared memory is always host-shared in containers regardless of flags

It removes IPC isolation — the container joins the host's IPC namespace, sharing `/dev/shm` and SysV IPC objects with every host process; prefer a larger `--shm-size` inside the container's own namespace
explain: `--ipc=host` dissolves the IPC namespace boundary: the container sees and can interfere with host and sibling shared-memory segments. The default is a private IPC namespace, it has nothing to do with networking, and `/dev/shm` is per-container unless host mode (or an explicit share) is chosen.

q: A container runs with `--memory 4g --memory-reservation 2g`. The host comes under memory pressure while the container sits at 3 GB. What happens?
options: The container is OOM-killed the moment it crosses 2 GB
Reservation and limit are two names for the same enforcement
The container is guaranteed its full 4 GB regardless of host pressure

The reservation is a soft limit: the container may use up to the 4 GB hard limit while memory is plentiful, but under pressure the kernel reclaims from it first — usage below the reservation is treated like any other container's
explain: `--memory-reservation` sets a soft threshold: below it the container is protected comparably to others, above it (up to the hard `--memory` cap) its pages are first in line for reclaim when the host is pressured. Crossing the reservation never directly kills, the two flags enforce different things, and no container is guaranteed memory the host does not have.

q: An old hardening guide sets `--kernel-memory 512m` on every container. On Docker 24 the flag warns it is deprecated. What is the current guidance?
options: Rename it to `--kmem 512m` — the flag was renamed, not removed
Keep it — compliance baselines still require the separate knob
Replace it with `--memory-reservation 512m`
Drop it — kernel memory accounting was folded into the unified cgroup controller, so `--kernel-memory` was deprecated and `--memory` covers the accounting
explain: Upstream deprecated `--kernel-memory` when kernel memory accounting merged into the main memory controller — the separate limit became meaningless. There is no `--kmem` rename (invented), baselines track the deprecation, and `--memory-reservation` is a soft-limit knob, not a kernel-memory one.

q: A Kubernetes Deployment uses `image: shop/api:2.0` — a tag rebuilt on every merge — with `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent`. New pushes never roll out to the existing nodes. Why?
options: `IfNotPresent` always pulls — the nodes must be out of disk
The Deployment needs `replicas: 0` before the new image is fetched
`imagePullPolicy` is a Docker-only concept that Kubernetes ignores

`IfNotPresent` reuses the node's cached `2.0` without ever checking the registry — with a mutable tag the kubelet cannot tell new from old; the robust fix is immutable tags or digests (changing the tag is what triggers a real rollout)
explain: `IfNotPresent` means exactly that: a cached image is never re-pulled, so a moving tag silently goes stale — the classic mutable-tag hazard. It does not always pull, zeroing replicas is irrelevant theater, and `imagePullPolicy` is a core Kubernetes pod-spec field.

q: The daemon sets a default writable-layer quota of 20 GB (`overlay2.size`), but ONE logging container legitimately needs 50 GB of writable layer. Which per-container override works?
options: `--memory 50g` — memory limits also bound the writable layer
Daemon storage defaults cannot be overridden per container
`--volume-size 50G` — the per-container quota flag
`docker run --storage-opt size=50G` — overrides the daemon's default quota for that container (the backing filesystem must support quotas, e.g. XFS with `pquota`)
explain: `--storage-opt size=` is the per-container quota override for drivers that support it (overlay2 on XFS with project quotas). `--memory` constrains RAM, not filesystem; per-container override is supported; and `--volume-size` does not exist (invented).

q: A critical database container and a batch worker share a host. Under memory pressure the database keeps getting OOM-killed first. Which flag biases the OOM killer toward the worker instead?
options: `--oom-kill-disable` on the database — the safe and recommended fix
`--memory` limits on the worker — limits already control OOM priority
The OOM killer's victim choice cannot be influenced
Raise `--oom-score-adj` on the worker (e.g. `500`) — a higher score makes the kernel pick it first; a negative value on the database protects it (range -1000 to 1000)
explain: `--oom-score-adj` directly tunes the kernel's OOM scoring per container — the designed knob for 'kill this one before that one'. `--oom-kill-disable` on the DB is dangerous (an unkillable leaking process can take the host down instead), memory limits bound usage rather than priority, and the score adjustment exists precisely because victim choice is tunable.

q: A legacy application breaks under the default AppArmor profile, but the host must keep enforcing AppArmor for everything else. How do you exempt just this container?
options: Switch the host to complain mode — required before any container can be exempted
`--privileged` — the only way to escape the default profile
AppArmor cannot be disabled per container
`--security-opt apparmor=unconfined` — disables AppArmor confinement for that container only; the host profile enforcement and other containers are unaffected
explain: `apparmor=unconfined` is the per-container opt-out — surgical, leaving host-wide enforcement intact. Host-wide complain mode is a bigger hammer than needed, `--privileged` does disable the profile but also grants every capability and device access (far beyond the ask), and per-container control is fully supported.

q: A pod's `securityContext` sets `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`. A teammate says that is the same as dropping all capabilities. What is the distinction?
options: It is identical to `cap-drop: [ALL]`
It forces the container to run as non-root
It is a Docker `security-opt`, not a Kubernetes field
It sets the kernel's `no_new_privs` bit — the process can never GAIN more privilege (e.g. via setuid binaries); it does not remove the capabilities the container already holds
explain: `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` engages `no_new_privs`: a one-way latch preventing privilege gain through setuid/setgid execution. It is orthogonal to the capability bounding set — existing caps stay. It does not imply `runAsNonRoot` (a root process can still run with no_new_privs), and it is a native Kubernetes securityContext field.

q: A 2019 Compose file (`version: "2.4"`) shares data via `volumes_from: [datacontainer]`. The team converts the file to Compose v3 for a Swarm deployment and the deploy rejects the key. What happened to `volumes_from`?
options: It was removed in the v3 format — v3 dropped several v2-only keys (`volumes_from`, `volume_driver`, `extends`, `links`); share a named volume mounted in each service instead
It was renamed to `volumes_share` in v3
v3 requires `volumes_from` to reference a Swarm service rather than a container
Nothing changed — the rejection must come from elsewhere; v3 supports `volumes_from`
explain: The v3 format (built for Swarm) removed `volumes_from` along with other single-host-era keys — the portable replacement is a shared named volume. There is no `volumes_share` rename (invented), v3 does not accept the key in any form, and the rejection is the format working as documented.

q: A pod references a ConfigMap that exists only in production (`log-level-overrides`). In dev the ConfigMap is absent and the pod refuses to start. How can the pod tolerate the missing ConfigMap?
options: Set `optional: true` on the ConfigMap volume (or `envFrom`) reference — the pod starts without it, and mounts it normally wherever it exists
ConfigMap references are optional by default — the dev cluster must be misconfigured
Use `subPath` — it skips ConfigMaps that do not exist
Mount an `emptyDir` with the same name as a fallback
explain: `optional: true` is the designed tolerance knob: missing ConfigMaps (or Secrets) no longer block pod startup. References are required by default, `subPath` only selects within an existing volume, and an emptyDir cannot conditionally stand in for a ConfigMap.

q: A team uses `local` PersistentVolumes (fast NVMe on each node), but pods sometimes schedule onto nodes that do not hold the volume's data. What is required for correct scheduling?
options: `nodeAffinity` on the PersistentVolume — the scheduler must be told which node(s) hold the data; `local` volumes REQUIRE nodeAffinity, otherwise data locality is ignored
Nothing — the scheduler auto-detects which node holds a local volume
Use `hostPath` instead — it is equivalent and needs no affinity
Set the StorageClass `volumeBindingMode: Immediate` — that fixes placement
explain: A `local` PV is just a path until `nodeAffinity` pins it to nodes — without it the scheduler treats the volume as anywhere-accessible and misplaces pods. Auto-detection does not exist, `hostPath` is a different (node-local, non-portable) mechanism with the same locality problem, and binding mode controls WHEN binding happens, not WHERE the data lives.

q:
A stack's Compose file declares:
volumes:
  db-data:
    external: true
The deploy fails: 'volume db-data not found'. The volume was never created. What is wrong?
options: `external: true` means 'must already exist' — create it first with `docker volume create db-data`, or drop `external: true` and let the stack create its own `stackname_db-data` copy
External volumes cannot be used in Swarm stacks
The volume declaration needs a `driver:` or it cannot be found
Stacks always prefix volume names, even external ones
explain: `external: true` opts out of lifecycle management: Compose/Swarm will use the volume but never create it, so a missing volume is a deploy error. External volumes work fine in stacks, no driver is required for the default local driver, and external names are used verbatim — prefixing applies only to stack-managed volumes.

q: Months of CI runs left hundreds of anonymous volumes. Which command lists ONLY the unused ones for review before pruning?
options: `docker volume ls --filter dangling=true` — shows volumes not referenced by any container
`docker volume ls --filter unused=true` — the unused filter
`docker volume ls` shows only unused volumes by default
`docker system df --volumes` — the review command
explain: `dangling=true` is the documented filter for unreferenced volumes — the safe review step before `docker volume prune`. There is no `unused` filter (invented), plain `ls` shows everything, and `system df` reports aggregate reclaimable space, not a per-volume list.

q: `docker volume rm db-data` fails with 'volume is in use', yet `docker ps` shows no running containers. What is holding the volume?
options: A STOPPED container still referencing it — a volume counts as in use until every referencing container (running or stopped) is removed; `docker rm` the container first
The volume is corrupted and must be reformatted
Only running containers count — this is a daemon bug
Re-run with `docker volume rm -f` — force bypasses the in-use check safely
explain: Volume references are held by container records, not by running processes — stopped containers pin their volumes, which is also why `docker volume prune` spares them. Corruption is not indicated, the behavior is by design rather than a bug, and `-f` does not override the in-use protection.

q: A Dockerfile contains `VOLUME /data`. Every `docker run` without `-v` creates a new anonymous volume, and `docker volume ls` grows without bound. Why?
options: The `VOLUME` instruction declares an anonymous-volume mount point — each container gets a fresh anonymous volume there unless you bind a named volume or host path; the anonymous volumes persist after container removal until pruned
`VOLUME` is documentation-only metadata, like `EXPOSE`
It is a storage-driver bug — `VOLUME` should reuse one volume
`VOLUME` creates a named volume per image
explain: `VOLUME` is a runtime instruction, not documentation: it guarantees the path is a volume, minting an anonymous one per container when nothing is explicitly mounted. Those anonymous volumes outlive their containers and accumulate until `docker volume prune`. It is not EXPOSE-like metadata, not a bug, and the volumes are anonymous (random hex IDs), not named.

q: The team labels production volumes `keep=true`. Which command prunes CI/anonymous volumes while sparing the labeled ones?
options: `docker volume prune --filter "label!=keep"` — prune honors label filters, so labeled volumes are excluded
`docker volume prune` never touches labeled volumes by default
Labels cannot be used to filter prune operations
`docker volume rm $(docker volume ls -q)` — then recreate what matters
explain: `docker volume prune --filter` supports label selectors, making `label!=keep` the surgical cleanup. Plain prune absolutely removes labeled volumes (labels are not protection by default), label filtering is supported, and mass-removing everything is the opposite of surgical.

q: `docker cp web:/var/www ./www-backup` lands files owned by root with flattened permissions, breaking a faithful restore. Which flag preserves ownership, permissions, and timestamps?
options: `docker cp -a` — archive mode preserves UIDs, GIDs, permission bits, and timestamps
No flag is needed — `docker cp` always preserves everything; the destination filesystem is at fault
`docker cp --preserve` — the preservation flag
Use `docker export` instead — it preserves permissions
explain: `-a`/`--archive` is cp's fidelity mode for exactly this backup/restore use case. Default `docker cp` does not guarantee preservation, there is no `--preserve` flag on docker cp (invented), and `docker export` flattens a container's filesystem to a tarball — it also excludes volumes and is not a selective copy tool.

q: An engineer bind-mounts a single config file: `-v /srv/app/config.yaml:/etc/app/config.yaml`. The host file does not exist yet, and the container fails to start — inspection shows Docker created `/srv/app/config.yaml` as an empty DIRECTORY on the host. What happened, and what is the stricter alternative?
options: With `-v`, Docker auto-creates a missing host path as a directory — so the 'file' became a directory and the mount is useless; `--mount type=bind` instead ERRORS on a missing source rather than creating one
Docker never creates missing bind-mount paths — the directory came from elsewhere
Bind mounts require the container-side path to exist first
Adding `:ro` prevents the auto-creation
explain: The `-v` shorthand's helpful auto-creation is type-blind: missing paths become directories, which silently breaks single-file mounts. `--mount type=bind` fails fast on a missing source, surfacing the real problem (the absent file). Docker does create the path (that is the bug's cause), the container path is created automatically too, and `:ro` changes writability — not creation behavior.

q: Stack `shop` declares a named volume `db-data` (not external). After deploy, `docker volume ls` shows `shop_db-data`. A standalone backup container run with `-v db-data:/data` finds the volume EMPTY. Why?
options: Stack deploy prefixes non-external volume names with the stack name — the real data lives in `shop_db-data`; the backup mounted a different, newly created empty `db-data`
Volumes cannot be shared between stacks and standalone containers
The volume was not populated because stack volumes skip the image-copy step
Standalone containers cannot use named volumes
explain: Like networks and secrets, stack-managed volumes are namespaced with the stack prefix — `db-data` in the Compose file is `shop_db-data` in reality. The backup's `-v db-data` referenced (and auto-created) a wholly separate empty volume. Sharing works fine once you use the real prefixed name, stack volumes populate normally, and standalone containers use named volumes routinely.

q: An engineer runs `docker system prune -a`, assuming volumes are safe, then finds named volumes holding real data are gone. What happened?
options: They must have also passed `--volumes` (or confirmed its prompt) — plain `prune` never touches volumes; `docker system prune --volumes` removes ALL unused volumes, including named ones with data
`prune -a` always deletes volumes — the `-a` includes them
Named volumes are deleted automatically when their containers stop
It is a known data-loss bug in prune
explain: Volume deletion is opt-in: plain `docker system prune` (even `-a`) leaves every volume alone, while `--volumes` extends pruning to all unused volumes — named or anonymous, data or not. `-a` only widens image pruning to all unused images, stopped containers do not delete their volumes, and this is documented behavior, not a bug.

q: An engineer runs `docker cp web:/app/data ./backup` and separately `docker cp web:/app/data/. ./backup2`, expecting identical layouts. Instead `backup` contains a `data/` subdirectory while `backup2` contains the files directly. What is the rule?
options: A trailing `/.` (or `/*`) copies the directory's CONTENTS into the destination; without it, the directory itself is copied as a subdirectory — mirroring classic `cp -r` semantics
The two forms are identical — the difference indicates a daemon bug
`docker cp` does not support trailing-slash forms
The contents form requires `docker cp -a`
explain: `docker cp` follows familiar copy semantics: naming the directory copies the directory, while `/.` addresses its contents. It is not a bug, trailing forms are supported, and `-a` controls attribute preservation — not which files are selected.

q: Two containers need a SHARED RAM-disk: fast scratch space, never persisted, with a strict 100 MB cap. Which creates it?
options: `docker volume create --driver local --opt type=tmpfs --opt device=tmpfs --opt o=size=100m scratch` — a named tmpfs-backed volume both containers mount with `-v scratch:/work`
`--tmpfs /work` on each container — both containers share the same RAM disk
tmpfs storage cannot be shared between containers or size-capped
Use the containers' default `/dev/shm` — it is shared across containers
explain: The local driver's mount options can back a NAMED volume with tmpfs — shareable, size-capped with `o=size=`, and RAM-resident. Per-container `--tmpfs` mounts are private to each container (not shared), tmpfs absolutely supports sharing and caps, and `/dev/shm` is per-container namespaced by default.

q: A container writes to an NFS-backed named volume as UID 999, but files land owned by `nobody` and the app cannot read them back — the NFS server applies root squash. Which volume option controls the client-side ownership mapping?
options: `--opt o=addr=10.0.0.5,rw,uid=999,gid=999` (with `type=nfs`, `device=:/exports/data`) — mount options set the ownership the NFS client presents; root squash itself is server-side policy
Run `chown` inside the container — ownership changes persist on NFS
NFS ownership cannot be influenced from the client mount options
`--privileged` — it bypasses the server's squash policy
explain: The local driver passes `o=` straight to the NFS mount, where `uid=`/`gid=` control presented ownership — the client-side half of the equation. `chown` as squashed-nobody is neutered by the server mapping, client mount options very much can set this, and no container flag overrides server-side squash policy.

q: CI runs `docker run -v ~/data:/data app`. It works on engineers' laptops but fails in CI with an invalid-path error mentioning a literal `~`. What is happening?
options: `~` is expanded by the SHELL, not by Docker — CI runs the command without shell expansion (or with a different HOME), so the literal `~` reaches the daemon and fails path validation; use `$HOME/data` or an absolute path
The daemon expands `~` using its own HOME, which differs in CI
Bind mounts do not support home directories
`--mount type=bind` expands `~` where `-v` does not
explain: Tilde expansion is shell behavior — Docker receives whatever string survives to the daemon, and a literal `~` is not a valid absolute path. The daemon performs no expansion, home directories bind-mount fine once expanded, and `--mount` is equally literal (its strictness differs, not its expansion).

q: A monitoring pod must see host mounts that appear AFTER the pod starts (newly attached backup disks under `/mnt`). A `hostPath` mount of `/mnt` only shows mounts present at pod start. Which setting propagates new host mounts into the pod?
options: `mountPropagation: HostToContainer` on the volumeMount — new host mounts propagate into the pod; `Bidirectional` would additionally propagate the pod's mounts back to the host (privileged and risky)
`hostPath` `type: DirectoryOrCreate` — it refreshes the mount table automatically
Nothing — a container's mount table is fixed at start time
Run the pod as privileged — propagation is automatic then
explain: Mount propagation is the kernel mechanism for exactly this: `HostToContainer` flows host-side mounts into the pod after start. `DirectoryOrCreate` only ensures the path exists at mount time, the mount table is not fixed (propagation exists for this), and privileged alone does not enable propagation — the field must still be set.

q: The team accepts that the Swarm routing mesh cannot split traffic by URL path (the earlier /api vs /web finding). Their cluster is Docker Enterprise with MKE. What provides Layer-7, path-based routing to Swarm services in that environment?
options: Publish both services with `--endpoint-mode dnsrr` — DNS round-robin handles path-based routing

Deploy the Interlock reverse-proxy extension and label the services — e.g. `com.docker.lb.hosts=shop.example.com`, `com.docker.lb.port=8080`, `com.docker.lb.network=frontend` — so Interlock routes by host/path to the right service
Add `--publish mode=l7,target=80` to each service
Nothing inside Docker EE does Layer-7 routing — put an external HAProxy in front and point it at the services' VIPs
explain: The routing mesh is Layer-3/4 (IPVS): it balances TCP/UDP, never HTTP paths. Interlock is Docker EE's built-in Layer-7 extension (nginx/HAProxy-based) that watches Swarm services and routes by hostname/path from `com.docker.lb.*` service labels. EXAM TRAPS: (A) dnsrr only changes service discovery to DNS round-robin — still no HTTP awareness. (C) `mode=l7` is an invented publish mode. (D) is plausible but wrong — Interlock is exactly the native EE answer, and VIPs are internal-only anyway.

q: Monitoring discovers containers by the label `team=payments`. The service was created with `docker service create --label team=payments ...`, but discovery finds zero containers, and `docker inspect` on a task's container shows no such label. What went wrong?
options: Labels cannot be queried on Swarm task containers at all
The label needs a `com.docker.` prefix to be visible on containers
`--label` sets labels on the SERVICE object; container-level labels need `--container-label team=payments`, which lands on each task's container
Service labels only propagate to containers after the first `docker service update`
explain: Swarm keeps two label namespaces: `--label` tags the service object (visible in `docker service inspect`), while `--container-label` tags every task's container (visible in `docker inspect` on the container). Monitoring that inspects containers needs the latter. EXAM TRAPS: (A) false — container labels are fully inspectable. (B) invents a prefix requirement. (D) invents a propagation delay.

q: A stack's services use images from a private registry. `docker stack deploy` runs on a manager where `docker login` succeeded, but tasks scheduled to workers fail with pull authentication errors. (The `docker service create` equivalent is `--with-registry-auth`.) What is the stack-level fix?
options: Run `docker login` on every worker node
`docker stack deploy --with-registry-auth -c app.yml shop` — the flag forwards the manager's registry credentials with the service specs so every node can pull
Add `registry_auth: true` under each service's `deploy:` section
Embed the credentials in the image reference as `user:pass@registry.corp/...`
explain: `docker login` is per-daemon; Swarm managers only distribute registry credentials to workers when told. `--with-registry-auth` on `stack deploy` (like on `service create`) ships the credential with the spec. EXAM TRAPS: (A) works but is operationally wrong — per-node logins don't scale and rot. (C) invents a Compose key. (D) invents an invalid, insecure image-reference syntax.

q: A Compose file declares a config `app_cfg` (file-based, NOT external) and the service references it as `app_cfg`. After `docker stack deploy -c shop.yml shop`, `docker config ls` shows `shop_app_cfg` — there is no `app_cfg`. The engineer fears the deploy created the wrong object. What happened?
options: Nothing is wrong — stacks namespace non-external resources by prefixing the stack name (`shop_app_cfg`); inside the file you keep referring to it as `app_cfg`
The deploy duplicated the config; delete `shop_app_cfg` and recreate it as `app_cfg`
File-based configs are always external — the missing `external: true` caused the rename
Two stacks named `shop` collided; rename the stack
explain: Stack deploy prefixes non-external networks, volumes, secrets, and configs with `<stack>_` so stacks don't collide; in-file references keep using the short name. Same mechanism as the `shop_db-data` volume confusion. EXAM TRAPS: (B) deleting it would break the service. (C) inverts the rule — `external: true` is what SKIPS prefixing. (D) invents a collision.

q: `docker service logs -f web` interleaves all 12 replicas with `web.1.<id>` prefixes, burying the one crashing task `web.7.abc123`. The engineer wants ONLY that task's stream. What works?
options: `docker service logs --filter task=web.7.abc123 web`
SSH to the node running web.7 and run `docker logs` on its container
`docker logs web.7.abc123` on the manager
`docker service logs web.7.abc123` — service logs accepts a task name/ID and shows just that task's logs
explain: `docker service logs` multiplexes every task's stream, but passing a task name/ID scopes it to that task. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents a `--filter` flag. (B) works but is manual toil — find the node, find the container. (C) repeats the earlier exec trap: a task ID is not a container ID, and the container probably isn't on the manager.

q: A cost-saving runbook scales the dev `web` service to 0 every night (`docker service scale web=0`) and back to 3 each morning. An engineer worries the nightly scale-down deletes the service's named volumes, and that Monday's tasks somehow resume the exact Friday containers. What actually happens?
options: The scale-down deletes the named volumes; Monday starts with empty data

Tasks are ephemeral: scale-to-0 shuts every task down, and scale-up creates brand-new tasks (new task IDs; slot numbers 1-3 are reused). Named volumes persist on their nodes and reattach by name — data survives wherever a task lands on the same node
The exact same task containers are frozen on Friday and thawed on Monday
Scaling a service to 0 deletes the service definition itself
explain: Scale-to-0 is not hibernation: tasks are destroyed and recreated fresh (only the slot numbering repeats). Volumes are separate objects with their own lifecycle — they persist node-locally and reattach by name. EXAM TRAPS: (A) confuses task ephemerality with volume deletion (volumes die on `volume rm`/prune, not on scale-down). (C) imagines freeze/thaw. (D) confuses `scale web=0` with `service rm`.

q: A backup taken by MKE 3.6.0 is restored onto fresh hosts where the team installed MKE 3.7.0 first. The restore fails. What is the rule?
options: Backups are forward-compatible; the failure must be a wrong passphrase

Backups are tied to the original hosts' certificates and cannot move
explain: MKE restores require version parity: the restoring MKE must match the version that took the backup. Standard path is install the old version, restore, then upgrade. EXAM TRAPS: (A) misdiagnoses as a passphrase problem. (B) invents a `--force` migration. (D) invents certificate-binding.

q: A Kubernetes hire asks for the equivalent of a global Swarm service that must roll its update one node at a time: the log-agent DaemonSet may have at most 1 pod unavailable during the rollout. Which spec expresses this?

A DaemonSet with `updateStrategy: {type: OnDelete}`

EXAM TRAPS: (B) uses the wrong object — a Deployment doesn't guarantee one pod per node. (C) `OnDelete` means pods update only when manually deleted — the opposite of rolling. (D) is nonsense.

q: After `docker stack rm shop`, the overlay network `backend` (declared `external: true` in the Compose file) still exists in `docker network ls`. The engineer expected full cleanup. What is correct?

explain: `external: true` means 'pre-existing, managed elsewhere': the stack uses it but its lifecycle is not the stack's. Only stack-created resources are removed. EXAM TRAPS: (A) misreads normal behavior as failure. (B) invents a `--prune` flag for `stack rm`. (C) misdiagnoses deliberate design as a leak (though manual `network rm` is fine if truly unwanted).

q: A global monitoring agent runs on 50 nodes. `docker service update --image agent:2.0 agent` restarts all 50 tasks at once, creating a fleet-wide monitoring gap. How do you pace the rollout?

EXAM TRAPS: (A) abandons the one-per-node guarantee. (C) is false — in-place updates work. (D) misuses a placement cap that global mode already implies.

q: A vendor image's app drains gracefully on SIGQUIT but dies uncleanly on SIGTERM, and the Dockerfile STOPSIGNAL cannot be changed (signed image). At deploy time, how do you make Swarm stop tasks with SIGQUIT?

EXAM TRAPS: (A) confuses the SIGNAL with the GRACE PERIOD (the timeout before SIGKILL). (B) invents an env var — STOPSIGNAL is a Dockerfile instruction, not runtime env. (D) falsely claims no override exists.

q: The zombie-process problem (an app running as PID 1 never reaps its children) is fixed for standalone containers with `--init`. The workload now moves to a Swarm service. What carries the fix over?
options: `docker service create --init ...` — Swarm services support the init shim per task

EXAM TRAPS: (B) falsely limits the flag to `docker run`. (C) invents a Compose key. (D) invents orchestrator reaping — the kernel still needs a subreaper in the PID namespace.

q: A recent Kubernetes convert asks how to keep workloads off control-plane nodes — the K8s equivalent of Swarm's manager-avoidance constraint. What do you tell her?
options: Put `nodeSelector: {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: ''}` on every workload
Nothing — Kubernetes schedules on control-plane nodes by default and that is fine
Label the workers and constrain workloads to them

explain: Kubernetes uses taints/tolerations: the control plane taints itself `NoSchedule`, so ordinary pods are excluded unless they explicitly tolerate it. EXAM TRAPS: (A) inverts the selector — that would TARGET control-plane nodes. (B) is false. (C) is workable but not the built-in mechanism the question asks for.

q: `kubectl drain node7` refuses to proceed when DaemonSet pods are present unless `--ignore-daemonsets` is passed, yet `docker node update --availability drain node7` on a Swarm node running global tasks just works. What is the behavioral difference?

explain: Swarm's drain is unconditional: every task on the node (replicated AND global) is shut down and rescheduled elsewhere (global tasks simply don't come back while drained). kubectl treats DaemonSets as node furniture and refuses to evict them without explicit opt-in. EXAM TRAPS: (A) inverts Swarm's behavior. (C) confuses `pause` (no new scheduling, tasks stay) with `drain` (tasks evicted). (D) is false.

q: A Kubernetes rollout is going sideways and the engineer wants to FREEZE it mid-rollout to investigate — not roll back yet, not continue. What is the command?

Set `--update-failure-action pause` on the Deployment
`kubectl rollout pause deploy/api` — freezes the rollout; `kubectl rollout resume deploy/api` continues it
Delete the ReplicaSet

(B) is the classic cross-tool trap: `--update-failure-action` is a real flag, but it belongs to `docker service`, not kubectl. (D) is destructive.

q: An engineer runs `docker stack deploy -c prod.yml api` on a nightly schedule 'to make sure it is applied', but worries each run restarts all services. What actually happens with an unchanged file?
options: Nothing restarts — deploy is declarative; the orchestrator diffs desired vs actual state and only rolls services whose spec changed
Every service restarts; deploy is imperative
Only services with an `update_config` restart
You must pass `--no-recreate` to avoid restarts
explain: Stack deploy reconciles: unchanged specs produce no task churn, which is why blind nightly redeploys are harmless (if pointless). EXAM TRAPS: (B) mistakes the declarative model for an imperative one. (C) invents conditional logic. (D) invents a flag.

q: The MKE cluster needs an 11th worker node. The MKE install command was only ever run on managers. What is the correct way to add the worker?
options: Run the `mirantis/ucp install` command on the new worker too
Workers cannot be added after install; rebuild the cluster
Copy `/var/lib/docker/swarm` from a manager to the worker
Join the swarm with the worker token (`docker swarm join --token <worker-token> <manager>:2377`); MKE's agent components deploy to the node automatically — there is no MKE install step on workers

EXAM TRAPS: (A) misapplies the install to workers. (B) is false. (C) is dangerous — Raft state must never be cloned.

q: A Dockerfile fetches `https://artifacts.corp/data.tar.gz` with ADD. The team wants the build to FAIL if the downloaded bytes do not match the known SHA-256. What is the BuildKit-native way?
options: `COPY --checksum=sha256:<digest> ...`
`ADD --checksum=sha256:<digest> https://artifacts.corp/data.tar.gz /data/` — the checksum is verified during the build and a mismatch fails it
`ADD --verify sha256:<digest> https://...`

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI wants build cache to travel WITH the pushed image — no separate cache configuration on runners, no extra registry repositories. Which cache exporter fits that requirement?

`--cache-to type=local`

EXAM TRAPS: (A) inverts the two backends. (B) is false. (D) exports cache to a local directory — it doesn't travel with the image.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A compliance tool ingests images only as OCI layout tarballs (not Docker-format archives). How do you build straight to that format?

`docker save` the image afterwards
Pass `--output type=docker`
OCI layout requires `docker manifest` commands

EXAM TRAPS: (B) `docker save` produces Docker-format tars (and needs a local image first) — the wrong format. (C) `type=docker` is the default Docker format — the opposite of what's asked. (D) is nonsense.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Multi-arch builds (`linux/amd64,linux/arm64`) run the compile stage under slow QEMU emulation. The compile itself is platform-independent Go code. How do you compile natively and only package per-arch?

Set `QEMU_CPU=max`
Use `--load` instead of `--push`
Split stages: `FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang AS build` compiles natively, then `COPY --from=build` the binary into a final stage built for `$TARGETPLATFORM`

EXAM TRAPS: (A) gives up the architecture. (B) invents a variable. (C) is unrelated to emulation speed.

q: The team runs `registry:2` with a corporate CA-signed certificate for `registry.corp`. Which container configuration enables TLS on the registry itself?

Set `REGISTRY_HTTP_TLS_CERTIFICATE=/certs/registry.crt` and `REGISTRY_HTTP_TLS_KEY=/certs/registry.key` on the registry container (with the cert files mounted in)
Add `registry.corp` to the daemon's `insecure-registries`
Registries cannot terminate TLS themselves; a reverse proxy is mandatory

q: Three teams share one CI host and fight over the default builder's cache. The platform team wants each pipeline to have its own isolated builder. What creates and selects one?

Set `DOCKER_BUILDER=team-a` in the environment

Edit daemon.json to add a builder definition

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Every base-image bump invalidates all subsequent COPY layers even when the copied files did not change, because layer identity chains to the parent. Which BuildKit COPY option breaks that chain for better reuse?

`COPY --independent`
Pass `--cache-from` on the build
Nothing — layer chains cannot be broken

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: After switching the pipeline to `docker buildx build --push`, pushes to the company's OLD registry fail with errors about an unknown manifest media type. The same Dockerfiles pushed fine before the switch. What is happening, and the fix?

Multi-arch pushes are unsupported; go back to single-arch builds
The registry disk is full

q: The release engineer needs the manifest list of `shop/api:2.0` without enabling experimental CLI features (the `docker manifest inspect` route needs them). What works with no daemon or CLI config change?

`docker pull shop/api:2.0` and inspect locally
`docker images --digests`
Nothing — manifest inspection always needs experimental mode

q: A Compose-based pipeline must pass the CI commit SHA into the build as `APP_VERSION` without developers editing the Dockerfile per commit (a merge-conflict hazard). What is the Compose-native way?

Build args cannot come from Compose; shell out to `docker build` directly

q: A build using `COPY --link` fails with `unknown flag: --link`, although BuildKit is enabled and the daemon is current. What is going on?

`--platform` was not passed to the build

Set `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0`

q: A Dockerfile chains five RUN steps with `&& \` continuations into one layer, but it is unreadable. The team wants one layer with natural multi-line scripting and no backslash chains. What is the BuildKit-native form?

Keep five separate RUN steps — readability beats layer count
A heredoc: `RUN <<EOF` on its own line, then the script lines, then `EOF` — one layer, natural multi-line script

q: The pipeline must FAIL the build when a critical or high CVE is found in the image, but only report (not fail) on medium/low. Which command gates it?

`docker scout cves --fail-on critical`
`docker scout cves --severity critical,high`

q: A new release manager needs her own Notary delegation key for the `shop/api` repo (per-tag signing rights). How is the key created?

`docker trust key generate rita` — creates the keypair; then `docker trust signer add --key rita.pub rita shop/api` delegates signing rights
`docker key generate rita`

q: The team wants the CI system notified the moment an image is PUSHED to their `registry:2` instance — no polling. What is the registry-native mechanism?
options: Poll `GET /v2/_catalog` every minute
MSR webhooks — event notifications are only available in the commercial registry
Configure `notifications.endpoints` in the registry config — the registry POSTs push/pull/tag events to the webhook URL
`docker events` on the registry host

q: Developers push rapid builds to `dev/website`. When a build is tagged `-stable`, it should automatically appear in `qa/website` — without giving developers push access to the QA repo. Which MSR feature does this?

Repository mirroring to Docker Hub
Give the dev team admin rights on both repositories
An MSR promotion policy on `dev/website` (Promotions tab) — criteria like tag name ending in `-stable`, vulnerability counts, or license — auto-pushes matching images to `qa/website`
explain: MSR promotion policies create image pipelines between repos based on tag, vulnerability, license, or component criteria — no cross-team access needed. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the manual version of what the policy automates. (B) is a different feature (mirroring). (C) violates the stated access requirement.

q: Shared CI runners accumulate build cache until disks fill. The team wants to keep 50 GB of the hottest cache and prune the rest. Which command?

`docker builder prune --filter until=24h`
`docker builder prune --all`
Delete `/var/lib/docker/buildkit` by hand

q: A secure facility's servers have no internet access and no internal package mirror. The team must install Docker Engine on fresh RHEL hosts. What is the supported path?

Install from the static binaries tarball — download once on a connected machine, extract, and install the binaries plus the systemd units per the documented procedure
`apt-get install docker.io` from the distro repositories
Copy `/usr/bin/docker` from an existing host

q: On a host with an older-but-supported kernel, the daemon refuses to start with overlay2, logging that the kernel version check failed — though the distro backported the needed features. What unlocks overlay2?

Upgrade the kernel — there is no override

Set `"storage-driver": "overlay"`

q: The platform team needs the resolver option `ndots:2` (try short names against search domains first) applied to every container on a host. Where does this daemon-wide setting live?

The daemon's `--dns` flag
Per-container `--dns-opt` only — there is no daemon-wide setting
`"dns-opts": ["ndots:2"]` in daemon.json — applied to every container's resolv.conf

q: Rootless Docker setup fails for user `ci`, with an error about subordinate ID ranges. What is missing?

Membership in the `docker` group
`--privileged` on the daemon
A kernel using cgroup v1

q: An engineer manages prod through a Docker context. A teammate needs the same access. What is the native way to hand it over?

`docker context export prod > prod.dockercontext` and share that file; the teammate runs `docker context import prod prod.dockercontext`
Copy `~/.docker/config.json`
Contexts cannot be shared; everyone recreates them by hand

q: Where does the Docker daemon read its configuration file on Windows Server?

The Windows registry
`C:\ProgramData\docker\config\daemon.json`
`daemon.json` is not supported on Windows

q: A volume plugin is installed but DISABLED. The team must set its `API_TOKEN` setting before enabling it. How?

`docker plugin set vendor/plugin API_TOKEN=s3cret` while it is disabled, then `docker plugin enable vendor/plugin`

q: A `docker build --squash` fails, saying the feature needs the daemon's experimental mode (the earlier squash finding). How do you enable it?

Enable experimental in the CLI config (`~/.docker/config.json`)
Pass `--experimental` to `docker build`
Squash was removed; use multi-stage builds instead

q: With the Splunk log driver, the app STALLS whenever the Splunk backend is slow — logging backpressure blocks the application. How do you decouple them?
options: Raise `max-size`
Set `"log-opts": {"mode": "non-blocking", "max-buffer-size": "4m"}` — the driver buffers in memory and drops instead of blocking the app when the backend lags
Switch the daemon back to json-file
Raise the container's CPU limit

q: A volume plugin has a security fix in a newer version. The plugin is currently enabled and in use. What is the native upgrade path?

Uninstall and reinstall from scratch
`docker plugin disable vendor/plugin`, then `docker plugin upgrade vendor/plugin`, then `docker plugin enable vendor/plugin` — settings are preserved across the upgrade
Plugins update themselves automatically
explain: Plugins upgrade via disable → `plugin upgrade` → enable, preserving their configured settings. EXAM TRAPS: (A) plugins aren't images — `docker pull` is the wrong object. (B) works but pointlessly loses configuration. (D) is false.

q: The company is deploying Mirantis Secure Registry (DTR 2.9-era) alongside MKE. What is true about the install?
options: MSR installs fully standalone with no other dependencies
Install it from a Swarm worker with `docker run`
MSR is installed through the MKE web UI
It requires a running MKE/UCP cluster — install with `docker run -it --rm docker/dtr:2.9.x install --ucp-url https://mke.corp --ucp-username admin`, run from a manager node
explain: MSR/DTR is not standalone: it bootstraps onto an existing MKE (UCP) cluster via the `docker/dtr install` image, which needs UCP credentials and manager access. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is false — the UCP dependency is the whole point. (B) uses the wrong node role. (C) invents a UI install flow.

q: The MKE backup covers the control plane. The team also needs a dedicated backup of MSR's own metadata (repositories, policies, scan results). What backs up MSR itself?
options: `docker run -i --rm docker/dtr:2.9.x backup --ucp-url https://mke.corp ... > msr-backup.tar` — MSR has its own backup command, separate from the MKE backup
The MKE backup already includes all MSR metadata
Copy `/var/lib/registry` off the MSR nodes
MSR metadata cannot be backed up
explain: `docker/dtr backup` captures MSR's metadata independently of the MKE control-plane backup — two systems, two backups. EXAM TRAPS: (B) conflates the two. (C) grabs blob storage but misses the metadata database. (D) is false.

q: The team moves the Docker data-root to `/mnt/docker` on an SELinux-enforcing host. Containers now fail with permission errors even though DAC permissions are correct. What is the fix?
options: Run `setenforce 0`
Label the new path for container use: `semanage fcontext -a -t container_var_lib_t '/mnt/docker(/.*)?' && restorecon -Rv /mnt/docker`
Add `:z` to every volume mount
Reinstall Docker with SELinux disabled
explain: The Docker data directory needs the `container_var_lib_t` SELinux type; a moved data-root loses it. EXAM TRAPS: (A) disables MAC entirely — the sledgehammer. (C) `:z`/`:Z` relabel shared CONTENT mounts, a different scope. (D) invents a flag and downgrades security.

q: The `ops` team must manage Docker without sudo and without joining the `docker` group (auditors want a distinct group). How does the daemon grant socket access to a different group?
options: `chmod 777 /var/run/docker.sock`
Only the `docker` group can ever own the socket
Set `"group": "ops"` in daemon.json — the daemon assigns the socket to that group on startup
Create a symlink to the socket owned by `ops`
explain: The daemon's `group` option controls which group owns `docker.sock`. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the insecure classic. (B) is false. (D) is nonsense — permissions follow the socket, not the link.

q: Rootless Docker works for the `ci` user — until they log out, at which point the daemon dies and nightly builds fail. What is the fix?
options: Launch the daemon under `nohup`
Switch back to rootful Docker
Add the user to the `docker` group
`loginctl enable-linger ci` — keeps the user's systemd manager (and the rootless daemon) alive after logout
explain: Rootless Docker runs as a user systemd service; without lingering, logout tears down the user manager and the daemon with it. EXAM TRAPS: (A) fights the wrong layer. (B) abandons the rootless requirement. (C) is irrelevant — rootless doesn't use the docker group.

q: The MKE cluster must schedule a Windows-only workload. What is true about adding Windows workers to MKE?
options: Join Windows nodes to the swarm with the worker token — no MKE install step on workers; schedule the workload with a platform constraint (`node.platform.os == windows`)
Run the MKE install command on each Windows node
MKE does not support Windows workers
Windows containers must run on manager nodes
explain: Workers — Windows or Linux — just join the swarm; MKE agents deploy automatically, and the OS constraint steers the Windows workload. EXAM TRAPS: (B) misapplies the managers-only install. (C) is false. (D) is false and dangerous.

q: An overlay network `secure` was created WITHOUT `--opt encrypted`. Compliance now requires encryption. The engineer looks for `docker network update --opt encrypted secure`. What will they find?
options: There is no such update path — encryption is set at creation time only; recreate the network with `--opt encrypted` (and reattach the services)
`docker network update --opt encrypted secure` works fine
Restart the daemon with `--encrypted-networks` to convert all overlays
Encryption can be toggled per-container with `--opt encrypted` on `docker run`
explain: Overlay encryption is a create-time decision — there is no `docker network update` at all, and no in-place toggle. Plan a recreate (new network, move services, remove the old). EXAM TRAPS: (B) invents a subcommand. (C) invents a daemon flag. (D) misplaces a network-level option at the container level.

q: Running `docker run -d -p 80 nginx`, the engineer finds the site answering on some random high port. What did `-p 80` do?
options: Bound host port 80 to the container
Published container port 80 to a RANDOM host port (Docker picks from the ephemeral range); `docker port <container>` reveals which
Errored — the form is invalid without a host port
Exactly what `-P` does
explain: A lone container port in `-p` means 'publish it, you pick the host port'. EXAM TRAPS: (A) describes `-p 80:80`. (C) is false — the form is valid. (D) `-P` publishes ALL exposed ports; `-p 80` publishes just the one named.

q: In Compose, a metrics sidecar must share the `web` service's network stack (localhost scraping, like the `container:` mode). What is the Compose form — and the Swarm caveat?
options: `network_mode: host`
Put both services on the same user-defined network
`network_mode: "service:web"` — the sidecar shares web's network namespace. Caveat: `docker stack deploy` IGNORES `network_mode` (like `security_opt`), so this is Compose/`docker compose up` only
`links: [web]`
explain: `network_mode: "service:<name>"` is Compose's port of `--network container:`. It is on the verified list of options Swarm ignores. EXAM TRAPS: (A) shares the HOST's stack, not web's. (B) confuses 'same network' with 'same network STACK' — localhost still differs. (D) `links` is legacy and doesn't share namespaces.

q: The team runs `docker run -d -p 10.0.0.5:80:80 -p 192.168.1.10:8080:80 nginx`. A reviewer claims the second `-p` conflicts with the first. Who is right?
options: The reviewer — one container port maps to exactly one host binding
The second `-p` silently replaces the first
Only the first `-p` takes effect
The command is valid — one container port can be published on multiple host IP/port combinations; TCP and UDP are separate spaces too
explain: Port publishing is a list: the same container port may appear on several host IPs/ports, and the same numeric port may serve TCP and UDP independently. EXAM TRAPS: (A/B/C) all invent a one-to-one restriction that doesn't exist.

q: Containers on overlay `app-net` cannot reach each other across two specific nodes. `docker network inspect app-net` on a manager shows a `Peers` section. What does it tell you?
options: The gossip/VXLAN peer list — every node participating in the overlay should appear; a missing node points at blocked gossip (TCP/UDP 7946) or VXLAN (UDP 4789) between those nodes
The list of containers attached to the network
The Raft quorum members
Nothing actionable — `Peers` is informational only
explain: `Peers` is the overlay's membership view from gossip; a node absent there never joined the data plane. EXAM TRAPS: (B) confuses `Peers` with `Containers` (which is local-node-only). (C) confuses overlay gossip with Raft. (D) dismisses the primary diagnostic.

q: A service uses `--endpoint-mode dnsrr` and publishes `-p 80:80`. A teammate claims the routing mesh cannot load-balance a DNSRR service's published port. Is that right?
options: Yes — dnsrr disables the mesh; use `mode=host` instead
No — DNSRR only removes the internal VIP (service discovery becomes DNS round-robin); published ports still flow through the routing mesh and load-balance across tasks
Yes — dnsrr services cannot publish ports at all
Only UDP published ports work with dnsrr
