explain: The VIP is what you give up with dnsrr (the earlier stateful-TCP finding); the L4 mesh for published ports is unaffected. EXAM TRAPS: (A) and (C) falsely claim the mesh or publishing breaks. (D) invents a protocol restriction.

q: A global node-exporter needs BOTH: direct per-node access on host port 9100 (per-node scraping) AND mesh-routed access on 19100. Can one service declare both publish modes?
options: No — one publish mode per service
Only by creating two separate services
Yes — `--publish mode=host,target=9100,published=9100 --publish mode=ingress,target=9100,published=19100` on the same service; the mode is per port-mapping, not per service
Host mode and ingress mode can never mix in one cluster
explain: Each `--publish` is independent: mix host-mode (direct, per-node) and ingress-mode (mesh) mappings on one service freely. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents a per-service mode restriction. (B) doubles the operational surface for no reason. (D) is false.

q: An app requires its FQDN to be `web.corp.internal` inside the container. `--hostname web` alone yields just `web`. What completes it?
options: `--dns-search corp.internal`
`--add-host web.corp.internal:127.0.0.1`
Set the FQDN from inside the container at runtime
`--domainname corp.internal` — the container's FQDN becomes `web.corp.internal`
explain: `--hostname` plus `--domainname` compose the FQDN, exactly like a host. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--dns-search` affects name RESOLUTION, not the machine's own name. (B) plants a static hosts entry — it doesn't set the hostname. (C) the hostname is a container property set at creation.

q: Three legacy hostnames must resolve inside a container, but corporate DNS cannot be changed. What is the per-container mechanism?
options: Multiple `--add-host` flags (`--add-host db1:10.0.0.5 --add-host db2:10.0.0.6 ...`); in Compose, `extra_hosts:` — the entries land in the container's `/etc/hosts`
Edit `/etc/hosts` inside the running container
Pass the IPs with `--dns`
Only one `--add-host` is allowed per container
explain: `--add-host`/`extra_hosts` injects static name→IP mappings per container. EXAM TRAPS: (B) is ephemeral — and echoes the earlier lesson that the host's file doesn't propagate. (C) confuses DNS SERVERS (`--dns`) with DNS RECORDS. (D) is false — repeat the flag freely.

q: Stacks `billing` and `shop` must share one overlay network. Each stack declaring its own `backend` network keeps them isolated. What is the sharing pattern?
options: Declare `backend` in both Compose files — the same name means the same network
Create it once (`docker network create -d overlay backend`), then declare it `external: true` in both Compose files — both stacks attach to the same network
Have `shop` use `billing`'s default network
Networks cannot be shared across stacks
explain: `external: true` attaches to a pre-existing network instead of creating a stack-private one — the cross-stack sharing mechanism (and why `ping db` vs `ping billing_db` behaved the way it did). EXAM TRAPS: (A) each stack creates its OWN `backend`. (C) default networks are stack-private. (D) is false.

q: The team wants the container's port 80 on a RANDOM host port, but bound ONLY to loopback — not all interfaces. Which form?
options: `-p 127.0.0.1::80` — an empty host-port field means Docker picks a random one, on 127.0.0.1 only
Not possible — random host ports always bind all interfaces
explain: The `ip::container-port` form combines a pinned interface with a random port. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `-P` randomizes but binds all interfaces. (B) pins loopback but fixes the port at 80. (D) is false.

q: A game server needs host port 7777 for BOTH TCP and UDP. The engineer runs `-p 7777:7777 -p 7777:7777/udp`. Valid?
options: No — the second mapping conflicts with the first
No — the `/udp` suffix is not real syntax
Only if the Dockerfile EXPOSEs both protocols
Yes — TCP and UDP port spaces are independent; the same host port number can serve both
explain: Port allocation is per-protocol: 7777/tcp and 7777/udp coexist. EXAM TRAPS: (A) imagines one shared space. (B) denies real syntax. (C) repeats the EXPOSE myth — EXPOSE documents; `-p` works regardless.

q: Every task of the `api` service needs the company resolver (10.2.0.53) and `corp.internal` suffix search — the per-container DNS settings, but expressed at service level. Which service flags?
options: `docker service create --dns 10.2.0.53 --dns-search corp.internal --dns-option ndots:2 ...` — services accept the same DNS flags as `docker run`
`--network-opt dns=10.2.0.53`
DNS can only be set daemon-wide for Swarm services
Bake the resolver into the image's `/etc/resolv.conf`
explain: `docker service create` supports `--dns`, `--dns-search`, and `--dns-option` per task. EXAM TRAPS: (B) invents a flag. (C) is false. (D) fights Docker — resolv.conf is managed, and baking it breaks portability.

q: A service attaches to overlays `frontend` and `backend`. How many VIPs does it get?
options: One VIP total, on the first network listed
One per attached network — `docker service inspect` shows a VirtualIP entry for each; tasks are reachable through either
VIPs only exist on the ingress network
None — multi-network services silently switch to dnsrr
explain: The VIP is a per-network construct: each attached overlay gets its own virtual IP for the service. EXAM TRAPS: (A) imagines a single global VIP. (C) confuses the service VIP with the mesh. (D) invents an automatic mode switch.

q: A user-defined bridge network is created on manager1, but containers on manager2 cannot join it. What is the scoping rule?
options: The network needs `--attachable`
Bridge networks replicate after a gossip delay — wait a few minutes
Bridge networks are LOCAL-scoped — they exist on one host only; multi-host container networking needs a (swarm-scoped) overlay network
Create an identically named bridge on every node
explain: Driver scope matters: `bridge`/`host`/`null` are local to one daemon; `overlay` is swarm-scoped. Same name on two hosts is two networks. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--attachable` is an overlay concept. (B) invents replication. (D) creates isolated same-named networks — no connectivity.

q: Trying `docker network create --dns 10.0.0.53 mynet` fails with `unknown flag: --dns`. Where do DNS settings actually belong?
options: The flag is valid on newer daemons — upgrade
`--opt dns=10.0.0.53` on network create
DNS is fully automatic; never configure it
Per-container `--dns`/`--dns-search` at run/create time, or daemon-wide `"dns"` in daemon.json — networks do not take DNS flags
explain: DNS is a container/daemon concern, not a network property. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the flag doesn't exist at any version. (B) invents a driver option. (C) is false — corporate resolvers are a routine need.

q: `docker run --network frontend --network backend app` is issued expecting dual attachment from the start. What happens?
options: `docker run` takes a single `--network`; attach the second one at runtime with `docker network connect backend <container>`
Both attach — the first listed wins for DNS
The container gets two interfaces automatically
Multi-network containers require Compose
explain: `docker run` accepts one `--network`; extra attachments are runtime operations via `docker network connect` (and detachable the same way). EXAM TRAPS: (B) invents multi-attach. (C) describes the END state after `connect`, not what the single command does. (D) is false.

q: A host remaps container UIDs into subordinate ranges via user namespaces (`userns-remap` set to `default`). One legacy container MUST see real host UIDs (it manages host files by UID). How do you exempt just that container?
options: Run it `--privileged`
`docker run --userns=host ...` — opts that container out of remapping, back to host UIDs
Run it `--user root`
Per-container exemption is impossible; remapping is all-or-nothing
explain: `--userns=host` disables the remap for one container. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--privileged` doesn't touch UID mapping. (C) root is still remapped under userns-remap. (D) is false.

q: Inside a container, `cat /proc/kcore` returns empty though the host's is huge, and several `/proc` and `/sys` paths show as masked. What is this?
options: An AppArmor denial
A dropped Linux capability
Docker's default masked paths — sensitive host kernel interfaces are masked (over-mounted) in every container; customize with `--security-opt mask=...` / `unmask=...`
A side effect of rootless mode
explain: The daemon masks paths like `/proc/kcore`, `/proc/keys`, `/sys/firmware` by default in all containers — independent of AppArmor/capabilities. EXAM TRAPS: (A) AppArmor is a different mechanism. (B) capabilities gate syscalls, not these mounts. (D) masking applies to rootful containers too.

q: A pod must run its app as UID 999 and group 3000 — the image defaults to root and cannot be rebuilt. What is the pod-level enforcement?
options: `fsGroup: 3000` in the securityContext
Add a `USER` instruction — requires rebuilding the image
`docker run --user 999:3000`
`securityContext: {runAsUser: 999, runAsGroup: 3000}` — the kubelet enforces the process identity regardless of the image default
explain: `runAsUser`/`runAsGroup` override the image's default user at runtime. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `fsGroup` sets supplementary group ownership for VOLUMES, not the process UID. (B) requires the forbidden rebuild. (C) is the wrong tool — this is Kubernetes, not the Docker CLI.

q: The `payments` namespace must enforce the Pod Security Standards `restricted` profile. What does `restricted` require of every container, beyond the baseline?
options: `runAsNonRoot: true`, `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` (or localhost), and dropping ALL capabilities — the strictest built-in profile
Just `privileged: false`
Only a read-only root filesystem
Nothing new — `restricted` is only a label
explain: `restricted` hardens on three axes: non-root user, default seccomp, and zero added capabilities (plus no privilege escalation). EXAM TRAPS: (B) baseline already covers privileged. (C) read-only root is good practice but not the whole profile. (D) denies the enforcement.

q: A debug container was granted `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` to strace a flaky app (the minimal grant). The security team wants it removed after the incident. Why is lingering SYS_PTRACE a big deal?
options: It silently disables the seccomp filter
It lets the process trace other processes — reading/writing their memory and injecting syscalls; combined with a shared PID namespace or a breakout primitive it is a potent escalation path
It is equivalent to `--privileged`
It only affects the container's own processes, so it is harmless
explain: ptrace is process-memory access: powerful for debugging, dangerous to leave. The grant should be incident-scoped. EXAM TRAPS: (B) is false. (C) overstates — it's one powerful cap, not the full set. (D) understates the blast radius.

q: The `payments` namespace needs a default-deny posture: no pod talks to anyone unless an explicit policy allows it — ingress AND egress. Which NetworkPolicy delivers it?
options: A policy with `policyTypes: [Ingress]` and an empty ingress rule list
A policy with an empty `podSelector` and no `policyTypes`
`podSelector: {}` with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` and no rules — selects all pods and denies everything both directions until allow-policies are added
NetworkPolicies cannot deny traffic; they can only allow it
explain: An empty-rule policy selecting all pods in both directions is the standard default-deny-all; finer allow-policies then punch holes. EXAM TRAPS: (A) leaves egress wide open (the earlier exfiltration finding). (B) without policyTypes the policy enforces nothing. (D) is false — empty rules mean deny.

q: A monitoring ClusterRole needs to `get`/`list` NODES (cluster-scoped, not namespaced). The admin created a `Role` and a `RoleBinding` in `monitoring`. Why doesn't it work?
options: The verbs are wrong — nodes need `watch`
Bind the ClusterRole with a RoleBinding instead
RBAC does not cover nodes
Roles cannot grant access to cluster-scoped resources — node access requires a ClusterRole (plus ClusterRoleBinding)
explain: `Role`/`RoleBinding` are namespace-scoped; cluster-scoped resources like nodes need `ClusterRole`/`ClusterRoleBinding`. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the verbs are fine. (C) is the subtle trap — a RoleBinding referencing a ClusterRole still only grants permissions WITHIN that namespace. (D) is false.

q: Release manager Rita generated her delegation key on her old laptop (`docker trust key generate rita`). On the new laptop she needs the SAME key — rotation would break existing delegations. How?
options: `docker trust key load rita-key.pem --name rita` — imports the existing private key under her signer name
Generate a fresh key — delegations follow the signer name, not the key
`ssh-add rita-key.pem`
Copy `~/.docker/trust` over and hope for the best
explain: `trust key load` imports an existing private key so delegations (which bind the KEY) keep working. EXAM TRAPS: (B) inverts the binding — delegations follow the key material. (C) is the wrong tool. (D) is unsupported hackery.

q: A Compose file sets `security_opt: [- seccomp:/path/custom.json]` for a service. `docker stack deploy` prints `Ignoring unsupported options: security_opt` and deploys anyway. The team assumed their custom seccomp profile was active. What is the reality?
options: The deploy failed — the warning means the service was not created

Swarm services cannot carry custom seccomp/AppArmor options — `stack deploy` ignores `security_opt` (like `privileged`, `cap_add`, `devices`); tasks run under the daemon defaults. Harden with standalone `docker run` or accept the defaults
The profile path must be a URL, not a local file
security_opt works, but only when nested under `deploy:`
explain: `security_opt` is on the verified list of Compose options Swarm ignores — the deploy warns and continues WITHOUT it. EXAM TRAPS: (A) misreads a warning as a failure. (C) invents a URL requirement. (D) invents a placement rule.

q: Compliance asks: 'Who deployed what, and when, on the MKE cluster last quarter?' `docker events` on a worker shows only local container noise. Where is the authoritative trail?
options: Nowhere — MKE does not log API actions
The Swarm Raft logs
MKE's audit logs — the control plane records authenticated API actions (who did what, when); that is the compliance trail
The join-token history
explain: MKE keeps audit logs of API activity — the who/what/when record auditors want. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is false. (B) Raft holds encrypted cluster STATE, not an action audit trail. (D) is nonsense.

q: A Deployment uses `image: shop/api` (no tag — defaults to `:latest`) with no `imagePullPolicy` set. Nodes re-pull on every pod creation even though the image is cached. Why?
options: A kubelet bug — cached images are always reused
`IfNotPresent` is the default for every tag
The kubelet never caches `:latest`
The default policy is `Always` for `:latest` (and `IfNotPresent` for pinned tags) — `:latest` re-pulls by default
explain: The default is tag-dependent: `:latest` (or untagged) → Always; anything else → IfNotPresent. The mirror image of the earlier IfNotPresent-stale-tag problem. EXAM TRAPS: (A) denies documented behavior. (B) states the default backwards for `:latest`. (C) confuses caching with policy.

q: A container runs its app as `appuser` (Dockerfile USER). An engineer execs in to inspect a data file and lands as root instead — `docker exec` ignored the image's USER. How do you exec as the app user?
options: `docker exec --user appuser -it <container> sh` — exec takes its own `--user`, independent of the image's USER
USER applies to exec too; the image must be broken
Exec in as root, then `su appuser`
Pass `--privileged` to the exec
explain: `docker exec --user` sets the exec session's identity; the image USER only governs the container's main process. EXAM TRAPS: (B) contradicts the established behavior. (C) works but the flag is the direct answer. (D) is unrelated.

q: A monitoring agent needs the HOST's cgroup hierarchy (host-wide per-service CPU accounting) — the cgroup analogue of `--pid=host`. What is the namespaced equivalent?
options: Bind-mount `-v /sys/fs/cgroup:/sys/fs/cgroup`
`docker run --cgroupns=host ...` — shares the host's cgroup namespace, the cgroup analogue of `--pid=host`
Run the agent `--privileged`
Impossible — the cgroup view is always namespaced
explain: `--cgroupns=host` joins the host's cgroup namespace so the agent sees the true hierarchy. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the bind-mount shows host paths but the namespace still virtualizes the view — the namespace flag is the correct mechanism. (C) is overkill and doesn't change namespaces. (D) is false.

q: The platform team wants the `restricted` PSS profile but fears breaking 200 existing pods overnight. How do they preview violations without enforcing?
options: Enforce immediately and roll back whatever breaks
Pod Security Standards cannot preview — only enforce
Label the namespace `pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted` (and/or `audit: restricted`) — violations are warned/recorded, not blocked; flip to `enforce:` after cleanup
Run a third-party scanner instead
explain: PSS has three modes per namespace: enforce (block), audit (record), warn (warn). Warn/audit first, enforce after remediation — the safe migration path. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is reckless. (B) denies real modes. (D) ignores the native mechanism.

q: After hardening a container with `--cap-drop ALL`, `ping` fails with `Operation not permitted`. What is the minimal capability to restore ping?
options: `--cap-add SYS_ADMIN`
Ping needs no capabilities
Re-add ALL capabilities
`--cap-add NET_RAW` — ping needs raw sockets, and that is the only capability it requires
explain: ping crafts ICMP via raw sockets → `NET_RAW`. Least privilege means adding back just that. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the sledgehammer cap. (B) is false — unprivileged ping fails. (C) defeats the hardening.

q: A container runs `--read-only`, yet DNS resolution works fine. The engineer expected `/etc/resolv.conf` to be unwritable and DNS to break. Why does it still work?
options: `--read-only` does not actually protect anything
DNS is resolved by the daemon on the container's behalf
Docker always mounts `/etc/hostname`, `/etc/hosts`, and `/etc/resolv.conf` as separate writable mounts — even with `--read-only` — so identity and DNS keep working
You must also pass `--tmpfs /etc` for DNS to work
explain: Those three files are per-container managed mounts, always writable regardless of `--read-only`. EXAM TRAPS: (A) denies the protection. (B) misplaces resolution in the daemon. (D) invents a requirement.

q: No cluster volume plugin is available, but there is an NFS server at 10.0.0.5 exporting `/exports/data`. What is the exact `docker volume create` for it?
options: `docker volume create --driver nfs nfsshare`
`docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=10.0.0.5,rw --opt device=:/exports/data nfsshare`
`docker volume create -v nfs://10.0.0.5/exports/data nfsshare`
Mount it on the host and bind-mount — Docker cannot consume NFS natively
explain: The `local` driver's mount options (`type=`, `o=`, `device=`) can mount NFS (or CIFS) directly — no plugin needed. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents an `nfs` driver. (C) invents URL syntax. (D) denies the native capability.

q: The NFS volume must be declared in a Compose file's top-level `volumes:` instead of created by hand. What is the declaration?
options: `driver: nfs` under the volume
A `bind:` entry pointing at the host's NFS mount

`volumes:
  nfsshare:
    driver: local
    driver_opts:
      type: nfs
      o: addr=10.0.0.5,rw
      device: ":/exports/data"`
Compose cannot declare NFS volumes
explain: Top-level volumes accept `driver_opts` mapping 1:1 to `docker volume create --opt`. EXAM TRAPS: (A) uses a nonexistent driver. (B) is a different mechanism (host pre-mount). (D) is false.

q: A singleton pod must be the ONLY pod in the whole cluster able to mount a volume — even another pod on the SAME node must be refused. Which access mode?
options: `ReadWriteOnce`
`ReadWriteMany`
Access modes cannot express this
`ReadWriteOncePod` — single-pod exclusivity, cluster-wide
explain: `ReadWriteOncePod` restricts the volume to exactly one pod anywhere; `ReadWriteOnce` allows several pods on the same node. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the per-node trap. (B) is the opposite. (C) is false.

q: Each pod in a Deployment must mount its OWN subdirectory of a shared volume, named after the pod (`/data/<pod-name>`). The pod name is only known at runtime. How?
options: `subPathExpr: $(POD_NAME)` with `POD_NAME` populated from `fieldRef: metadata.name` — the expression expands per pod
`subPath: $POD_NAME`
Hand-create one PVC per pod
Not possible in Kubernetes
explain: `subPathExpr` expands `$(VAR)` references; plain `subPath` does NOT expand — the classic trap. EXAM TRAPS: (B) is exactly that trap. (C) doesn't scale. (D) is false.

q: A 2 MB ConfigMap is mounted by 500 pods; every update triggers watch storms and occasional mid-rollout inconsistency. The config changes rarely and never in place. What helps?
options: Mount it with `readOnly: true`
`immutable: true` on the ConfigMap — the kubelet caches it without watches; updates require recreating the object, which suits rarely-changed config
Use a Secret instead
Split it into 500 ConfigMaps
explain: Immutable ConfigMaps trade in-place updates for watch-free caching — ideal for static config at scale. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is a mount option, unrelated to watches. (C) has identical mechanics. (D) is silly.

q: An engineer writes a Secret manifest with the password in PLAINTEXT under `data:` and the API server rejects it. What is the plaintext-friendly field?
options: Base64-encode it into `data:` by hand
Put the password in an annotation
`stringData:` — write plaintext; the API server base64-encodes it into `data:` for you
Secrets cannot hold passwords
explain: `stringData` is the write-only plaintext convenience; the server populates `data:`. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the valid manual alternative — but not the field asked for. (B) misuses annotations. (D) is false.

q: A pod must mount the single host FILE `/etc/allowed-ips.conf` (not a directory). Which hostPath type — and how strict is it?
options: `type: Directory`
`type: FileOrCreate` — creates an empty file if missing
`type: DirectoryOrCreate`
`type: File` — mounts a single file; the pod FAILS to start if the file does not exist, which is the strictness you want for an allowlist
explain: `File` demands the file exist — fail-closed for security inputs. EXAM TRAPS: (A)/(C) are directory types. (B) is the dangerous trap: silently creating an EMPTY allowlist file.

q: A Java app wants its heap sized from the container's MEMORY LIMIT without hardcoding it. The limit is set in the pod spec. How does the value reach the app as an environment variable?
options: `valueFrom: {resourceFieldRef: {resource: limits.memory}}` — the kubelet injects the container's own limit as env
`fieldRef` pointing at an annotation
Mount `/sys/fs/cgroup` and parse the limit at startup
Hardcode the same number in the app config
explain: `resourceFieldRef` exposes the container's own requests/limits as env vars (or files) — the resource twin of the downward API's `fieldRef`. EXAM TRAPS: (B) `fieldRef` is for pod metadata, not resources. (C) is manual toil. (D) drifts out of sync.

q: An image ships default configs at `/app/conf`. The team mounts a tmpfs there for runtime overrides — and the defaults VANISH (a tmpfs starts empty; it has no copy-up like named volumes). How do you get the image's files INTO the tmpfs?
options: Use a named volume instead of tmpfs
Long syntax: `--mount type=tmpfs,dst=/app/conf,tmpcopyup` — copies the image's existing files up into the tmpfs at mount time
Add `--opt nocopy`
COPY the defaults in the entrypoint script
explain: `tmpcopyup` is tmpfs's answer to volume copy-up: seed the RAM-disk from the image. EXAM TRAPS: (A) changes the lifecycle the team chose tmpfs for. (C) `nocopy` is a VOLUME option — and inverted. (D) is manual toil.

q: A staging namespace needs a writable COPY of the production PVC's data — same storage class, no manual disk surgery, and no VolumeSnapshot exists. What is the native expression?
options: Create a VolumeSnapshot first
`kubectl cp` the data between pods
A new PVC with `dataSource: {name: prod-data, kind: PersistentVolumeClaim}` — the provisioner clones the source PVC
Edit the PV's `claimRef` to point at the new PVC
explain: A PVC can be a `dataSource` for another PVC — provisioner-side cloning, no admin steps. EXAM TRAPS: (A) snapshots are the other answer, but none exists here. (B) is slow manual toil. (D) is dangerous claim surgery.

q: Two containers share one named volume `data`, but each must see ONLY its own subdirectory (`tenant1/`, `tenant2/`). This is plain Docker, not Kubernetes. How?
options: `--mount type=volume,src=data,dst=/app,subpath=tenant1`
Create two separate named volumes
Bind-mount the subdirectories from the host
`--mount type=volume,src=data,dst=/app,volume-subpath=tenant1` — Docker's subpath equivalent for named volumes
explain: Docker's option is `volume-subpath`; Kubernetes calls the same idea `subPath` — the cross-platform naming trap. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is exactly that trap. (B) evades the requirement. (C) needs host paths that may not exist.

q: A ConfigMap holds keys `tls.crt` and `tls.key`; the app expects files named `cert.pem` and `key.pem`. How do you rename keys to filenames in ONE volume mount?
options: `items: [{key: tls.crt, path: cert.pem}, {key: tls.key, path: key.pem}]` on the configMap volume — each key lands at the given filename
Rename the keys in the ConfigMap itself
Two separate `subPath` volumes
ConfigMap keys cannot be remapped to different filenames
explain: `items` maps keys to arbitrary paths in a single mount. EXAM TRAPS: (B) breaks other consumers of the keys. (C) works but is verbose — items is the idiomatic one-mount answer. (D) is false.

q: A legacy app reads its DB password from the ENVIRONMENT, not a file. The password lives in a Kubernetes Secret. How does it reach the container's env?
options: Mount the Secret as a volume
`env: [{name: DB_PASS, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db, key: password}}}]` — or `envFrom: {secretRef: {name: db}}` for the whole Secret
Secrets cannot become environment variables
Copy the password into the image's ENV
explain: `secretKeyRef`/`envFrom` project Secret values into env vars — the env twin of Secret volumes. EXAM TRAPS: (A) yields files, not env. (C) is false. (D) bakes the secret into the image.

q: A Compose file bind-mounts `./data:/data`, but `./data` does not exist on fresh checkouts and the deploy should create it. (`docker run -v` auto-creates host paths — what about Compose?)
options: Compose short syntax auto-creates it too, always
Mark the volume `external: true`
Long syntax: `type: bind, source: ./data, target: /data, bind: {create_host_path: true}`
Add `RUN mkdir /data` to the Dockerfile
explain: `bind.create_host_path: true` is the explicit opt-in for host-path creation in Compose long syntax. EXAM TRAPS: (A) confuses `docker run -v`'s auto-create with Compose short syntax. (B) is a different concept. (D) creates an IMAGE directory, not the host path.

q: Three containers share a 20 GB dataset via one named volume, and none may modify it. What is the mount form?
options: `--read-only` on each container
`chmod -R a-w` the volume's data on the host
Named volumes cannot be mounted read-only
`-v models:/models:ro` — the `:ro` suffix makes the named-volume mount read-only in that container
explain: `:ro` (or `readonly` in `--mount`) makes that container's mount read-only while others stay read-write. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--read-only` locks the whole rootfs — heavier than needed. (B) is host-side hackery. (C) is false.

q: A Swarm service needs a shared tmpfs (RAM-disk) visible to its tasks — but `docker service create` has no `--tmpfs` flag. How do you get a tmpfs through the volume system?
options: `docker volume create --driver local --opt type=tmpfs --opt device=tmpfs --opt o=size=100m,uid=1000 tmpshare` — a tmpfs-backed named volume, mountable by services
`docker service create --tmpfs /scratch`
`docker volume create --opt type=memory tmpshare`
Swarm services cannot use tmpfs at all
explain: The `local` driver can mount a tmpfs as a named volume — consumable by services like any volume. EXAM TRAPS: (B) invents a service flag. (C) invents a driver type. (D) is false.

q: Ten pre-provisioned PVs are labeled `tier=gold`. A PVC must bind ONE of them — but the engineer does not know the PVs' exact names. What is the label-based binding?
options: `storageClassName: gold`
Omit any selector and let it bind whichever PV is free
`volumeName: pv-gold-3`
`selector: {matchLabels: {tier: gold}}` on the PVC — binds a PV carrying matching labels
explain: PVC `selector` binds by PV labels without knowing names. EXAM TRAPS: (A) confuses StorageClasses (dynamic provisioning) with selection. (B) may grab the wrong tier. (C) `volumeName` works but requires the exact name the question rules out.

q: A CI pipeline deploys stacks to the MKE collection `/Production` using a dedicated service account. The pipeline suddenly fails with `access denied` on every deploy. An admin 'fixed' it last week by adding the service account to a team that holds the `View Only` role on `/Production`. The pipeline only needs to create and update Swarm services — nothing else. What is the correct least-privilege fix?
options: Create a grant binding the service account subject to the `Scheduler` role on the `/Production` collection — Scheduler is the purpose-built role for deploying and managing services, without cluster-admin rights
Make the service account a member of the `admins` org — org membership automatically confers deploy rights
Keep `View Only` but add the service account to three more teams — stacked team memberships accumulate into deploy rights
Assign the `Restricted Control` role — it is the MKE role designed for CI/CD deploy pipelines
explain: MKE access = grants, and a grant binds a subject (user, team, or service account) + a role to a collection. Teams alone grant nothing, and `View Only` cannot create services. EXAM TRAPS: (B) org admin is maximum privilege, the opposite of least privilege. (C) team memberships don't stack into rights without a grant. (D) `Restricted Control` is broader than needed (container exec/logs) and is not the deploy role — `Scheduler` is.

q: Two tenants share one MKE cluster. Tenant A's developers must never see Tenant B's services, and vice versa. An engineer proposes putting both tenants' services in the default `/Shared` collection and relying on Kubernetes namespaces for isolation. What is the correct MKE-native design?
options: Keep `/Shared` — MKE automatically hides services from users outside their Kubernetes namespace

Create `/TenantA` and `/TenantB` collections, move each tenant's services into its own collection, and grant each tenant's team a role only on its collection — collections are the MKE access boundary for both Swarm and Kubernetes resources
Create two MKE orgs — orgs are the hard isolation boundary and collections are only cosmetic labels
Run `docker swarm ca --rotate` — rotating the CA re-keys tenant isolation
explain: Collections are MKE's RBAC boundary: a grant gives a subject a role on a collection, and anything outside the granted collections is invisible. EXAM TRAPS: (A) Kubernetes namespaces are not MKE collections — MKE RBAC doesn't read them. (C) orgs group users/teams for administration; the resource boundary is the collection. (D) CA rotation reissues TLS certs; it has nothing to do with authorization.

q: After an incident, the team runs `docker service ps payments` to trace a failed rollout, but only the 5 most recent task entries exist — older failures aged out before the postmortem. They need ~30 entries retained going forward. What changes this?
options: `docker service update --history-retain 30 payments` — retention is a per-service setting
Add more manager nodes — task history scales with Raft quorum size
Run `docker swarm update --task-history-limit 30` — the swarm-wide retention setting (default 5) controls how many historic task entries `docker service ps` keeps
`docker service ps --all-time payments` — the flag bypasses retention
explain: Task history retention is a swarm-level setting, default 5, raised with `docker swarm update --task-history-limit`. EXAM TRAPS: (A) no per-service `--history-retain` flag exists. (B) manager count affects fault tolerance, not history depth. (D) `--all-time` is invented — once entries age out of Raft, they're gone.

q: Before patching the kernel on `node-3`, an engineer runs `docker node update --availability pause node-3`, expecting its 12 tasks to migrate elsewhere first. Ten minutes later the tasks are still on `node-3` and the patch window is burning. What went wrong, and what was the right command?
options: Pause migrates tasks but needs `--force` — rerun as `docker node update --availability pause --force node-3`
Nothing — the Swarm equivalent is `kubectl drain node-3`, which was never run
The node must be removed from the swarm with `docker swarm leave` before patching

`pause` only stops NEW task scheduling — existing tasks stay put. The engineer wanted `docker node update --availability drain node-3`, which gracefully shuts tasks down and reschedules them onto other nodes
explain: Availability has three states: `active` (normal), `pause` (no new tasks, existing keep running), `drain` (existing tasks are shut down and rescheduled elsewhere). EXAM TRAPS: (A) no `--force` flag exists for availability. (B) `kubectl drain` is Kubernetes — cross-tool confusion. (C) leaving the swarm is drastic and unnecessary.

q: A 3-manager Swarm loses two managers to simultaneous disk failures. The survivor can't reach quorum: `docker node ls` fails and nothing schedules. Backups of the swarm state exist, but the replacement VMs have different IP addresses. What recovers the cluster?
options: `docker swarm join` the replacements to the survivor — a single manager can admit new members without quorum

On the surviving manager, run `docker swarm init --force-new-cluster --advertise-addr <new-ip>` — it rebuilds a single-manager cluster from the local Raft state; then join fresh managers/workers and restore workloads
`docker node demote` the two dead managers — demotion restores quorum to the survivor
Restore the backup onto one replacement VM and `docker swarm join` it — backups carry quorum with them
explain: `--force-new-cluster` is the disaster-recovery path: it forces the local node to become a single-manager swarm from its Raft data, discarding the lost managers. EXAM TRAPS: (A) join requires quorum on the existing cluster. (C) demote is a Raft operation — it also needs quorum. (D) a restored backup can't join a quorum-less cluster; the force-new-cluster step comes first.

q: A 5-manager Swarm spans two datacenters: 3 managers in DC-A, 2 in DC-B. The inter-DC link drops. Which side keeps scheduling, and what happens if one more manager on the surviving side then crashes?
options: DC-A (3 of 5) keeps quorum and keeps scheduling; if one of those 3 crashes, quorum is lost everywhere — 2 of 5 is not a majority, so the cluster stops scheduling (running tasks keep running) until quorum is restored
Both sides keep scheduling — Swarm uses active-active multi-master replication
DC-B takes over because the minority side is promoted automatically
The whole cluster freezes the moment any partition occurs — Swarm has no partition tolerance
explain: Raft quorum = majority: 3 of 5. The minority side goes read-only; the majority side keeps working. Losing one more on the majority side leaves 2/5 — no quorum anywhere, so no new scheduling, updates, or joins, but already-running tasks are untouched. EXAM TRAPS: (B) split-brain scheduling would corrupt state — Raft forbids it. (C) nothing auto-promotes. (D) partitions are tolerated by the majority side.

q: A 12-replica service is constrained to `node.role==worker`, but all 12 tasks pile onto workers in `us-east-1a`, starving the other AZs. Nodes carry the label `az=1a|1b|1c`. Which placement setting spreads replicas evenly across AZs?
options: `--placement-pref spread=node.role` — spread accepts any node attribute
`docker service create --max-per-node 4 ...` — caps replicas per node
`--placement-pref spread=node.labels.az` — a spread preference distributes tasks evenly across the distinct values of the label
`--update-parallelism 4` — parallelism controls placement spread
explain: `--placement-pref spread=node.labels.<key>` tells the scheduler to balance tasks across the label's values. EXAM TRAPS: (A) spread only accepts node/engine label keys, not `node.role`. (B) `--max-per-node` doesn't exist as a service flag. (D) update parallelism paces rollouts; it doesn't place tasks.

q: A clustered app requires every task's hostname to be unique and stable per slot (e.g. `kafka-1`, `kafka-2`). Setting `--hostname kafka` gives every task the same name and the cluster fails to form. Which service option fixes it?
options: `--hostname '{{.Container.ID}}-kafka'` — Container.ID is a supported template field
`--hostname '{{.Replica.Number}}-kafka'` — Replica.Number is the slot index
Bake a unique hostname into the image with `RUN hostname kafka-$RANDOM` — each task gets its own value
`--hostname '{{.Task.Slot}}-kafka'` — Swarm evaluates Go templates per task; supported fields include `.Service.Name`, `.Task.Slot`, `.Task.ID`, and `.Node.Hostname`
explain: Swarm templates `--hostname` (and `--mount`, etc.) per task. `.Task.Slot` gives the stable 1..N index. EXAM TRAPS: (A)/(B) `Container.ID` and `Replica.Number` are not template fields. (C) image-baked values are identical in every task — the template is evaluated per task at scheduling time.

q: A 3-node Galera cluster runs as a Swarm service. With the default endpoint mode, each node resolves the service name to the same virtual IP, so gossip/membership traffic hairpins through the load balancer and the cluster never forms. What fixes service discovery for this workload?
options: Publish the Galera port with `--publish mode=host` — host mode disables the VIP

Recreate the service with `--endpoint-mode dnsrr` — DNS round-robin makes the service name resolve to the individual task IPs (also reachable as `tasks.<service>`), so members gossip directly with each other
Add two more replicas — Galera quorum needs 5 nodes
Switch the service to `--mode global` — global mode implies DNS round-robin
explain: The default VIP mode load-balances through one virtual IP — fatal for gossip protocols that need each member's real address. `dnsrr` returns the task IPs via DNS. EXAM TRAPS: (A) publish mode affects ingress, not internal discovery. (C) more replicas don't change endpoint mode. (D) global and dnsrr are independent settings.

q: An API container deadlocks: the process stays up, so Swarm reports the task `Running`, but every request times out and the VIP keeps routing traffic to it. Restarts are manual. Which mechanism makes Swarm detect and replace the wedged task automatically?
options: Define a `HEALTHCHECK` (or `--health-cmd`) that exercises the real request path — Swarm marks repeatedly-unhealthy tasks for shutdown and reschedules replacements
`--restart-condition any` — it restarts tasks whose health checks fail
`--update-delay 30s` — delayed updates give deadlocks time to clear
Health status is cosmetic in Swarm — run an external monitor that calls the Docker API
explain: Swarm watches health status: a task that stays unhealthy is shut down and replaced, restoring the desired state. EXAM TRAPS: (B) restart-condition governs container EXITS, not health state — a deadlocked process never exits. (C) update-delay paces rollouts. (D) is false — health-driven replacement is built in.

q: A bad deploy is rolling back too slowly: `--update-delay 60s --update-parallelism 1` makes the rollback take an hour. The team runs `docker service update --rollback web` but the rollback inherits the same sluggish pacing. How do they roll back faster?
options: Rollbacks always reuse the update config — the only fix is redeploying with a new image tag
`docker service rollback web` — the dedicated rollback command accepts `--fast`
`docker service update --rollback --rollback-parallelism 5 --rollback-delay 10s web` — rollback behavior defaults to the update config but can be overridden with `--rollback-*` flags
Delete and recreate the service — a rollback can never be faster than the original update
explain: `--rollback-delay`, `--rollback-parallelism`, `--rollback-order`, `--rollback-failure-action`, etc. override the update config for the rollback operation. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the misconception the question exploits — the override flags exist precisely for this. (B) `docker service rollback` is not a command; it's `service update --rollback`. (D) recreation loses service identity, VIP, and history.

q: The compose file for stack `shop` no longer defines the `worker` service, but after `docker stack deploy -c shop.yml shop`, `docker stack services shop` still lists `worker` running the old image. Why, and what removes it?
options: The compose file is cached — redeploy with `docker stack deploy --refresh -c shop.yml shop`
`stack deploy` never removes services — `docker stack rm shop` plus a full redeploy is the only way
The worker tasks are wedged — drain every node with `docker node update --availability drain`
By default `stack deploy` only adds/updates; it never deletes services missing from the file. Redeploy with `docker stack deploy --prune -c shop.yml shop` (or `docker service rm shop_worker`)
explain: Stack deploy is additive by default — a safety choice so a truncated file can't nuke the stack. `--prune` reconciles: services in the swarm but absent from the file are removed. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--refresh` is invented. (B) rm+redeploy works but causes a full outage — unnecessary. (C) the tasks aren't wedged; they're simply not managed anymore.

q: A contractor was given the Swarm worker join token and their engagement ends today. The token may have been pasted into a shared chat. Existing workers must keep running undisturbed. What invalidates the leaked token?
options: `docker swarm leave` on every worker, then rejoin them with a fresh token
`docker swarm join-token --rotate worker` — rotation issues a new worker token and invalidates the old one; already-joined nodes are unaffected
Rotate the manager token — worker tokens derive from it and expire automatically
Tokens cannot be rotated — the only option is rebuilding the swarm
explain: `--rotate` generates a new join token for that role and revokes the old one; cluster membership is unaffected since tokens are only checked at join time. EXAM TRAPS: (A) churning every worker is unnecessary. (C) manager and worker tokens are independent. (D) rotation is a single command.

q: A service uses `--constraint 'node.labels.gpu==true'`. The admin added the label via `"labels": ["gpu=true"]` in the node's `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and restarted the daemon, but tasks never schedule — `docker node inspect` shows no `gpu` label under `Spec.Labels`. What is the mismatch?
options: Daemon.json `labels` are *engine* labels (matched by `engine.labels.gpu`), not node labels. Node labels live in the swarm spec — set them with `docker node update --label-add gpu=true <node>` — the `node.labels.gpu==true` constraint matches those
Labels in daemon.json need a `com.docker.` prefix to be visible to the scheduler
Constraints only match engine labels — `node.labels` constraints were removed in recent versions
The daemon must be reloaded with `kill -SIGHUP` for constraint labels to register
explain: Two different label stores: daemon.json `labels` → `engine.labels.*` (per-engine config); `docker node update --label-add` → `node.labels.*` (swarm spec, visible in `docker node inspect`). The constraint referenced the wrong store. EXAM TRAPS: (B) no prefix requirement exists. (C) `node.labels` constraints are fully supported. (D) SIGHUP reloads some daemon options, but it can't move a label between stores.

q: An engineer debugs a 12-task service by `docker exec`-ing into one task's container and tailing its log file. They miss errors occurring on the other 11 tasks. What is the Swarm-native way to see the aggregated stream?
options: `docker service ps --logs web` — ps gained a logs flag
SSH to each node and run `docker logs` per container — Swarm has no log aggregation
`docker service logs --since 15m --tail 100 web` — streams the combined logs of all tasks in the service, with `--since`/`--tail`/`--follow` supported
`docker logs` only works on standalone containers — install a logging plugin first
explain: `docker service logs` aggregates every task's stdout/stderr in one stream. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `service ps` has no `--logs`. (B) manual SSH scales terribly and misses rescheduled tasks. (D) `docker logs` works on any container; service logs is built in, no plugin needed.

q: A monitoring agent must run on every node EXCEPT the two GPU workers (which carry the node label `gpu=true`). The team creates it with `--mode global`. What keeps the agent off the GPU nodes?
options: Nothing — global mode ignores all placement constraints by design
Use `--replicas <node-count-minus-2>` instead of global mode — replica counts are the only way to skip nodes
Run `kubectl taint` on the GPU nodes — Swarm honors Kubernetes taints
Add `--constraint 'node.labels.gpu != true'` — placement constraints apply to global services too: one task lands on every node satisfying the constraint
explain: Constraints filter the candidate set for ANY mode, including global — the scheduler places one task per node that passes the constraint. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the core misconception. (B) replica math breaks the moment nodes change. (C) `kubectl taint` is Kubernetes — cross-tool confusion.

q: An admin tries `docker node demote` on the last remaining manager to make the cluster 'worker-only'. The command is refused. A teammate suggests `docker swarm leave --force` on that manager instead. What is the actual outcome of each?
options: Both work — demote is only refused while other managers exist

Demote is refused because a swarm cannot have zero managers (Raft needs at least one). `swarm leave --force` on the last manager destroys the swarm — services keep running on workers but are no longer orchestrated
`docker node demote` on the last manager converts it to a worker and the swarm keeps working manager-less
The cluster auto-promotes a worker to replace it, so either command is safe
explain: Swarm forbids demoting the final manager — zero managers means no Raft, no scheduler. Force-leaving it dissolves the swarm entirely (containers keep running, orchestration ends). EXAM TRAPS: (A) inverts the rule. (C) a manager-less swarm cannot exist. (D) Swarm never auto-promotes workers.

q: CI runs `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --load -t app:ci .` and fails with an error about `--load` with multiple platforms. The team needs both architectures in the registry. What is the correct fix?
options: Push instead of load: `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push -t registry/app:ci .` — `--load` can only import a single-platform image into the local image store; `--push` writes the multi-arch manifest list to the registry
Add `--multi-load` — the flag that enables multi-platform loads
Switch to plain `docker build` — the classic builder handles multi-platform natively
Use `--output type=docker` with both platforms — the docker output type supports manifest lists
explain: `--load` moves the result into the local (single-platform) image store, so it rejects multi-platform builds. `--push` stores the manifest list in the registry. EXAM TRAPS: (B) `--multi-load` is invented. (C) classic `docker build` is single-platform. (D) `type=docker` output is also single-platform-only.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Python image reinstalls 400MB of pip packages on every build because `requirements.txt` changes often, defeating layer caching. The team wants the download cache to persist across builds without landing in the final image. Which Dockerfile instruction does this?
options: `VOLUME /root/.cache/pip` — volumes persist across builds
`RUN --mount=type=bind,source=/root/.cache,target=/root/.cache pip install ...` — bind mounts share the host cache
`RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install ...` — a BuildKit cache mount persists the directory across builds but never becomes an image layer
`COPY --cache /root/.cache /root/.cache` before the pip install
explain: `type=cache` mounts are BuildKit-managed persistent caches: shared across builds, scoped (shared/private/locked), never committed to layers. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `VOLUME` is runtime-only; builds have no volumes. (B) build bind mounts can't reach arbitrary host paths — that's the security boundary cache mounts replace. (D) `COPY --cache` is invented.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Go build needs a private SSH key to fetch internal modules. The current Dockerfile has `COPY id_rsa /root/.ssh/` — the key ends up in an image layer, visible to anyone who pulls the image. What is the safe pattern?
options: Pass it as `ARG SSH_KEY` — build args are never stored in the image
Use a multi-stage build and `COPY` the key only in the builder stage — earlier stages are discarded from the final image
Add `id_rsa` to `.dockerignore` — then the COPY silently skips it and the build still works
`RUN --mount=type=ssh go mod download` with `docker buildx build --ssh default .` — the SSH agent socket is available only for that RUN step and never lands in any layer
explain: `type=ssh` forwards the SSH agent into the build step without persisting anything — nothing to leak. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `ARG` defaults appear in `docker history`, and the value is one `ENV` away from the image config. (B) the key still sits in the builder stage's layers in the build cache. (C) `.dockerignore` would break the COPY — and ignoring doesn't help a file you actually need.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A corporate pull-through mirror is configured via `registry-mirrors` in daemon.json. Pulls of `nginx` fly, but pulls of `ghcr.io/org/app:2.0` still go direct to the internet and get blocked by the firewall. Why doesn't the mirror handle them?
options: The mirror needs `docker login` credentials before it proxies anything
`registry-mirrors` only applies to Docker Hub (`docker.io`). Pulls from other registries like `ghcr.io` bypass the mirror configuration entirely
Mirrors only cache images already pulled once — `ghcr.io` images need `--pull always` first
The daemon must be restarted with `--registry-mirror-fallback=false`
explain: `registry-mirrors` is strictly a Docker Hub mirror setting; the daemon tries the mirror first and falls back to Hub. Other registries are contacted directly — they need their own mirror/proxy setup. EXAM TRAPS: (A) mirrors work anonymously for pulls. (C) pull-through mirrors fetch on demand. (D) no such flag exists.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An engineer leaves the team. They were added as a delegated signer on `registry/org/app` via `docker trust signer add`. Deleting their key file from the CI server doesn't revoke their ability to sign — the delegation lives in Notary. What actually removes their signing rights?
options: `docker trust signer remove <name> registry/org/app` — removes the signer from the repository's delegation, so their signatures are no longer trusted
`docker trust revoke registry/org/app:1.4` — revokes the signer's key
Delete the `~/.docker/trust` directory on the CI server
Run `docker notary key rotate` — rotation automatically drops old signers
explain: Delegations are server-side: `signer add/remove` manages who may sign for the repo. EXAM TRAPS: (B) `trust revoke` removes trust data for a TAG, not a signer. (C) local key deletion doesn't touch the Notary server's delegation. (D) rotation replaces keys; it doesn't prune the delegation list.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Production runs `app:1.2`. Upstream rebuilt `1.2` with different code (same tag, new digest) and the next redeploy pulled the changed bits, causing an incident. How does the team make the reference immutable?
options: Switch to `app:latest` — latest is content-addressed
Set `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` in the compose file
Pin the digest: `app@sha256:<digest>` — tags are mutable pointers, digests are immutable content addresses
Enable Docker Content Trust — it pins tags to digests automatically
explain: A digest reference can only ever resolve to those exact bytes; a tag can be repointed at any time. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `latest` is the MOST mutable tag. (B) `imagePullPolicy` is Kubernetes, and it doesn't freeze tag contents anyway. (D) Content Trust verifies signatures — it doesn't rewrite your reference into a digest.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A site has no internet and no registry. The team needs three images (`app:2.0`, `db:5.7`, `proxy:1.1`) moved from the build network to the isolated site via USB. Which workflow preserves tags and layer sharing?
options: `docker export` each container — exports include image tags and history
Copy `/var/lib/docker` to the USB drive — the directory is portable across hosts
`docker push` to a `file://` URL — the registry client supports file URLs
`docker save -o bundle.tar app:2.0 db:5.7 proxy:1.1`, carry the tarball, then `docker load -i bundle.tar` — save preserves all tags, history, and shared layers in one archive
explain: `save` serializes images (tags, history, shared layers deduplicated) to a tarball; `load` restores them. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `export` is for CONTAINERS — flat filesystem, no tags/history. (B) `/var/lib/docker` is driver- and host-specific, never portable. (C) no `file://` push exists.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile contains `ARG NPM_TOKEN` followed by `ENV NPM_TOKEN=$NPM_TOKEN`. A security review flags that anyone who pulls the image can recover the token. The developer objects: 'build args aren't stored in the image.' Who is right?
options: The developer — `ARG` values never appear in `docker history` or `docker inspect`

The reviewer — the `ARG` line itself may be safe, but `ENV` bakes the value into the image config, visible via `docker inspect` (and `docker history` shows the ENV assignment). Use `RUN --mount=type=secret` so the token never lands in any layer
Both wrong — tokens in Dockerfiles are encrypted at rest by BuildKit
The reviewer is right, but the fix is `.dockerignore` — it excludes secrets from layers
explain: `ENV` persists in the image config — `inspect` shows it, `history` shows the assignment, and every derived image inherits it. `ARG`-only values passed via `--build-arg` don't persist, but the moment they're copied to `ENV` they're baked in. EXAM TRAPS: (A) confuses ARG-with---build-arg safety with the ENV copy. (C) BuildKit encrypts nothing in the final image. (D) `.dockerignore` only filters the build CONTEXT, not Dockerfile instructions.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile has `ADD release.tar.gz /opt/`. The engineer expected `/opt/release.tar.gz` as a single file, but the build explodes the archive into `/opt/` and the app can't find the tarball. What is the minimal fix, and why did this happen?
options: `ADD --no-extract release.tar.gz /opt/` — the flag disables extraction
Rename the file to `release.tgz` — only the `.tar.gz` extension auto-extracts
Use `COPY release.tar.gz /opt/` — `ADD` auto-extracts local tar archives into the destination, `COPY` never does
Extract it in a previous build stage — `ADD` cannot handle archives at all
explain: `ADD` has two magic behaviors `COPY` lacks: auto-extracting local tarballs and fetching remote URLs. When you want the archive as a file, `COPY` is the precise tool. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--no-extract` is invented. (B) the extension doesn't matter — any recognized tar auto-extracts. (D) `ADD` handles archives fine; the complaint is about WHERE it put the files.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An image is 2.4GB. The Dockerfile downloads a 900MB SDK, builds the app, then a later `RUN rm -rf /sdk` 'cleans up' — but the image stays 2.4GB. Why didn't the cleanup shrink the image, and what fixes it?
options: `rm` doesn't work inside builds — use `docker image prune` after the build
Enable the experimental `--squash` flag — squashing is the only way to remove files from layers
The SDK is still referenced by the build cache — run `docker builder prune`

Each `RUN` is a separate layer; deleting files in a later layer only whiteouts them — the bytes remain in the earlier layer. Chain download, build, and cleanup in a single `RUN` so the SDK never lands in a committed layer
explain: Layers are additive: a delete in layer N+1 hides but never removes layer N's bytes. The fix is one `RUN` that downloads, builds, and cleans up before the layer commits. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `rm` works fine — it's the layering that defeats it. (B) `--squash` is experimental and a blunt instrument for a Dockerfile bug. (C) builder prune cleans the CACHE, not the image.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Users report the app crashes on ARM servers but works on x86. The tag is `app:2.0`. Before rebuilding, how does the engineer verify which architectures the published manifest actually covers?
options: `docker buildx imagetools inspect app:2.0` — lists the manifest's platforms (e.g. `linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`) without pulling anything
`docker inspect app:2.0` — shows every architecture in the remote manifest
`docker history app:2.0` — history includes the architecture matrix
Pull it on an ARM host — there is no way to inspect a remote manifest
explain: `imagetools inspect` queries the registry and prints the manifest list with platforms/digests. EXAM TRAPS: (B) `docker inspect` describes the LOCAL image only. (C) history shows layer commands, not platforms. (D) is the defeatist trap — remote inspection is exactly what imagetools is for.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Pulls from the on-prem registry `registry.corp:5000` fail with `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` (self-signed corporate CA). The quick hack — `insecure-registries` — was rejected by security since it disables TLS verification. What is the proper fix?
options: `docker pull --insecure registry.corp:5000/app` — per-pull insecurity
Install the corporate CA certificate into the Docker certs directory (`/etc/docker/certs.d/registry.corp:5000/ca.crt`) on every engine — TLS stays fully verified, just against the corporate CA
`docker login --tls-skip-verify registry.corp:5000`
Disable TLS on the registry and use plain HTTP — internal networks don't need TLS
explain: `certs.d/<host>:<port>/ca.crt` is the documented trust anchor for registries with private CAs — verification stays on. EXAM TRAPS: (A)/(C) both flags are invented. (D) plain HTTP exposes credentials and image content; `insecure-registries` exists for lab use, not production.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: The registry volume grows every week even though old tags are deleted via the API. `df` shows no relief. What reclaims the orphaned blobs, and what state must the registry be in?
options: `docker system prune` on the registry host — it cleans registry blobs
Deleting a tag deletes its blobs immediately — the disk growth must be logs, not blobs

Run `registry garbage-collect /etc/docker/registry/config.yml` — tag deletion only removes manifests; unreferenced blobs are reclaimed by garbage collection, which must run with the registry in read-only mode (or stopped)
Restart the registry container — startup runs garbage collection automatically
explain: The registry is content-addressed: deleting a tag removes the manifest pointer, but blobs are shared and only freed by GC. GC must not race with pushes, hence read-only/stopped. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `system prune` is client-side. (B) is the misconception the question exploits. (D) restarts run no GC.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI overwrote the `prod-stable` tag with a broken build and production auto-deployed it. The team wants `prod-*` tags to reject overwrites at the registry. Where is this enforced?
options: In the Dockerfile — `LABEL immutable=true` makes the tag immutable
With `docker tag --lock prod-stable` — tags support a lock flag
With Docker Content Trust — signed tags cannot be overwritten
In MSR repository settings — the immutable-tags policy rejects pushes to a tag that already exists, so promotion workflows must mint new tags
explain: MSR's immutable tag rules evaluate at push time: an existing tag can't be repointed. EXAM TRAPS: (A) labels describe images; they enforce nothing. (B) `--lock` is invented. (C) Content Trust verifies WHO signed, not whether the tag moved — a validly-signed overwrite still overwrites.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: After `docker rmi app:old`, `docker system df` shows no space reclaimed. `docker images` still lists `app:current` with the SAME image ID. Why?
options: `rmi` removed only the `app:old` tag — the layers are still referenced by `app:current` (same image ID), so nothing is deleted until the last tag (and any containers) referencing the image are gone
`docker rmi` never deletes layers — only `docker system prune` does
The image is still in the build cache, which `rmi` cannot touch
You must pass `--force` for any space to be reclaimed
explain: `rmi` untags first and deletes only when the reference count hits zero — same image ID under two tags means one `rmi` just drops a name. EXAM TRAPS: (B) `rmi` absolutely deletes unreferenced images. (C) build cache is separate from the image store. (D) `--force` is for containers-using-the-image, not for space.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A developer runs `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push` on the default builder and gets an error that the `docker` driver doesn't support multi-platform builds. What's the fix?
options: Add `--load` — loading enables multi-platform on the docker driver

Create a `docker-container` driver builder (`docker buildx create --driver docker-container --use`) — it runs the build inside a BuildKit container with full multi-platform support (plus QEMU for cross-architecture emulation)
Install QEMU — emulation alone unlocks multi-platform on the docker driver
Set `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0` — the classic builder handles manifest lists
explain: The default `docker` driver builds in-process and is single-platform; the `docker-container` driver runs real BuildKit with multi-platform support. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--load` is single-platform-only. (C) QEMU provides emulation but the driver still rejects the request. (D) the classic builder predates manifest lists.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Before pushing `app:2.0`, a developer wants a quick overview of its vulnerabilities and base-image recommendations — not a CI gate, just orientation. Which command fits?
options: `docker scan app:2.0` — the built-in vulnerability scanner
`docker scout cves --exit-code --only-severity critical app:2.0` — the exit-code mode is the quick overview
`docker scout quickview app:2.0` — summarizes the image's vulnerabilities and upgrade recommendations
`docker scout --deep app:2.0` — deep mode is the summary view
explain: `scout quickview` is the human-readable summary; `scout cves` is the detailed CVE list (with `--exit-code` for CI gates). EXAM TRAPS: (A) `docker scan` (the Snyk integration) was removed. (B) confuses the gating mode with the overview mode. (D) `--deep` is invented.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: During a routine Engine upgrade, every container on the host stops and restarts, causing a 4-minute outage. The team wants containers to keep running across daemon restarts and upgrades. Which daemon setting does this?
options: `--restart always` on every container — restart policies survive daemon upgrades without downtime
Run everything as Swarm services — the orchestrator restarts them instantly with no gap
Set `live-restore` to `false` — disabling live-restore keeps containers alive
Set `live-restore` to `true` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` — the new daemon process re-attaches to already-running containers instead of stopping them
explain: `live-restore: true` keeps containers running across daemon restarts/upgrades — the old daemon hands them off. EXAM TRAPS: (A) restart policies restart containers AFTER the daemon returns; the outage still happens. (B) Swarm reschedules fast but tasks still flap. (C) inverts the flag.

q: The team switches the daemon's default log driver to `gelf` to ship to Graylog. Immediately, `docker logs web` fails with 'configured logging driver does not support reading'. They still need `docker logs` for on-call debugging. What is the reality, and the fix?
options: Only `json-file`, `journald`, and `local` support `docker logs` reads — remote drivers (`gelf`, `syslog`, `fluentd`) are write-only from the engine's perspective. Revert the default to `json-file` (or `local`) and ship logs with a forwarder sidecar if centralization is needed
`docker logs --driver gelf web` — the driver flag selects the reader
Add a `read: true` key under `log-opts` in daemon.json
Logs are cached locally for 24 hours regardless of driver — just wait and retry
explain: Dual-mode logging isn't a thing: the engine either keeps local logs (json-file/journald/local → `docker logs` works) or streams them away (remote drivers → `docker logs` errors). EXAM TRAPS: (B) no such flag. (C) no such log-opt. (D) no local cache exists with remote drivers.

q: An admin needs to enable daemon debug logging on a production host without stopping containers. Restarting the daemon would cause an outage. Which approach applies the change without a restart?
options: All daemon.json changes require a full daemon restart — schedule a maintenance window
Set `debug` to `true` in daemon.json, then `kill -SIGHUP <dockerd-pid>` (or `systemctl reload docker`) — `debug` is one of the reloadable options; `storage-driver` and `data-root` are NOT
Edit daemon.json — the daemon watches the file and applies every key live
Pass `--debug` to the `docker logs` command — debug is a client-side flag
explain: SIGHUP/`systemctl reload` applies a documented subset (debug, labels, insecure-registries, etc.) without restart; structural options like storage-driver/data-root need a full restart. EXAM TRAPS: (A) overgeneralizes. (C) no file-watching exists. (D) confuses client and daemon flags.

q: `/var/lib/docker` has filled the root filesystem. The team has a fresh 500GB mount at `/data`. What is the safe migration procedure?
options: Set `data-root` to `/data/docker` and restart — the daemon migrates existing data automatically
Symlink `/var/lib/docker` to `/data/docker` while the daemon keeps running
Stop the daemon, `rsync -a /var/lib/docker/ /data/docker/`, set `data-root` to `/data/docker` in daemon.json, start the daemon — the engine never moves existing data for you
Run `docker system prune -a` — pruning permanently solves a full disk
explain: `data-root` only tells the daemon WHERE to look — it copies nothing. The safe move is stop → rsync → repoint → start. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the daemon starts EMPTY on the new path; old data is orphaned. (B) symlinking a live graph driver risks corruption. (D) pruning buys time but doesn't relocate storage.

q: Compliance requires that developers CANNOT run `docker exec` into production containers, while the platform team can. There is no engine-native RBAC in open-source Docker. What enforces this?
options: A seccomp profile — seccomp filters Docker API calls
MKE collections — they restrict `docker exec` on any engine
Remove developers from the `docker` group — group membership controls exec granularity
An authorization plugin (`--authorization-plugin=...` on the daemon) — AuthZ plugins intercept every API request and can allow/deny `POST /containers/.../exec` per policy
explain: AuthZ plugins are the engine's request-interception point: allow/deny per API endpoint and user. EXAM TRAPS: (A) seccomp filters SYSCALLS inside containers, not API calls. (B) MKE RBAC governs MKE-managed clusters, not raw engine API. (C) the `docker` group is all-or-nothing — membership equals root-equivalent.

q: An admin installs a v2 volume plugin on the manager with `docker plugin install rexray/ebs`. The command hangs waiting for input, and later tasks scheduled on workers fail with 'plugin not found'. What two things went wrong?
options: v2 plugins require privilege grants — pass `--grant-all-permissions` (or approve interactively); and plugins are node-local, so the plugin must be installed on EVERY node that will run the workload, not just the manager
Plugins install cluster-wide automatically — the hang means the plugin name is misspelled
Volume plugins only work with `docker run -v`, never with Swarm — use NFS mounts instead
The plugin needs `--privileged` on the daemon — grant flags are for containers, not plugins
explain: v2 plugins declare required privileges (network, mounts, devices) that must be granted at install; and a plugin lives on the node where it's installed — Swarm doesn't distribute it. EXAM TRAPS: (B) nothing propagates plugins. (C) volume plugins work fine in Swarm once installed per-node. (D) `--privileged` is a container flag, unrelated to plugin grants.

q: A legacy host still uses the `devicemapper` storage driver. The team wants `overlay2`. They flip `storage-driver` to `overlay2` and restart — all images and containers vanish from `docker images`/`docker ps`. What happened, and what was the correct migration?
options: `overlay2` deleted the data on first start — restore from backup; the flag flip itself was correct

Storage drivers are not convertible in place: each driver keeps its own directory tree. The old data still sits under the devicemapper directory but is invisible to `overlay2`. Correct path: push/save images and back up volumes FIRST, then switch the driver, then re-pull/restore
The daemon needs `--storage-opt dm.migrate=true` to convert the graph
`devicemapper` is the compiled-in default and cannot be changed on an existing host
explain: The graph driver reads only its own backend directory — switching drivers abandons the old tree (data intact on disk, unusable). Migration is backup → switch → restore. EXAM TRAPS: (A) nothing was deleted. (C) no migrate flag exists. (D) drivers are freely switchable; the cost is the data move.

q: An app in a container dies with 'too many open files' at ~1024 connections, though the host allows a million. What raises the container's limit?
options: Raise the host limit with `sysctl` — containers inherit the host's current value
`docker run --pids-limit 4096` — the pid limit also caps file descriptors
`docker run --ulimit nofile=65536:65536 ...` — container ulimits default conservatively (1024 soft) independent of the host's settings
`--privileged` — privileged containers get unlimited file descriptors
explain: Containers get Docker's default ulimits (nofile 1024:4096-ish), not the host's; `--ulimit` sets them per container (or `default-ulimits` daemon-wide). EXAM TRAPS: (A) host sysctl doesn't propagate into the container's ulimit. (B) pids-limit caps processes, not FDs. (D) privileged doesn't touch rlimits.

q: A container runs with `--memory 1g` and gets OOM-killed even though the host has free swap. The team wants the container to use NO swap at all (predictable tail latency). Which setting does that?
options: `--memory-swap -1` — negative one disables swap
`--oom-kill-disable` — the kernel will page to swap instead of killing
Remove `--memory` — without a memory limit, swap is never used
`--memory 1g --memory-swap 1g` — setting memory-swap EQUAL to memory means the combined RAM+swap ceiling equals the RAM limit, i.e. zero swap
explain: `--memory-swap` is the TOTAL (RAM+swap) allowance; equal to `--memory` leaves no room for swap. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `-1` means UNLIMITED swap. (B) disabling the OOM killer doesn't grant swap — the host OOMs instead. (C) an unlimited container can absolutely use swap.

q: Pulling `mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022` on a Windows Server 2019 Docker host fails to start the container. The same image runs on a 2022 host. What is the rule?
options: Windows containers share the host kernel — with process isolation the image's OS build must be less than or equal to the host's build. Use an `ltsc2019`-based image on the 2019 host (or `--isolation=hyperv`, which runs its own kernel)
Windows images are host-independent — the failure must be a corrupt pull; re-pull
Server 2019 requires the `ltsc2022` image — newer images are backward compatible with older hosts
Windows containers only run on Windows 11 — Server hosts are unsupported
explain: Process-isolated Windows containers share the host kernel, so image build ≤ host build. Hyper-V isolation virtualizes the kernel and relaxes the match. EXAM TRAPS: (B) ignores kernel sharing. (C) inverts the compatibility direction. (D) Server 2019/2022 both support Windows containers.

q: A runbook from 2019 says to install 'Docker UCP' using the `docker/ucp` image. On a fresh 2024 host the image doesn't exist and the install fails. What happened?
options: UCP was removed from Docker Enterprise — orchestration is Swarm-only now
UCP was renamed to MKE (Mirantis Kubernetes Engine) and DTR to MSR — install the MKE/MSR images instead; `docker/ucp` references are pre-rename and stale
The image moved to `docker.io/library/ucp` — same name, new namespace
UCP install now requires a Kubernetes cluster first — bootstrap Kubernetes, then install UCP
explain: Mirantis renamed Universal Control Plane → MKE and Docker Trusted Registry → MSR. Old runbooks referencing `docker/ucp` / `docker/dtr` are outdated. EXAM TRAPS: (A) MKE absolutely still exists. (C) no such namespace move. (D) MKE installs onto a Swarm cluster it manages — no pre-existing Kubernetes needed.

q: `docker system df` shows 14GB reclaimable under 'Build Cache' but only 200MB under Images. `docker system prune -a` is considered too destructive (it would remove unused images the team wants to keep). What reclaims just the build cache?
options: `docker image prune -a` — it includes the build cache
`docker volume prune` — build cache is stored as volumes
`docker builder prune` — prunes only the BuildKit build cache, leaving images, containers, networks, and volumes alone
Build cache cannot be pruned independently — restart the daemon to clear it
explain: `builder prune` is the scoped tool: `--filter` and `--keep-storage` give further control. EXAM TRAPS: (A) image prune touches images, not build cache. (B) build cache isn't volumes. (D) restarts don't clear it.

q: After Docker is installed, the host loses connectivity to the corporate VPN subnet `172.17.0.0/16` — the default docker0 bridge claims the same range. Containers are already running. What fixes the conflict?
options: Assign containers static IPs outside `172.17.0.0/16` with `--ip` on `docker run`
Change the VPN subnet — Docker's bridge range is fixed and cannot move
Run `docker network prune` — it releases the conflicting subnet
Set `bip` to `10.200.0.1/24` (with a matching `fixed-cidr`) in daemon.json and restart the daemon — `bip` defines docker0's bridge address, moving it off the conflicting range
explain: `bip` (bridge IP) re-addresses docker0; `fixed-cidr` bounds container IPs within it. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--ip` needs a user-defined network with a matching subnet — and doesn't move docker0. (B) Docker's range is fully configurable. (C) prune deletes unused networks; it doesn't re-address docker0.

q: On a Rootless Docker host, `docker run -p 80:80 nginx` fails with 'permission denied' binding port 80, but `-p 8080:80` works. Why?
options: Rootless daemons run as an unprivileged user, which cannot bind ports below 1024 — serve on a high port (or lower `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start`)
Rootless Docker doesn't support port publishing at all — the 8080 case only worked by accident
Port 80 is reserved by the rootless network namespace — use `--network host` instead
The container needs `--privileged` to bind low ports
explain: Binding <1024 requires `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, which the unprivileged user lacks — a kernel rule, not a Docker bug. EXAM TRAPS: (B) publishing works fine above 1024. (C) `--network host` is disallowed in rootless mode. (D) `--privileged` grants container capabilities, not host bind rights for an unprivileged user.

q: MSR runs 3 replicas, but pushes sometimes 404 on pull from another replica — each replica stores images on its own local disk. What makes MSR storage consistent across replicas?
options: Enable Raft replication for the MSR backend — replicas sync image data automatically
Configure a shared storage backend (NFS, S3, or another supported object store) in the MSR admin settings so all replicas read and write the same image store
Run `rsync` on a cron between the replica data directories
MSR replicas share storage by default — the 404s must be a load-balancer issue
explain: MSR replicas are stateless only when the image store is shared — local-disk storage is per-replica by default. EXAM TRAPS: (A) Raft replicates MSR's metadata DB, not blob storage. (C) rsync between live registry backends corrupts. (D) is the misconception causing the incident.

q: The engine cannot pull through the corporate HTTP proxy — `docker pull` times out, though `curl` works (the shell has `http_proxy` set). Why doesn't the daemon see the proxy, and where is it configured?
options: The daemon reads the shell's `http_proxy` — just `export` it before starting dockerd
Set an `http-proxy` key in daemon.json — the engine reads proxy config from there

The daemon doesn't inherit shell environment variables under systemd — configure a systemd drop-in (`/etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/http-proxy.conf` with `Environment=HTTP_PROXY=...`), then `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart docker`
Pass `--proxy` on every `docker pull`
explain: Under systemd the daemon's environment comes from unit files, not your shell — hence the drop-in. EXAM TRAPS: (A) works only if you launch dockerd by hand from that shell. (B) daemon.json has no proxy keys. (D) `--proxy` is invented.

q: ML engineers run `docker run --gpus all ...` and get `unknown or invalid runtime name: nvidia`. The hosts have NVIDIA drivers and GPUs. What's missing?
options: The NVIDIA container runtime isn't registered with the daemon — install the `nvidia-container-toolkit` (which registers the `nvidia` runtime under daemon.json `runtimes`) and restart the daemon; `--gpus` maps to that runtime
`--privileged` — GPU access requires privileged mode
GPUs are only available to Swarm services, not `docker run`
Pass `--device /dev/nvidia0` instead — `--gpus` is deprecated
explain: `--gpus` is a frontend for a registered runtime; without the toolkit's `runtimes` entry the name doesn't resolve. EXAM TRAPS: (B) privileged doesn't create a runtime.
