(C) `--gpus` works fine on single engines. (D) `--gpus` is current; `--device` is the manual partial workaround, not the fix.

q: Compliance mandates encryption of container-to-container traffic on Swarm overlay networks. An engineer points out Swarm already uses mutual TLS and declares the requirement met. The auditor disagrees. Who's right, and what actually encrypts the data plane?
options: The engineer — mutual TLS encrypts all overlay traffic, control and data

The auditor — mutual TLS only protects the control plane (Raft, gossip). Application traffic on overlays is VXLAN-encapsulated but NOT encrypted unless the network is created with `--opt encrypted` (IPsec/AES-GCM); encryption can't be added to an existing network — it must be recreated
Both wrong — overlay encryption needs `--opt secure=true` at swarm init
The auditor is right, but the fix is `--publish mode=encrypted` on each service
explain: Swarm has two planes: control (always mTLS) and data (VXLAN, plaintext by default). `--opt encrypted` enables IPsec ESP for the data path at network CREATE time. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the exact misconception. (C) `--opt secure` is invented. (D) publish mode has no `encrypted` value.

q: Containers on overlay networks can't reach the corporate subnet `172.18.0.0/16` — return traffic dies. `ip route` shows `docker_gwbridge` owns `172.18.0.0/16` (its default). The swarm is already initialized. What changes the gwbridge subnet?
options: Edit `bip` in daemon.json — `bip` controls docker_gwbridge
`docker network update --subnet 10.99.0.0/16 docker_gwbridge`

Remove and recreate it: `docker network rm docker_gwbridge`, then create it again with `--subnet 10.99.0.0/16` and the `com.docker.network.bridge.name=docker_gwbridge` option (alternatively, set `default-address-pools` in daemon.json BEFORE the host joins the swarm)
gwbridge subnets are fixed at swarm init and can never be changed
explain: `docker_gwbridge` is a plain bridge network that can be removed and recreated with a chosen subnet (do it when no overlay traffic is flowing). EXAM TRAPS: (A) `bip` addresses docker0, not gwbridge. (B) no `network update --subnet` exists. (D) is false — recreation is documented.

q: A macvlan network works with `docker run` on each host, but `docker service create --network macvlan-net` fails — Swarm doesn't recognize the node-local network. What's the supported pattern for macvlan in Swarm?
options: macvlan is unsupported in Swarm — use host-mode publishing instead
Create the macvlan network with `--scope swarm` directly — scope is the only missing piece
Enable promiscuous mode on the swarm managers — that propagates the network definition

Create an identical `--config-only` macvlan network on every node, then create one `--scope swarm` network with `--config-from` referencing it — services attach to the swarm-scoped network while each node applies its local macvlan config (parent interface, VLAN)
explain: Swarm-scoped networks can't carry node-specific options (parent interfaces differ per host), so the config-only + config-from pattern separates local config from swarm scope. EXAM TRAPS: (A) macvlan works in Swarm via this pattern. (B) `--scope swarm` alone still needs the per-node config. (C) promiscuous mode is a NIC requirement for macvlan traffic, not a propagation mechanism.

q: Security forbids promiscuous mode on host NICs, which rules out macvlan, but containers need directly-routable corporate IPs (no NAT, no encapsulation). Which driver and mode fits?
options: ipvlan `l3` mode (`-o ipvlan_mode=l3`) — containers share the parent's MAC, the host routes their subnets, no promiscuous mode needed, and container IPs are directly routable
macvlan with `-o macvlan_mode=bridge` — bridge mode doesn't need promiscuous mode
Overlay with `--opt encrypted` — encryption replaces the need for routability
ipvlan `l2` mode — L2 is the routed mode
explain: ipvlan L3 makes the host act as a router for container subnets with a single MAC — no promiscuous mode, no bridge learning. EXAM TRAPS: (B) macvlan ALWAYS needs promiscuous mode (distinct MACs per container). (C) encryption and routability are unrelated. (D) inverts the modes — L2 is switched, L3 is routed.

q: Behind the routing mesh, the app's audit log shows every client's IP as a Swarm node IP — the mesh SNATs ingress traffic. The team needs true client IPs AND must keep Swarm scheduling. What publishing change preserves the source IP?
options: `--publish mode=ingress` — ingress mode preserves the source IP

`--publish mode=host,target=80` — host mode bypasses the routing mesh and binds the port directly on the nodes running the task, preserving the client source IP (trade-off: the port is only bound where tasks run, no mesh-wide balancing on that port)
`--network host` on the service — host networking preserves IPs for services
Add an external load balancer in front — it restores the original client IP
explain: Ingress mode goes through IPVS + SNAT (node IP seen); host mode binds the published port on the task's node directly — no SNAT. EXAM TRAPS: (A) ingress is the mode CAUSING the SNAT. (C) Swarm services don't support `--network host`. (D) an external LB still sees the SNATed node IP.

q: A config-management agent needs the IP of EVERY task of service `db` (for rolling config pushes), not the VIP. `nslookup db` returns one virtual IP. What DNS name returns all task IPs?
options: `db.swarm` — the `.swarm` suffix lists task addresses
Query the VIP with `dig +short` — the VIP round-robins all task IPs
`tasks.db` — the embedded DNS serves A records for each task IP under `tasks.<service>`, and this works in both VIP and dnsrr endpoint modes
Task IPs aren't in DNS — scrape `docker service ps` and `docker inspect` each task
explain: `tasks.<service>` is the documented per-task DNS name on overlay networks, independent of endpoint mode. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `.swarm` suffix is invented. (B) the VIP is a single virtual IP — it never expands. (D) works but is fragile compared to DNS.

q: Two containers on the DEFAULT bridge can't resolve each other by name (`ping db` fails) though IPs work. The same setup works on a user-defined network. What's the difference?
options: The default bridge needs `--dns 8.8.8.8` on each container for name resolution
Container names only resolve with `--link` — the working setup must be using links
The default bridge resolves names only for the first 24 hours after creation
The default `bridge` network has no embedded DNS — automatic name resolution (via `127.0.0.11`) exists only on user-defined networks; on the default bridge you need legacy `--link` or IPs
explain: Embedded DNS is a user-defined-network feature; the legacy default bridge predates it. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--dns` sets UPSTREAM resolvers, it doesn't create name records. (B) inverts the history — links are the legacy workaround. (C) invented time limit.

q: The database tier must be reachable by the app tier but have NO route to the internet — not even DNS exfiltration via egress. Which network option enforces this?
options: `docker network create --internal db-net` — internal networks block all external connectivity while allowing inter-container traffic
Don't publish the DB ports — unpublished containers have no egress path
`-o com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false` — it blocks external access
Put the DB on the default bridge — it's isolated from the internet by default
explain: `--internal` drops the gateway route — containers talk to each other but can't leave the network. EXAM TRAPS: (B) publishing controls INGRESS; egress is unaffected. (C) `icc=false` blocks container-TO-container traffic — the opposite direction. (D) the default bridge has full egress via masquerading.

q: Two untrusted workloads share one bridge network (for IPAM reasons they can't be split), but compliance forbids any direct container-to-container traffic between them. External connectivity must keep working. What's the network-level control?
options: `--internal` on the network — it blocks container-to-container traffic
`docker network create -o com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false ...` — disables inter-container communication on the bridge while external connectivity remains
A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy — it applies to Docker bridge networks
Publish no ports — unpublished ports block east-west traffic
explain: `enable_icc=false` programs iptables to drop bridge-forwarded container-to-container packets; the gateway path (external) is untouched. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--internal` kills external too. (C) NetworkPolicy is Kubernetes-only. (D) publishing is about ingress, not east-west.

q: A Diameter signaling service needs SCTP on port 3868. The engineer assumes Swarm only does TCP/UDP and plans to bypass Docker networking with host networking. What is the Swarm-native option?
options: Swarm indeed supports only TCP/UDP — host networking is the only path for SCTP
`--publish mode=sctp` — sctp is a publish mode
`docker service create --publish published=3868,target=3868,protocol=sctp signaling` — Swarm overlay networks support SCTP port publishing; `protocol` accepts `tcp`, `udp`, or `sctp`
`--publish protocol=all` — publishes TCP, UDP, and SCTP at once
explain: SCTP support was added to Swarm overlay networking — the long `--publish` syntax takes `protocol=sctp` (short syntax: `-p 3868:3868/sctp`). EXAM TRAPS: (A) is outdated. (B) `mode` is `ingress`/`host`, not a protocol. (D) `protocol=all` is invented.

q: Containers need IPv6 addresses. An engineer adds `ipv6` set to `true` in daemon.json, restarts, and containers still get only IPv4. What's missing?
options: IPv6 requires Swarm mode — single engines can't assign IPv6
Pass `--ipv6` to `docker run` — it's a per-container flag
IPv6 works automatically once the daemon flag is set — the containers must be misconfigured
A fixed IPv6 subnet must also be assigned (`fixed-cidr-v6`, e.g. `fd00:db8::/64`); for user-defined networks, create them with `docker network create --ipv6 --subnet fd00:db8:1::/64`
explain: Enabling the flag without an address pool gives the daemon nowhere to allocate from. `fixed-cidr-v6` (daemon) or `--ipv6 --subnet` (per network) provides the range. EXAM TRAPS: (A) single engines do IPv6 fine. (B) no `--ipv6` run flag exists. (C) the flag alone allocates nothing.

q: An engineer 'fixes' slow DNS by overwriting a container's `/etc/resolv.conf` (which pointed at `127.0.0.11`) with the corporate nameserver. Immediately, `ping web` (a Swarm service name) fails while external names resolve. What broke?
options: `127.0.0.11` is Docker's embedded DNS server — it resolves service and container names on user-defined networks. Replacing it bypasses Docker's name resolution entirely. The right way to add upstreams is `--dns`, which the embedded server forwards to
`127.0.0.11` is a link-local bug — the engineer's fix was correct and `ping web` should work
Service names only resolve over TCP — the corporate DNS blocks TCP/53
The engineer should have used `--dns-search` instead of replacing resolv.conf
explain: The embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 answers for Docker names and forwards everything else to the daemon's configured upstreams. Overwriting resolv.conf removes Docker from the path. EXAM TRAPS: (B) 127.0.0.11 is by design. (C) invents a TCP requirement. (D) `--dns-search` sets search domains, it doesn't restore the resolver.

q: From INSIDE a container, `curl http://<host-ip>:8080` (the service's own published port) times out, but external clients reach it fine and `curl http://localhost:80` from inside works. What pattern should the team avoid?
options: The published port is broken — republish it with `mode=host`

Hairpin NAT: reaching your own published port via the host IP from inside the container is unreliable — connect via the service DNS name or the container port directly instead of looping through the host's published port
The container needs `--network host` to reach host IPs
It's a firewall issue — open 8080 in the host iptables
explain: Hairpinning (container → host IP:published → back into the container) isn't a supported path; DNAT rules don't cover it. Use the service name (VIP/dnsrr) or localhost:container-port. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the port works externally — nothing's broken. (C) host networking is a sledgehammer for a dialing mistake. (D) external clients prove the firewall is fine.

q: A log-shipper sidecar must scrape `localhost:9090` on the app container (the app only binds loopback). Two containers on the same bridge network can't reach each other's localhost. How do they share the loopback interface?
options: `--link app:localhost` — links share the loopback interface
Publish 9090 and scrape the host IP — equivalent to localhost
`docker run --network container:app shipper` — the shipper joins the app's network namespace, sharing its loopback, interfaces, and IPs
`--ipc shareable` on the app — ipc mode shares the network stack
explain: `--network container:<name>` puts both containers in one net namespace — localhost is literally shared. EXAM TRAPS: (A) links are legacy and never shared localhost. (B) host IP:published is a different path (and hairpin-prone). (D) `--ipc` shares memory/semaphores, not networking.

q: At scale, auto-created overlay networks keep grabbing `10.0.x.0/24` subnets that collide with the corporate WAN. The team wants all future Swarm-managed networks carved from `10.200.0.0/16` in `/24` chunks. Where is this set?
options: `docker swarm init --subnet 10.200.0.0/16` — init takes the pool
Per network with `--subnet` — there is no global default for this
It happens automatically — Docker avoids subnets already in use on the host
`default-address-pool` in daemon.json (e.g. `base` `10.200.0.0/16`, `size` 24) on every node before swarm init — the pool feeds automatic subnet allocation for new networks
explain: `default-address-pool` defines the bases Docker carves auto-allocated subnets from; it must be set consistently before the swarm is initialized. EXAM TRAPS: (A) no `--subnet` on init. (B) per-network `--subnet` works but doesn't change the DEFAULT. (C) Docker avoids host-local conflicts only, not WAN-wide ones.

q: The `ingress` network's auto-assigned subnet overlaps a new partner VPN. The team needs ingress on `10.99.0.0/24`. How?
options: `docker network rm ingress`, then `docker network create --ingress --subnet 10.99.0.0/24 ingress` — ingress is a regular overlay network that can be removed and recreated (do it when no published ports are in use)
`docker network update --subnet 10.99.0.0/24 ingress` — update changes the subnet in place
Leave and rejoin the swarm on every node — ingress regenerates with a fresh subnet
ingress subnets are immutable — rebuild the cluster
explain: The ingress network is special-purpose but not special-kind — remove and recreate it with the desired subnet. EXAM TRAPS: (B) no subnet update exists. (C) rejoining regenerates nothing about ingress. (D) is defeatist and wrong.

q: The corporate firewall already uses UDP 4789 for another VXLAN product, conflicting with Swarm's overlay data path. Swarm init succeeds but overlay traffic is blackholed. What avoids the conflict?
options: Change the ingress published ports — they use UDP 4789
`docker swarm init --data-path-port 5789` — the VXLAN data-path port (default UDP 4789) is configurable at init (and join) time
Enable `--opt encrypted` — encryption changes the VXLAN port
VXLAN ports are kernel-fixed and cannot change — move the other product
explain: `--data-path-port` exists precisely for VXLAN port conflicts; it must match on all nodes. EXAM TRAPS: (A) published ports are unrelated to the VXLAN underlay. (C) encryption wraps the payload; the UDP port stays 4789. (D) is false — configurability is documented.

q: An engineer attaches a config with `--config app.conf` and the app looks for it at `/run/secrets/app.conf` — not found. `docker exec` shows the file at `/app.conf`. Why?
options: Configs only attach with `--config-add` on update, not at create time
The config was never created — `docker config ls` would be empty
Unlike secrets (default `/run/secrets/<name>`), configs default to `/<config-name>` at the container's root — the app must read `/app.conf`, or the service must set an explicit `target=`
Configs are encrypted at rest and need a decrypt key to materialize in the container
explain: The number-one config/secret mix-up: different default mount paths. Secrets → `/run/secrets/<name>` (tmpfs); configs → `/<name>` (bind). EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--config` works at create. (B) the file EXISTS — at the wrong path. (D) configs are NOT encrypted at rest (that's the point of secrets).

q: The database password must rotate. The service was created with `--secret db_pass`. An engineer tries `docker secret update db_pass` — no such command. What is the correct rotation?
options: `docker exec` into each task and rewrite `/run/secrets/db_pass` — the tmpfs is writable by root
Delete and recreate the service — secrets are bound at create time forever
`docker service update --secret db_pass=newvalue` — the flag accepts inline values

`docker secret create db_pass_v2 -`, then `docker service update --secret-rm db_pass --secret-add source=db_pass_v2,target=db_pass svc` — secrets are immutable, so rotation means a new secret object plus a service update (tasks are recreated with the new mount); remove the old secret afterward
explain: Swarm secrets are immutable — there is deliberately no update path. Rotation = new object + `--secret-rm/--secret-add` in one update (the `target=` keeps the in-container path stable). EXAM TRAPS: (A) `/run/secrets` mounts are read-only tmpfs. (B) recreation works but is needlessly disruptive. (C) `--secret` takes no inline values.

q: Compliance: the TLS key secret must be readable ONLY by the app user (uid 1000), not world-readable. By default secrets mount `0444`. How is this tightened?
options: `--secret source=tls.key,target=tls.key,uid=1000,gid=1000,mode=0400` — per-secret uid/gid/mode are set at attach time (the writable bit is always ignored, the executable bit may be set)
`chmod 400 /run/secrets/tls.key` in the entrypoint — the mount is writable at startup
`chown 1000` the secret files under `/var/lib/docker` on each host — secrets are host files
Secrets can't restrict read access — use a config instead
explain: The long `--secret` syntax carries `uid=`, `gid=`, `mode=` — least privilege at mount time. EXAM TRAPS: (B) the mount is read-only; chmod fails. (C) secrets live in the Raft store, not host files. (D) configs are world-readable too — and unencrypted.

q: A deploy bot was granted `Full Control` on `/Production` 'to make CI work'. Security demands least privilege: the bot only creates, updates, and removes Swarm services. Which role, and how is it applied?
options: `View Only` — it allows deployments initiated by CI

Replace the grant with the `Scheduler` role on `/Production` — a grant binds a subject (user/team/service account) plus a role to a collection; `Scheduler` is the purpose-built deploy-services role, while `Full Control` is cluster-admin
Move the bot into the `admins` team but set the team to read-only
Roles are advisory in MKE — `Full Control` is the only role that can deploy
explain: MKE's default roles escalate None → View Only → Restricted Control → Scheduler → Full Control. `Scheduler` deploys/manages services without node/cluster admin. EXAM TRAPS: (A) View Only can't create anything. (C) combines two wrong ideas — admins team isn't read-only. (D) roles are enforced, not advisory.

q: CI deploys with a departed admin's personal MKE account. The account gets deactivated and every pipeline breaks at 2 AM. What's the durable pattern?
options: Share one admin account named `ci-admin` — shared accounts never get deactivated
Embed a client bundle in the repo — bundles don't expire
Create a dedicated MKE service account, grant it the `Scheduler` role on the target collection(s), and download its client bundle for CI — service accounts aren't tied to a human's employment status
Use LDAP authentication per pipeline run — interactive logins are the most secure option for CI
explain: Service accounts are non-human identities with their own client bundles — immune to offboarding. EXAM TRAPS: (A) shared admin credentials are an audit nightmare. (B) client bundles DO expire and embedding them in git leaks credentials. (D) per-run interactive LDAP breaks automation.

q: A container runs a legacy setuid-root binary. An attacker exploiting the app could use it to escalate to root inside the container. Which option neutralizes the setuid vector without rewriting the app?
options: `--cap-drop ALL` — dropping capabilities clears the setuid bit
`--read-only` — read-only filesystems ignore setuid bits
`--user 1000` — non-root users can't execute setuid binaries
`--security-opt no-new-privileges` — the kernel blocks privilege escalation via setuid/setgid binaries and file capabilities for the container's processes
explain: `no-new-privileges` is the precise control: exec'd binaries can't gain privileges beyond the calling process. EXAM TRAPS: (A) capability drops don't clear setuid bits. (B) read-only doesn't ignore setuid either. (C) non-root users CAN execute setuid binaries — that's exactly what makes them dangerous.

q: A monitoring agent needs the `mount` syscall, which Docker's default seccomp profile blocks. The team considers `--privileged`. What's the precise alternative?
options: A custom seccomp profile — `--security-opt seccomp=/etc/docker/agent-profile.json` allowing just the needed syscalls — keeps the default-deny posture for everything else
`--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` — it's equivalent to a custom profile
`--cap-add SYS_ADMIN` — capabilities override seccomp blocks
Switch to an AppArmor profile — AppArmor manages syscalls
explain: Seccomp is the syscall filter: a custom profile adds back only what's needed instead of removing all filtering. EXAM TRAPS: (B) `unconfined` disables the filter entirely — works but abandons the protection. (C) capabilities and seccomp are independent gates; both must allow. (D) inverts the LSM roles — AppArmor confines files/capabilities, seccomp filters syscalls.

q: A container bind-mounts a host directory. Files created by root INSIDE the container appear as root-owned on the host — a breakout could chown host files. The team can't run the app as non-root (it binds low ports). What maps container-root to an unprivileged host user?
options: `--user 0:0` — explicitly pinning root enables the UID mapping
`--userns-remap default` on the daemon — user namespaces map container UIDs (including root) to subordinate host UIDs from `/etc/subuid`/`/etc/subgid`, so container-root is unprivileged on the host
`userns_mode: host` in the compose file — it isolates UIDs in Swarm
An SELinux label (`--security-opt label=type:container_t`) — labels remap UIDs
explain: User-namespace remapping shifts the container's entire UID range (root → e.g. host uid 100000). EXAM TRAPS: (A) `--user 0:0` IS host root — the problem, not the fix. (C) `userns_mode: host` DISABLES remapping (and is Swarm-ignored anyway). (D) SELinux labels confine access; they don't remap UIDs.

q: A monitoring container mounts `-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro`. The team believes `:ro` makes it safe — 'read-only means it can't change anything.' What's the reality?
options: They're right — read-only socket mounts can only list containers
The `:ro` flag is silently ignored for sockets — it mounts read-write anyway

Read-only refers to the MOUNT, not the API — the daemon API has no read-only mode; anyone who can talk to the socket can start privileged containers and take the host. Never mount the socket into untrusted workloads; use a filtered API proxy instead
Sockets can't be mounted into containers at all — the command fails
explain: `:ro` stops the container from replacing the socket FILE; it does nothing to the API, which is full control by design (equivalent to root on the host). EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the dangerous misconception. (B) the flag applies, just irrelevantly. (D) socket mounts are common — that's the problem.

q: An engineer opens `~/.docker/config.json` and finds an `auth` value that decodes from base64 to `user:password`. They conclude the registry password is encrypted. A laptop theft later exposes it in seconds. What should have been configured?
options: Nothing — base64 IS encryption; the thief just got lucky
`chmod 600 config.json` — file permissions are the documented credential protection
`docker logout` after every pull — logout deletes the credential from the registry server
A credential helper (`credsStore`, e.g. `desktop`, `secretservice`, or `pass`) — helpers store passwords in the OS keychain/secret store instead of base64 in config.json
explain: base64 is ENCODING, not encryption — anyone can decode it. Credential helpers delegate to the OS keychain. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the core misconception. (B) permissions help but the secret is still recoverable. (C) `logout` only removes the local entry; the password was already exposed.

q: Compliance requires containers to run with an immutable root filesystem, but the app writes temp files to `/tmp` and a PID file to `/run`. How do both requirements hold?
options: `docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run app` — the root filesystem is read-only while tmpfs mounts provide writable scratch space that never persists
Read-only mode is incompatible with any writes — the requirement can't be met, request an exception
`-v /tmp` — an anonymous volume makes the whole filesystem writable again
Build the image with `chmod -R a-w /` — equivalent to `--read-only`
explain: `--read-only` + `--tmpfs` is the standard hardened pattern: immutable image layers, ephemeral writable scratch. EXAM TRAPS: (B) gives up too early — tmpfs is made for this. (C) a volume on /tmp doesn't make `/` writable; it just covers /tmp (and persists). (D) file permissions aren't a mount-level guarantee and break the app.

q: Security policy requires periodic CA rotation. An admin runs `docker swarm ca --rotate` on a manager. What actually happens to the cluster?
options: Every node must leave and rejoin — rotation immediately invalidates all node certificates
The old CA is replaced and node certificates are automatically reissued against the new CA — workloads are unaffected; existing certificates otherwise expire on their original schedule
Rotation only affects the Raft logs — TLS certificates are permanent and never rotate
The cluster must be recreated with `docker swarm init --force-new-cluster`
explain: Swarm manages its PKI: rotation swaps the CA and reissues node certs automatically — no rejoin, no workload impact. EXAM TRAPS: (A) describes a manual PKI, not Swarm's. (C) node certs DO expire/rotate (default 3-month validity). (D) force-new-cluster is for quorum loss, not rotation.

q: CI talks to a Docker daemon exposed on TCP `2375` (plain HTTP). Anyone on the network can now control the daemon — equivalent to root on the host. What's the correct way to expose the daemon API?
options: It's fine on a private network — the Docker API over HTTP is safe behind a firewall
Switch to port `2376` — the port number itself enables encryption

Serve the API with mutual TLS (`--tlsverify --tlscacert=ca.pem --tlscert=server.pem --tlskey=server-key.pem`, port 2376 by convention) with `DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1` on clients — never expose the unauthenticated API to a network
Put a password on `docker login` — that authenticates daemon API access
explain: The daemon API is root-equivalent; `--tlsverify` enforces mutual TLS so only holders of client certs can connect. EXAM TRAPS: (A) 'private network' is not authentication. (B) port numbers enable nothing. (D) `docker login` authenticates to REGISTRIES, not the daemon.

q: An attacker can't forge signatures but replays last month's signed `app:1.2` metadata, hiding a critical patch (freeze attack). Which part of Docker Content Trust / Notary defeats this?
options: The `root` role — root keys expire quickly, blocking replays
The `snapshot` role — it prevents mix-and-match of package versions
Digest pinning — clients always pull by digest, ignoring metadata
The `timestamp` role — timestamp metadata carries a short expiry, so clients reject stale/replayed repository metadata even when the signatures are valid
explain: TUF's roles split duties: timestamp = freshness (short-lived, defeats freeze/replay), snapshot = consistency, targets = integrity, root = trust anchor. EXAM TRAPS: (A) root is the long-lived trust anchor. (B) snapshot stops mix-and-match, not replays. (C) digest pinning helps deployments but the question asks about the Notary mechanism.

q: A vulnerability scanner flags that the app container runs as root. The Dockerfile ends with `CMD ['./app']`. What's the standard fix, and can operators still override it?
options: Add `RUN useradd -r appuser` and `USER appuser` before CMD — the process then runs unprivileged; operators can still override per-run with `docker run --user`
`chmod +s ./app` — setuid lets it run with non-root privileges safely
Root inside containers is harmless because of namespaces — suppress the finding
`--privileged=false` — that drops the container to a non-root user
explain: `USER` sets the runtime UID; `--user` overrides it per invocation. EXAM TRAPS: (B) setuid goes the WRONG direction (gains privilege). (C) user namespaces aren't on by default — container root is a real risk. (D) `--privileged` is about capabilities/devices, not the UID.

q: The team needs to confine which FILE PATHS a container can read (e.g. deny `/etc/shadow`), but the default `docker-default` AppArmor profile doesn't cover it. What's the workflow?
options: Switch to a seccomp profile — seccomp profiles filter file paths
Write a custom AppArmor profile, load it on the host with `apparmor_parser`, and run with `--security-opt apparmor=my-profile` — AppArmor is the path/capability LSM, seccomp is the syscall filter
`--cap-drop ALL` — capabilities control file path access
AppArmor profiles ship inside images — add the profile to the Dockerfile
explain: AppArmor confines file/network/capability access by path; profiles live on the HOST and are referenced by name. EXAM TRAPS: (A) inverts the LSM roles — seccomp filters syscalls, not paths. (C) capabilities gate privileged OPERATIONS, not path reads. (D) the kernel loads profiles from the host, not the image.

q: First deploy: `docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres`. The engineer expected an EMPTY volume, but the container's initialized DB files appear in `pgdata`. On the second run with a host bind mount instead, the directory stays empty and Postgres fails. What explains the difference?
options: Postgres behaves differently under bind mounts — it's an application quirk
Bind mounts populate from the image; named volumes never do
Docker populates a NEW named volume with the image's existing content at the mount point — bind mounts never populate (the host directory wins as-is, empty or not)
The volume was pre-created by another container with seed data
explain: Named-volume initialization copies the image's directory content into a fresh volume — one-time, at first mount. Bind mounts map the host path verbatim. EXAM TRAPS: (A) it's engine behavior, not Postgres. (B) inverts the rule. (D) invents a seeder.

q: A container mounts `-v /mnt/data:/data`. Later, an admin mounts a new disk at `/mnt/data/archive` ON THE HOST. The container never sees `/data/archive`. What mount option fixes visibility of subsequently-mounted host paths?
options: `--privileged` — privileged containers see all host mounts
Restart the container — mounts are evaluated once at start, then frozen
Mount with `:ro` — read-only mounts propagate submounts automatically
Bind propagation `rshared`: `-v /mnt/data:/data:rshared` (or `--mount type=bind,bind-propagation=rshared`) — makes the bind point share mount/unmount events with the host
explain: Bind propagation controls whether submounts propagate: `rshared` (both ways), `rslave` (host→container), `rprivate` (default, none). EXAM TRAPS: (A) privileged doesn't change propagation. (B) restarts don't help — the mount was private at creation. (C) `:ro` affects writability, not propagation.

q: A Swarm service needs a shared read-write filesystem across tasks on different nodes. A plain named volume is node-local — tasks on node B can't see node A's data. What's the portable recipe?
options: `docker volume create -d local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=10.0.0.5,rw --opt device=:/exports/app appdata` (same name on every node), then `--mount type=volume,src=appdata,dst=/data` — the local driver's NFS options mount the same export everywhere
Use a bind mount of the NFS path — binds are automatically shared across Swarm nodes
Named volumes replicate between nodes automatically in Swarm
Set `--replicas 1` — one task means no sharing problem
explain: The `local` driver accepts `type=`/`o=`/`device=` mount options — an NFS-backed volume with the same name on each node gives every task the same filesystem. EXAM TRAPS: (B) binds require the path on every host AND don't travel with the service. (C) named volumes never replicate. (D) dodges the requirement.

q: A Swarm service needs a 2GB writable scratch space that lives ONLY in RAM (never touches disk). What mount does this?
options: `-v scratch:/scratch` — named volumes are RAM-backed by default
`--mount type=tmpfs,dst=/scratch,tmpfs-size=2147483648` — tmpfs mounts are in-memory, per-task, and discarded when the task stops
`--tmpfs` isn't supported for services — use a config for scratch space
Set the storage driver to `tmpfs` in daemon.json
explain: `type=tmpfs` with `tmpfs-size` (bytes) and optional `tmpfs-mode` gives per-task RAM disks. EXAM TRAPS: (A) named volumes are disk-backed. (C) `--mount type=tmpfs` IS the service form (`--tmpfs` is the `docker run` shorthand). (D) no such storage driver.

q: The team needs a nightly backup of the `dbdata` named volume. What's the standard agentless pattern?
options: `docker volume export dbdata > backup.tar` — volumes have a native export
Copy `/var/lib/docker/volumes/dbdata/_data` while the DB runs — live copies are always consistent

`docker run --rm --volumes-from db -v /backups:/backup ubuntu tar czf /backup/dbdata.tar.gz -C /var/lib/postgresql/data .` — a throwaway container mounts the volume and archives it (stop the DB first, or use its native dump tool, for consistency)
`docker commit db` — the commit includes volume data
explain: `--volumes-from` + tar is the classic: any image with tar can archive any volume without touching daemon internals. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `volume export` doesn't exist. (B) live file copies of a running DB can be corrupt — and `_data` paths are driver internals. (D) `commit` EXCLUDES volume contents by design.

q: `docker compose up` creates anonymous volumes (from the image's `VOLUME` instructions). After `docker compose down`, `docker volume ls` still shows them, slowly filling the disk. What removes them with the stack?
options: `docker compose down` removes them automatically — they must be named volumes if they survived
`--rm` on `docker compose up` — it cleans volumes on exit
Anonymous volumes can't be removed once created — rebuild the images without `VOLUME` instructions
`docker compose down -v` — the `-v` flag removes named volumes declared in the compose file AND anonymous volumes attached to the stack's containers (never external volumes)
explain: `down -v` is the cleanup flag: anonymous + compose-managed named volumes go; `external: true` volumes are left alone. EXAM TRAPS: (A) plain `down` keeps volumes by design (data safety). (B) `--rm` is a `docker run` flag. (C) they're removable — just not automatically.

q: An app accidentally overwrote its config file mounted from a named volume, taking down the service. The config must be readable but never writable by the container. What enforces this?
options: Mount it read-only: `-v appconf:/etc/app:ro` (or `--mount type=volume,src=appconf,dst=/etc/app,readonly`) — the kernel denies writes regardless of the container's UID
`chmod 444` the files inside the image — mount options don't matter once perms are set
Use a secret instead — secrets are the only read-only mount type
Set the volume driver to `readonly` mode — drivers enforce access mode
explain: `:ro`/`readonly` mounts are enforced by the kernel — even root in the container gets EROFS. EXAM TRAPS: (B) root in the container can re-chmod; only the mount flag is a hard gate. (C) secrets are read-only too, but they're for sensitive data and Swarm-only. (D) no such driver mode.

q: A service needs a volume created with driver-specific options (e.g. NFS mount options) at service-create time. `docker service create -v myvol:/data` accepts no driver options. How are driver options passed for service volumes?
options: They can't be — services only support plain named volumes without options

Use the long form: `--mount type=volume,src=myvol,dst=/data,volume-driver=local,volume-opt=type=nfs,volume-opt=o=addr=10.0.0.5` — `--mount` supports `volume-driver` and `volume-opt`; the `-v` shorthand does not
Pre-create the volume with options, then `-v` is fine — the question's premise is wrong
Put the driver options in the image's `VOLUME` instruction
explain: `--mount` is the full-featured form: `volume-driver`, `volume-opt`, `readonly`, etc. `-v` is a shorthand subset. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is false — `--mount` covers it. (C) pre-creating works but doesn't answer 'at service-create time'. (D) `VOLUME` takes only a path.

q: An admin runs `docker volume prune` expecting to reclaim a volume belonging to a STOPPED container. The volume survives. Why?
options: Prune is broken for stopped containers — use `docker volume rm -f`
Stopped containers' volumes are always deleted — the admin must have mistyped the volume name
`docker volume prune` only removes volumes not referenced by ANY container — a stopped container still references its volumes, so they're kept. Remove the container (or `docker rm -v`) first
Prune requires `--all` to touch stopped containers' volumes
explain: 'Unused' means unreferenced by any container, running OR stopped — prune is conservative by design. EXAM TRAPS: (A) nothing's broken. (B) inverts the rule. (D) no `--all` flag on volume prune.

q: A multi-tenant host needs a 10GB cap per tenant's Docker volume. The storage driver is overlay2. An engineer proposes `docker volume create -o size=10G`. What happens?
options: The volume is capped at 10GB — the local driver enforces `size`
The option is accepted but silently ignored — the volume is uncapped
Docker creates a 10GB loop device backing each volume
The `size` option only exists for the deprecated devicemapper driver — overlay2 has no native per-volume quota. Enforce quotas at the filesystem layer (e.g. XFS project quotas) outside Docker
explain: Docker has no volume-size enforcement on overlay2 — `size` was a devicemapper `storage-opt`. Quotas must come from the filesystem underneath. EXAM TRAPS: (A) is the wishful reading. (B) is close but misses the point — the option isn't meaningful here at all. (C) describes nothing Docker does.

q: An engineer runs `docker cp web:/etc/nginx/conf.d ./backup` expecting the directory's CONTENTS in `./backup`, but gets `./backup/conf.d/...` instead. What copies just the contents?
options: `docker cp web:/etc/nginx/conf.d/. ./backup/` — the trailing `/.` copies contents rather than the directory itself
`docker cp -r web:/etc/nginx/conf.d ./backup` — `-r` flattens the directory
`docker cp` can't copy directory contents — pipe `tar` through `docker exec` instead
Add a trailing slash to the destination — destination slashes control flattening
explain: `docker cp` follows archive semantics: `src/.` means 'contents of src'. EXAM TRAPS: (B) `-r` is implied for directories; it doesn't flatten. (C) `cp` handles this natively. (D) destination slashes don't change the behavior.

q: Two containers need a SHARED memory-only workspace that survives container restarts but not host reboots. `--tmpfs` is per-container (not shared, not named). What provides a named, shareable RAM-backed volume?
options: A regular named volume — the local driver is RAM-backed

`docker volume create -d local -o type=tmpfs -o device=tmpfs -o o=size=100m,uid=1000 tmpspace` — the local driver's `type`/`device`/options can back a named volume with tmpfs, mountable by many containers
Bind-mount `/dev/shm` — it's shared across containers
tmpfs can't be shared between containers — use a regular volume and accept disk I/O
explain: The `local` driver is a mount-option passthrough: `type=tmpfs` gives a named, multi-container, RAM-backed volume. EXAM TRAPS: (A) named volumes are disk-backed. (C) `/dev/shm` is per-container (though size-tunable). (D) is false — this recipe exists precisely for sharing.

q: A volume plugin is installed on the Swarm manager only. Services using it fail on workers with 'volume driver not found'. What's the fix?
options: Restart the workers — plugins propagate to the cluster on daemon restart
Reinstall with `--grant-all-permissions` — permission grants gate cluster propagation
Install the plugin on EVERY node that will run the workload — plugins are node-local; Swarm does not distribute them
Deploy the plugin as a `--mode global` service — global mode distributes plugins
explain: Plugins live on the node where installed — the scheduler doesn't ship them. Every node needing the driver installs it identically. EXAM TRAPS: (A) restarts propagate nothing. (B) grants affect install-time privileges, not distribution. (D) global services are workloads, not plugin delivery.

q: After `docker stack rm shop`, the team redeploys and finds YESTERDAY's database rows still present. They expected `stack rm` to delete the named volumes. What is the actual behavior?
options: `stack rm` deletes volumes — the data must be coming from the image's seed data
Volumes are deleted only with `stack rm --volumes`
The database re-seeded itself — the volumes were deleted correctly
`docker stack rm` removes services, networks, secrets, and configs but NEVER named volumes — data persists by design; remove volumes explicitly with `docker volume rm`
explain: `stack rm` is deliberately non-destructive to data — volumes outlive the stack. EXAM TRAPS: (A) inverts the behavior. (B) `--volumes` doesn't exist on stack rm. (C) the rows came from the surviving volume, not a reseed.

q: A service mounts `-v appdata:/app` AND `-v ./config:/app/config`. The app sees the config files AND the rest of `/app` from the volume. A teammate claims the second mount hides the entire volume. Who's right?
options: The observed behavior is correct — mounts resolve most-specific-path-wins: `/app/config` comes from the bind, everything else under `/app` from the volume
The teammate — any overlapping mount shadows the entire parent mount
Docker rejects overlapping mounts — the service shouldn't have started
The first mount always wins — `/app/config` shows volume data
explain: Mounts are evaluated by path specificity — nested mounts coexist, the deeper path wins for its subtree. EXAM TRAPS: (B) describes shadowing that doesn't happen. (C) overlapping mounts are legal. (D) order doesn't decide; specificity does.

q: `docker pull` fails with 'no space left on device', but `df -h` shows 40GB free on `/var/lib/docker`. What's the likely cause, and the confirming command?
options: The registry is out of space — check the registry's logs
Inode exhaustion from thousands of small layers/files — `df -i` shows 100% inode use; prune unused images/containers or reformat with more inodes
`df -h` lies inside containers — run it on the host instead
The pull needs `--storage-opt size=50G` to proceed
explain: 'No space left' with free bytes = out of inodes — classic on filesystems with millions of small layer files. `df -i` confirms. EXAM TRAPS: (A) a full registry returns a different error. (C) `df` was already on the host path. (D) no such pull-time storage-opt.

q: Priya belongs to two MKE teams. Team 'deployers' holds a grant giving it a role that can create and update services on the /production collection; team 'auditors' holds a grant giving it a read-only role on the same /production collection. When Priya browses /production in the MKE UI, what can she do?
options: Only view resources — the more restrictive read-only grant caps her access
Everything the service-management role allows — MKE grants are additive, so her effective access is the union of all grants across her teams and the broader grant wins
Nothing — overlapping grants on the same collection cancel each other out
Only the actions both roles share — MKE intersects overlapping grants
explain: An MKE grant maps a subject (user, team, org, or service account) to a role on a resource set (a collection). When several grants cover the same subject, the effective permission is the UNION of all of them — they never cancel or intersect. EXAM TRAPS: (A) 'restrictive wins' is invented — MKE has no deny/override rule like that. (C) grants never cancel each other. (D) intersection is not a thing in MKE RBAC.

q: The platform team binds their MKE cluster to Active Directory over LDAP. During a full AD outage, the on-call engineer must scale a service immediately. Which statement is true?
options: Nobody can log in — binding LDAP disables all local MKE accounts including the built-in admin
Only users whose LDAP passwords were synced into MKE before the outage can log in
Local MKE accounts (including the built-in admin) still authenticate against MKE's own backend, so the on-call engineer can log in locally; LDAP users cannot until AD recovers
MKE automatically fails over to cached LDAP credentials for every user
explain: LDAP/AD is an ADDITIONAL auth backend, not a replacement — local users keep authenticating against MKE itself, which is exactly why the built-in admin remains as break-glass. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invented — binding LDAP never disables local accounts. (B) MKE never stores or syncs LDAP passwords; it binds to the directory at login. (D) there is no automatic cached-credential failover for directory users.

q: A 5-replica service is created with --placement-pref 'spread=node.labels.zone' on a 2-zone Swarm cluster. `docker service ps` shows 3 tasks in zone-a and 2 in zone-b. The engineer files a ticket: 'spread is broken, it should be even.' How do you respond?
options: Working as designed — spread distributes tasks as evenly as possible, and 5 replicas across 2 zones cannot divide evenly, so 3/2 is the correct best-effort result; a hard constraint would have failed scheduling instead
The preference syntax is wrong — it must be --placement-pref 'even=node.labels.zone'
One zone's nodes are missing the label — spread only counts labeled nodes, so relabel and the tasks will rebalance to 3/3
Spread preferences only apply at service creation for the first replica; the rest are random
explain: Placement PREFERENCES are soft (best-effort): the scheduler spreads tasks across the label values as evenly as it can — with 5 replicas and 2 zones, 3/2 is mathematically the best spread. EXAM TRAPS: (B) invents an 'even=' operator — the operator is 'spread='. (C) 3/3 would need 6 replicas; missing labels would skew harder, not produce a near-even split. (D) invented — preferences apply to every scheduling decision.

q: An engineer adds "labels": ["env=prod"] to daemon.json on three workers and restarts the daemons. A service created with --constraint 'node.labels.env==prod' leaves every task Pending, while `docker node ls` shows all nodes Active and Ready. What is wrong?
options: The daemons must re-join the swarm after any label change
Constraints cannot match labels at all — only placement preferences can
Pending means the image is missing on those nodes; the labels are fine

daemon.json "labels" are ENGINE labels, matched with engine.labels.env==prod — node.labels.* only matches labels set with `docker node update --label-add`; the constraint is looking in the wrong label namespace
explain: Two different label namespaces exist: engine labels (daemon.json "labels" / dockerd --label, matched as engine.labels.X) and node labels (`docker node update --label-add`, matched as node.labels.X). The constraint queried node.labels but the value lives in engine.labels, so nothing matches and tasks pend. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invented — no re-join needed. (B) constraints match labels fine. (C) a missing image shows a pull error on the task, not a scheduling Pending caused by an unmatched constraint.

q: CI uses a docker-container buildx builder for --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64. The amd64 stage passes, but the arm64 RUN steps fail with 'exec format error'. The builder was created successfully. What is missing?
options: The docker-container driver does not support arm64 at all

QEMU/binfmt emulation is not registered on the host — cross-architecture RUN steps need binfmt handlers to execute foreign binaries; install them with `docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install all`, then rebuild
Multi-arch builds require two separate builders, one per architecture
'exec format error' means the Dockerfile itself is corrupt
explain: Building for another arch is only half the story — EXECUTING its RUN steps needs QEMU via binfmt_misc, registered with the tonistiigi/binfmt helper. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the driver supports any platform QEMU can emulate. (C) one builder handles many platforms. (D) misreads an emulation error as file corruption.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A monorepo holds 12 microservices, each with its own Dockerfile, build args, and target registry tag. The team wants ONE command in CI that builds all twelve images correctly. Which approach fits?
options: A shell for-loop over `docker build` — buildx bake cannot handle multiple Dockerfiles
`docker compose build` — it automatically discovers every Dockerfile in subdirectories
Merge everything into one giant multi-stage Dockerfile

Define one target per service in a docker-bake.hcl file (or reuse the existing compose file, which bake reads natively) — a single `docker buildx bake` then builds every target with its own context, Dockerfile, args, and tags
explain: `docker buildx bake` builds many targets in one invocation from HCL/JSON definitions — and it natively reads compose files, so the compose services become bake targets. EXAM TRAPS: (A) bake exists precisely for multi-image builds. (B) compose build only builds services defined in that compose file, discovering nothing. (C) merging unrelated services into one Dockerfile destroys independent versioning and caching.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: The security team requires SLSA build provenance attached to every production image so auditors can verify exactly how each image was built. The team builds with buildx. What satisfies this?
options: Build with --provenance=true and push — buildx generates signed SLSA provenance attestations that travel with the image in the registry (`--provenance=mode=min` trims them if size is a concern)
Enable Docker Content Trust — it provides the same SLSA provenance
Add a LABEL with the git SHA — that is provenance
Do nothing — provenance is attached automatically on every docker build
explain: BuildKit can emit SLSA provenance attestations at build time (--provenance=true); they are pushed alongside the image as OCI attestations and verifiable by auditors. EXAM TRAPS: (B) DCT is Notary-v1 SIGNING (publisher identity), not SLSA build provenance — related but different. (C) a LABEL is an unverifiable self-claim, not a signed attestation. (D) provenance is opt-in and requires pushing (attestations need registry support).
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A customer contract requires an SBOM to be delivered with every shipped image. The team builds with buildx. How do they ship the SBOM with the image itself?
options: COPY the SBOM into the image — SBOMs must travel as an image layer
SBOMs can only be produced by external scanners after the push, never at build time
Build with --sbom=true and push — buildx generates the SBOM and attaches it as an attestation referencing the image; `docker buildx imagetools inspect` reveals it
`docker sbom` is a Swarm-only command and cannot run in CI
explain: --sbom=true makes BuildKit generate a software bill of materials and attach it as an OCI attestation linked to the image, without bloating the image layers. EXAM TRAPS: (A) COPYing the SBOM in adds a layer and pollutes the runtime image. (B) build-time generation is exactly what --sbom does. (D) invents a Swarm restriction — SBOM flags are buildx build options.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An audit flags ~/.docker/config.json on a build agent containing "auth": "dXNlcjpwYXNzd29yZA==" for the corporate registry, calling credential storage insecure. What is the right response?
options: Dismiss it — the base64 encoding is Docker's encryption

Acknowledge it — that value is merely base64-encoded and readable by anyone with the file; configure a credential helper (credsStore/credHelpers, e.g. docker-credential-pass) so secrets live in the OS keychain instead of the JSON file
Delete config.json — Docker does not need it to authenticate
chmod 600 the file — that fully resolves the finding
explain: The "auth" field is base64 ENCODING, not encryption — trivially reversible. The fix is a credential helper (credsStore for all registries or credHelpers per-registry) that keeps secrets in the OS keychain/secret store. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the classic encoding-vs-encryption confusion. (C) deleting the file breaks registry auth entirely. (D) 600 helps but the secret is still on disk in reversible form — the helper is the real fix.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: The team sets "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"} in daemon.json and restarts the daemon. A week later the OLDEST containers still have multi-gigabyte JSON log files. Why?
options: max-size only applies to Swarm services, not standalone containers
The values must be given in bytes — '10m' is not a valid unit
Log rotation requires the 'local' driver, not json-file
Daemon log options apply only to containers created AFTER the change — existing containers keep the options they were created with, so they must be recreated to pick up rotation
explain: Log driver and log-opts are per-container settings captured at CREATE time; the daemon.json defaults only seed NEW containers. Restarting the daemon does not retroactively reconfigure running containers. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invented scoping — max-size/max-file are valid for any json-file container. (B) 10m/3 are valid units. (C) json-file is exactly the driver that supports max-size/max-file rotation.

q: The monitoring team wants Prometheus to scrape DOCKER DAEMON metrics (engine internals), but nothing is listening. `docker stats` works fine. How is the daemon's metrics endpoint enabled?
options: Set "metrics-addr": "127.0.0.1:9323" in daemon.json and restart the daemon — it then exposes Prometheus-format engine metrics; note the endpoint has no auth by default, so bind it to localhost or protect it
Use `docker stats` — it already exposes daemon metrics
Daemon metrics require Swarm mode
Install a third-party metrics plugin
explain: metrics-addr enables the daemon's Prometheus endpoint (9323 conventionally) — separate from container stats. EXAM TRAPS: (B) `docker stats` reports CONTAINER resource usage, not engine internals. (C) invents a Swarm requirement. (D) no plugin needed — it's built in.

q: On a rootless Docker host, throughput to published container ports is far lower than the identical workload on rootful Docker. The app and image are the same. What explains it?
options: Rootless mode throttles bandwidth by design
The workload needs --network host to perform

Rootless cannot program host iptables, so published-port traffic flows through RootlessKit's user-mode networking stack — functional but slower than rootful iptables DNAT; it is an accepted rootless trade-off, not a misconfiguration
Rootless mode does not support port publishing
explain: Rootless networking is user-mode (slirp/RootlessKit port driver) because an unprivileged daemon can't own iptables — correctness preserved, throughput reduced. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents intentional throttling. (B) host networking 'fixes' it by abandoning isolation. (D) false — publishing works, just slower.

q: An engineer runs `docker context create prod --docker host=ssh://ops@prod-01` then `docker context use prod`. `docker context ls` shows prod as current (*), yet `docker ps` still lists LOCAL containers. What is overriding the context?
options: Contexts only work with TLS endpoints, not SSH
The DOCKER_HOST environment variable is set — environment variables take precedence over the active context; unset it to let the context apply
The context must be imported with `docker context import` before use
SSH contexts require agent forwarding to be enabled
explain: Precedence is: DOCKER_HOST env var > active context > default socket. A stale exported DOCKER_HOST silently wins over `docker context use`. EXAM TRAPS: (A) SSH hosts are fully supported context endpoints. (C) invents an import step — create+use is sufficient. (D) agent forwarding is unrelated to endpoint selection.

q: A container is started with --log-driver syslog --log-opt syslog-address=tcp://logs.corp:514. `docker logs web` returns 'configured logging driver does not support reading'. Is logging broken?
options: No — syslog is a non-local driver: logs stream to the syslog server, and `docker logs` / `docker service logs` only work with local drivers (json-file, journald); check the syslog server, nothing is lost
Yes — the container must be recreated with the json-file driver
Yes — tcp:// is not a valid syslog-address scheme
No, but only until the next daemon restart, after which `docker logs` starts working with any driver
explain: `docker logs` reads from the LOCAL log store; non-local drivers (syslog, gelf, fluentd, awslogs...) forward entries and keep nothing readable locally — the error message is expected behavior, not data loss. EXAM TRAPS: (B) recreating with json-file would abandon the SIEM feed for no reason. (C) tcp:// and udp:// are both valid schemes. (D) invents a restart side effect.

q: The fleet logs with --log-driver gelf. On hosts running Engine 20.10+, `docker logs` still returns entries; on older hosts it errors with 'does not support reading'. What explains the difference?
options: The GELF driver gained read support in Engine 20.10
The newer hosts have journald installed, which backfills the reads
Someone installed a GELF reader plugin on the newer hosts

Engine 20.10 introduced DUAL LOGGING: a local cache kept alongside the remote driver, so `docker logs` keeps working with gelf/syslog and friends; it is tunable via --log-opt cache-disabled, cache-max-size, and cache-max-file
explain: Dual logging (20.10+) maintains a local ring-buffer cache in parallel with the configured remote driver, restoring `docker logs` for non-local drivers. EXAM TRAPS: (A) no driver 'gained' read support — the cache did it. (B) journald is a separate driver, irrelevant here. (C) invents a plugin — the behavior is built into the engine.

q: Only the payments service must ship logs to the SIEM over syslog; every other service keeps the json-file default. How is this configured?
options: Change the daemon default to syslog — per-service log drivers are not possible
`docker service create --log-driver syslog --log-opt syslog-address=udp://siem:514 payments` — services accept their own --log-driver/--log-opt, independent of the daemon default
Deploy a sidecar on each payments task that tails the json-file logs
Run `docker service logs --driver syslog` after creating the service
explain: `docker service create` supports --log-driver and --log-opt per service, overriding the daemon default for just that service's tasks. EXAM TRAPS: (A) false — per-service drivers exist precisely for this. (C) an unnecessary sidecar for a built-in feature. (D) invents a --driver flag on `docker service logs`.

q: A standalone debug container on a manager must join the app's overlay network to curl a service VIP. `docker network connect app_net debug` fails with 'network is not attachable'. What is the fix?
options: Retry with `docker network connect --attachable app_net debug`
Join the node to the swarm first — only swarm nodes can use overlays

Recreate the network with `docker network create -d overlay --attachable app_net` — a non-attachable overlay serves Swarm services only; attachable must be set at creation and cannot be added to an existing network
Connect the debug container to docker_gwbridge instead
explain: Overlay networks default to service-only; standalone containers need --attachable, which is a create-time property — there is no way to retrofit it, so the network must be recreated. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents a connect-time flag. (B) the node is already a manager; membership is not the issue. (D) docker_gwbridge carries egress traffic, not the overlay's service VIPs.

q: A legacy monitoring agent fails inside a container on the `unshare` syscall with EPERM, though it runs fine on the host. `docker info` shows seccomp enabled with the default profile. What is the right move?
options: Run with --security-opt seccomp=unconfined or a custom profile permitting the syscall — the default seccomp profile blocks ~44 syscalls; do not reach for --privileged, which disables seccomp and the rest of the isolation with it
Add --cap-add SYS_ADMIN — capabilities override seccomp blocks
Rebuild the image — the binary must be corrupt
seccomp profiles cannot be changed per container; the agent must run on the host
explain: The default seccomp profile denies risky syscalls including unshare/clone-namespace variants; per-container override is via --security-opt seccomp=. EXAM TRAPS: (B) capabilities and seccomp are independent filters — a capability grant does not unblock a seccomp-denied syscall. (C) misdiagnoses a policy denial as image corruption. (D) false — per-container seccomp is a standard --security-opt.

q: A container is denied writing to a /proc/sys path and the host audit log shows apparmor="DENIED". The team maintains a custom AppArmor profile for this app. How is it applied to the container?
options: Set apparmor= in daemon.json — AppArmor profiles are daemon-global
`docker run --security-opt apparmor=my-app-profile` — containers use the docker-default profile unless overridden per container with --security-opt
Add --cap-add SYS_RESOURCE — that clears AppArmor denials
AppArmor profiles only apply to Swarm services, not standalone containers
explain: Docker applies the docker-default AppArmor profile to every container unless --security-opt apparmor=<profile> names another loaded profile. EXAM TRAPS: (A) there is no daemon-global profile switch. (C) capabilities do not override MAC denials. (D) invents a Swarm-only restriction.

q: Hardened containers run with --security-opt no-new-privileges:true. The app's healthcheck shells out to /bin/ping (setuid root) and now fails with 'operation not permitted'. What is the best fix?
options: Drop no-new-privileges — ping requires privilege escalation
Run chmod u-s /bin/ping on the host
Run the container --privileged instead

Keep no-new-privileges and add --cap-add NET_RAW so ping works via capability instead of setuid — no-new-privileges exists precisely to stop setuid binaries gaining privilege, so capabilities are the intended replacement
explain: no-new-privileges blocks setuid/setgid elevation; the correct pattern is replacing the setuid mechanism with a granular Linux capability (NET_RAW for ping). EXAM TRAPS: (A) surrenders the hardening for one binary. (B) modifies the host, not the container's execution context. (C) --privileged grants everything, the opposite of hardening.

q: After enabling "userns-remap": "default" in daemon.json, a container writing to a pre-existing named volume gets permission denied. The same volume worked before the change. Why?
options: userns-remap encrypts volume contents with the remap key
All images must be rebuilt after enabling user namespaces

Container root is now mapped to an unprivileged host UID (the dockremap user from /etc/subuid); files in the volume are still owned by the old host UID, which the remapped root cannot write — chown the volume data into the remapped subordinate range
Named volumes are incompatible with user namespace remapping
explain: userns-remap maps container UIDs (including root=0) into a subordinate host range, so previously root-owned volume files become foreign-owned. Fix ownership into the mapped range (or re-seed the volume). EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents encryption. (B) images are UID-agnostic at the layer level — no rebuild needed. (D) false — volumes work fine once ownership is reconciled.

q: `docker info` warns: 'devicemapper: usage of loopback devices is strongly discouraged for production use' on a RHEL 7 host. What is the proper fix?
options: Ignore it — the message is informational only

Provision direct-lvm: create a real thin pool (pvcreate/vgcreate/lvcreate) and point the daemon at it with "storage-opts": ["dm.thinpooldev=..."] — loop-lvm is test-only; alternatively move to overlay2 on a supported kernel and filesystem
Switch to the vfs storage driver
Attach additional loopback devices to spread the load
explain: The default loopback devicemapper setup is for testing; production needs direct-lvm on a dedicated thin pool (or overlay2, the modern default, where the kernel/filesystem allow). EXAM TRAPS: (A) the warning is explicit about production. (C) vfs is the slowest, copy-everything driver — worse, not better. (D) more loopbacks don't fix the fundamental loop-lvm problem.

q: dockerd fails to start with the overlay2 driver on a host where /var/lib/docker sits on XFS. `xfs_info` shows ftype=0. What is wrong?
options: overlay2 requires d_type support, and XFS formatted without ftype=1 lacks it — back up /var/lib/docker, reformat with mkfs.xfs -n ftype=1, and restore (ext4 supports d_type by default; this is the classic overlay-on-XFS gotcha)
overlay2 does not support XFS at all — only ext4 works
The kernel is too old for any overlay filesystem
Set the storage-opt overlay2.override_kernel_check=true
explain: overlay/overlay2 need d_type directory-entry type support from the backing filesystem; XFS only provides it when formatted with ftype=1, and the only fix is a reformat. EXAM TRAPS: (B) XFS works fine once ftype=1. (C) misdiagnoses a filesystem-format issue as a kernel issue. (D) override_kernel_check bypasses kernel version checks — irrelevant to d_type.

q: CI runs `docker plugin install vieux/sshfs` and hangs on the interactive prompt 'Do you grant the above permissions?'. How should CI install the plugin non-interactively?
options: Pipe 'yes' into the command via stdin
Plugins cannot be installed non-interactively — pre-bake them into the machine image instead
`docker plugin install --disabled` skips the permission prompt
`docker plugin install --grant-all-permissions vieux/sshfs` — grants the requested privileges without prompting (the plugin enables by default unless --disabled is passed)
explain: --grant-all-permissions is the designed non-interactive path for plugin privilege grants. EXAM TRAPS: (A) piping yes is fragile and not the supported mechanism. (B) false — the flag exists precisely for automation. (C) --disabled only defers activation; the grant prompt is handled by --grant-all-permissions.

q: A stateful Swarm service reschedules across nodes and the team needs its data volume to follow the task using EBS storage. They install REX-Ray. How are volumes provisioned?
options: Docker auto-converts existing local volumes to REX-Ray volumes
`docker volume create` with no driver — REX-Ray transparently intercepts all volume creation
`docker volume create -d rexray/ebs --name dbdata` (or --volume-driver on service create) — REX-Ray is a volume driver/plugin, and it must be installed on every node where tasks may land
REX-Ray replaces the Docker volume API entirely
explain: REX-Ray plugs in as a volume DRIVER selected with -d/--volume-driver; scheduling only succeeds where the driver is present, so install it cluster-wide. EXAM TRAPS: (A) no auto-conversion exists. (B) without -d you get the local driver. (D) it extends the volume subsystem via the plugin API, not replacing it.

q: The CI pipeline must deploy services to MKE nightly. The team debates sharing the tech lead's admin login in the pipeline versus creating a dedicated identity. What is the correct approach and why?
options: Create an MKE service account and grant it only the role it needs on the target collection — a non-human identity with least privilege that keeps an audit trail; sharing a human admin login destroys accountability and over-privileges the pipeline
Share the admin login — service accounts exist but cannot be granted roles
Commit the lead's client bundle into the repo — client bundles are read-only so this is safe
CI cannot authenticate to MKE at all — SSH into the managers and run docker commands there
explain: MKE service accounts are first-class grant subjects for automation: least-privilege role on a scoped collection, auditable as the pipeline. EXAM TRAPS: (B) false — service accounts are grantable subjects like users and teams. (C) bundles carry full client certs and committing them leaks credentials. (D) invented — MKE's API is the supported automation path.

q: One MKE cluster serves three departments that need strong RBAC isolation from each other. How should orgs and teams model this?
options: One team per department and no orgs — orgs are just UI folders with no RBAC meaning
Orgs cannot contain teams — model everything with collections only
Create one org per department, put each department's teams inside its org, and scope grants to each org's collections — orgs group teams so each department gets its own RBAC boundary
A user can only ever belong to a single org, so create three clusters
explain: Orgs are the top-level grouping: teams live inside orgs, and grants referencing an org's teams/collections give each department an isolated boundary on a shared cluster. EXAM TRAPS: (A) orgs are real RBAC subjects for grants, not cosmetic. (B) teams DO live inside orgs. (D) invented single-org restriction — and one cluster with orgs is exactly the multi-tenancy pattern.

q: MKE runs Swarm and Kubernetes orchestrators side by side. A developer needs kubectl access to the Kubernetes orchestrator. How do they get credentials?
options: kubectl talks to the Swarm managers directly — no setup is needed
Download the Kubernetes client bundle/kubeconfig from the MKE UI — MKE issues per-user credentials for its Kubernetes API alongside the Swarm endpoint
Install kubectl on a manager node and copy /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
MKE's Kubernetes API is Swarm-only — use `docker stack` commands instead
explain: MKE is dual-orchestrator: the UI/API issues the user a kubeconfig (client bundle) for Kubernetes exactly as it issues certs for Swarm — per-user, RBAC-enforced. EXAM TRAPS: (A) kubectl needs the K8s API endpoint and certs. (C) /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf is the kubeadm path, not MKE. (D) invented — the K8s orchestrator is fully usable.

q: Migrating from Kubernetes, a team defines 'init' behavior expecting init containers to run before app containers in their Swarm service. Tasks start, but the init logic never runs. Why?
options: Init containers require --init on `docker service create`
Init steps must be declared under a deploy.init key in the compose file
Swarm only runs init containers for global-mode services
Swarm has no init-container concept — every task container starts independently with no ordering; bake sequencing into the entrypoint script or gate readiness with healthchecks
explain: Init containers are a Kubernetes primitive; Swarm schedules each task's containers independently with no phased startup. EXAM TRAPS: (A) --init installs tini as PID 1 for zombie reaping — unrelated to startup ordering. (B)/(C) invent compose keys and mode restrictions that don't exist.

q: A compose file uses depends_on with `condition: service_healthy` so the API waits for the DB. `docker compose up` honors it, but after `docker stack deploy` the API crashes on boot because the DB is not ready yet. Why?
options: `docker stack deploy` ignores depends_on entirely — short syntax and long syntax alike; Swarm schedules tasks independently with no startup ordering, so the compose health-gate only works under `docker compose`
condition: service_healthy requires Swarm mode to function
The DB image is missing a HEALTHCHECK instruction
depends_on long syntax is only valid in v2 compose files
explain: depends_on (including the long-syntax health condition) is a Compose-orchestrator feature that `docker stack deploy` silently ignores — a classic Swarm-vs-Compose gap. EXAM TRAPS: (B) backwards — it works in Compose, not Swarm. (C) a missing healthcheck would break the compose path too, which works. (D) long syntax is valid in the compose spec used by both.

q: The team signs images with Docker Content Trust today. A vendor ships signatures made with notation (Notary v2). Will the team's existing verification (`DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 docker pull`) verify those signatures?
options: Yes — Docker Content Trust and notation are the same trust system

No — DCT is Notary v1 (TUF metadata on a notary server, managed with `docker trust`); Notary v2/notation stores signatures as OCI artifacts in the registry itself — different systems, and MSR 2.x content trust speaks v1
Yes, once the vendor is added with `docker trust signer add`
No — notation signatures only verify on Windows container hosts
explain: Notary v1 (DCT: TUF repo metadata, separate notary server) and Notary v2 (notation: signatures as OCI referrers in the registry) are incompatible trust systems. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the central confusion — same word 'notary', different protocols. (C) `docker trust signer add` manages v1 delegations only. (D) invents a platform restriction.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI must push DCT-signed images non-interactively. How are the signing passphrases supplied?
options: Commit them in the repo next to the Dockerfile so the pipeline can read them
Pass them via --build-arg at build time
DCT cannot run non-interactively — disable content trust in CI

Inject them as protected CI variables with DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 — DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST_REPOSITORY_PASSPHRASE (plus ROOT/OEM passphrases as needed); add the CI key once via `docker trust signer add` delegation instead of sharing the repository key
explain: DCT honors passphrase env vars for automation, and delegation (`docker trust signer add`) lets CI sign with its own key rather than the precious repo key. EXAM TRAPS: (A) committing passphrases leaks signing identity. (B) build-args persist in image history/metadata. (C) false — env-var passphrases are the designed non-interactive path.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 docker pull registry.corp/app:v3` fails with 'no trust data for v3'. The registry is healthy and the tag exists. What is the most likely cause?
options: The registry disk is full
The image layers are corrupt
The tag was never signed — DCT refuses unsigned content by design; sign and push it (or pull without DCT if policy allows) rather than treating it as corruption or an outage
The notary server needs a restart
explain: 'no trust data' is DCT's explicit unsigned-content refusal, not a corruption or outage signal. EXAM TRAPS: (A)/(B) invent infrastructure causes for a policy verdict. (D) a notary outage produces a connection error, not 'no trust data'.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Java API needs ~90s to warm up. Its HEALTHCHECK (interval 10s, retries 3) flags it unhealthy during warmup and the orchestrator kill-restarts it in a loop. What is the correct fix?
options: Add --start-period=120s to the HEALTHCHECK — failures inside the start period do not count toward retries, giving slow starters a grace window without weakening real failure detection
Set --retries=100 so it eventually passes
Remove the HEALTHCHECK entirely
Raise --interval to 120s
explain: --start-period is the designed warmup grace: the container gets that long before unhealthy counts begin. EXAM TRAPS: (B) huge retries delay detection of GENUINE failures forever. (C) surrenders health monitoring. (D) a 120s interval makes every check sluggish, including real outages.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A compose file defines an optional 'debug' service with profiling tools that must NOT start during a normal `docker compose up`. How is this expressed?
options: Comment the service out when it is not needed
Give it `profiles: ['debug']` — profiled services are excluded by default and start only with `docker compose --profile debug up` (or COMPOSE_PROFILES=debug)
Profiles only work with `docker stack deploy`
Wire it behind depends_on so it never resolves
explain: Compose profiles selectively enable services; unlisted profiles stay dormant. EXAM TRAPS: (A) manual editing defeats the purpose. (C) backwards — profiles are a Compose feature, ignored by stack deploy. (D) abuses depends_on for something it cannot do.

q: A developer's inner loop is slow: every code tweak needs a full `docker compose up --build`. They want code changes synced into the running container, rebuilding only when dependencies change. What fits?
options: Bind-mount everything — no watch mode exists in Compose
`docker compose watch` redeploys the whole stack on every file save
Watch mode only works against Swarm stacks

Add a `develop.watch` section (sync rules for code paths, rebuild triggers for dependency files) and run `docker compose watch` — code syncs live without a rebuild; dependency changes trigger rebuilds
explain: `docker compose watch` implements sync (file sync, no rebuild) vs rebuild actions per path rules in develop.watch. EXAM TRAPS: (A) denies a real feature. (B) misstates it as full redeploy — sync is the point. (C) invents a Swarm restriction.

q: The platform team keeps a shared base compose file (logging, networks) that every app's compose file should extend — declared INSIDE the file, not via CLI flags. What works?
options: `extends:` — it includes whole compose files
There is no in-file mechanism — `-f base.yml -f app.yml` is the only way
Top-level `include:` listing the base file — Compose merges included files into one project model declaratively
Top-level `import:` — the compose file-inclusion directive
explain: `include:` composes multiple files into a single project from inside the YAML. EXAM TRAPS: (A) extends works per-SERVICE from another service definition, not whole-file inclusion. (B) -f merging works but is CLI-driven, not what was asked. (D) invents an `import:` keyword.

q: A service sets `env_file: [.env.prod]` containing API_URL=old, and also `environment: {API_URL: new}`. `docker compose config` renders API_URL=new. Why?
options: `environment:` entries take precedence over `env_file` — the explicit mapping wins (and .env files separately drive variable INTERPOLATION in the compose file, a different mechanism)
`env_file` always wins over `environment:`
The file that sorts last alphabetically wins
Compose merges the two sources nondeterministically
