explain: Compose env precedence: `docker compose run -e` > `environment:` > `env_file` > Dockerfile ENV. The .env interpolation role is separate from container env. EXAM TRAPS: (B) states the precedence backwards. (C)/(D) invent ordering rules — it is deterministic.

q: An old runbook says to run Linux containers on Windows Server via LCOW. What is the current guidance?
options: LCOW is the production path for Linux containers on Windows
LCOW was experimental and is deprecated — the supported path for Linux containers on Windows today is the WSL 2 backend, not LCOW
LCOW requires Hyper-V isolation to be disabled first
LCOW and the WSL 2 backend are the same thing
explain: Linux Containers on Windows (Hyper-V-isolated LinuxKit VM) was an experiment; Docker moved to the WSL 2 backend and LCOW was dropped. EXAM TRAPS: (A) states the deprecated path as current. (C) invents a prerequisite. (D) conflates two different architectures.

q: On a fresh Windows Server 2022 install with Docker Engine, `docker run mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022` fails with an hcsshim error about the container feature. The image and daemon are fine. What is missing?
options: Hyper-V must be disabled for Windows containers
LCOW must be enabled for Windows images
The image tag is incompatible with the daemon
The Windows 'Containers' OS feature is not installed — enable it (Install-WindowsFeature Containers) and reboot; the Host Compute Service cannot create containers without it
explain: Windows containers need the OS Containers feature; without it hcsshim fails no matter how correct the image/daemon are. EXAM TRAPS: (A) Hyper-V is needed for Hyper-V isolation, not the problem here. (B) LCOW is Linux-containers-on-Windows — irrelevant to Windows images. (C) misblames the tag.

q: ML inference images are ~8GB and task startup is dominated by pulling layers. The team hears eStargz enables 'lazy pulling'. What is eStargz?
options: A new image format that replaces OCI
A registry variant that streams layers over HTTP/3

A containerd snapshotter: eStargz-formatted images let the runtime fetch only the files the container actually reads, so startup does not wait for the full pull — it works with existing registries via Docker's containerd image store
A Docker Hub premium feature for faster pulls
explain: eStargz (with the stargz snapshotter, and nydus as its sibling) adds chunk-level lazy fetch to OCI-compatible images — partial reads on demand. EXAM TRAPS: (A) it EXTENDS OCI, not replacing it. (B) invents a transport story. (D) it is an open snapshotter, not a Hub upsell.

q: A k3s edge node runs containerd with no Docker daemon. The admin wants a docker-like CLI to run a one-off debug container. What fits?
options: nerdctl — the containerd-native CLI with docker-compatible syntax (`nerdctl run`), built for environments without dockerd
`docker run` — it works fine without the daemon
`ctr run` — the only containerd CLI, with UX identical to docker
Nothing — install the full Docker Engine; containerd cannot run containers alone
explain: nerdctl targets containerd directly with familiar docker-style commands — the standard answer on k3s/finch-class hosts. EXAM TRAPS: (B) the docker CLI is useless without dockerd. (C) ctr exists but is low-level with different UX. (D) false — containerd is a complete runtime.

q: Release images are tagged v2.4.0 in MSR. The team wants to guarantee that tag can NEVER be overwritten by a later push. Which MSR feature does this?
options: Docker Content Trust signing on the repository
Immutable tags — once pushed, MSR rejects any push that would overwrite an immutable tag, protecting releases from accidental or malicious retagging
A promotion policy from staging to production
Repository pruning with a keep-last-1 rule
explain: Immutable tags make the tag write-once: subsequent pushes to that tag are refused. EXAM TRAPS: (A) signing proves publisher identity; it doesn't block overwrites by a key holder. (C) promotion moves images between repos — unrelated. (D) pruning DELETES old tags, the opposite of protection.

q: A contractor's engagement ends. They held an MKE client bundle for CLI/API access. How is their access revoked?
options: Wait — client bundles expire automatically after 24 hours
Delete the bundle files from their laptop
Rotate the cluster CA
Remove or disable their user (or their team's grant) in MKE — the bundle's client certificates authenticate AS that identity, so removing the identity kills the access; bundles do not self-expire
explain: A client bundle is just credentials for an identity; revocation happens at the identity/grant level in MKE. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents auto-expiry — bundles live until the identity is gone. (B) you can't reach their laptop. (C) CA rotation is massive overkill for one departure.

q: Policy: images with critical CVEs must never reach the production MSR repository. The pipeline pushes to a staging repo first. How can MSR enforce the gate automatically?
options: Have a human eyeball scan results before each release
It cannot — MSR scanning only reports, it never gates
Enable MSR image scanning on push and add a promotion policy gated on scan results — images promote from staging to production only when no blocking CVEs are found
Block pushes of any image containing OS packages
explain: MSR (DTR) scans on push and its promotion policies can require clean scan results before promoting between repositories — the automated quality gate. EXAM TRAPS: (A) manual review doesn't scale and isn't enforcement. (B) denies a real gating feature. (D) unworkable — nearly every image has OS packages.

q: The team exposes the Docker API on TCP 2375 for a monitoring tool. Security flags it immediately. What is the issue and the fix?
options: Port 2375 serves the API as plaintext HTTP with NO authentication — anyone reaching it gets root-equivalent control of the host; serve it with --tlsverify on 2376 (or keep it on a protected local socket), never as plaintext TCP
Port 2375 requires a password by default, so the finding is wrong
Just move to port 2376 without TLS — the port number is the protection
Firewall rules alone make plaintext 2375 safe
explain: An unauthenticated Docker API = remote root. The fix is mutual TLS (--tlsverify, conventionally 2376) or no TCP exposure at all. EXAM TRAPS: (B) 2375 has zero auth. (C) the port number provides nothing; TLS does. (D) firewalls reduce exposure but the service itself stays unauthenticated.

q: A Swarm service needs scratch space for session files that must NEVER hit disk and must vanish when the task ends. Which mount is right?
options: A named volume — its data vanishes when the task stops
`--mount type=tmpfs,destination=/sessions` (optionally tmpfs-size=…) — tmpfs lives in memory, never touches disk, and dies with the task
A bind mount to the host's /tmp
tmpfs mounts are not supported for Swarm services
explain: tmpfs mounts are memory-backed and task-scoped — exactly the ephemeral, disk-free semantics asked for, and they work on services. EXAM TRAPS: (A) named volumes PERSIST beyond the task. (C) host /tmp is disk (usually) and shared. (D) invents a Swarm restriction.

q: A service created with --volume-driver customdrv runs fine on 3 nodes, but tasks landing on 2 other nodes fail with 'driver not found' mount errors. Why?
options: The driver name is misspelled — it only worked on 3 nodes by luck
Swarm replicates volume drivers to all nodes automatically
The service should use --mount instead of --volume-driver
Volume drivers are node-local plugins — the driver must be installed on EVERY node where tasks may land; either install it cluster-wide or constrain the service to driver-ready nodes
explain: Volume plugins live on the node, not in the Swarm — the scheduler doesn't install them. A task landing where the driver is absent fails to mount. EXAM TRAPS: (A) a typo would fail everywhere. (B) invents driver replication. (C) --mount still names the same driver.

q: On a RHEL 7 host using the devicemapper driver, what does a proper direct-lvm setup actually require?
options: Nothing — the default loopback files are production-ready
Only setting dm.basesize in daemon.json

A dedicated block device carved into a thin pool (pvcreate → vgcreate → lvcreate for the thin pool and its metadata), then daemon.json "storage-opts": ["dm.thinpooldev=/dev/mapper/<pool>"...] — loop-lvm is test-only
Formatting the block device as XFS first
explain: direct-lvm = LVM thin pool on real block storage, handed to the daemon via dm.thinpooldev; the loopback default is explicitly test-only. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the exact anti-pattern the docker info warning calls out. (B) basesize tunes container rootfs size, not the loopback problem. (D) the thin pool is LVM-managed, not a formatted filesystem.

q: An engineer switches the daemon from overlay2 to devicemapper for a test, then switches back. All images and containers are gone. What happened?
options: Changing the storage driver points the daemon at a fresh, empty backend — images and containers stored under the old driver are not migrated and become invisible; back them up (or push images) before switching drivers
devicemapper deletes /var/lib/docker on startup
The images were corrupted by the driver switch
Any daemon restart wipes local images
explain: Each storage driver keeps its own directory tree under /var/lib/docker; switching drivers abandons the old tree (it's still on disk, just unused). EXAM TRAPS: (B) invents deletion — the data is orphaned, not deleted. (C) nothing is corrupted. (D) restarts never wipe images.

q: After deleting hundreds of stale tags from an MSR repository, disk usage barely drops. The deletions succeeded — the tags are gone. Why is the space not freed?
options: MSR retains deleted tags for 30 days before freeing them
MSR stores tag data outside the monitored disk
Deleting a tag only removes the tag reference — the underlying blobs are reclaimed by MSR's garbage collection, which runs on its own schedule (or on demand); until GC runs, the disk stays full
Disk metrics only refresh after a daemon restart
explain: Tags are pointers to manifests/blobs; deletion unpoints them, and only garbage collection sweeps the now-unreferenced blobs. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents a retention policy. (B) misplaces the storage. (D) invents a metrics-refresh requirement.

q: CI pushes nightly tags into an MSR repo and it grows without bound. The team wants to automatically keep only recent nightly tags. What is the built-in mechanism?
options: Configure a repository pruning policy (e.g., keep the N most recent tags matching a pattern) — MSR prunes the rest on its schedule
Delete old tags by hand every Friday
Pruning runs automatically with no configuration
Mark the nightly tags immutable
explain: MSR/DTR pruning policies retain recent tags (by count/pattern) and remove the rest — the automated retention control. EXAM TRAPS: (B) manual toil instead of the feature. (C) false — policies must be configured. (D) immutable tags PREVENT deletion/overwrite, the opposite of pruning.

q: A failed update triggers a rollback, but the rollback itself stalls halfway, leaving mixed versions. The team wants the ROLLBACK phase to pause on failure for inspection instead of pushing through. Which setting controls that?
options: --update-failure-action pause — that already covers rollbacks
--rollback-parallelism 0
Rollback behavior cannot be configured

--rollback-failure-action pause — the rollback phase has its OWN failure-action setting, independent of --update-failure-action (which governs the update phase); set it on the service or at update time
explain: Update and rollback are separate phases with separate knobs: --update-failure-action vs --rollback-failure-action (pause|continue). EXAM TRAPS: (A) the near-identical flag trap — update-failure-action does NOT govern rollbacks. (B) invents semantics for parallelism 0. (C) denies real configurability.

q: Before a major MKE upgrade, the team plans backups. What must be captured?
options: Only the Swarm raft logs from one manager

The MKE/UCP backup (cluster configuration, certificates, and Swarm state via the docker/ucp backup procedure) AND the MSR metadata backup separately — they are independent components with independent backups; one does not cover the other
Nothing — upgrades never touch cluster state
Just the daemon.json files from each node
explain: MKE (UCP) and MSR (DTR) back up independently: UCP backup covers swarm state/certs/config, DTR/MSR backup covers registry metadata — you need both for a full restore. EXAM TRAPS: (A) raft logs alone miss certs, configs, and all registry data. (C) upgrades absolutely can mutate state. (D) daemon.json is node config trivia, not cluster state.

q: Go builds re-download all modules on every `docker build` even though go.mod hasn't changed. How can the module cache persist across builds without bloating the image?
options: COPY the module cache into the final image
BuildKit has no cache mounts — accept the re-downloads
Use RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod so the cache persists across builds but is NOT committed to any image layer
Switch from COPY to ADD for go.mod
explain: BuildKit cache mounts persist build scratch (module caches, apt caches) across builds while staying out of the image. EXAM TRAPS: (A) ships megabytes of cache in production. (B) denies a core BuildKit feature. (D) ADD vs COPY is irrelevant to caching.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile defines stages base → build → test → release. CI wants to execute the test stage WITHOUT producing the release image. How?
options: `docker build --target test` — builds up to and including the named stage, skipping everything after it
Comment out the release stage temporarily
--target also tags the resulting image automatically
Multi-stage Dockerfiles cannot stop mid-way
explain: --target stops the build at the named stage — the standard way to run test/debug stages in CI. EXAM TRAPS: (B) manual editing instead of the flag. (C) --target does NOT tag anything; add -t if you want a tag. (D) denies the feature.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Builds must reach an internal artifact proxy that only accepts clients on the host network. RUN curl fails under the default build network. What is the fix?
options: RUN steps cannot access any network — vendor the artifacts into the context
Build with --network=none for maximum compatibility
Bake the proxy credentials into the final image
`docker build --network=host` — the build container shares the host's network stack for RUN steps (default is an isolated bridge; --network=none would isolate it completely)
explain: `docker build --network=` controls the network namespace of RUN steps: host shares the host stack when the proxy demands it. EXAM TRAPS: (A) false — RUN has network by default. (B) none is the opposite direction. (C) leaks credentials into layers.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile declares ARG API_KEY, the build passes --build-arg API_KEY=secret (build steps see it), but the RUNNING container's $API_KEY is empty. Why?
options: ARG values are masked at runtime for security

ARG exists only at BUILD time — to carry a value into runtime you must assign it to an ENV (e.g. ENV API_KEY=$API_KEY); and for real secrets prefer BuildKit --mount=type=secret over baking them into layers at all
--build-arg was not actually passed
ENV instructions cannot reference ARG values
explain: ARG is build-scoped; only ENV (and friends) persist into the container's environment. The stem confirms the build-arg worked, so the gap is purely ARG-vs-ENV scope. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents masking. (C) contradicts the stem. (D) false — ENV can expand ARGs.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: After hand-editing daemon.json, the admin wants to check the file WITHOUT restarting the daemon (production hours). How?
options: `dockerd --validate` — parses and validates daemon.json against the daemon's schema and exits without starting anything
There is no way — restart and read the logs
python -m json.tool is sufficient validation
`docker config validate daemon.json`
explain: dockerd --validate is the Docker-aware config check: it catches unknown keys and bad values, not just JSON syntax. EXAM TRAPS: (B) denies the built-in validator. (C) json.tool catches syntax errors but not semantic ones (e.g., misspelled keys). (D) invents a docker CLI subcommand.

q: After `docker system prune -a`, disk usage is still dominated by old named volumes. Why weren't they removed?
options: prune -a does not remove images, only containers
The volumes must be in use — prune only removes unused ones
`docker system prune` never touches volumes unless --volumes is passed — named volumes are deliberately excluded by default as a data-safety guard
The daemon must be stopped before pruning volumes
explain: Volumes are excluded from system prune by default; --volumes opts in. The guard exists because volume data is often irreplaceable. EXAM TRAPS: (A) -a absolutely removes unused images. (B) even unused volumes survive without --volumes. (D) invents a downtime requirement.

q: A legacy Dockerfile relying on classic-builder behavior breaks under BuildKit. The team needs the classic builder for this one build only. How?
options: The classic builder was removed — rewrite the Dockerfile
DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0 docker build . — the env var selects the classic builder for that invocation
Delete the # syntax= directive line
Use `docker buildx build --driver docker`
explain: DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0 falls back to the classic builder per-invocation. EXAM TRAPS: (A) false — classic builder still ships. (C) the syntax directive only matters to BuildKit anyway. (D) buildx IS BuildKit regardless of driver.

q: Rootless dockerd fails at startup: 'newuidmap not found in PATH'. What is missing?
options: Kernel user-namespace support
A reboot to enable rootless mode
The user must be root after all
The uidmap package providing the setuid newuidmap/newgidmap helpers — rootless operation needs those helpers to set up the UID mapping; install uidmap and retry
explain: Rootless Docker delegates subordinate UID/GID setup to the setuid newuidmap/newgidmap binaries from the uidmap package. EXAM TRAPS: (A) a kernel gap would fail differently. (B) no reboot needed. (C) defeats the entire purpose of rootless.

q: Containers must resolve internal corporate names via the corporate DNS at 10.0.0.2, but the Docker host itself uses a public resolver. Where is container DNS configured?
options: Per container with --dns 10.0.0.2, or daemon-wide with "dns": ["10.0.0.2"] in daemon.json — the container's resolv.conf is built from these, independent of the host's resolver (--dns-search/--dns-opt tune search domains and options)
Edit /etc/resolv.conf inside each running container
Containers always inherit the host's DNS — it cannot be changed
Set the nameserver in the Dockerfile
explain: Container DNS is explicit: --dns (per container) or daemon.json dns (default for all) — the host's resolver is irrelevant. EXAM TRAPS: (B) in-container edits are ephemeral. (C) states the exact misconception. (D) DNS is runtime config, not image content.

q: An admin dashboard container started with -p 8080:80 is reachable from the internet. The team wants it bound to localhost only. What is the fix?
options: Add host firewall rules — Docker cannot bind selectively
Recreate it with -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 — the optional IP field in the publish spec binds the host port to localhost only
Switch the container to --network host
The publish syntax does not support IP addresses
explain: -p [IP:]hostport:containerport — omitting the IP binds all interfaces (0.0.0.0); 127.0.0.1 scopes it to loopback. EXAM TRAPS: (A) Docker binds selectively just fine. (C) host networking exposes MORE. (D) denies real syntax.

q: Containers need outbound IPv6 connectivity. The engineer adds --ipv6 to `docker run` and gets an error. What is the right approach?
options: --ipv6 is a valid `docker run` flag — the engine must be broken
Docker cannot do IPv6 at all
Use --network host for IPv6
IPv6 is a DAEMON-level setting — enable "ipv6": true with a "fixed-cidr-v6" in daemon.json (plus per-network settings); no per-container --ipv6 flag exists
explain: IPv6 is configured on the daemon (and networks), not per container — the flag the engineer reached for doesn't exist. EXAM TRAPS: (A) asserts a nonexistent flag. (B) false — Docker routes IPv6 fine once enabled. (C) host networking is not the IPv6 mechanism.

q: One container attaches to the frontend and backend networks. It must be reachable as 'web' on frontend and 'api-internal' on backend. How?
options: Set two hostnames on the container
The hostname automatically changes per network
Connect with --network-alias web on the frontend network and --network-alias api-internal on the backend network — aliases are per-network, unlike the single container-wide hostname
Network aliases require Swarm mode
explain: --network-alias registers a name on ONE network's DNS; repeat per network for different names. EXAM TRAPS: (A) a container has exactly one hostname. (B) invents adaptive hostnames. (D) aliases work on any user-defined network.

q: The corporate network already uses 10.0.0.0/8 everywhere. `docker swarm init` would auto-create overlay networks from its default pool and collide. How is this avoided?
options: Init with --default-addr-pool 10.20.0.0/16 (and --default-addr-pool-mask-length as needed) — the pool for auto-created networks is fixed AT INIT; changing it later requires leaving and re-initializing the swarm
Change the pool anytime with `docker swarm update`
Overlay subnets cannot be customized
Set --data-path-port to avoid the collision
explain: --default-addr-pool reserves the CIDR space Swarm carves overlay subnets from, and it's init-time-only. EXAM TRAPS: (B) no update path exists. (C) denies the customization. (D) data-path-port is the VXLAN UDP port (4789), unrelated to addressing.

q: A compromised container fork-bombs, exhausting the host's PID space and destabilizing neighboring containers. It ran with default settings. Which control would have contained the blast radius?
options: --memory limits — they cap process counts as well
`docker run --pids-limit 256` (compose: pids_limit) — caps processes/threads in the container's cgroup, so the fork bomb hits the container's own ceiling instead of the host's PID space
Fork bombs are impossible inside containers
--cpus limits the number of processes
explain: pids-limit is the cgroup pids controller applied per container — the direct fork-bomb defense. EXAM TRAPS: (A) memory limits don't bound task counts. (C) denies a classic attack. (D) CPU shares don't limit process count.

q: Compliance demands containers run with the absolute minimum Linux capabilities. Today they run with Docker's default ~14 capabilities. What is the correct pattern?
options: Enumerate each unwanted capability in --cap-drop
Capabilities cannot go below the Docker default
Rely on --privileged=false, which already minimizes them
`--cap-drop ALL` followed by `--cap-add` of only what is needed (e.g. --cap-add CHOWN) — deny-by-default, then grant the minimal set; verify with the CapDrop/CapAdd fields in `docker inspect`
explain: Drop-all-then-add is the least-privilege pattern; enumerating drops is fragile against future defaults. EXAM TRAPS: (A) allowlist-by-subtraction breaks when defaults change. (B) denies the mechanism. (C) non-privileged still carries the default capability set.

q: Before an audit, the team wants to check daemon and container configuration against the CIS Docker Benchmark. What fits, and what does it actually do?
options: Docker Bench for Security — it automatically remediates any misconfiguration it finds
Nothing — the CIS benchmarks do not cover Docker
Run Docker Bench for Security — it CHECKS configuration against the CIS benchmark and reports pass/warn/notes; it changes nothing itself
The benchmark scripts only apply to Swarm managers
explain: Docker Bench is an audit script, not a remediation tool — it reports, you fix. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the dangerous 'it fixes itself' myth. (B) the CIS Docker Benchmark very much exists. (D) invents a Swarm-only scope.

q: A vulnerability scan flags that all containers run as root — the image has no USER directive. What is the fix, and what must be watched?
options: Add `USER app` (creating the user in the image) or pass --user on run/service create so the process runs unprivileged — and ensure that user has filesystem permissions on any mounted volumes, or writes will fail
Root inside a container is harmless because of namespaces
--privileged defaults to false, so running as root is already safe
USER only takes effect with --privileged
explain: Dropping root via USER/--user is baseline hardening; the classic follow-on bug is volume permission denials for the non-root UID. EXAM TRAPS: (B) root-in-container is still high-risk (kernel exploits, misconfigurations). (C) conflates privileged mode with the root user. (D) invents a dependency.

q: On an SELinux-enforcing host, a NAMED volume works fine, but a BIND mount of the same data gives 'permission denied' inside the container. Why the difference?
options: Named volumes bypass SELinux entirely
Bind mounts are fundamentally incompatible with SELinux
The two mounts contain different data

Docker automatically labels named-volume content for container access, but bind-mounted host paths keep their existing SELinux labels — the bind mount needs :z/:Z (or a manual chcon) to become accessible
explain: SELinux decisions use labels: Docker sets them on volume content it manages, but never relabels arbitrary host paths unasked — hence :z/:Z. EXAM TRAPS: (A) volumes are labeled, not exempt. (B) bind mounts work fine once labeled. (C) the data is identical; the labels differ.

q: How do you back up a named volume's data into a tarball on the host?
options: `docker volume export data > backup.tar`
`docker run --rm -v data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup busybox tar czf /backup/data.tar.gz -C / data` — a throwaway container holding both mounts does the copy; there is no `docker volume export` command
tar up /var/lib/docker/volumes/data directly while containers run
Named volumes cannot be backed up
explain: The documented pattern is a transient container with the volume plus a host bind for the archive. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents a `docker volume export` command. (C) copying the raw volume dir under a live daemon risks inconsistent data. (D) denies the standard pattern.

q: Two standalone hosts must share a dataset over NFS, with no volume plugin to install. How?
options: `docker volume create -d local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=10.0.0.5,rw --opt device=:/exports/data shared` — the LOCAL driver's type=nfs option mounts NFS directly; no plugin required
Impossible — NFS always needs a third-party volume plugin
Use a bind mount — bind mounts work across hosts
`docker volume create --driver nfs shared`
explain: The built-in local driver accepts type=nfs with mount opts — the plugin-free NFS path. EXAM TRAPS: (B) states the plugin myth. (C) bind mounts are strictly local paths. (D) invents a 'nfs' driver name.

q: A container bind-mounts /mnt/data. Later the host mounts a new disk UNDER /mnt/data, but the container never sees it. Why, and what is the fix?
options: Bind mounts are snapshots — recreate the container to pick up the new mount
The container needs --privileged to see host submounts

Mount propagation defaults to rprivate — the container's mount namespace does not receive the host's new submount; use a shared propagation mode (e.g. -v /mnt/data:/data:rshared, with the host side shared too)
Docker does not support nested mounts
explain: rprivate means mount/unmount events don't propagate into the container; rshared/rslave opt into propagation. EXAM TRAPS: (A) recreating works but misses the mechanism — propagation is the real fix. (B) privileged is unnecessary. (D) denies supported functionality.

q: A manager was rebooted after the swarm was initialized with --autolock. The daemon is up, but `docker node ls` fails: 'Swarm is encrypted and needs to be unlocked'. What is needed?
options: Re-initialize the swarm with `docker swarm init`
Run `docker swarm unlock` and enter the unlock key (generated and shown at init — stored by the operator); if the key was exposed, rotate it afterward with `docker swarm unlock-key --rotate`
Restart the daemon once more — the lock clears itself
Nothing — autolock only encrypts worker join tokens
explain: Autolock encrypts Raft logs/TLS keys at rest; after a daemon restart the manager needs the unlock key. EXAM TRAPS: (A) re-init would DESTROY the swarm. (C) the lock persists across restarts by design. (D) autolock protects manager state, not join tokens.

q: A cluster runs exactly 2 managers. One manager dies. The survivor cannot schedule services or process updates — the cluster is effectively read-only. Why, and what is the guidance?
options: The survivor needs `docker swarm init --force` to seize control
Two managers tolerate one failure, so something else must be wrong
Promote a worker — the cluster will auto-restore quorum

Raft quorum for 2 managers is 2 — losing one loses quorum, freezing all writes. Run 3 or 5 managers (odd numbers): 3 tolerates 1 failure, 5 tolerates 2. Even manager counts add nodes without adding fault tolerance
explain: Quorum = floor(n/2)+1: for n=2 that's 2, so ANY single loss halts the control plane. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents a force-seize that would split-brain. (B) states the exact myth that causes this outage. (C) promotions are themselves writes — impossible without quorum.

q: A worker needs a kernel upgrade. The admin must gracefully evict its tasks first. Should they use `docker node update --availability pause` or `--availability drain`?
options: drain — it evicts the node's tasks (rescheduled elsewhere) and blocks new placements; pause only stops NEW tasks from being scheduled while existing ones keep running, which suits investigation, not maintenance
pause — it evicts all tasks from the node
They are identical — either works
Remove the node from the swarm instead
explain: drain = evict + reschedule + no-new-tasks (maintenance); pause = freeze scheduling only (diagnostics). EXAM TRAPS: (B) states pause backwards — pause never evicts. (C) conflates two distinct states. (D) removal is destructive overkill.

q: A monitoring agent must run on every WORKER node but must NOT run on managers. Which service definition does this?
options: --mode global alone — it covers managers too, violating the requirement
replicated with --constraint 'node.role==worker' and --replicas set to today's worker count

`docker service create --mode global --constraint 'node.role==worker'` — global places one task per node MATCHING the constraint, so managers are excluded and future workers are picked up automatically
Global mode cannot take placement constraints
explain: Global mode honors constraints: one task per matching node, self-maintaining as workers join. EXAM TRAPS: (A) unconstrained global hits managers. (B) a fixed replica count rots on every cluster change. (D) denies real constraint support.

q: The team builds amd64 and arm64 images separately with the classic builder and wants ONE tag that serves the right architecture to each client. How is that assembled?
options: `docker manifest create registry.corp/app:v2 --amend registry.corp/app:v2-amd64 --amend registry.corp/app:v2-arm64`, then annotate OS/arch and `docker manifest push` — a manifest list unites per-arch images under one tag (buildx --platform does this in a single step on modern toolchains)
Push both images to the same tag — the registry merges them automatically
Manifest lists are created automatically on push
Use `docker trust` to merge the architectures
explain: A manifest list (fat manifest) is the multi-arch pointer; `docker manifest` assembles it from per-arch pushes. EXAM TRAPS: (B) two pushes to one tag overwrite each other. (C) nothing is automatic with separate builds. (D) trust is signing, not manifests.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: After pushing a multi-arch image, how do you verify which platforms the tag actually serves?
options: `docker inspect registry.corp/app:v2` — it lists every platform
Pull the tag on one machine of each architecture
The registry web UI always shows the platform list
`docker buildx imagetools inspect registry.corp/app:v2` — reads the manifest list from the registry, showing platforms, per-arch digests, and attached attestations
explain: imagetools inspect resolves the tag remotely and prints the manifest list — the authoritative answer. EXAM TRAPS: (A) `docker inspect` shows only the LOCAL platform's manifest. (B) toil that proves nothing about the list. (C) UI coverage varies; the CLI is definitive.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile does `COPY . /app` followed by `RUN chown -R app:app /app`. The image is larger than expected and rebuilds are slow. What is the better pattern?
options: chown must run as its own layer — this is already optimal
`COPY --chown=app:app --chmod=755 . /app` — ownership and mode are set AT COPY time: no extra layer, smaller image, better layer caching
Use ADD instead of COPY — it sets ownership automatically
File ownership is irrelevant inside containers
explain: --chown/--chmod on COPY avoids the duplicate-layer rewrite that RUN chown causes (the files exist twice across layers). EXAM TRAPS: (A) defends the wasteful pattern. (C) ADD doesn't set ownership. (D) ownership matters for non-root USER execution.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI suddenly fails with 'toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit'. The Dockerfiles haven't changed. What is the fix?
options: Wait out the window and retry — nothing else helps
The limit is per image name — retag the image
Authenticate the pulls (`docker login`) — anonymous pulls get the lowest quota while authenticated accounts get far higher limits; for heavy CI also consider a registry mirror or pull-through cache
Rate limits only apply to pushes, so this error is impossible
explain: Hub throttles anonymous pulls hardest; authenticating raises the quota substantially — the standard CI fix, plus caching for scale. EXAM TRAPS: (A) passive waiting instead of the auth fix. (B) invents per-name accounting. (D) denies the well-known pull limit.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: After configuring the daemon's proxy for internet pulls, pulls from the INTERNAL registry at 10.20.0.5:5000 start failing — the traffic is being sent to the egress proxy. What is the fix?
options: Add the internal addresses to NO_PROXY in the dockerd systemd proxy drop-in (Environment="NO_PROXY=10.20.0.5,10.0.0.0/8"), then daemon-reload and restart — the daemon honors no-proxy exceptions; without them even internal pulls route to the proxy
Remove the proxy configuration entirely
Internal registries cannot coexist with a configured proxy
Add the registry to insecure-registries instead
explain: Proxy env for the daemon needs NO_PROXY/NO_PROXY exceptions for internal hosts — the classic 'proxy broke internal pulls' fix. EXAM TRAPS: (B) sacrifices internet pulls. (C) false — exceptions are the designed coexistence. (D) insecure-registries is about TLS, not routing.

q: Pulling from a test registry over plain HTTP fails with 'http: server gave HTTP response to HTTPS client'. How is this fixed?
options: Retry with `docker pull --insecure-registry test-registry:5000`
Docker cannot use registries without TLS, ever
Enable TLS on the client side only
Add it to daemon.json as "insecure-registries": ["test-registry:5000"] and restart the daemon — registry TLS policy is DAEMON configuration; no per-pull insecure flag exists
explain: Docker defaults to HTTPS for registries; opting out is a daemon-level insecure-registries entry. EXAM TRAPS: (A) the classic invented flag — pull has no such option. (B) false — insecure registries are supported via config. (C) TLS is negotiated with the server; client-only settings don't apply.

q: An ML container needs GPU access and nvidia-container-toolkit is installed on the host. How does the container actually get the GPU?
options: Run the container --privileged — the only way to reach GPUs
`docker run --gpus all ...` — the toolkit hooks GPU devices and libraries into the container; verify with nvidia-smi inside
GPUs attach automatically once the toolkit is installed
Bind-mount /dev/nvidia0 by hand
explain: --gpus is the supported interface (all, or device IDs); the toolkit handles device nodes, libraries, and driver wiring. EXAM TRAPS: (A) privileged is the overkill myth. (C) installation alone attaches nothing. (D) manual device binds miss the userspace libraries.

q: An app logs 'too many open files' inside containers but never on the host, whose limits are high. Why?
options: Containers inherit the invoking user's shell limits, so the app must be misreading them
Raise the host's limits even higher
Containers receive the DAEMON's default ulimits, not your shell's — set --ulimit nofile=65536:65536 on run/service create, or set default-ulimits in daemon.json
ulimits cannot be changed for containers
explain: The daemon (usually started by systemd with its own LimitNOFILE) seeds container ulimits — your interactive shell limits are irrelevant. EXAM TRAPS: (A) states the exact misconception. (B) tuning the wrong layer. (D) denies --ulimit/default-ulimits.

q: A Swarm service must publish a port in HOST mode (bypassing the ingress routing mesh to preserve client source IPs), but the short -p syntax cannot express the mode. How is it done?
options: The short syntax supports it: -p 8080:80,mode=host
Host-mode publishing is impossible for Swarm services
Put the service on --network host instead
Use the long publish syntax: --publish published=8080,target=80,protocol=tcp,mode=host — the mode field is only available in the long form
explain: mode=host|vip|ingress is a long-syntax-only field on service publish. EXAM TRAPS: (A) invents short-syntax support. (B) denies a real feature. (C) --network host discards Swarm networking entirely — a different, blunter tool.

q: The database network must allow app↔database traffic but have NO route to the internet. How is this built?
options: `docker network create --internal dbnet` — internal networks block external access while keeping inter-container connectivity intact
Simply don't publish any ports — that also blocks egress
Create the network with --icc=false
Internal networks also block container-to-container traffic, so this can't be done
explain: --internal drops the gateway/egress path but leaves container-to-container traffic working. EXAM TRAPS: (B) publishing controls INGRESS; egress stays open. (C) icc=false blocks container-to-container — the opposite axis. (D) states the opposite of --internal semantics.

q: What does `docker network prune` remove?
options: Every network, including ones in use
Only the default bridge network
Only UNUSED networks — any network with connected containers or endpoints is left alone
Networks and their attached volumes
explain: Prune is safe by default: only networks with no endpoints are removed. EXAM TRAPS: (A) in-use networks are protected. (B) invents a single-target scope. (D) volumes are a separate prune.

q: Two containers share a user-defined bridge but must NOT communicate directly with each other — traffic may only flow via published ports through the host. How?
options: Move them to separate networks

Disable inter-container communication on the bridge (--opt com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false at create, or --icc=false on the daemon) — containers stay mutually isolated while published ports keep working
icc=false also disables published ports, so add explicit ACCEPT rules
Connect them with --link, which blocks traffic by default
explain: ICC=false cuts container-to-container traffic on the bridge; ingress via published ports is unaffected. EXAM TRAPS: (A) works but redesigns around the actual feature. (C) states the opposite — published ports still function. (D) --link is legacy and ENABLES access, not blocks.

q: A build needs a private package-feed token during a RUN step, but the token must NOT end up in any image layer. The team currently passes it via --build-arg. What is wrong, and what is the fix?
options: --build-arg values persist in image history and metadata — use RUN --mount=type=secret,id=feedtoken with `docker build --secret id=feedtoken,src=./token.txt`: the secret is mounted only for that RUN step and never committed to a layer
build-args are never persisted anywhere
Switch to ENV — it is more secure than ARG
Build-time secrets are impossible in Docker
explain: Build-args leak via `docker history`/metadata; BuildKit secret mounts exist precisely for build-time credentials. EXAM TRAPS: (B) the dangerous myth. (C) ENV is WORSE — baked into the runtime environment. (D) denies the secret-mount feature.

q: The team loses the private key used to sign their DCT repository. What is the actual consequence?
options: The registry admin can regenerate the identical key
All previously signed tags become unverifiable

They cannot publish NEW signed tags with that key — recovery means rotating to a new key/delegation, and clients pinned to the old trust must adopt the new one; this is why offline root keys and delegation exist
Nothing — signing keys are optional metadata
explain: Existing signatures verify with the PUBLIC key (still published), but new signatures need the private key — hence rotation and delegation practices. EXAM TRAPS: (A) private keys can't be regenerated by anyone. (B) confuses signing ability with verification. (D) dismisses the whole trust model.

q: Company policy mandates MFA for all admin access, enforced through the corporate SAML identity provider. How does MKE integrate?
options: MKE cannot use external identity providers
MKE caches SAML passwords locally for offline authentication
Enforce MFA inside MKE's local user settings
Point MKE's SAML auth backend at the identity provider — authentication (including MFA) is delegated to the IdP; MKE maps the asserted identity to its users/teams for RBAC
explain: MKE delegates auth to the IdP via SAML/LDAP and applies its own RBAC to the asserted identity — MFA lives at the IdP. EXAM TRAPS: (A) denies real IdP support. (B) SAML never gives MKE the password. (C) MFA can't be bolted onto local auth to satisfy the IdP mandate.

q: The team pins every production image by digest. A teammate argues Docker Content Trust signing is now redundant. Is it?
options: Yes — a digest proves who published the image
No — digest pinning proves WHAT bits you run (immutability), while DCT signing proves WHO published them (authenticity); they defend against different attacks and complement each other
Yes — Docker Content Trust is deprecated
Digests change on every pull, so pinning is meaningless anyway
explain: Digests stop tag-mutation attacks; signatures stop publisher-impersonation attacks. Dropping either leaves a hole. EXAM TRAPS: (A) conflates integrity with authenticity. (C) DCT is not deprecated. (D) digests are content-addressed and stable.

q: Every redeploy of a compose app leaks disk: `docker volume ls` shows dozens of random-hex volumes. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The compose file uses ANONYMOUS volumes (-v /data with no name) — each recreate mints a fresh one while the old one lingers; switch to named volumes and clean up with `docker volume prune`
Named volumes leak by design — nothing to do
`docker rm` removes anonymous volumes automatically
Volume names cannot be listed
explain: Anonymous volumes are recreated per container and orphaned on replace — the classic compose disk leak. EXAM TRAPS: (B) blames named volumes. (C) only `docker rm -v` removes them. (D) denies `docker volume ls`.

q: One container's runaway writes fill the shared disk, starving its neighbors. The team wants a per-container disk cap. What works?
options: --storage-opt size=10G works on every driver and filesystem
Per-container disk quotas are impossible
Set --tmpfs-size — it caps all container writes

Use --storage-opt size=10G — but it requires a supporting backend (devicemapper, or overlay2/zfs on filesystems with project quotas such as XFS with pquota); it is NOT universal, so check the driver/filesystem first
explain: size= is backend-dependent: devicemapper natively, overlay2/zfs only with quota-capable backing fs. EXAM TRAPS: (A) states universality that doesn't exist. (B) denies the feature. (C) tmpfs-size only bounds tmpfs mounts.

q: An image bakes default config into /app/config. Mounting a NAMED volume there shows the defaults, editable. But a BIND mount to an empty host dir shows an empty /app/config. Why the difference?
options: Named volumes are broken and should not be used
On FIRST use, Docker populates a named volume with the image's content at the mount path — deliberate seeding behavior; bind mounts never populate, they simply overlay the host directory
Bind mounts populate too — the host dir must be non-empty
Mounting deletes the image content in both cases
explain: Volume initialization copies image content into a fresh named volume once; bind mounts have no such step. EXAM TRAPS: (A) dismisses the feature. (C) states the opposite. (D) nothing is deleted.

q: The backup agent runs in a restricted context that can only read /data/volumes. The team wants named volumes' data to live at predictable paths under /data/volumes/<name> on the node — no shared storage involved. What provides this?
options: Replace all named volumes with bind mounts at hardcoded paths
Symlink /var/lib/docker/volumes subdirectories into /data/volumes

The local-persist volume plugin — it maps named volumes to deterministic host paths (`docker volume create -d local-persist -o mountpoint=/data/volumes/<name> --name <name>`); the volume stays node-local, just addressable where the backup agent can reach it
Move the entire /var/lib/docker directory to /data
explain: local-persist pins a named volume to a chosen host path — volume semantics with a fixed location. EXAM TRAPS: (A) abandons volume management for toil. (B) symlinks under the daemon's directory are fragile. (D) relocating all of /var/lib/docker is massive overkill for one backup path.

q: `docker info` shows 'Storage Driver: vfs' and disk usage is enormous with painfully slow builds. What is the story?
options: vfs is the recommended production storage driver
Swarm requires the vfs driver
Disk usage is unrelated to the storage driver choice
vfs performs a full filesystem copy per layer with no copy-on-write — simple and robust, but enormously wasteful; it is a fallback/debugging driver, not for production — move to overlay2
explain: vfs = naive full copies, no CoW, no sharing between layers — correct but the slowest, most wasteful driver. EXAM TRAPS: (A) states the opposite of guidance. (B) invents a Swarm requirement. (C) driver choice dominates disk usage.

q: A platform team publishes a shared `base.yaml` in a Git repo with hardened logging and resource defaults, and each app team keeps its own `compose.yaml`. An engineer tries `extends:` pointing at the remote file so the app project can reuse it, but Compose rejects remote references in `extends`. Which construct is actually designed for pulling another Compose file into the project, and how does it differ from `extends`?
options: Use `include:` — it merges additional Compose files (local paths or URLs) into the project as extra services, networks, and volumes; `extends`, by contrast, reuses individual service definitions by merging one service's fields into another within files Compose can already read
Use `extends:` with a `!reset` tag — that enables remote URLs in extends
`include:` only works for local files, never URLs, so the shared file must be vendored into every repo
Pass both files with `docker compose -f base.yaml -f compose.yaml up` — that is byte-identical to `include:`, so `include:` was deprecated
explain: `include` (Compose 2.20+) is the composition mechanism: it pulls whole additional Compose files — local paths or remote URLs — into the current project. `extends` is the reuse mechanism: it copies/merges fields from one service definition into another. The engineer's mistake was using the reuse tool for a composition job. Wrong options: `!reset` is a YAML merge tag for overriding extends, not a URL enabler; `include` explicitly supports URLs; and `-f` merging vs `include` differ in project-directory resolution and interpolation context — `include` is not deprecated.

q: A developer runs `docker compose watch` on a dev project. Edits under `./src` sync into the running container instantly, while editing `requirements.txt` triggers a rebuild. A teammate claims 'watch rebuilds the image on every save, so it's just a slower `docker compose up --build`.' The watch section declares `action: sync` for `./src` and `action: rebuild` for `requirements.txt`. What actually happens on each change type?
options: Watch only works with `docker stack deploy`, so in a plain Compose project it silently falls back to polling `up --build`
`sync` actions require the container to have an SSH daemon; without one, watch rebuilds everything
Every file change rebuilds the image — the teammate is right; `sync` is just a label for the rebuild strategy
`sync` copies changed files straight into the running container with no rebuild or restart; `rebuild` rebuilds the image (and recreates the container) — the two actions behave differently by design
explain: Watch rules are per-path actions: `sync` streams file changes into the running container (fast, no rebuild), `rebuild` rebuilds the image when dependencies change, and `restart` just restarts the container. The teammate conflated the actions. Wrong options: watch is a local dev workflow for `docker compose` — it has nothing to do with Swarm stacks; and sync uses the Docker API exec/copy path, not SSH.

q: A compose file defines `app`, `db`, and a `debug-tools` service carrying `profiles: ["debug"]`. `docker compose up -d` starts `app` and `db` but not `debug-tools`. On-call needs the debug container running right now, without editing the file. Which command does it, and what is the underlying rule?
options: `docker compose --profile debug up -d` — services carrying a profile are excluded from default startup and only start when their profile is enabled; equivalently `COMPOSE_PROFILES=debug` works
`docker compose up -d --force-profiles` — profiles are mandatory and the flag overrides them
Profiles only affect `docker stack deploy`, so `up` should have started it — this is a Compose bug; restart the daemon
`docker compose up debug-tools` can never start a profiled service; the profile must first be removed from the file
explain: Profiles are opt-in groups: any service with a `profiles:` list is skipped unless one of its profiles is enabled via `--profile` or `COMPOSE_PROFILES`. The exam-relevant subtlety: explicitly naming the service (`docker compose up debug-tools`) ALSO starts it even without the profile — so option D's 'never' is false. Wrong options: there is no `--force-profiles` flag, and profiles are a Compose client concept, unrelated to Swarm deploys.

q: A stack file declares the `api` service with `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy`. After `docker stack deploy`, `api` starts before the database is healthy and crashes on boot. The engineer concludes Compose health conditions are broken. What is actually happening?
options: The `condition:` syntax is invalid — Swarm only accepts the short `depends_on: [db]` list form, so the whole key was rejected

Swarm's orchestrator ignores `depends_on` entirely — startup ordering is a single-engine Compose concept; `docker stack deploy` schedules all services as soon as their constraints are satisfiable, so `api` must implement retry/backoff against the database itself
The healthcheck on `db` was misconfigured, so the condition could never evaluate — fix the healthcheck and ordering works
`service_healthy` requires the `db` service to use `--endpoint-mode dnsrr`; with the default VIP mode the condition is skipped
explain: Swarm does not honor `depends_on` (short or long syntax) — it is one of the Compose keys the stack deploy path ignores, along with `build`, `container_name`, and `restart`. Ordering guarantees simply don't exist in the orchestrator, so services must be resilient to dependencies starting later (retry loops, wait-for-it patterns). Wrong options: the long syntax with `condition: service_healthy` is valid Compose; a healthcheck fix can't create ordering Swarm never implements; endpoint mode has no bearing on startup order.

q: A repo has `docker-bake.hcl` defining targets `api` and `worker` plus the implicit `default` group. CI runs `docker buildx bake`, tags are set in the file, but nothing is pushed to the registry. The engineer assumed bake pushes by default, like they believed `docker buildx build` does. What is the actual push behavior?
options: The `default` group only builds the first target alphabetically; `worker` was never built
Bake pushes every target automatically — the registry must be rejecting the push; check authentication

Bake only pushes when a target sets `push = true` or the invocation passes `--push`; by default it just builds (and with no output configured, results stay in the build cache). The engineer's mental model was wrong on both counts — plain `docker buildx build` doesn't push either without `--push`
Bake files must be JSON — the HCL file was silently ignored and nothing built at all
explain: Buildx never pushes unless told: `--push` on the CLI or `push = true` in the bake target. Bake's `default` group builds all targets, honoring each target's outputs. Wrong options: authentication failures produce explicit errors, not silent no-push; HCL is a first-class bake format (docker-bake.hcl / .json / .override variants all work); the default group includes every target, not just one.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI builds from `docker-bake.hcl`, where the `api` target pins `tags = ["registry/app:release"]`. For an emergency hotfix the team must build the same target with tag `registry/app:hotfix-42` WITHOUT editing the file or duplicating the target. Which invocation does it?
options: `docker buildx bake --build-arg TAGS=registry/app:hotfix-42 api` — build args override bake target fields
Copy the file to `docker-bake.hotfix.hcl`, edit the tag, and run `docker buildx bake -f docker-bake.hotfix.hcl api` — bake targets are immutable at invocation time
Bake always uses the tags in the file; the only override is rebuilding with plain `docker buildx build -t`
`docker buildx bake --set api.tags=registry/app:hotfix-42 api` — `--set` overrides target fields with `target.key=value` syntax, so the file stays untouched
explain: Bake's `--set` flag overrides any target attribute at invocation time (`--set <target>.<field>=<value>`, with `*` as a wildcard target). It's the designed mechanism for CI parameterization without file surgery. Wrong options: `--build-arg` feeds Dockerfile ARG, not bake metadata; duplicating the HCL file works but defeats bake's purpose and is exactly what `--set` avoids; and plain `docker build` loses the target's platforms, cache, and secret configuration.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile uses `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token pip install ...`. Locally, `docker buildx build --secret id=token,src=./token.txt .` works, but CI fails with 'secret not found'. A teammate proposes `--build-arg TOKEN=$(cat token.txt)` as the portable fix. Why is the teammate's fix dangerous, and what is the correct CI change?
options: Pass `--secret id=token,src=...` (or the CI secret equivalent) in the CI build invocation too; the teammate's `--build-arg` expands the token into a RUN layer, where it stays visible in `docker history` and in the image config forever — secret mounts, by contrast, never end up in any layer
Secret mounts only work with the `docker` build driver, not `docker-container`, so CI must switch drivers
The correct fix is `ENV TOKEN` in the Dockerfile — environment variables are stripped at push time
Build args are fine — ARG values never persist in the image, so the teammate's fix is safe and simpler
explain: `--build-arg` values are interpolated into the Dockerfile instructions and baked into layer history (`docker history` shows the full `RUN curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ..."` line). BuildKit secret mounts expose the secret only to that single RUN step and never commit it to a layer. The CI fix is to supply the secret the same way locally — via `--secret` wired to the CI system's secret store. Wrong options: ENV is equally baked into the image config and visible in `docker inspect`; secret mounts work with the container driver (they require BuildKit, not a specific driver).
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A workstation's `~/.docker/config.json` contains both `"credsStore": "osxkeychain"` and `"credHelpers": {"registry.internal.example": "pass"}`. The engineer runs `docker login registry.internal.example` and is asked where the credential lands. Where does it go?
options: Into the macOS keychain, because `credsStore` is the global default and always wins
Base64-encoded in the `auths` section of config.json — `docker login` always writes `auths`
Into the `pass` credential helper, because a per-registry `credHelpers` entry takes precedence over the global `credsStore` for that registry
Nowhere — with both configured, Docker refuses to store the credential and uses it for the session only
explain: Precedence is: `credHelpers` (per-registry) beats `credsStore` (global default). So this registry's credential goes to `pass`; every other registry falls back to the macOS keychain. Wrong options: `credsStore` is the fallback, not the winner; `docker login` only writes base64 `auths` when NO helper/store is configured (and that encoding is obfuscation, not encryption); Docker never silently session-only stores on login.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An admin manages three remote engines. They export `DOCKER_HOST=ssh://admin@node2`, yet `docker context ls` still shows `default` with the `*` marker. `docker ps` lists node2's containers. Confused, they ask a colleague which setting is actually in effect. What is the answer?
options: Neither — mixing `DOCKER_HOST` with contexts corrupts the CLI state and every command fails until `docker context use default` is run
The SSH connection goes to node2 but authentication uses the `default` context's TLS certs
The `default` context — the `*` marker is authoritative and environment variables are only read when no contexts exist
`DOCKER_HOST`, because environment variables override the active context; the `*` merely shows which context WOULD be used if the variable were unset
explain: The Docker CLI resolves the daemon endpoint with a clear precedence: `DOCKER_HOST` (and friends like `DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY`) override whatever context is active. `docker context ls`'s asterisk shows the active context, which only applies when the env vars are unset. Contexts themselves are purely client-side state in `~/.docker/contexts`. Wrong options: env vars are not a fallback — they're the override; nothing is corrupted; and TLS material comes from the endpoint's own config, not blended across sources.

q: During a daemon upgrade on a host with `"live-restore": true` in daemon.json, all containers kept running — the team was impressed. A month later, after a scheduled host reboot for a kernel patch, every container was down and an incident was filed claiming 'live-restore is broken'. Is it?
options: Yes — live-restore is supposed to survive host reboots; the kernel patch must have wiped the container state

No — live-restore only keeps containers running across daemon restarts/upgrades/crashes; a host reboot stops everything, and containers come back only via restart policies (`--restart unless-stopped`/`always`) plus the daemon starting on boot
No — live-restore only applies to Swarm services, not standalone containers, so the standalone ones were never protected
Yes — but only because live-restore requires the `containerd` image store; with the default storage it silently disables itself
explain: Live restore bridges daemon downtime: the daemon can stop, crash, or upgrade while containerd keeps workloads alive. A host reboot is outside that contract — the kernel is gone, so everything stops, and recovery depends on restart policies and the daemon's own autostart. It is also off by default and must be set before the daemon starts. Wrong options: live-restore covers standalone and Swarm containers alike; and it has no dependency on the containerd image store.

q: After enabling `"userns-remap": "default"` on a host, a container that bind-mounts a host directory starts getting permission-denied writing files it used to write fine. On the host, those files are owned by root. `docker exec` shows the app running as root inside the container. What changed?
options: With userns-remap, container root (uid 0) maps to an unprivileged subordinate UID (the `dockremap` range from /etc/subuid), so host files owned by real root are now inaccessible — the directory must be chowned to the mapped subordinate range
Userns-remap forces all containers to run as the `nobody` user; the app must be rewritten to drop privileges itself
The bind mount now requires the `:Z` SELinux flag or the kernel denies the write
Userns-remap is incompatible with bind mounts — the data must be moved into a named volume
explain: User namespaces remap the container's UID 0 to a high, unprivileged host UID (default `dockremap:231072:65536` in /etc/subuid). Host-root-owned bind-mount content is suddenly owned by 'someone else' from the container's mapped perspective. The fix is `chown`ing the host path into the subordinate range (or using named volumes, whose ownership Docker manages). Wrong options: the app still runs as root *inside* its namespace; `:Z` is an SELinux relabeling concern, orthogonal; bind mounts work fine under remap once ownership is fixed.

q: Containers on a user-defined bridge cannot resolve an internal corporate domain that the host itself resolves fine. The engineer works around it per-container with `docker run --dns 10.0.0.53`, but wants it fleet-wide so every new container inherits it. Which daemon setting does this, and what does it NOT change?
options: `--dns` can only be set per container; there is no daemon-wide equivalent — the workaround is the solution
Set `"dns-search"` instead — `"dns"` only affects the default bridge, not user-defined networks

`"dns": ["10.0.0.53"]` in daemon.json — it sets the default upstream DNS servers containers use for external lookups; it does NOT replace the embedded 127.0.0.11 resolver on user-defined networks, which keeps serving container-name queries and forwards upstream to these servers
`"dns": ["10.0.0.53"]` in daemon.json — it replaces 127.0.0.11 entirely, so container-name resolution stops working
explain: The daemon-wide `dns` list becomes the default upstream resolver for containers (it lands in their resolv.conf / is used by the embedded server as forwarder). The embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 remains authoritative for container names on user-defined networks — the two are complementary, not replacements. Wrong options: container-name resolution is untouched; a daemon-wide setting absolutely exists; `dns-search` sets search domains, a different knob.

q: A monitoring system must scrape metrics from EACH task of a Swarm service individually. With the default endpoint mode, scraping the service name only ever reaches one task's metrics. Which endpoint mode exposes every task, and how does it change client behavior?
options: `--endpoint-mode dnsrr` — DNS queries for the service name return the IP of every task, so the scraper must iterate over all returned addresses itself; there is no single virtual IP doing the balancing anymore
`--endpoint-mode vip` — the virtual IP already fans out to all tasks, so the scraper just needs to add more replicas
`--endpoint-mode host` — a Swarm endpoint mode that publishes every task on the host network
Endpoint mode only affects published ports; service-name DNS always returns all tasks regardless
explain: VIP mode (default) gives one virtual IP with kernel-level (IPVS) load balancing — perfect for clients, useless for per-task scraping. DNSRR mode makes the embedded DNS return every task IP, pushing the fan-out decision to the client. Wrong options: adding replicas under VIP still hides tasks behind one IP; there is no `host` endpoint mode (that's `--network host`, a different concept); endpoint mode directly controls service-name DNS answers.

q: A service publishes `-p 8080:80` in the default ingress mode with two tasks on one node — both serve traffic fine. After redeploying with long-syntax `mode=host` publishing, the second task fails to start with a port conflict. What did ingress mode provide that host mode doesn't?
options: Ingress mode is just an alias for host mode; the conflict is a firewall issue on that node
Host mode requires `--endpoint-mode dnsrr`; without it, ports collide
The conflict proves host mode is unsupported in Swarm — published ports only work in ingress mode

Ingress mode load-balances 8080 through the routing mesh, so the port is bound once per node by the mesh, not once per task — host mode binds the host's port 8080 directly in each task, so two tasks on one node collide
explain: Ingress-mode publishing goes through the swarm routing mesh: every node listens on the published port and routes to a task anywhere. Host-mode publishing bypasses the mesh and binds the port in the task's network namespace on its host — one task per port per node, full stop. That's the trade-off: host mode removes a hop but sacrifices the mesh's any-node serving. Wrong options: they're distinct modes, not aliases; endpoint mode is orthogonal; host-mode publishing is fully supported.

q: A one-off debug container is started with `docker run --network myoverlay nginx`, where `myoverlay` is a Swarm overlay network carrying the app's services. It fails: the network 'cannot be used' by standalone containers, though every Swarm service attaches fine. What is missing?
options: The overlay must be created with `--attachable` — without it, only Swarm-managed tasks may join; standalone `docker run` containers are rejected
The container must be started with `docker service create` — overlays can never carry standalone containers
The debug container needs `--network-alias` matching a service name to be admitted
Overlay networks only work on manager nodes; the command ran on a worker
explain: `--attachable` explicitly opens a Swarm overlay to manually-attached standalone containers (the classic debugging use case). Without it, the network is exclusive to service tasks. The flag is set at `docker network create` time. Wrong options: attachable overlays absolutely carry standalone containers; network aliases are for DNS, not admission; overlays span all nodes — managers vs workers is irrelevant here.

q: A `db-net` overlay was created with `--internal`. The app reaches the database, but the database cannot pull OS patches from the internet — intended. The team now wants the DB to fetch updates through a proxy container without exposing the DB itself. Which statement about `--internal` is true and enables this design?
options: `--internal` only blocks external egress from containers on that network; a proxy container attached to BOTH `db-net` and an external network can ferry traffic, while the DB itself stays isolated
`--internal` is equivalent to `--opt encrypted` — it encrypts traffic rather than isolating it
Internal networks reject all inbound connections, so even the app couldn't reach the DB — the network was miscreated
`--internal` disables the embedded DNS, so the proxy design can't work — the flag must be removed
explain: `--internal` cuts the network's external route (no default gateway to the outside) while leaving intra-network connectivity and DNS intact. The standard pattern is exactly the dual-homed proxy: one container straddling the internal and external networks. Wrong options: DNS keeps working on internal networks; encryption is the separate `--opt encrypted`; and inbound from attached containers is the whole point — only external egress is blocked.

q: A team reserves `10.5.0.10` for a logging collector by creating the network with `--subnet 10.5.0.0/24 --aux-address "collector=10.5.0.10" --ip-range 10.5.0.128/25`. Weeks later, a container started with `--ip 10.5.0.10` fails with 'address already allocated', and the team is confused because nothing holds that IP. What do `--aux-address` and `--ip-range` actually do?
options: `--aux-address` permanently assigns the IP to the named host, so `--ip` can never reuse it — the collector must be a Swarm service instead
Nothing — both flags are documentation-only; Docker's IPAM ignores them

`--aux-address` excludes the address from the dynamic pool (reserving it for manual `--ip` use), and `--ip-range` restricts which subnet slice dynamic assignment draws from; the failure means the reservation was created but the address was ALSO handed out earlier — aux-address only takes effect at network creation and can't retroactively reclaim an already-leased IP
`--aux-address` reserves the IP, so the `--ip` failure proves another container already claimed 10.5.0.10 — find it with `docker network inspect`
explain: `--aux-address` carves named exclusions out of the pool IPAM allocates dynamically — the standard way to keep a static IP from colliding with DHCP-style assignment. `--ip-range` narrows the dynamic slice. The trap: both are create-time IPAM inputs. If 10.5.0.10 was leased dynamically BEFORE the network was recreated with the reservation (or the container holding it wasn't recreated), the exclusion can't evict the existing lease. Wrong options: aux-address doesn't bind the IP to anything — it withholds it; the flags are fully honored by IPAM; and 'already allocated' here reflects the stale pre-reservation lease, not a second claimant.

q: A container is hardened with `--cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE` so its non-root app can bind port 443. On startup the entrypoint script's `chown app:app /data` fails with 'Operation not permitted'. A teammate says 'just run as root — root bypasses capability checks.' What is the minimal correct fix, and why is the teammate wrong?
options: Add `--cap-add=CHOWN` — file ownership changes require `CAP_CHOWN`, which was dropped with ALL; and the teammate is wrong because capability checks apply even to uid 0 once the capability is dropped from the bounding set — root without CAP_CHOWN still can't chown
Run as root — the teammate is right; uid 0 bypasses all capability checks regardless of `--cap-drop`
Add `--privileged` — chown requires full privilege; capabilities can't grant it piecemeal
Remove `--cap-drop=ALL` — dropping ALL is all-or-nothing and can't be combined with `--cap-add`
explain: `chown` needs `CAP_CHOWN`; with ALL dropped, even uid 0 is denied — capabilities are enforced against root too once removed from the bounding set. That's precisely why `--cap-drop=ALL` is such a strong hardening primitive. The fix stays surgical: add back only CHOWN (FOWNER/SETUID/SETGID neighbors only if the app proves it needs them). Wrong options: root does not bypass dropped caps; `--privileged` is a sledgehammer for a scalpel problem; drop-ALL plus selective add-back is the canonical least-privilege pattern.

q: A team adopts `--read-only` for all containers. An engineer worries this will break service discovery: 'If the root filesystem is read-only, Docker can't update `/etc/hosts` and `/etc/resolv.conf` when containers start and stop — name resolution will go stale.' What actually happens to those files under `--read-only`?
options: The engineer is right — `--read-only` freezes `/etc/hosts`, so containers must use `--add-host` for every dependency at creation time

Docker bind-mounts `/etc/hosts`, `/etc/hostname`, and `/etc/resolv.conf` into every container as writable mounts, independent of `--read-only` — the flag locks the image layers, not these runtime-managed files, so name resolution keeps working
Name resolution bypasses files entirely — the embedded DNS never consults `/etc/hosts`, so the question is moot
`--read-only` is silently ignored when the container is attached to a user-defined network, which is why resolution keeps working
explain: Even on `--read-only` containers, Docker mounts /etc/hosts, /etc/hostname, and /etc/resolv.conf as individual writable bind mounts (managed by the daemon, living outside the container's rootfs). `--read-only` applies to the image's layers only. So the daemon keeps rewriting hosts entries as the network changes, and the embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) keeps resolving container names. Wrong options: no `--add-host` workaround is needed; the embedded DNS DOES fall through to /etc/hosts semantics for some lookups, but that path still works because the file is a writable mount; and `--read-only` is enforced regardless of network type.

q: An admin sets `DOCKER_HOST=tcp://manager:2376` to reach a remote daemon that was configured with `--tlsverify`. Every command fails at the TLS handshake. The daemon is up and port 2376 is reachable. What is the client missing?
options: Remove `--tlsverify` from the daemon — it is incompatible with remote TCP access
Nothing — `--tlsverify` on the daemon auto-issues client certificates on first connection; the failure must be a firewall rule

The client must present certificates: set `DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1` and `DOCKER_CERT_PATH` (or pass `--tlsverify --tlscacert --tlscert --tlskey`) pointing at the CA, client cert, and key — without them the daemon rejects the handshake
Connect to port 2375 instead — TLS-enabled daemons listen on 2375 and upgrade opportunistically
explain: `--tlsverify` means the daemon requires mutually-authenticated TLS: clients must present a cert signed by the daemon's CA. The CLI gets that material from `DOCKER_CERT_PATH` (ca.pem, cert.pem, key.pem) plus `DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1`, or the explicit `--tls*` flags. Wrong options: no auto-issuance exists (that's what makes it secure); 2375 is the conventional *unencrypted* port — connecting there to a TLS daemon fails differently and downgrading is the opposite of the goal; `--tlsverify` is precisely the flag FOR remote TCP access.

q: A team must distribute two files to Swarm tasks: a database password and a 2MB license file. An engineer puts both into Swarm secrets, but `docker secret create license ./license.bin` is rejected. What is the correct split, and why?
options: Both must be secrets — the rejection is a bug; retry with `docker secret create --force`

Put the password in a secret and the 2MB license in a config — secrets are capped at 500KB and are encrypted at rest (raft log) and in transit, while configs have no such size cap but are NOT encrypted, making them right for large non-sensitive files
Split the license into five 400KB secrets — secrets are the only swarm-native distribution mechanism
Bake both files into the image — swarm distribution is deprecated for files over 500KB
explain: Swarm secrets are limited to 500KB each and are the encrypted channel (encrypted in the raft logs, TLS in transit, mounted as tmpfs in the container). Configs use the same distribution machinery without encryption or the tight size cap — the right home for large non-sensitive blobs like license files. Wrong options: there is no `--force` for secret create; chunking a license across secrets is operational madness; baking secrets into images is the canonical anti-pattern.

q: Tasks spread across three Swarm nodes need shared read-write file storage. An engineer runs `docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=10.0.0.10,rw --opt device=:/exports/data shared` and it works on every node. A teammate insists 'the local driver can't do NFS — you need a volume plugin like rex-ray.' Who is right?
options: Both are wrong — NFS volumes can only be declared in a Compose file, not created via the CLI
The engineer got lucky — the volume works on one node but the data won't actually be shared
The teammate — `local` only manages host directories; NFS requires a third-party volume plugin
The engineer — the `local` driver accepts `type`, `device`, and `o` mount options and can mount anything the kernel supports, including NFS and CIFS; no plugin is needed for basic NFS
explain: The local driver's `--opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=... --opt device=:/path` passes straight through to the kernel mount — NFS, CIFS, tmpfs-style mounts are all fair game with zero plugins. Plugins like rex-ray add orchestration (provisioning cloud disks per node), not the ability to speak NFS. Wrong options: CLI creation is fully supported; and NFS is genuinely shared storage — every node's mount points at the same server export.

q: `docker run -v /data/incoming:/app/incoming` auto-creates `/data/incoming` on the host when missing, but the equivalent `--mount type=bind,source=/data/incoming,target=/app/incoming` fails with 'source does not exist'. CI 'fixed' it by pre-creating directories. What behavioral difference is this, and which is the safer default?
options: `--mount` is deprecated — `-v` is the only supported bind syntax, and the error is a deprecation warning

`--mount` requires the bind source to exist and fails fast otherwise, while `-v` silently creates it as root; `--mount`'s explicitness is safer — auto-created root-owned directories are a classic source of permission bugs
`-v` validates the source and `--mount` doesn't — the behaviors are reversed from what was observed
Both auto-create; the `--mount` failure was caused by a typo in `target=`
explain: This is the documented `-v` vs `--mount` divergence: `-v` is lenient (creates missing host paths as root), `--mount` is strict (bind sources must pre-exist). The strictness is the safer default — a typo'd path fails loudly instead of conjuring a root-owned directory that later breaks non-root containers. Wrong options: `--mount` is the modern recommended syntax, not deprecated; the observed behaviors are as stated, not reversed.

q: A session cache must never touch disk and must vanish with the container. The engineer proposes `docker run --tmpfs /cache:size=100m,mode=1777`. A teammate warns 'tmpfs is disk-backed on some drivers' and suggests a named volume instead. Who is right?
options: The engineer — tmpfs is RAM-backed (swappable, never written to the container's filesystem), scoped to the container's lifetime, and sized/capped explicitly; a named volume would persist the cache on disk past container removal, defeating both requirements
Neither — sensitive ephemeral data must use Swarm secrets, which are the only RAM-backed mount
The engineer is right about RAM, but tmpfs cannot be size-limited — the `size=` option is ignored
The teammate — tmpfs mounts are backed by the storage driver, so they persist like volumes
explain: tmpfs mounts live in host memory (page cache, swappable under pressure), never in the storage driver, and evaporate with the container — the textbook fit for sensitive ephemeral scratch. Named volumes persist on disk by design.
