Wrong options: storage drivers are not involved in tmpfs; secrets are RAM-backed too but are for distribution of small sensitive values (500KB cap), not a 100MB cache; and `size=`/`mode=` are honored tmpfs options.

q: A host carries 40 volumes: 30 disposable scratch volumes and 10 critical data volumes labeled `keep=true` at creation (`docker volume create --label keep=true data1`). The admin wants one command that prunes the scratch volumes while provably sparing the labeled ones. Which single command achieves this, and how does the filter keep the labeled volumes out of the deletion set?
options: `docker volume prune --filter "label=keep"` — the filter selects volumes to DELETE, so this deletes exactly the labeled ones (the opposite of what is wanted)
`docker volume prune` prompts per volume — just answer 'no' ten times

`docker volume prune --filter "label!=keep"` — prune deletes unused volumes, and the label filter narrows the candidate set first: only unused volumes WITHOUT the keep label are removed; labeled volumes are excluded from deletion even if unused
Labels cannot be set on volumes — use a naming convention and `--filter "name!=data*"` instead
explain: Prune filters are ANDed with the 'unused' criterion: the command considers only unused volumes, then keeps only those matching the filter — `label!=keep` matches volumes lacking the label, so the ten labeled data volumes are excluded from the deletion set. This is the standard protect-prune pattern (labels double as documentation). WRONG options: `label=keep` would select the critical volumes FOR deletion — the classic inverted-filter footgun; prune never prompts per volume; and `--label` is fully supported on `docker volume create`.

q: A Swarm was initialized with `--autolock`. After a manager reboots for patching, `docker node ls` on it fails: the swarm is locked and the unlock key was never stored anywhere safe. The other two managers are healthy. What is the recovery path?
options: Restart the Docker daemon — the lock clears automatically once the daemon rejoins the Raft quorum
The unlock key is printed in the daemon logs on every boot; grep the journal and run `docker swarm unlock`
Wait 24 hours — locked managers auto-unlock after the Raft snapshot interval elapses

The key cannot be recovered on the locked node; from a healthy manager, remove the locked node (`docker node demote` / `docker node rm --force`), rotate the key with `docker swarm unlock-key --rotate`, record the new key, and rejoin the node fresh
explain: Autolock encrypts Raft logs at rest; a restarted manager cannot read them without the key, and there is no backdoor — a lost key means that manager's local state is unrecoverable. The supported recovery is surgical: drop the node from the cluster, rotate the key cluster-wide (rotation is safe on healthy managers), and rejoin. This is why runbooks demand the key in a vault at init time. Wrong options: no auto-clear, no log printout, and no timeout — the lock is indefinite by design.

q: A worker join token was pasted into a chat log. The admin immediately runs `docker swarm join-token --rotate worker` and distributes the new token. A teammate worries that all 40 existing workers will drop out of the cluster when the old token dies. What actually happens on rotation?
options: Rotation is a two-phase process: old tokens keep working for 24 hours, then all nodes must rejoin
Workers stay, but managers must re-issue their certificates with `docker swarm ca --rotate` before the new token is valid
Existing workers are unaffected — the token is only checked at join time; rotation invalidates the old token for NEW joins only
All workers using the old token are expelled within the Raft snapshot interval and must rejoin with the new token
explain: Join tokens are single-use-at-join credentials: the manager validates the token when a node joins, then issues it a mutual-TLS certificate. After that, membership rides on the certificate, not the token — rotating the token only closes the door to new joins with the leaked value. No rejoin storm, no grace period. Wrong options: there is no expiry-driven expulsion; and CA rotation is a separate operation for certificates, unrelated to join tokens.

q: An operator deploys stack `mystack` passing two compose files: `docker stack deploy -c base.yaml -c prod.yaml mystack`. Both files define the `web` service: base.yaml sets `replicas: 2`, prod.yaml sets `replicas: 6` and adds a logging driver. After deploy, web runs 6 replicas with prod's logging. A teammate expected base.yaml to win 'because it was listed first.' What is the multi-file merge rule?
options: Only `deploy:` keys merge; `replicas` is ignored in stack files entirely
The first `-c` file always wins — the deploy is buggy and should be reported

Later files override earlier ones on conflicting keys (same rule as `docker compose -f` stacking) — prod.yaml's values win; use file order deliberately to layer base config under environment overrides
Conflicting keys across files are a deploy error — the files must define disjoint services
explain: Compose file stacking is last-wins: each additional `-c` file overrides the merged result of the previous ones, key by key. That's the entire point of the base+override pattern (base.yaml for shared config, prod.yaml for environment deltas). Wrong options: first-wins is backwards; conflicts are the feature, not an error; and `replicas` under `deploy:` is honored by Swarm.

q: A nightly report is deployed as `docker service create --mode replicated-job --replicas 4 reportgen:3.1`. The four tasks run, exit 0, and sit in 'Complete' state. A teammate insists completed job tasks will restart forever like crashed replicas and wants `--restart-condition none` added. What is the actual lifecycle?
options: Replicated-job tasks run to completion: a task that exits 0 is done and is NOT restarted — the mode exists precisely for finite batch work, unlike `replicated` mode which maintains long-running tasks. The default restart condition for jobs is `on-failure`, so only failed tasks retry
The teammate is right — all service modes restart exited tasks; `--restart-condition none` is required to stop the loop
Job tasks are deleted immediately on success, so 'Complete' tasks indicate a scheduler bug
Replicated-job ignores `--replicas` and runs exactly one task; the other three are orphans
explain: Job modes (`replicated-job`, `global-job`) model run-to-completion work: success is terminal, and only non-zero exits are retried (default `on-failure`). That's the whole point versus `replicated` mode, which converges toward N *running* tasks forever. Wrong options: no restart loop exists to suppress; completed tasks are retained per `--task-history-limit` for inspection, not leaked; and `--replicas` is honored — four tasks ran.

q: A Compose stack file contains a `secrets:` block: - source: tls_key, target: server.key, uid: '101', gid: '101', mode: 0400`. After deploy, the container sees `/run/secrets/server.key` owned by 101:101 with mode 0400. A teammate claims 'in Swarm the secret always lands under its source name — `target` is a Compose-only fiction.' Who is right?
options: `target` works but `uid`/`gid` are silently ignored — secrets are always owned by root
Long syntax is only valid for configs; secrets only support the short syntax in stacks
The teammate — Swarm mounts secrets at `/run/secrets/<source>` and ignores `target`, `uid`, `gid`, and `mode`

The observed behavior is correct: the long syntax's `target` renames the file inside the container, and `uid`/`gid`/`mode` set ownership and permissions (default mode is 0444 when unspecified) — the teammate is describing the SHORT `- tls_key` syntax, where the filename defaults to the source name
explain: The long secret syntax is fully honored by Swarm: `target` sets the in-container filename, `uid`/`gid`/`mode` set ownership/permissions (defaults: root-owned, 0444). The teammate confused it with the short syntax, where the mount name indeed defaults to the source name. Wrong options: ownership and mode are honored (that's why 0400 secrets are possible); and long syntax works for both secrets and configs.

q: A security scan flags `docker history app:2.0` output showing `RUN curl -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJ..." https://artifacts/api` — the full token, in plain text. It was passed with `--build-arg TOKEN=...`. The team debates fixes. Which statement correctly diagnoses the leak and the safe pattern?
options: Build args are safe because ARG values are stripped from the final image — the scanner is reading the build cache, not the image

The token is baked into the layer's history because `--build-arg` interpolates into the Dockerfile instruction text; anyone with the image can read it via `docker history`. The safe pattern is a BuildKit secret mount (`RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token ...` with `--secret` at build time), which never lands in any layer
Switch the ARG to an ENV — environment variables are redacted from `docker history`
Add the token to `.dockerignore` — ignored files can't leak into history
explain: `--build-arg` performs textual substitution into RUN instructions, and that text is permanently recorded in layer metadata — `docker history` on any machine with the image reveals it. BuildKit `--mount=type=secret` exposes the secret only to that RUN step's mount namespace; nothing is committed. Wrong options: ARG is NOT stripped (it's in the image config/history); ENV is equally visible in `docker inspect`; `.dockerignore` controls build context files, not instruction text.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI builds are slow because every pipeline re-runs `npm install` from scratch. The team enables `--cache-to type=inline` and builds get faster — but every image grows by ~200MB and the team can't figure out why. A teammate suggests switching to `--cache-to type=registry,ref=app:buildcache`. What is the difference between the two cache backends?
options: Inline cache is a no-op — the speedup came from something else; registry cache is the only real backend

`type=inline` embeds the build cache metadata INTO the pushed image config (bloating every image), while `type=registry` stores cache as separate manifests under `ref` — the image stays lean. The 200MB growth is the inline cache riding along in the image
Registry cache only works with Docker Hub — inline is the portable option
Both backends bloat the image identically; the size growth is from the application layers
explain: Inline cache piggybacks on the image itself: cache metadata is embedded in the image config, so every pull carries it (hence the bloat). Registry cache (`type=registry,ref=...`) writes cache blobs as a separate, dedicated manifest — the deliverable image stays clean. The pattern: inline for simple cases, registry cache when image size matters (always, in production). Wrong options: inline is real and effective; registry cache works with any OCI registry; and app layers don't explain cache-correlated growth.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A `daemon.json` sets `"registry-mirrors": ["https://mirror.corp:5000"]`. Pulls of Docker Hub images now flow through the mirror, but `docker push corp/app:1.0` still targets the upstream registry, and pushing directly to the mirror's address fails. The team asks whether the mirror is misconfigured. What is the actual contract of a registry mirror?
options: Mirrors are pull-through caches ONLY — the daemon consults them on pull, but pushes always go to the canonical upstream registry; you cannot push to a mirror address and have it appear upstream
The mirror needs `"insecure-registries"` before it accepts pushes — add it and pushes will replicate upstream
Mirrors handle pushes but only for official images — `corp/app` is a user repo, so it bypasses
Pushes go to the mirror first and replicate lazily; the failure means replication is still in flight — wait and retry
explain: A registry mirror is a read-side cache: on pull, the daemon tries the mirror first and falls back upstream; the push path never consults mirrors. Pushing to the mirror's own address just writes into that registry's storage under its own name — it doesn't forward upstream. Wrong options: `insecure-registries` is about HTTP/plain trust, unrelated to push routing; there is no official-image distinction; and no lazy replication exists in the mirror protocol.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: `docker image prune -a --filter "until=240h"` reclaimed 40GB, but it also deleted last month's release image `app:3.2`, which is referenced by a (currently stopped) Compose project — not by any existing container. The team expected `-a` to remove only 'dangling' images. What does `-a` actually do?
options: `-a` removes all images not referenced by the Dockerfile cache — the stopped Compose project doesn't count as a reference
`-a` only removes dangling images; `app:3.2` must have been dangling (untagged), so the team mislabeled it

Without `-a`, prune removes only dangling (untagged) images; WITH `-a`, it removes all images not used by at least one existing container — a Compose file reference or a stopped project is not 'use'; only container references (and their image ancestry) protect an image
`-a` removes images older than the `until` filter regardless of use — the filter overrides the usage check
explain: The two prune modes: default = dangling only; `-a` = everything unused, where 'used' means referenced by an existing container (running or stopped). A Compose file sitting on disk creates no reference — only `docker compose up` creating containers does. The `until` filter further narrows by creation age but never overrides the usage rule. Wrong options: the build cache is a separate `docker builder prune` concern; `app:3.2` was tagged, not dangling; and `until` filters, it doesn't bulldoze the usage check.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An admin wants verbose logging from the `vieux/sshfs` volume plugin and runs `docker plugin set vieux/sshfs DEBUG=1`. It fails: the plugin must be disabled first. They `docker plugin disable vieux/sshfs`, set the option, and re-enable — but a teammate warns 'disabling will break the volumes using it.' What is the correct lifecycle understanding?
options: Plugin options can only be set at install time — the plugin must be removed and reinstalled with `-e DEBUG=1`
Disabling a plugin never affects existing volumes — the teammate is wrong; volumes are independent of plugin state
`docker plugin set` works on running plugins; the error means DEBUG isn't a valid option

`docker plugin set` only works on disabled plugins — that's why it failed; and disabling a plugin whose volumes are in use by containers is blocked/unsafe, so quiesce or remove dependent containers first, then disable -> set -> enable
explain: Managed plugin configuration (`docker plugin set`) mutates the plugin's rootfs/env, which is only safe while the plugin is stopped — hence the disabled-required rule. And disable isn't free: containers actively using the plugin's volumes hold it busy, so you must stop/remove dependents first (the daemon refuses or you risk I/O errors). The lifecycle is disable -> set -> enable. Wrong options: no reinstall needed; volumes backed by a disabled plugin lose their driver; and the error was about state, not the option name.

q: Installing MKE on a manager node with the documented `mirantis/ucp` install invocation (bind-mounting the Docker socket, `--host-address 10.0.0.5 --interactive`) aborts on an engine version check. The host runs a brand-new Docker Engine released last week. What best explains the preflight failure?
options: The `--interactive` flag is incompatible with `--rm` — rerun without `--rm`
MKE must be installed on a worker node, not a manager — the installer detects the manager role and refuses
MKE only supports specific, validated Engine versions — a newer-than-supported engine fails the preflight check; the fix is installing a supported Engine release, not forcing the install
`--host-address` must be a DNS name, not an IP — the version check error is a misleading wrapper
explain: MKE (UCP) ships against a validated Engine matrix; the installer preflights the engine version and refuses unsupported ones — newer included. This is deliberate: the control plane depends on specific Engine behaviors. The install itself runs on a manager (it bootstraps the Swarm control plane), `--host-address` takes an IP fine, and `--rm`+`--interactive` is the documented invocation. Wrong options: manager is the CORRECT node; the address format is fine; the flag combo is standard.

q: An MKE admin runs the documented backup command and gets an encrypted tarball, then is asked for a passphrase during a restore drill — a passphrase nobody recorded. The admin hopes the passphrase is recoverable from the cluster. Is it, and what is the operational lesson?
options: Yes — the passphrase is stored in the `ucp-config` ConfigMap and can be extracted with `kubectl`
Yes — any cluster admin can regenerate it with `docker/ucp backup --reveal-passphrase`

No — the backup is encrypted with the passphrase supplied at backup time; without it the tarball is unrecoverable. The lesson: store the passphrase in the vault alongside the backup, and test restores — also note restores require the SAME MKE version that produced the backup
No — but the backup is only encrypted at rest on disk; copying it to another MKE cluster decrypts it automatically
explain: UCP/MKE backup encryption is passphrase-based and the passphrase exists nowhere in the cluster by design — lose it and the backup is cryptographically unrecoverable. Two companion facts: restore targets must run the same MKE version (no cross-version restores), and an untested backup is just a tarball of hope. Wrong options: no in-cluster copy exists; no reveal command exists; encryption doesn't magically lift on another cluster.

q: A container running a legacy binary dies with 'Operation not permitted' on a `mount`-family syscall. It runs fine with `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`. The team wants to keep the default seccomp profile for every other workload. What is the right approach?
options: Set `"seccomp": "unconfined"` in daemon.json — seccomp can only be toggled daemon-wide

Write a custom seccomp profile JSON that allows just the needed syscall (based on the default profile) and pass `--security-opt seccomp=/path/custom.json` for that container — the default profile blocks ~44 syscalls and stays in force for everything else
Seccomp only applies to `--privileged` containers, so the binary must be requesting privilege escalation — rewrite it
Add `--cap-add=SYS_ADMIN` — capabilities and seccomp are the same mechanism, so the capability re-enables the syscall
explain: Docker applies a default seccomp profile (blocking ~44 risky syscalls) to every non-privileged container. The surgical fix is a custom profile: copy the default, allow the one syscall, and attach it per-container. Capabilities are a SEPARATE mechanism (they gate what a process may do; seccomp gates which syscalls it may invoke) — adding SYS_ADMIN doesn't punch through a seccomp denial. Wrong options: seccomp is per-container, not daemon-only; it applies to all containers by default, not just privileged ones.

q: A compliance rule requires encrypted container-to-container traffic. The team creates `docker network create --opt encrypted --driver overlay secure-net` and packet captures on the hosts now show ESP packets. What exactly is encrypted, what is NOT, and what is the cost?
options: The VXLAN data-plane between nodes is encrypted with IPsec; the Swarm control-plane (Raft/gossip) was already encrypted via mutual TLS regardless; published-port ingress traffic is NOT encrypted by this flag; expect measurable CPU overhead on throughput-heavy workloads
Everything including published ports is encrypted end-to-end, with no performance cost — encryption is hardware-offloaded
Only DNS queries are encrypted; data traffic still flows as plain VXLAN — the ESP packets are the control plane
`--opt encrypted` requires `--attachable`, otherwise it silently creates an unencrypted network
explain: `--opt encrypted` enables IPsec for the overlay data plane (node-to-node VXLAN). The control plane (manager Raft, gossip) is always mutual-TLS encrypted — that was never optional. Ingress/published traffic enters via the routing mesh unencrypted by this flag (that's a TLS-at-the-app concern). The trade-off is CPU: encryption costs throughput, so it's scoped to networks that need it. Wrong options: no free lunch on CPU; DNS isn't the encrypted thing; and `attachable` is orthogonal.

q: A Swarm service must talk to two isolated tiers: `docker service create --network frontend --name api api:2.0` works, but the team also needs it on `backend`. An engineer claims 'a service can only attach to ONE network — you need two services.' Is that true, and what does multi-network attachment look like?
options: Multiple `--network` flags are accepted but only the last one takes effect — silently
Multi-network services require `--endpoint-mode dnsrr` — with VIP mode the second network is ignored
The engineer is right — one network per service is a Swarm hard limit; split the service

A service can attach to MULTIPLE networks (`--network frontend --network backend`, or `docker service update --network-add backend api`): the task gets an interface and a VIP on each, and DNS resolves the service name per-network. The engineer's limit doesn't exist
explain: Swarm services are multi-network citizens: each `--network` adds an attachment with its own VIP and DNS registration, and `--network-add`/`--network-rm` mutate attachments on a live service via rolling update. This is the standard frontend/backend segmentation pattern (public ingress on one net, database on another, no routing between them except through the service). Wrong options: no one-network limit exists; all listed networks attach; endpoint mode is orthogonal to attachment count.

q: Containers need IPs on the corporate LAN, but the switch team refuses macvlan: each container's unique MAC would blow their MAC-table limits. Which driver gives each container its own LAN IP WITHOUT a unique MAC per container, and what is the trade-off?
options: The default bridge with `--ip` — bridge containers share the host MAC automatically
Overlay — it assigns LAN IPs natively and shares MACs

ipvlan in L2 mode — containers share the host interface's MAC while getting distinct IPs; the trade-off is the host itself can't directly reach the containers' IPs without extra routing, and the underlay sees one MAC for many IPs
macvlan in bridge mode — it shares the MAC by default; the switch team is mistaken
explain: ipvlan L2 multiplexes many container IPs onto the parent interface's single MAC — exactly the MAC-table-friendly answer (macvlan, by contrast, mints a MAC per container and needs promiscuous mode). The known quirk: the local host can't talk to its own ipvlan-L2 container IPs directly (traffic hairpins oddly), a standard exam footnote. Wrong options: macvlan is the MAC-per-container driver; the default bridge NATs behind the host IP (no LAN IPs); overlays use VXLAN, not LAN addressing.

q: A legacy container relies on `--link db:database`, which injects `DB_PORT`-style environment variables and a `/etc/hosts` entry. The team migrates to a user-defined network and the env vars vanish, breaking the app's config. What changed, and what is the supported modern replacement?
options: `--link` only functions on the default bridge — on user-defined networks it's silently ignored, so the env-var/hosts injection never happens; the supported replacement is the network's embedded DNS (reach the dependency by container/service name) plus explicit `-e` variables for any config the app needs
User-defined networks block environment variables — pass `--env-file` instead, which works everywhere
`--link` was removed entirely — the container should have failed to start
The env vars moved to `docker inspect` — read them from the API at runtime
explain: `--link` is legacy default-bridge-only machinery: it wrote /etc/hosts entries and injected `ALIAS_PORT`-style env vars. On user-defined networks Docker provides embedded DNS instead (name resolution by container or service name) and expects explicit `-e`/`--env-file` for configuration — deterministic, not magic. The migration fix: point the app at the DNS name and declare the env vars explicitly. Wrong options: env vars work fine on user-defined networks when declared; `--link` still exists (deprecated, default bridge only); nothing moved into `docker inspect`.

q: The CI system needs to deploy to MKE's `/Prod/Web` collection, but the team refuses to put a human admin's client bundle in the pipeline. What is the least-privilege way to credential the pipeline?
options: Share the admin's bundle — pipelines are trusted, so impersonation concerns don't apply

Create a dedicated local service-account user in MKE, grant it the Scheduler role scoped to the `/Prod/Web` collection, and have the pipeline download THAT user's client bundle — the pipeline gets exactly deploy rights in one collection, and the credential is attributable and revocable independently of any human
Give the pipeline the LDAP bind DN — LDAP credentials double as MKE API tokens
Client bundles can't be scoped — the pipeline needs Full Control or nothing
explain: The pattern is a purpose-built identity: a service account (local MKE user) + a minimal grant (Scheduler × /Prod/Web) + its own client bundle. That yields least privilege (deploy-only, one collection), attribution (audit logs name the pipeline), and clean rotation (rotate the service account without touching humans). Wrong options: sharing the admin bundle gives the pipeline full admin — the exact incident the team wants to avoid; LDAP bind creds aren't API tokens; and bundles inherit whatever grants their owner has, so scoping works fine.

q: An admin downloads their MKE client bundle and posts it in the team channel 'so everyone can manage the cluster'. The security team objects at once. What is a client bundle, and why is sharing it a problem?
options: A bundle is per-user: it contains that user's certificates (Swarm + Kubernetes) and embedded permissions — sharing it lets anyone impersonate the admin with their full access; every user must download their own bundle
A bundle is cluster-wide and read-only — sharing it is harmless; security is mistaken
Bundles contain only the cluster CA — they grant no access by themselves
Sharing is fine if the bundle is password-protected — the zip password is the access control
explain: The client bundle is a personalized credential set: client certs minted for THAT user, encoding their grants. Handing it out is credential sharing — recipients inherit the downloader's permissions (here, admin). The fix is each human/service account fetching its own bundle from the web UI. Wrong options: bundles are not cluster-wide or read-only; they absolutely authenticate; and the zip is a transport container, not the authorization boundary.

q: Security asks two questions about Swarm node identity: how often do node TLS certificates rotate, and can the Swarm use the corporate PKI instead of its own CA? The admin answers from the defaults. What is correct?
options: External CAs are supported but disable mutual TLS — traffic falls back to plaintext
Node certificates never rotate — they last the life of the node; and Swarm can't use an external CA

Node certificates auto-rotate roughly every 90 days (the default rotation period), and `docker swarm init --external-ca` (or join with one) lets an external CA sign node certificates instead of the built-in root CA
Certificates rotate every 24 hours, which is why `docker swarm ca --rotate` must run daily via cron
explain: Swarm runs its own PKI: each node gets a mutual-TLS certificate that the swarm automatically reissues on a ~90-day rotation — no operator action, no restarts. For corporate-PKI integration, `--external-ca` points the swarm at an external CA for signing (the mesh stays mutual-TLS either way). Wrong options: rotation is automatic (that's the point of `ca --rotate` being for the ROOT CA, a rare manual event); and external CAs don't weaken the transport — they just change who signs.

q: The team set the daemon flag `--icc=false` to isolate tenants on the default bridge, but a NEW user-defined bridge network still allows its containers to talk to each other. They want icc disabled on that network too, without affecting others. What is the mechanism?
options: Pass `--opt com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false` at `docker network create` — user-defined bridges accept per-network bridge options, so icc can be disabled selectively; the daemon `--icc` flag only ever governed the default bridge
Restart the daemon — `--icc=false` applies to user-defined networks created after the flag is set
icc can't be disabled on user-defined networks — redesign around Swarm encrypted overlays
Set `--icc=false` on `docker run` per container — it's a runtime flag, not a daemon flag
explain: The daemon `--icc` flag is default-bridge-only (a legacy control). User-defined bridges expose the same control per network via the `com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc` driver option at creation time — selective, no daemon-wide blast radius. This is the intended tenant-isolation knob for custom bridges. Wrong options: no restart changes the scoping; encrypted overlays solve a different problem (confidentiality, not segmentation); and `--icc` is not a `docker run` flag.

q: `docker compose down -v` in a project with a named `dbdata` volume declared in the Compose file wiped the database. The engineer protests: 'I thought `-v` only removes ANONYMOUS volumes.' What does `down -v` actually remove?
options: Only anonymous volumes — named volumes are safe; the data loss must have come from something else
`down -v` removes the containers AND all volumes declared in the Compose file — named ones included — plus the project's networks. Named volumes are only safe from `down` WITHOUT `-v`
`down -v` removes containers but never touches any volume; `-v` only affects networks
It removes named volumes only if they are empty — the database volume must have been empty
explain: `docker compose down` removes containers and networks; `-v/--volumes` extends that to named volumes declared in the compose file — this is THE data-loss footgun of the Compose CLI. Anonymous volumes attached to the project's containers go too. The protection is plain `down` (volumes survive) or external volumes. Wrong options: nothing about anonymity protects a declared named volume from `-v`; and emptiness is irrelevant.

q: A backup runbook does `docker run --rm -v dbdata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/db.tgz -C /data .` while the database container is RUNNING. Restores sometimes come back corrupt. The team blames tar. What is the real problem and the correct pattern?
options: The `-C /data .` syntax corrupts archives — use absolute paths in tar
`--rm` deletes the volume after the backup — the corruption is the volume being removed mid-read
Tar can't read volume mounts — use `docker cp` instead, which snapshots consistently

A filesystem-level copy of a LIVE database's files is inherently inconsistent (WAL/journal mid-write); tar faithfully copied a torn state. Stop the container (or use the database's native dump tool) for a consistent backup; the helper-container + tar pattern itself is sound for quiesced data
explain: The helper-container tar pattern is the idiomatic volume backup — the flaw is timing, not tooling. Copying a running DB's data files races its writes; you get a torn, unrecoverable image. Either stop the container first (downtime, but consistent) or use the DB's own dump (pg_dump/mongodump) for hot backups. Wrong options: `docker cp` has the identical consistency problem; `-C` is correct tar usage; `--rm` removes the helper container, never the volume.

q: A shared config directory is mounted into three containers: two with `:ro`, one with `:rw`. The `:ro` containers crash trying to write a lock file. The team asks two things: how to fix the lock file, and whether `:ro` protects the data from the `:rw` container. What are the answers?
options: Remount everything `:rw` — `:ro` is volume-wide, so one `:ro` mount forces all containers read-only and the design is impossible
Use `--read-only` on the `:rw` container instead — that makes the whole volume read-only
`:ro` is enforced by the kernel across all mounts of the volume — the `:rw` container's writes will be denied too

Point the lock file at a tmpfs or a separate writable mount — `:ro` is per-mount, so the `:rw` container can still write the shared data; `:ro` constrains only the container it's set on, it is not a volume-wide lock
explain: Read-only is a property of the MOUNT, not the volume: each container's mount flags are independent. The `:rw` container writes happily while the `:ro` ones are denied — which is exactly the desired sharing pattern (config consumers read-only, one writer). The crashing containers need their lock file redirected to a writable location (tmpfs is the classic). Wrong options: nothing is volume-wide here; `--read-only` locks the container's rootfs, not its volumes; the kernel enforces per-mount flags independently.

q: `docker info` warns: 'WARNING: the devicemapper storage driver is using loopback devices — strongly discouraged for production.' The host has a spare 200GB block device. What is the production-grade fix, and what must happen to existing Docker data?
options: Ignore the warning — loopback devicemapper is fine for production as long as the loop file is on SSD

Configure direct-lvm: create the thin pool on the block device and set `dm.thinpooldev` (plus related `dm.*` options) in daemon.json — but changing the storage driver (or its backing) makes the existing `/var/lib/docker` content inaccessible, so images must be pushed/saved and volumes backed up BEFORE the switch
Just add the block device with `--storage-opt dm.directlvm_device` at `docker run` time — storage options are per-container
Switch to `overlay2` by editing daemon.json — the driver migrates devicemapper data automatically
explain: Production devicemapper means direct-lvm: a real block device backing the thin pool (`dm.thinpooldev`, `dm.use_deferred_deletion`, etc.), because loopback files serialize I/O and risk corruption under load. The unavoidable cost: Docker's storage is driver-specific, so switching drivers/backing orphans `/var/lib/docker` — migrate first (push images to a registry, back up volumes). Wrong options: the warning is real and load-bearing; storage drivers are daemon-wide, not per-container; and no automatic migration exists between drivers.

q: A Compose stack sets `deploy.update_config: {parallelism: 2, delay: 30s, failure_action: rollback, monitor: 60s, max_failure_ratio: 0.2, order: start-first}`. During a rollout, 3 of the first 10 updated tasks fail their healthchecks. What does the orchestrator do?
options: Pauses the update indefinitely — `failure_action` only accepts `pause` or `continue`, so `rollback` is ignored and the default pause applies
Continues the rollout — `max_failure_ratio` counts only crashed tasks, not unhealthy ones
`monitor` restarts the failed tasks after 60s and the rollout proceeds — `max_failure_ratio` is advisory

The 30% failure rate exceeds `max_failure_ratio: 0.2`, so the update is declared failed and `failure_action: rollback` reverts the service to the previous spec — `monitor: 60s` was the per-task health observation window that detected the failures
explain: Update supervision works in three parts: `monitor` is how long each updated task is watched before it's considered successful; `max_failure_ratio` is the tolerated fraction of failures; `failure_action` (pause|continue|rollback) decides what happens when the ratio is breached. 3/10 = 0.3 > 0.2 triggers rollback. Wrong options: `rollback` is a valid failure_action; healthcheck failures count as failures; `monitor` observes, it doesn't restart.

q: An operator runs `docker stack deploy -c new.yaml mystack --prune` to roll out a trimmed architecture. The `worker` service (present in the old file, absent in new.yaml) disappears. A teammate panics: 'prune also deletes the volumes and configs — we lost data!' What does `--prune` actually remove?
options: Prune is the default behavior — the flag is a no-op kept for compatibility
Everything not in the new file: services, networks, volumes, configs, and secrets — the teammate is right to panic

`--prune` removes services (and unused networks) that belong to the stack but are no longer defined in the file; volumes, configs, and secrets are NOT removed — data is safe. Without `--prune`, the orphaned `worker` service would have kept running
`--prune` only renames orphaned services with a `-orphan` suffix — nothing is ever deleted
explain: `--prune` garbage-collects the stack's SERVICES (and networks left unused) that the new file no longer declares — it exists precisely because plain `stack deploy` never deletes, only converges. Volumes/configs/secrets are data-plane objects Docker never prunes implicitly. Wrong options: no data objects are touched; nothing is renamed; and prune is strictly opt-in.

q: A node needs a kernel patch. The admin runs `docker node update --availability drain node3` and all 20 of its tasks reschedule at once, causing a traffic blip. For the next node they want no new tasks scheduled there, but the RUNNING tasks left alone until they finish draining naturally. Which availability value does that, and what is the drain/pause distinction?
options: `--availability pause` — pause stops the scheduler from placing NEW tasks on the node while leaving running tasks untouched; `drain` actively evicts and reschedules everything. For rolling maintenance, drain nodes one at a time (or pause first, then drain during a quiet window) instead of draining all at once
`--availability drain` is the only option — pause doesn't exist; the blip is unavoidable
`--availability active` — setting it back to active after drain prevents the blip
Delete the node with `docker node rm` — availability flags don't affect running tasks
explain: Three states: `active` (normal), `pause` (no new tasks, running ones stay), `drain` (evict everything, reschedule elsewhere). The blip came from mass eviction; the controlled pattern is one node at a time. `pause` is the 'stop sending work here' state — it never moves running tasks, so patching a paused node would kill them in place. Wrong options: pause absolutely exists; re-activating doesn't undo an eviction; and node rm is for cluster membership, not maintenance.

q: A 5-replica API service keeps landing 4 of its tasks on nodes in rack A and 1 in rack B — a rack failure would take out 80% of capacity. The admin wants tasks SPREAD evenly across racks. Nodes carry the label `rack=a|b|c`. Which scheduling construct expresses 'spread, not pack' — and why is it not the same thing as a constraint?
options: Add `--constraint 'node.labels.rack==a'` — constraints spread tasks across the labeled values
Use `--replicas 5 --update-parallelism 5` — parallelism controls placement spread

Set `--placement-pref 'spread=node.labels.rack'` — placement PREFERENCES are soft: the scheduler best-effort spreads tasks across distinct label values (racks), unlike constraints which are HARD requirements that would pin all tasks to one rack value
Placement spread is automatic — the observed packing proves the labels are misconfigured
explain: Constraints are hard filters (node must match); placement preferences are soft spread hints — `spread=node.labels.rack` tells the scheduler to distribute tasks across distinct rack values as evenly as possible. The 4-and-1 packing is the scheduler's default bin-pack-ish behavior without guidance. Wrong options: a constraint on rack==a would pin EVERYTHING to rack A (the opposite of resilience); parallelism governs update batching, not placement; and no automatic rack-awareness exists without the preference.

q: A `.dockerignore` contains `data/` on one line and `!data/seed.csv` on the next, but `COPY . /app` still omits `seed.csv`. The engineer insists negation patterns always work. What is the actual rule, and what related `.dockerignore` fact trips people up?
options: Negation is unsupported in `.dockerignore` — only `.gitignore` supports `!`; the line is ignored
The `!` must come FIRST in the file — order matters and later patterns can't re-include

You can't re-include a file inside an excluded DIRECTORY — `data/` excludes the whole tree and `!data/seed.csv` can't punch through it; re-include the dir first (`!data/`, then `!data/seed.csv`, or use `data/*` style). Related gotcha: `Dockerfile` and `.dockerignore` themselves are ALWAYS sent to the daemon, even if listed
`COPY` doesn't respect `.dockerignore` — only `ADD` does
explain: Docker's ignore matcher can't descend into an excluded directory to re-include a child — the parent exclusion wins. The fix is to exclude granularly (`data/*` then `!data/seed.csv`) or re-include the directory path too. The companion exam fact: Dockerfile and .dockerignore are always in the build context regardless of ignore rules. Wrong options: `!` negation is fully supported; order is last-wins (not first-wins); and both COPY and ADD respect .dockerignore.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile defines two stages, `golang AS builder` followed by `alpine AS final`. CI runs `docker build --target builder -t app:debug .` expecting the small final image, but gets a 900MB image containing the Go toolchain. The engineer thinks `--target` selects which stages to PUSH. What does `--target` actually do?
options: `--target` only works with `docker buildx build`, not `docker build` — the flag was ignored
Multi-stage builds always produce all stage images tagged separately — `--target` filters which get tagged
It selects the target REGISTRY — the flag was misused; the image name controls what gets built

`--target` stops the build at the named stage and the RESULT is that stage's image — `--target builder` deliberately produces the builder image (toolchain included); to get the small image, target `final` or omit `--target`
explain: `--target` sets the final stage of the build: everything up to and including that stage is built, and that stage's filesystem IS the resulting image. It's the standard way to extract build-stage artifacts (tests, debug shells) — and the standard footgun when you name the wrong stage. Wrong options: it has nothing to do with registries; it's supported by classic `docker build` too; and untargeted stages aren't separately tagged outputs.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An air-gapped site transfer: `docker save app:1.0 | gzip > app.tgz` on the connected host, then `gunzip -c app.tgz | docker load` on the isolated host. The image arrives but the team's deploy script referencing `app:latest` fails — that tag doesn't exist on the isolated host. The engineer blames `docker save` for dropping tags. What actually happened?
options: `docker save` strips all tags by design — only digests survive; retagging after load is mandatory
Compressed saves lose tag metadata — save without gzip to keep tags
`docker load` assigns a random tag — the deploy script must discover it via `docker images`

`docker save` preserves every tag and digest the image had at save time — but `app:latest` was never tagged on that image; save can't invent tags. Tag it before saving (`docker tag app:1.0 app:latest`) or retag after load
explain: `docker save` faithfully archives all repo tags pointing at the saved images — the failure is upstream: nobody ever created the `latest` tag on the source host (a `docker build -t app:1.0` doesn't also make `latest`). The fix is tagging before save or after load. Wrong options: save doesn't strip tags; compression is transparent to metadata; load preserves tag names exactly.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: CI has pushed `app:stable` on every release for months. Today the push is rejected: the MSR repository now has IMMUTABLE TAGS enabled and `app:stable` already exists. The team considers deleting and recreating the repository. What is the right response?
options: Immutable tags only apply to `latest` — `stable` should have worked; this is an MSR bug
Delete and recreate the repo — immutable tags can't be disabled once enabled

Immutable tags prevent OVERWRITING an existing tag — the pipeline must push unique tags per build (e.g. `app:1.4.2`, git SHA) instead of reusing `stable`. Don't nuke the repo: that destroys scan history, permissions, and promotion policies. If a floating tag is needed, use a mutable-tag repo or update the immutable-tag policy deliberately
Push with `--force` — immutability is advisory and force overrides it
explain: Immutable tags are a supply-chain guardrail: a tag, once pushed, can't be repointed — defeating tag-mutation attacks. The compatible CI pattern is unique tags per build (semver/SHA), with promotion or a separate mutable alias for 'current'. Deleting the repo is data destruction (policies, scan results, webhooks). Wrong options: the setting is toggleable by repo admins, but the fix is the tagging strategy, not fighting the control; no `--force` override exists; immutability applies to all tags when enabled.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: `docker trust inspect --pretty registry.corp/app:1.0` shows signers, but the same command for `registry.corp/app:2.0` shows 'No signatures'. Both images were built by the same CI. pulling `registry.corp/app:2.0` with content-trust enforcement fails. What does this prove about how trust data is scoped?
options: Trust is per-TAG: signatures are recorded against the exact tag pushed with DCT enabled — `2.0` was pushed without signing (or by a different pipeline step), so it has no trust data regardless of `1.0`
Trust is per-IMAGE DIGEST — the two tags point at different digests, so this is expected and both should verify
The Notary server is down — trust inspect falls back to empty results instead of erroring
`docker trust inspect` only shows delegations, not signatures — the output is meaningless for verification
explain: Notary/DCT trust metadata is attached per repository TAG: pushing `1.0` with `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` signs tag `1.0` only. The `2.0` failure means that tag was pushed unsigned (DCT off, different job, or `--disable-content-trust`). With DCT=1 on pull, unsigned tags are rejected — the enforcement working as designed. Wrong options: digests don't carry the trust record, tags do; a downed Notary errors, it doesn't return empty; and `trust inspect` shows exactly the signers whose signatures exist.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: The corporate WAN uses 172.16.0.0/12, but fresh Docker hosts keep creating bridge networks in 172.17-19.0.0/16, colliding with real corp subnets. The admin sets `"default-address-pools": [{"base": "10.200.0.0/16", "size": 24}]` in daemon.json, then restarts the daemon. What changes for future networks, and what stays as-is?
options: The setting only affects Swarm overlay networks — the default bridge always stays 172.17.0.0/16
`default-address-pools` is a Swarm init flag, not a daemon.json key — the file entry is ignored
All existing networks are renumbered into 10.200.0.0/16 on daemon restart — the collision is fixed retroactively

The pools only change which ranges Docker carves NEW networks from (each new bridge/overlay gets a /24 out of 10.200.0.0/16); EXISTING networks keep their old subnets and must be recreated to move. The `size` is the per-network prefix length, `base` the supernet Docker subdivides
explain: `default-address-pools` redefines the CIDR space for networks Docker auto-creates (docker0, user-defined bridges, and Swarm overlays) — but only for networks created AFTER the change; it's an allocation input, not a renumbering tool. `base`/`size` define the supernet and the slice per network. Existing colliding networks must be removed and recreated (migrate workloads first). Wrong options: nothing is retroactively renumbered; it covers bridge AND overlay defaults; and it is a genuine daemon.json key.

q: On an MKE 3.x cluster, one team deploys with `docker stack deploy` and another with `kubectl apply` — both against the same cluster, both working. A new hire asks: 'So which orchestrator does MKE actually run — Swarm or Kubernetes?' What is the accurate answer?
options: MKE 3 is Swarm-only — `kubectl` talks to a translation proxy that schedules Swarm services
The cluster runs whichever orchestrator was chosen at install time — this one must have been installed in dual mode by mistake

MKE 3 runs BOTH: Swarm and Kubernetes orchestrators coexist, and each workload targets one of them — `docker stack deploy` goes to Swarm, `kubectl` to Kubernetes. The client bundle even ships credentials for both
MKE 3 is Kubernetes-only — the `docker stack deploy` success is a compatibility shim that converts Compose to Kubernetes manifests
explain: MKE 3.x is a dual-orchestrator platform: Swarm and Kubernetes run side by side, and the workload's tooling selects the target. That's why the client bundle contains both a Swarm client cert and a kubeconfig. There's no shim or translation — native APIs both ways. Wrong options: neither orchestrator is emulated; and dual-orchestrator is the standard MKE 3 architecture, not an install mistake.

q: A Java fleet keeps hitting 'too many open files'. Per-container `--ulimit nofile=65536:65536` fixes it, but with 200 services the team wants the limit applied fleet-wide without editing every spec. What daemon-level setting provides the default, and how does per-container configuration interact with it?
options: Ulimits are Swarm-only — standalone containers can't get fleet-wide defaults
There is no daemon-wide ulimit — every container must pass `--ulimit` individually

Set `"default-ulimits": {"nofile": {"Hard": 65536, "Soft": 65536}}` in daemon.json — it becomes the default for every new container; an explicit `--ulimit` on `docker run`/`service create` still overrides it per-container
Set it in `/etc/security/limits.conf` — the daemon inherits host limits automatically
explain: Daemon `default-ulimits` sets the baseline ulimits for all containers created afterward — the fleet-wide fix. Per-container `--ulimit` remains the override, so exceptions are still possible (precedence: explicit flag > daemon default > kernel default). New containers only — existing ones keep their creation-time values (same create-time-snapshot rule as log-opts). Wrong options: the daemon-wide setting absolutely exists; limits.conf governs login sessions, not container namespaces; and it applies to all containers, Swarm or not.

q: A repository owner wants CI to sign images but will NOT put the repository's root signing key in the pipeline. They run `docker trust signer add --key ci.pub ci-signer registry.corp/app` and hand CI the ci-signer's private key. What trust relationship does this establish?
options: CI can now push anything — delegations are equivalent to sharing the root key
Nothing — `docker trust signer add` only works with the now-removed Notary server; with modern registries it's a no-op

The delegation authorizes `ci-signer`'s key to sign tags for that repository WITHOUT the root key ever leaving the owner's HSM — pulls with content trust verify the delegation chain. The owner can revoke it anytime with `docker trust signer remove`, rotating CI access without touching the root key
Delegations are per-TAG — the owner must re-run the command for every new version tag
explain: Notary delegations are the least-privilege signing pattern: the repo's root key certifies a delegate key for the repository, and that delegate signs pushes. Verifiers follow the chain root -> delegate. Compromise response is `signer remove` (plus rotation), no root-key ceremony. This is exactly how teams keep the offline root key offline while CI signs every build. Wrong options: delegation is scoped authority, not root equivalence; `trust signer` is live functionality; and delegations cover the repository (per-tag signing happens under that authority, no re-delegation per tag).

q: A Swarm service `web` publishes port 80. The team needs to ALSO expose 443 with zero downtime and without editing the original create command in the runbook. Which command does it, and how does the change roll out?
options: `docker service update --publish-add published=443,target=443 web` — port publishing is part of the service spec, so it's a rolling update honoring `update_config`; there is no way to hot-add a port without an update
Ports can't be changed after creation — the service must be removed and recreated
`docker service update --publish-add` restarts ALL tasks simultaneously regardless of `update_config`
Edit `/var/lib/docker/swarm` directly — the spec is a local file
explain: `--publish-add`/`--publish-rm` (and `--network-add`/`--network-rm`) mutate the service spec through the normal update path — rolling, honoring parallelism/delay. Published ports are spec fields, not hot-pluggable socket options, so an update (however gentle) is mandatory. Wrong options: recreate is unnecessary; the rollout is rolling, not simultaneous; and the raft state is not a hand-editable file.

q: Two database services — `redis` on network `cache-net` and `memcached` also on `cache-net` — no wait, they're on DIFFERENT networks: redis on `net-a`, memcached on `net-b`. An app container attaches to both networks and must reach each via the hostname `cache`. The engineer sets `--network-alias cache` on both db services. Will `ping cache` from the app resolve, and to what?
options: Aliases must be globally unique — the second `--network-alias cache` is rejected
The alias resolves to both IPs simultaneously — the app gets round-robin across redis and memcached
Network aliases only work in Swarm — standalone containers ignore them

It resolves on each network to that network's service — network aliases are scoped PER NETWORK, so `cache` on net-a hits redis and `cache` on net-b hits memcached; the same alias can mean different things on different networks without conflict
explain: Aliases (like the automatic service-name alias) live in the embedded DNS *per network*. Scoping is what makes the design work: one logical name, different backends per network segment. There's no global uniqueness requirement, no cross-network merging, and aliases work for standalone containers on user-defined networks too. Wrong options: no uniqueness enforcement; no cross-network round-robin; Swarm isn't required.

q: Overlay traffic crosses a corporate VPN whose underlay MTU is 1400. Large responses between services hang; small requests work. The engineer suspects the overlay. What is the mechanism and the fix?
options: VXLAN encapsulation adds ~50 bytes of overhead — a 1500-byte container MTU produces 1550-byte underlay frames that the 1400-MTU VPN drops (or fragments badly). Fix: create the overlay with `--opt com.docker.network.driver.mtu=1350` (or similar under-1400 value) so container frames fit after encapsulation
Increase the overlay MTU to 9000 — jumbo frames fix VPN fragmentation
MTU is negotiated automatically — the hang must be a firewall rule
Set the MTU on `docker run` with `--mtu` — it's a per-container flag
explain: The classic PMTU black hole: container sends 1500B, VXLAN adds its header, the VPN can't pass 1550B and drops (often without proper ICMP feedback through the tunnel). The fix is lowering the OVERLAY's MTU so encapsulated frames fit the underlay — the driver option `com.docker.network.bridge.mtu` / overlay equivalent at `docker network create` time. Wrong options: jumbo makes it worse; nothing auto-negotiates through VXLAN; and MTU is a network-create option, not a `docker run` flag.

q: Hosts have two NICs: a 1G management NIC and a 25G data NIC. The team wants Swarm's VXLAN data-plane on the 25G NIC but keep cluster management on the 1G NIC. `docker swarm init --advertise-addr <1G-IP>` handles management. Which flag steers the data path, and what does it NOT do?
options: `--listen-addr` — it binds both control and data to the fast NIC
NIC selection is automatic — Swarm benchmarks interfaces and picks the fastest
`--data-path-port` — it selects the NIC for VXLAN traffic

`--data-path-addr` — it sets the address/port used for the VXLAN data path, independent of `--advertise-addr` (control plane); it does NOT change the VXLAN UDP port (that's `--data-path-port`, default 4789) and does NOT affect Raft/gossip addressing
explain: Swarm separates control (`--advertise-addr`) from data (`--data-path-addr`): the data-path address is the interface VXLAN traffic uses. Port stays `--data-path-port` (default UDP 4789). This is the multi-homed fast-data-plane pattern. Wrong options: `--data-path-port` is the PORT knob, not the address; `--listen-addr` is the local API socket; and no auto-benchmarking exists.

q: A Dockerfile ends with `USER 1001`. At runtime the app fails: 'no matching entry in passwd' from a library call, and files `COPY`'d into the image are unreadable. The engineer argues 'numeric UIDs are invalid — USER needs a name.' What are the actual rules?
options: Numeric UIDs are invalid — the engineer is right; USER requires a name resolvable at build time

Numeric `USER 1001` is VALID — the container runs as uid 1001. But with no `/etc/passwd` entry, anything calling `getpwuid()` fails, and files COPY'd as root (owned by 0) may be unreadable. Fix: create the user in the Dockerfile (`useradd`) or `chown` the files to 1001 — don't just switch back to root
The kernel rejects unknown UIDs — the container can't start at all; the error proves the image is corrupt
Add `--user 1001` at `docker run` — Dockerfile USER is ignored when the image is pulled from a registry
explain: Docker happily runs numeric UIDs with no passwd entry — the kernel doesn't care. Userland does: `getpwuid()`-dependent libraries (Java, some Go libs, NSS) fail, and root-owned files stay root-owned. The fix is making the image coherent: create the user (passwd entry + home) and chown app files. Wrong options: numeric USER is legal; the container starts fine (the failure is in-app); and Dockerfile USER is honored — `docker run --user` merely overrides it.

q: An MSR repository enables 'require signed images'. CI pushes WITHOUT content trust, and the push is REJECTED. Meanwhile, pulls of the previously-signed tags under content-trust enforcement still succeed. The team asks: where is this enforced, and what must CI change?
options: Enforcement is server-side on the registry — the repo policy rejects unsigned pushes regardless of client settings; CI must push with `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` (or otherwise sign) so the tag carries a signature. The pull succeeding is expected: existing signed tags remain verifiable
Enforcement is client-side only — the rejection came from the CI Docker daemon's DCT setting, not the server
CI must sign with a different key per tag — one signature can't cover the repo
Signed-image enforcement only blocks `latest` — the CI tag must have been `latest`
explain: MSR/DTR repository policies are server-side gates: the registry itself refuses unsigned pushes when enforcement is on — no client setting bypasses it. CI's fix is signing at push time (DCT=1 with the repo's delegation keys). Pulls of already-signed tags are unaffected (that's the point: the policy protects the repo's contents, and verification is the consumer's job). Wrong options: the daemon didn't reject anything; signatures are per-tag (one key can sign many tags); enforcement covers all tags.

q: After a container-escape CVE, the team enables `"userns-remap": "default"`. Leadership asks: 'So even if an attacker gets root in the container and breaks out, they're harmless now?' What is the accurate security claim?
options: Yes — userns-remap is a complete sandbox; escapes are impossible

Mostly: with remap, container uid 0 maps to an UNPRIVILEGED host UID (the dockremap subordinate range), so a breakout lands the attacker as a nobody-like user WITHOUT host root — sharply limiting impact. But it's defense-in-depth, not a sandbox: kernel exploits, misconfigurations, and `--privileged` can still escalate. It complements seccomp/AppArmor/capability-dropping, it doesn't replace them
No effect — the mapping only applies to file ownership, not process credentials
It makes escapes MORE likely — the remap adds kernel attack surface
explain: User namespaces are a privilege-containment boundary: they convert 'root in container' into 'unprivileged on host', so the highest-value escape outcome (host root) is off the table. The honest caveat: it's one layer — it doesn't fix kernel bugs or bad configs, and it composes with (not replaces) seccomp, AppArmor, dropped capabilities, and read-only filesystems. Wrong options: 'impossible' overclaims; the mapping covers processes AND files; and the kernel attack-surface argument is backwards — userns REDUCES the value of an escape.

q: `docker inspect` on a running container shows `"Env": ["DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3t", ...]` — the password was passed with `docker run -e`. The deploy script is in a shared repo. The team says 'only root can run docker, so it's fine.' Why is this still a secret-management failure, and what is the proper channel?
options: It's fine — the team is right; docker access implies root and root can read everything anyway

`docker inspect` exposes env to ANYONE with Docker API access (not just root — any CI job, monitoring, or compromised container with socket access), and the value is also baked into the shared runbook/repo. The proper channel is a Swarm secret (or external secret store injected at runtime) — never plaintext in `-e`, Compose files, or images
Env vars are encrypted by the daemon — inspect shows ciphertext; the team misread the output
Move it to `--env-file` — env files are encrypted at rest by Docker
explain: Environment is the leakiest secret channel: visible in `docker inspect` to every API consumer, often logged, committed to repos, and inherited by child processes. 'Only root' ignores the real threat model (CI systems, socket-mounted sidecars, repo visibility). Swarm secrets (tmpfs-mounted, encrypted in transit/at rest in raft) or a vault agent are the proper channels. Wrong options: the daemon encrypts nothing about env; `--env-file` just moves the plaintext to a file.

q: A legacy runbook shares data with `docker run --volumes-from db app`. A new engineer asks whether to standardize on this. The mounts show up in both containers. Should the team standardize on this pattern?
options: Standardize on it — `--volumes-from` is the recommended sharing pattern and copies data efficiently

`--volumes-from` works but is LEGACY: it shares the source container's MOUNTS (not copies data), creating an implicit dependency on the source container's lifecycle. The modern pattern is named volumes mounted explicitly into each container (`-v shared:/data` on both) — explicit, lifecycle-independent, and visible in `docker volume ls`
`--volumes-from` copies the data at container start — it's safe but slow for large datasets
It only works with bind mounts — named volumes can't be shared this way
explain: `--volumes-from` replays the source container's volume mounts into the new container — no copying, just shared references, which means the data's availability is coupled to the source container existing (or at least its volumes surviving). Named volumes mounted in both containers give the same sharing with explicit, auditable wiring and no container-to-container dependency. Wrong options: nothing is copied; and it works with any volume type, named included.

q: `docker system df` reports 60GB 'reclaimable' under Images. The admin is tempted to run `docker image prune -a` but fears deleting a rarely-used-but-critical image. What is the safer investigation and cleanup sequence?
options: `docker system df -v` breaks down usage per image/container/volume — identify what's actually unused, then prune surgically: `docker builder prune` for build cache first (usually the bulk of 'reclaimable'), then `docker image prune -a --filter "until=..."` or label filters rather than a blind `-a`
Reclaimable means safe — just run `docker image prune -a`; Docker never deletes anything important
`docker system df` already deleted the reclaimable space — the report IS the cleanup
Reclaimable space can only be freed by restarting the daemon
explain: 'Reclaimable' = not referenced by any container — but 'unreferenced' includes that critical quarterly-report image. `-v` gives the per-object breakdown so cleanup is informed. The safe order: build cache first (`docker builder prune` — pure intermediate, biggest win), then filtered image pruning (age/label filters) instead of naked `-a`. Wrong options: reclaimable ≠ unimportant; `df` is read-only; no restart is involved.

q: An engineer budgets disk for 100 containers from a 2GB image as 200GB. `docker system df` after starting them shows barely 3GB used. They suspect the reporting is broken. What explains the numbers?
options: The reporting is broken — each container really uses 2GB; `docker system df` samples randomly

Image layers are SHARED read-only via copy-on-write: all 100 containers reference the same 2GB of layers; each container adds only its thin writable layer (often megabytes). Budget ~2GB + 100 × writable-layer size, not 100 × image size
Docker compresses container filesystems 60:1 by default — the 3GB is compressed
The containers share one kernel, so their filesystems are deduplicated in RAM, not on disk
explain: Union filesystems (overlay2 et al.) are the whole point: the image's layers are mounted read-only and SHARED; each container gets a private writable top layer where only its changes live (copy-up on write). 100 idle containers ≈ one image + 100 tiny diffs. The engineer's mental model was VM-style (full copy per instance). Wrong options: df is accurate; no 60:1 compression exists; kernel-sharing doesn't deduplicate disk.

q: An admin explores a volume directly: `ls /var/lib/docker/volumes/myvol/_data` shows the files, and they edit one while the app container is running. It works. A colleague says this is fine and faster than the helper-container dance. What is the guidance?
options: It's the recommended approach — direct `_data` edits are faster and Docker documents them as the primary backup method

It works but it's UNSUPPORTED while mounted: live edits race the application's writes (torn files, corrupt DBs), bypass nothing safety-wise but sidestep every consistency guarantee; inspect the mountpoint for debugging, but mutate via a helper container (`--volumes-from` or `-v myvol:/data`) with the app stopped/quiesced — and never assume the path layout is a stable API
The `_data` directory is a symlink farm — edits there don't affect the container
Direct edits are blocked by the daemon — the admin must have disabled a security feature
explain: `Mountpoint` from `docker volume inspect` is genuinely useful for forensics, but live mutation races the app — same torn-write problem as live DB file copies. The helper-container pattern (mount the volume in a throwaway container) is the supported mutation path, ideally with the app stopped. Also: `/var/lib/docker` internals aren't a stable API (rootless, different drivers change layouts). Wrong options: it's not the recommended path; `_data` is the real data; nothing blocks it — which is exactly why discipline matters.

q: The Swarm unlock key may have been exposed. An admin runs `docker swarm unlock-key --rotate` on a healthy manager and records the new key. A locked manager that reboots an hour later still accepts the OLD key from its local operator's notes. Should it?
options: Yes — rotation only affects future `swarm init` calls; existing keys keep working forever
Yes — the old key unlocks with a warning, and the warning is the only effect of rotation
No — but the locked manager is now permanently bricked; rotation destroys its Raft data

No — rotation invalidates the old key cluster-wide: any manager that (re)locks needs the NEW key. Managers that are currently running and unlocked are unaffected — rotation only matters at the next lock/unlock event
explain: Unlock-key rotation re-keys the Raft encryption: the old key immediately stops working for any FUTURE unlock. Running, unlocked managers don't notice (they're already decrypted in memory). The operational consequence: update the vault FIRST, because the next locked reboot anywhere demands the new key. Wrong options: old keys don't linger; no data is destroyed — the node just can't decrypt until given the right key.

q: `docker service ps web` shows a long tail of tasks in `Shutdown`, `Complete`, and `Failed` states alongside the running ones. A new engineer tries `docker rm` on a shutdown task's container ID and is confused when the task row persists. What is the task-history model?
options: The states are live — `Shutdown` tasks are still consuming CPU and must be killed with `docker kill`
Task history is unlimited by default — the tail grows forever until `docker system prune`
Task rows are containers — `docker rm` should work; the persistence is a daemon bug

`docker service ps` shows the service's task HISTORY (controlled by `--task-history-limit`, default 5 per slot): shutdown/failed tasks are retained as records for debugging, not as runnable containers — you can't `docker rm` a task, and the container may already be gone. History is per task slot and rolls over
explain: Swarm keeps a bounded history of task attempts per slot (default 5) — that's what `service ps` renders. `Shutdown`/`Failed` rows are forensic records; the actual containers are typically already removed. You manage history with `--task-history-limit` (batch 7 covered the default-5), not with `docker rm` — tasks aren't standalone containers. Wrong options: no bug; shutdown tasks consume nothing; history is bounded, not infinite.

q: A mixed-OS Swarm has Linux and Windows nodes. A Linux-only image's tasks keep getting scheduled on Windows nodes and failing to start. The admin wants Linux nodes only, without hardcoding node hostnames. Which constraint does it, and why not a hostname?
options: `--constraint 'node.hostname==linux-*'` — glob patterns are the standard OS selector
`--placement-pref 'spread=node.platform.os'` — preferences are hard requirements
Mixed-OS swarms can't constrain by OS — the image must be made multi-arch instead

`--constraint 'node.platform.os==linux'` — platform constraints match the node's OS/arch; hostnames are brittle (nodes get replaced, hostnames change) while the platform label is intrinsic and maintained by the engine
explain: Swarm exposes `node.platform.os` and `node.platform.arch` as built-in node attributes — the correct selector for OS-specific images (Windows containers need Windows nodes and vice versa). Hostname constraints are an anti-pattern: they break the moment a node is replaced. Preferences (`spread=`) are soft hints, not requirements. Wrong options: no glob support in hostname constraints; multi-arch images solve a different problem (and Windows/Linux images differ fundamentally).

q: A stack references a private registry image `registry.corp/app:2.0`. `docker stack deploy` succeeds on the manager, but tasks on WORKER nodes fail with 'unauthorized: authentication required' while the manager's tasks run fine. The operator authenticated with `docker login` on the manager before deploying. What is missing?
options: Workers need `docker login` run on each of them — registry credentials are per-node and never distributed
The image must be made public — Swarm can't pull private images onto workers

Pass `--with-registry-auth` to `docker stack deploy` — the manager's registry credentials are only forwarded to worker nodes when this flag is set; without it, workers pull anonymously and private pulls fail. (The manager worked because its local daemon already had the credential.)
Private images must be pushed to every node's local image store first with `docker save`/`docker load`
explain: `docker login` authenticates ONE daemon. `stack deploy` ships the service spec to all nodes, but the registry credential only travels with it under `--with-registry-auth` — the classic 'works on the manager, unauthorized on workers' fingerprint. The manager's own tasks succeed because that daemon already holds the login. Wrong options: per-node logins don't scale and aren't the mechanism; Swarm pulls private images fine with auth; save/load per node defeats the orchestrator.

q: A Dockerfile uses `ADD app.tar.gz /opt/` and the team is surprised to find the archive EXTRACTED into `/opt/` instead of copied as a file. Elsewhere, `ADD https://example.com/tool /usr/local/bin/` fetches a remote file. They ask when to use ADD vs COPY. What is the rule?
options: ADD and COPY are identical — the extraction was done by the base image's entrypoint
COPY also extracts archives and fetches URLs — the team should keep using ADD for everything
Prefer COPY everywhere — it's transparent

ADD has magic: it auto-extracts local archives (tar, gzip) and can fetch remote URLs; COPY does neither — it only copies local context files verbatim. Best practice: use COPY by default, ADD only when you explicitly want extraction or URL fetching
explain: ADD's two extras are exactly the surprises: local archive auto-extraction and URL fetching. Because they're implicit, the Dockerfile best-practice guidance is COPY-first — explicit beats clever. (Bonus exam fact: ADD never auto-extracts REMOTE archives — a downloaded .tar.gz stays a file.) Wrong options: the behaviors differ observably; COPY doesn't fetch URLs or extract.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Node.js Dockerfile does `COPY . /app` FIRST, then `RUN npm ci`. Every code change re-runs the 3-minute `npm ci`. The fix the team debates: copy `package*.json` first, run `npm ci`, THEN copy the rest. Why does order matter?
options: It doesn't — layer caching is keyed on file hashes, so reordering changes nothing

Docker caches each layer and invalidates a layer (and ALL layers after it) when its inputs change: `COPY .` changes on every edit, busting the `npm ci` cache below it. Copying the dependency manifest first means `npm ci` only re-runs when dependencies actually change — order layers from least-frequently-changed to most
The real fix is `--no-cache` — caching is the problem, not the order
`npm ci` can't be cached at all — it always re-runs by design
explain: Layer cache invalidation is positional: a changed layer invalidates everything beneath it. Dependencies change rarely, code changes constantly — so the manifest copy + install must sit ABOVE the code copy. This 'order by change frequency' principle is the single biggest Dockerfile build-speed lever. Wrong options: caching is content-keyed per layer, so order is everything; `--no-cache` makes every build maximally slow; npm ci is perfectly cacheable.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Production deploys pin `app:1.4.2`. Last night the registry team re-pushed `1.4.2` with a hotfix, and prod silently picked up new code on the next rollout — no approval, no audit trail. The team wants the tag's MEANING frozen. What is the correct pinning?
options: Tags are immutable once pushed — the registry must have been misconfigured to allow the overwrite
Use `latest` — it always points at the newest approved build
Digest pins are only for Docker Hub — private registries don't support them

Pin by DIGEST: `app:1.4.2@sha256:<digest>` — tags are mutable pointers; digests are content-addressed and immutable. A digest pin guarantees the exact bits, and any re-push under the tag won't affect the deploy
explain: A tag is a mutable nickname; a digest is the image's content hash. `image:tag@digest` says 'this tag, AND exactly these bits' — the deploy becomes immune to tag mutation, which is both the supply-chain control and the auditability fix (the digest in the deploy record identifies the bits). Wrong options: tags are mutable by default (immutable tags are an opt-in registry policy); `latest` is the least-pinned reference possible; digests work on any OCI registry.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A developer `docker login`s on their Mac, then copies `~/.docker/config.json` to a Linux CI runner. CI pulls fail with 'unauthorized'. The config shows `"credsStore": "desktop"` and no `auths` entry. What's wrong?
options: Linux can't read macOS config files — the JSON format differs per OS
CI must use `docker login` with the SAME password but a different username — credentials are machine-bound
The config is corrupt — `docker login` always writes an `auths` entry; re-login on the Mac

With a `credsStore` configured, the actual secret lives in the OS credential store (macOS keychain / Docker Desktop credential helper), NOT in config.json — copying the file copies only the pointer. CI needs its own `docker login` (or a helper available on Linux) to get a real credential
explain: Credential helpers/stores exist precisely so secrets DON'T sit in config.json: `docker login` stores the password in the keychain/helper and writes only the store's NAME to the file. The file is useless without the backing store. CI's fix: authenticate there (its own login, ideally via the CI system's secret + `--password-stdin`). Wrong options: no `auths` entry is EXPECTED with a credsStore; the JSON format is identical; credentials aren't machine-bound, the STORAGE is machine-local.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An engineer joins a worker to MKE using the token from the MKE web UI, but runs plain `docker swarm join --token <mke-token> <manager-ip>:2377`. The join fails. What's wrong with the approach?
options: Nothing — MKE join tokens are standard Swarm tokens; the failure must be a firewall on 2377

MKE's join process isn't raw `docker swarm join`: the UI provides a join command/script that enrolls the node through MKE (agent install, labels, orchestrator registration) — the token is consumed by MKE's join flow, not the Swarm CLI. Using the token with `docker swarm join` bypasses MKE enrollment
Workers can't join MKE at all — only managers
The token needs `--advertise-addr` appended — tokens are incomplete without it
explain: MKE manages its own node lifecycle: the UI-issued token drives MKE's join bundle (which installs the agent, registers the node with both orchestrators, and applies labels). A raw `docker swarm join` would — even if the token worked — produce a Swarm member MKE doesn't manage. The tokens look similar but belong to different flows. Wrong options: 2377 isn't the issue; workers are normal MKE members; tokens don't take address suffixes.

q: An admin changes `"storage-driver": "overlay2"` to `"devicemapper"` in daemon.json and restarts. `docker images` is now EMPTY — all images, containers, and volumes are gone. The admin assumes the daemon deleted them. What actually happened, and what was the required precaution?
options: The daemon.json syntax was wrong — the driver didn't actually change and the empty list is a display bug
The daemon migrates data between drivers automatically — the empty list means the migration is still running; wait
