Each storage driver keeps its own separate directory tree under `/var/lib/docker` — switching drivers makes the old driver's data INVISIBLE (not deleted, just unreadable by the new driver). Precaution: push/save images and back up volumes BEFORE switching; the old data is only usable by switching back
devicemapper starts empty by design — the data was deleted on driver change as documented
explain: `/var/lib/docker/<driver>/` is per-driver: overlay2's layers are meaningless to devicemapper and vice versa. The data still sits on disk under the old driver's directory — invisible, not destroyed — and reappears if you switch back. The migration-safe path: push images to a registry, back up volumes, switch, re-pull/restore. Wrong options: no auto-migration exists; nothing is deleted (that's precisely why the disk is still full); and the driver did change — the emptiness is the proof.

q: A host runs ZFS with datasets, snapshots, and compression the team relies on. Docker auto-selected `overlay2`. The team wants the `zfs` storage driver to get ZFS-native behavior. What must be configured, and what constraints come with the choice?
options: Set `"storage-driver": "zfs"` in daemon.json (ZFS must be present on the host) — Docker then manages a dataset per layer/container, gaining ZFS snapshots/compression semantics; trade-off: the driver only works where ZFS exists (not portable to ext4 hosts), and switching drivers orphans the overlay2 data per the driver-change rule
Docker auto-detects ZFS and uses it — the overlay2 selection means ZFS isn't actually installed
The zfs driver is selected per-container with `--storage-driver zfs` on `docker run`
ZFS and Docker are incompatible — overlay2 is mandatory on ZFS hosts
explain: Docker has first-class `zfs` (and `btrfs`) drivers selected daemon-wide in daemon.json — but the filesystem must exist on the host; there's no auto-detection from the root fs. The zfs driver maps Docker layers to ZFS datasets (clone/snapshot semantics, compression inherited). Costs: host coupling (compose files referencing zfs-isms won't run on ext4) and the universal driver-switch data invisibility. Wrong options: no auto-detect; storage drivers are daemon-wide, never per-container; ZFS hosts run Docker fine.

q: Centralized logging is configured: `--log-driver gelf --log-opt gelf-address=udp://graylog:12201`. Logs arrive in Graylog, but `docker logs web` on the host now returns NOTHING. The team thinks the driver is broken. What is the expected behavior, and what are the options?
options: The driver IS broken — `docker logs` works with every log driver; file a bug

Only the `json-file` and `local` drivers support `docker logs` (they keep a local copy) — all other drivers (gelf, syslog, journald, etc.) stream to their backend and `docker logs` reads nothing. Options: read logs in Graylog, or enable DUAL LOGGING (json-file cache alongside gelf) if local `docker logs` access is required
GELF requires TCP — the UDP address silently drops the local copy; switch to `tcp://` and `docker logs` works
Run `docker logs` on the Graylog host — the command is backend-aware
explain: `docker logs` reads the daemon's LOCAL log files — which only exist for json-file/local drivers. Third-party drivers ship logs off-host and keep no local copy; that's by design, not breakage. The two sanctioned answers: use the backend (Graylog) as the log viewer, or configure dual logging (a local json-file cache + the remote driver) when operators need both. Wrong options: no bug; UDP-vs-TCP doesn't affect local readability; `docker logs` has no backend awareness.

q: MKE's preflight rejected a host running a brand-new Docker Engine: the Engine is NEWER than MKE's supported matrix. The team must pin the Engine to a supported release on Ubuntu. Which approach is correct?
options: Install `docker-ce` normally and let it stay latest — MKE's version check is advisory and can be skipped with `--force`

Pin the version at install time: `apt-get install docker-ce=<version> docker-ce-cli=<version> containerd.io` (and `apt-mark hold` / pin preferences to block upgrades) — MKE's support matrix is a hard requirement because the control plane depends on specific Engine behaviors; running newer risks subtle breakage the preflight is designed to catch
Downgrade with `docker engine downgrade` — the CLI manages Engine versions
MKE always supports the newest Engine — the preflight failure must be a clock-skew issue
explain: Engine version management is the OS package manager's job: `apt-get install docker-ce=5:24.0.7-1~ubuntu.22.04~jammy` style pins (exact version strings from `apt-cache madison`), plus holds/pinning so unattended upgrades don't drift you out of support. MKE's matrix is binding, not advisory — the installer enforces it because UCP/MKE is validated against specific Engine APIs. Wrong options: no `--force` bypass exists for the version gate; there is no `docker engine downgrade`; and newest-Engine support is never assumed.

q: A long-running debug container was started on network `frontend` only. Mid-investigation, the engineer needs it to reach a database on the isolated `backend` network — WITHOUT restarting the container (its shell history and temp files matter). What is the correct operation, and what changes in the container?
options: Networks can only be added via `docker service update --network-add` — standalone containers can't gain networks
Impossible — a container's networks are fixed at creation; restart it with both `--network` flags

Use `docker network connect backend <container>` — it hot-attaches a new interface to the running container: the container gains the backend IP, DNS entries, and aliases immediately, with no restart. `docker network disconnect` reverses it the same way
`docker network connect` only works on stopped containers — stop it, connect, start it
explain: `docker network connect/disconnect` mutate a RUNNING container's network attachments live: new veth, new IP, DNS updated — the standard 'oops, need another network' fix. (For Swarm services, the equivalent is `service update --network-add`, which rolls.) The container keeps its state, shell, and temp files. Wrong options: no restart needed; connect works on running containers; the service-update path is the Swarm analogue, not a prerequisite.

q: Two teams each create an overlay network without specifying a subnet. Both get auto-allocated subnets that OVERLAP (10.0.1.0/24 each). Services on net-a intermittently reach the WRONG service on net-b. What is the failure mechanism, and what preventive practice avoids it?
options: Overlays can't overlap — the second create should have failed; this is a daemon bug
The fix is `--opt encrypted` — encryption separates the address spaces
Overlap is harmless — the intermittency must be DNS caching

Overlapping overlay subnets cause cross-network misrouting: the VXLAN/iptables rules can't disambiguate identical destinations, so traffic leaks between the networks. Practice: assign explicit non-overlapping `--subnet` (and `--ip-range`) per network at creation, coordinated with the IPAM plan — especially on shared clusters
explain: Docker's default IPAM hands out from the same default pools, so uncoordinated `network create` calls CAN collide — and identical subnets on two overlays produce genuinely ambiguous routing (same destination, two VTEP sets). The fix is IPAM hygiene: explicit `--subnet` per network from a planned allocation, documented per team/environment. Encryption doesn't disambiguate addressing. Wrong options: no create-time overlap check exists across separate networks; DNS isn't the layer that's confused.

q: A firewall team asks which ports must be open BETWEEN Swarm nodes (not for clients). The cluster uses default ports. Which set is correct, and what is each for?
options: 2377 TCP (cluster management/Raft API), 7946 TCP+UDP (gossip/control-plane), 4789 UDP (VXLAN data-plane); plus IP protocol 50 (ESP) if overlay encryption is on — note 7946 needs BOTH TCP and UDP, a classic firewall omission
2377 UDP only — Swarm management is UDP-based for speed
2376 TCP only — the TLS daemon port carries all Swarm traffic
80/443 TCP — Swarm reuses the standard web ports for management
explain: The Swarm port trinity: 2377/TCP for manager API and Raft, 7946 TCP+UDP for gossip (failure detection, network state), 4789/UDP for VXLAN data. Encrypted overlays add IPsec (ESP, protocol 50). The exam-favorite traps: 2376 is the per-daemon TLS port (not Swarm), and opening 7946 TCP without UDP breaks gossip. Wrong options: no web-port reuse; management is TCP (Raft needs it).

q: An operator runs `docker service logs -f web` and gets interleaved logs from all 5 tasks, which is what they wanted. Then they need ONLY task 3's logs (task ID `web.3.xyz`). They try `docker service logs --filter task=web.3.xyz` and it errors. What is the correct approach?
options: The filter syntax is `--filter task-id=...` — retry with the right key

`docker service logs` aggregates across tasks and has NO per-task filter — for one task's logs, target the container directly: find which node runs it (`docker service ps web`) and run `docker logs <container-id>` there
Per-task logs don't exist — Swarm only stores the aggregated stream
Use `docker service logs --tail` — tail implies per-task
explain: `docker service logs` is the aggregate view (multiplexed, with task-name prefixes) — it deliberately has no task filter. The per-task view is `docker logs` against the specific container on its node (locate via `docker service ps`). The invented `--filter task=` flag is the exam trap: service logs supports `--since/--tail/-f`, not task filtering. Wrong options: no such filter key; per-task logs absolutely exist (that's what gets aggregated); `--tail` just limits lines.

q: In MKE, a grant gives Team-A the Scheduler role on collection `/Prod`. A service lives in `/Prod/Web`. Team-A can deploy to it. A teammate argues 'grants must name the exact leaf collection — this is a misconfiguration that accidentally works.' Who is right?
options: The teammate — collection grants are exact-match; `/Prod` should NOT cover `/Prod/Web`

The grant is correct: collections are HIERARCHICAL — a grant on `/Prod` covers everything beneath it (`/Prod/Web`, `/Prod/DB`, ...). That's the design: broad grants high in the tree, narrow grants at the leaves; the teammate's mental model would make every grant unmanageably specific
Hierarchy exists but only for VIEW roles — Scheduler requires leaf-level grants
Collections are flat — `/Prod/Web` is unrelated to `/Prod` despite the naming
explain: MKE collections form a tree, and grants inherit downward — the standard way to say 'this team owns all of Prod'. Leaf-level grants exist for exceptions (e.g. a contractor scoped to just `/Prod/Web`). The teammate's exact-match theory would force grants on every leaf — unworkable at scale. Wrong options: inheritance applies to all roles equally; and the slash naming IS the hierarchy, not cosmetic.

q: The company PKI team requires all internal TLS to chain to the corporate root CA. The Swarm was initialized with its own CA. Can the Swarm be made to use the corporate CA, and when is that decided?
options: Yes, anytime: run `docker swarm ca --rotate --external-ca` on a manager and all node certs are re-issued under the corporate CA

Only at init/join time: `docker swarm init --external-ca ...` (or join with `--external-ca`) directs Swarm to have node certificates signed by the external CA instead of the built-in one. An existing swarm can't be retrofitted — it would need to be recreated (or live with its own CA, which is the normal, supported posture)
No — Swarm's mutual TLS is hardcoded to its built-in CA
Yes — drop the corporate root cert into `/etc/docker/certs.d` and the swarm picks it up on the next cert rotation
explain: `--external-ca` is an init/join-time directive: it tells the swarm 'don't self-sign node certs; submit CSRs to this CA'. After the swarm exists with its own CA, there's no supported migration path — the PKI identity is foundational (it's what every node's identity chains to). Most orgs simply run Swarm's PKI alongside corporate PKI (it's automatic, rotated, and never exposed). Wrong options: no retroactive flag; the CA isn't hardcoded (external is supported, just at bootstrap); certs.d is for REGISTRY TLS, unrelated.

q: A monitoring agent needs raw network capture and access to host USB devices. The vendor's guide says `--privileged`. The security team pushes back and asks for the least-privilege equivalent. What is it, and what does `--privileged` actually grant that this replaces?
options: `--privileged` only adds capabilities — devices were never restricted, so `--device` is redundant
Run the agent on the host instead — containers can't do packet capture
There is no equivalent — device access fundamentally requires `--privileged`

`--cap-add=NET_RAW --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --device=/dev/bus/usb` (plus whatever specific device nodes) — `--privileged` grants ALL capabilities, lifts the device-cgroup restrictions (access to ALL host devices), and disables the default seccomp/AppArmor confinement; the targeted flags reproduce only the needed pieces. If the device set is truly dynamic, `--privileged` may be justifiable — but it must be a conscious exception, not the default
explain: `--privileged` is three things at once: all capabilities, all host devices, and confinement profiles lifted. Decomposing it: capabilities for the syscalls (`--cap-add`), devices for the hardware (`--device`), and the profiles stay ON by default (a hardening win over privileged). The exam point: 'privileged' is a bundle, and most of its uses need only one strand. Wrong options: device access has fine-grained flags; devices ARE cgroup-restricted by default (that's why --device exists); containers capture packets fine with NET_RAW.

q: Swarm tasks on AWS need EBS-backed persistent volumes that follow tasks when rescheduled. The team installs the rex-ray plugin: `docker plugin install rexray/ebs REXRAY_PREEMPT=true EBS_REGION=us-east-1 --grant-all-privileges`, then `docker volume create -d rexray/ebs --opt size=16 ebsvol`. A teammate asks why a PLUGIN and not a storage driver. What is the architecture?
options: Plugins can't provision cloud disks — the EBS volume must be pre-created in the AWS console
`REXRAY_PREEMPT=true` is dangerous and unsupported — volumes can never move between nodes

Volume plugins ARE the driver mechanism for network/cloud storage in Docker: the plugin implements the volume driver API (create/mount/unmount), so `-d rexray/ebs` provisions real EBS volumes per task; `REXRAY_PREEMPT` lets a rescheduled task force-detach the volume from the old node. A storage DRIVER (overlay2/devicemapper) is a different layer — it's the container filesystem, not shared volumes
rex-ray is a storage driver — the `-d` flag is an alias for `--storage-driver`
explain: Two different 'driver' concepts: STORAGE drivers (overlay2) = how container layers are stored; VOLUME drivers/plugins = how named volumes are provisioned — and plugins are Docker's extensibility point for the latter (EBS, EFS, NFS appliances). Rex-ray's preempt handles the reschedule case: the new node's plugin force-detaches the EBS volume from the dead node and attaches it locally. Wrong options: `-d` selects the volume driver, unrelated to storage drivers; rex-ray absolutely provisions via the EC2 API; preempt is the designed mechanism for task mobility.

q: An NFS-backed volume is created via the local driver (filesystem type nfs, server 10.0.9.25, export `/srv/nfs/share`, read-write). Mounts fail with 'permission denied', though `showmount` works and the export allows the host IP. The NFS server is v4-only. What is the likely missing option?
options: NFSv4 requires the version pinned: add `vers=4` to the volume's mount options — without it the client negotiates down and the v4-only server rejects the mount. Also check root-squash: container root maps to `nobody` on the server by default, so the export needs appropriate anon mapping or the container should write as a mapped user
The `device` must include the server: `device=10.0.0.10:/srv/nfs/share` — `addr=` is deprecated
NFS volumes require the `nfs` volume DRIVER, not `local` — recreate with `-d nfs`
Permission denied means the volume plugin isn't enabled — run `docker plugin enable`
explain: Two classic NFS gotchas in one: (1) version negotiation — a v4-only server rejects the client's default v3 attempt, so pinning `vers=4` (or `vers=4.2`) among the mount options is required; (2) root squash — the container's root is squashed to nobody server-side, so writes fail unless the export maps appropriately. The local-driver NFS mount is otherwise correct (server address plus device path is the documented form). Wrong options: `addr=` is current syntax; there is no `-d nfs` (it's the local driver with type=nfs); no plugin is involved.

q: A fresh named volume is mounted at `/app/data`, and the container starts WITH the image's default config files already present in `/app/data`. But when the SAME volume (now containing a customized config) is mounted into a second container, the image's defaults do NOT overwrite the custom file. And a bind mount never copies anything. What are the two rules?
options: Bind mounts also copy on first use — the team misobserved
Named volumes are cloned from the image on every mount — the second container should have gotten fresh defaults; this is a bug

Rule 1: Docker populates a NEW (empty) named volume with the image's content at that path — a one-time initialization. Rule 2: it only happens when the volume is empty; existing data is never overwritten. Bind mounts do neither: they shadow the image path with the host directory as-is
The copy happens on every container START — the second container's image must lack the defaults
explain: The populate-on-first-use behavior is a named-volume-only feature: `docker run -v myvol:/app/data` on an empty myvol seeds it from the image — the standard 'ship default configs in the image, let users customize the volume' pattern. Once seeded, the volume is authoritative; later mounts (any container) see the volume's data, never a re-seed. Bind mounts are pure shadowing: host dir wins, image content hidden, nothing copied. Wrong options: no per-start cloning; no bug; bind mounts never seed.

q: A noisy container's writable layer is growing without bound and threatening the host disk. The team wants a hard cap: `docker run --storage-opt size=10G`. It works on their devicemapper host but is rejected on the overlay2 hosts. What is the support story for per-container layer quotas?
options: `--storage-opt size=` is supported on devicemapper, zfs, and btrfs — but on overlay2 it requires an XFS backing filesystem with project quotas enabled (`pquota` mount option); on ext4-backed overlay2 the option is rejected. The team should either use XFS+pquota for overlay2 or enforce quotas at the orchestration layer
The option works on all drivers — the overlay2 rejection is a bug; upgrade the daemon
Quotas are set with `--ulimit fsize` instead — `--storage-opt` is for something else
`size=` caps the IMAGE size, not the writable layer — it's the wrong knob
explain: Per-container filesystem quotas are driver-dependent: devicemapper/zfs/btrfs implement `size=` natively; overlay2 can only enforce it via XFS project quotas (the `pquota` mount flag on the backing fs) — ext4 has no such mechanism, hence the rejection. This is a real capacity-planning constraint: disk-hungry containers need either the right backing fs or external enforcement (monitoring + eviction). Wrong options: no bug, it's documented; `fsize` ulimits cap single FILE sizes, not the layer; `size=` is exactly the writable-layer quota.

q: The FINAL question. A config file must be seeded into a RUNNING container that has no volume at the target path, and the change must persist in the container's writable layer (it's a throwaway debug container — no volume needed). The operator uses `docker cp config.yaml container:/etc/app/config.yaml`. A teammate says '`docker cp` only works on stopped containers and needs a volume.' What are the actual semantics?
options: The teammate is right — `docker cp` requires the container stopped and a mounted volume at the destination

`docker cp` streams a tar archive into/out of the container's filesystem via the daemon API — it works on RUNNING or stopped containers, needs no volume, and writes land in the writable layer (or the mounted volume, if the path is a mount). It preserves permissions/ownership from the tar stream, and `docker cp container:/path ./local` copies OUT just as easily — the go-to for ad-hoc file exchange without volumes or exec tooling
`docker cp` only copies OUT of containers, never into them
Copied files vanish on `docker restart` — cp writes to a tmpfs staging area
explain: `docker cp` is the daemon-mediated tar pipe: `CONTAINER:PATH` addressing both directions, any container state, no volume or exec prerequisites. Into the container = writes to the writable layer (or the volume backing that path); out of it = snapshot of current files. Permissions come from the tar headers (note: copying as root can create root-owned files — the usual follow-up gotcha). It survives restarts (it's real filesystem state, not tmpfs). Wrong options: no stopped/volume requirement; bidirectional; persistent.
